comment:
I would prefer to give this a "meh" rather than a flat yes/no, but that isn't an option. I only have 85 minutes on record but that was enough for me as I am a big proponent of first impressions and this game gives a bad one. While it may indeed get better further in, it is unlikely I will ever find out. Had I not got this game for $4 during a mega sale and paid the current $25 they are charging, I would have requested a refund. 
 To start off with, the sounds are ridiculously loud by default and the music is so loud it just covers up everything else that is happening like a thick blanket. After setting the global sound to 70% and the music all the way to 20% the music was *still* a touch too loud in some places if characters weren't talking loud enough. So it is already off to a bad start, but having sounds set to an ear bleeding maximum as default isn't all that unusual to be fair. So lets get into the game.
 The first thing I noticed about the game is the dialogue. It drags on like some terrible novel which, I know, the game is based on. I found myself knowing what was being communicated within the first sentence or two and just jamming skip through the rest of the drivel as it was doled out a few agonizing words at a time as each finished thought or sentence has a lengthy pause before it moves onto the next part. After that came the training. And what a overload of information that was.
 Having played many games of this "style": God of war, Elden ring etc. I found the introduction to the combat of this game jarring to say the least. Everything about the combat just *feels* clunky. The swordplay and the spell casting both feel like an afterthought. Put into the game so there would be an activity to do between lengthy, pause filled dialogues. 
 I played through the initial area of the open world and was not impressed. It was not clear what to do during quests from how things were explained so I ended up just following quest markers or the goals listed on the side of the screen instead of playing the game and looking at the world. The mount controls are bad, mapped in a different way than the character for some reason even though they do the same things. 
 Needs a pass over default sound levels. Needs a look at the long pauses in dialogue. Needs a rework and standardization of controls. 
 But all of this is not why I stopped playing and uninstalled the game. I did that because of a stupid, meaningless side quest I failed because my horse was too far away. Not because of anything I did or didn't do with the information I had available. But because when I hit the button to call my horse, it spawned too far away and by the time I ran backwards to it, mounted up and hit the dash button to get it up to speed, the quest failed.

Unfortunatety this is not the game for me. I have tried multiple times over the years to get into playing this game, everytime I am reminded why I can't: the combat is fundamentally unbalanced, janky, bloated and broken. If you follow the main campaign you go against some pretty dangerous people and monsters, while tricky fights you do a good amount of damage, especially if you combine all of the combat mechanics (bombs, oils, signs). The issue arises as soon as you venture anywhere into the open world. Stuck in Velen you will find quests bunched in villages but 1 will be a very simple monster hunt, and the other will give you a symbol saying you're too underlevelled to try it. If you are actually at the 'level; to fight then you can attempt a monster. But no amounts of oils and bombs can stop a monster from 2 hitting you, and in this game, where monsters can have insane jumps, leaps, dashes & invulnerability stages/massive regeneration and you're hitting the enemy for a 20th of their health, and they suddenly heal all that progress back, yeah it can feel pretty reductive. 

Resource hunting also feels close to USELESS. 100s of plants and resources you'll gather, you can turn that into maybe 2-3 oils/bombs, but everytime you need to make a specific item, ooh that's a unique resource that you haven't come CLOSE to finding sorry.

Not for me.

comment:
This game has beautiful views, interesting enemies, and fun combat, but that's about it. There is poor to no storytelling, and the game feels much longer than it should be, which makes it boring towards the end. Even a great game can become tiring if it goes on for too long without enough variety. If all it offers is cool combat and pretty views, stretching that over 100 hours just kills the fun. I think it would have been much better if it was around 30–40 hours long and didn't have so many huge areas.

The catacombs are also a good example of this. Doing one or two is fine, but after that they're all basically the same and just feel like filler.

I also really dislike the Souls style of not telling you ♥♥♥♥ and expecting you to look everything up on a wiki. Just give us normal quests so we don't have to do homework while playing. And if they implemented invading, would it really hurt to add proper co-op as well, so people who want to play with friends don't have to download the buggy "Seamless Co-op" mod?

The beautiful world, enemies, and combat are not enough for me to give this game a positive review. Maybe if it wasn't so long, I would have rated it differently, but overall it's a 6–7/10.

comment:
[h1]This Is Supposed to Be a Remaster?[/h1]

I originally posted my criticism in the Steam Discussions. The first post was deleted because I called the remaster “♥♥♥♥♥♥♥” and criticized the visual changes. I made a second post calling them out for deleting the first one, called them clowns for calling this a remaster when they ignored some of the game's biggest problems, and that post was deleted too. Then I was banned from posting for a few days for:

[quote]Insults in addition to arguing moderation publicly. Uninterested in civil and/or constructive discourse[/quote]

Apparently calling the people responsible for this a bunch of clowns was enough to hurt their feelings and justify deleting my posts and banning me from the forums.

Fine. You want constructive criticism? Here it is.


[h2]Visuals[/h2]

You ♥♥♥♥♥♥ with the game's color palette and art direction so much that you stripped away a lot of the original grit, darkness, tone, and contrast. The game now looks more like some high-fantasy setting than the gritty world it originally had.

And somehow these visual changes also came with:

[list]
[*]Shadows randomly disappearing and reappearing during dialogue camera switches, causing flickering.
[*]NPCs randomly T-posing, including the merchant during the horse chase quest in the starting area.
[*]Hair becoming ridiculously shiny and staying bright even in dim areas.
[*]NVIDIA HairWorks eating a noticeable amount of performance just to make the hair move around slightly.
[*]Snow deformation being removed.
[*]Grass sway being removed.
[/list]

Igni looks cartoonish and doesn't have the same serious appearance as the next-gen version. The new Quen effect is also ridiculously difficult to see. Yrden is probably the only effect where I can actually say the visual change is a clear improvement.


[h2]Performance[/h2]

Performance is bad overall.

I understand that improving the visuals can make the game more demanding. That's fine. What isn't fine is making the game more demanding while simultaneously making parts of it look worse.

FPS is unstable even with ray tracing disabled, so what exactly was the plan here?


[h2]Combat[/h2]

And then there's the biggest problem: [b]the combat.[/b]

The combat is still garbage, if not actually worse.

Hits don't always seem to register because the hitboxes are still abysmal. Blocking attacks barely produces any convincing visual or physical reaction. Some enemy attacks seem to hit you before the attack animation has even finished.

These are fundamental problems with the combat system that should have been addressed before anything else.

Instead, you spent your time changing the visuals.


[h2]Modders Already Most of This[/h2]

A lot of the other changes, such as the skill tree changes, removing the weight limit, removing gear degradation, and various other quality-of-life changes, are things modders had already addressed years ago.

So what exactly was the point of this “remaster”?

You had an opportunity to actually improve the game's biggest weaknesses, especially the combat, and instead you gave us a visual overhaul that makes the game more demanding, introduces visual bugs, removes some existing features, and still leaves the terrible combat largely untouched.

And then you expect people to treat this like some generous goodwill project.

[b]No.[/b]

You ♥♥♥♥♥♥ with the visuals, made the game more demanding, introduced bugs, removed things that were already in the game, and left some of its worst underlying problems alone.

[b]Maybe fix the actual game before calling it a remaster.[/b]

As for deleting criticism because you don't like the language used to express it, that's exactly why I'm leaving this review here instead of posting it on your forums again.

comment:
The gameplay is fun enough, there's some cool fashion, and if you like the aesthetic of the dystopian near future there's some interesting environmental design. But if you're here for cyber punk I got bad news for you, they forgot all the punk. This is cyber punk written by people who have clearly never engaged with the concept of punk past ripped clothing, studded belts, and angry tones. Their anti-corporate and anti-establishment sentiments are nearly exclusively shown through gangs and goons who just wanna destroy stuff. Other than that there's Johnny, who's depicted as every narcissistic angry dude at your local hardcore scene; the Mox, who are actually a great depiction of rough community oriented punks, but the most we see of them is from Judy (who do give credit is I think the best written character); And lastly the Nomads, who do I think the best job of depicting anti-establishment community first punk ideology but unfortunately don't engage with night city very much.

 There are a few more characters with compelling and interesting arcs but it all feels somewhat hollow and hopeless. I stopped playing the game not from boredom but just from feeling like there was no point. Not every game needs to have a  happy ending where the good guys win but in the world this game was released into and the following years it feels more like an oppressively pessimistic view of our own world rather than a genuine cyber punk game. The heart of cyber punk is the notion that even in the most oppressive times those of us at the lowest end of society can find community, stand for something, and enact change in a setting that serves as a warning for the things our current world is capable of. It feels like CD Project Red is only willing to engage with the surface level of that, they saw mohawks and body mods and didn't look any deeper than that, and it feels disappointing.

comment:
This game is proof that players will overlook any amount of garbage gameplay if the story is good.

Proponents will say "you can do anything!"  What they actually mean is "you have to do ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ everything".

Here's the 100% meta gameplay: before every battle encounter, you have to join your party, hide everyone, unjoin your party, take one member and launch your first attack.  This starts combat and freezes all enemies in place.  Now every member of your party that is not in combat is free to stalk around and get into position in ways that make absolutely no sense.  You *have* to do this because if you do not, your party starts grouped together and you get wiped out with AOE attacks.  Its such a bizarre meta, and this problem is already fixed!  In X-COM, when combat starts, everyone automatically spaces out and finds cover.

But wait, how does that work with scripted dialog sequences?  That's the neat part, it doesn't!  Characters teleport next to you when dialog starts, then they teleport away, back to their original position.  Why bother fixing this obvious oversight when you can just use DM maaaagic!

I have 170 hours in the game, all of them were waiting for the gameplay to not suck.  Most of it was manually moving items around the inventory.  Food goes to camp, gotta pick up every individual armor and weapon and sell it.  Oh, did you swap party members after a fight?  Well that party member's wares are not included when you click "sell wares".  You have to manually swap them back into your party before those wares get sold.

I hope you like having to read every random scrap of paper you find because you are punished if you don't.  How easy would it be to simply auto-read notes when you pick them up?

Speaking of reading, I hope you've been studying DND-ology for 15 years, because you're gonna need it to understand wtf you're doing while leveling.  Every level for every character is just endless reading for a million different skills.  Then you have to do the same thing for armor and weapons because almost every item has a unique effect.  Though honestly, it seems like the meta eventually turns into "big nuke that don't have attack rolls or saving rolls".

It's baffling to me that you can't swap characters in the middle of a conversation.  So if you're accidentally controlling the wrong character when a scripted encounter starts, you're completely ♥♥♥♥♥♥.  Oh, you were leading the party with tact-less Lae'zel?  It's a shame your 22 charisma MC can't take 2 steps forward and join the conversation.  Why?  Because ♥♥♥♥ you, they were busy writing logic gates rather than playtesting.

The whole game is like this.  From start to finish.  Endless frustration and tedium.  Quickloading over and over again for minor petty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.  If this were a visual novel or a prestige show on HBO, it would be amazing.  But I wanted a fun game and they did not deliver.

comment:
I never thought I’d ever rate The Witcher 3 negatively, because it’s my all time favorite game... but they completely screwed it up with the re-remaster.
The game already had Ray Tracing (which is important) in the so called “Next-Gen” version from 2022. Now, with the re-remaster, the game runs ONLY in Ray Tracing mode (so basically like the Next-Gen version), but with half the frame rate...

I have a 4090 and a 5800X3D. The Next-Gen version runs at 4K with DLSS Quality, max settings + Ray Tracing at around 60–70 FPS in Novigrad. With Frame Generation, I get around 120–140 FPS.

The remastered version, using the exact same save file and identical max settings, runs at only around 30-40 FPS with Ray Tracing, and barely over 60 FPS with Frame Generation.

I honestly wonder why nobody seems to care about optimization anymore, or why they keep pushing such an old engine to its limits over and over again. I mean, the Next-Gen version already had Ray Tracing. So what exactly is the reason for cutting the FPS in half with essentially identical Ray Tracing? This is just horribly optimized.

Then they changed the tone mapper, and the new version simply looks overexposed and almost like a camera Log profile. And that's despite the fact that I'm playing on a proper 4K OLED with properly configured HDR.

It completely destroys the look of the game and the original art style.

Anyway, I’ve gone back to the Next-Gen version. Thanks to Steam for making that possible through the game’s settings.

With a few mods, the game actually looks significantly better than the re-remaster while running at roughly twice the performance. So honestly, I can only recommend making your own “remastered” version with mods. It simply looks better and runs better.

comment:
I played this game way back when it was first released on PC, I played it on the PS4, and I played it on PC twice in the last 4 years. Great game then.

The remaster, on the other hand, is a ridiculous and degenerative experience. Anyone coming fresh to this, and only ever playing this version, will probably hate the experience.

In 4 hours I have seen the following:

*) Graphics glitches that are inconsistent even as glitches. Sometimes the exact same region or screen will glitch out in an entirely variant way. Consistently though, the colours vary, the water glows so bright you cannot bear it for long, and the grass will suddenly turn black. But not consistently. Sometimes it'll be fine. 

*) Gameplay is...broken. Variously broken. Again, not consistently. For the first hour it was fine, and today it is not. With no gameplay settings changes between the two play sessions, it has gone from so-so combat to getting one-shotted by pretty much everything that isn't a human being. Strangely, I'm invincible against humans. But a wolf? Nah. One bite...Geralt dead.

*) Cutscenes are...odd. The colour saturation changes dramatically, and everyone looks greyish/brown. As well, now, but not during the first session, when in conversation there is a persistent thrumming sound that is so loud it can drown out nuances in dialogue.

*) Combat is another kettle of drowners. But not a good one. The new features (are there any?) seem not to exist. Unless one of the features is that none of the applied skills apply. It could be a choice, I suppose, but maybe not. Maybe yet another bug. As well, HUD artefacts sometimes just disappear, but luckily your health doesn't matter anyhow, since that one-shot thing is a thing.

I could probably go on, but nah. The thing is, this is an old game that was refreshed and made much, much less playable. Unlike all the folks who can't even get it to run, it does run for me...and that makes it worse, because I got to see (sometimes), hear (sometimes), and feel (way too much) how broken it seems to be.

comment:
Elden ring i would say is a good game, but massively overrated & personally not for me. I think the game's true rating would be more along a 7/10 (good) but instead i will be rating it a 6/10 (above average) taking into account my personal preference.

Elden ring's main issue is that it takes the souls formula and proceeds to cannibalize itself in the pursuit of the desire to always get "harder" for difficulties sake rather than simply trying to make a enjoyable & engaging game that is balanced while also being hard. Rather than bosses (mostly starting in the mid-to-late game and encompassing all of the DLC) being able to be fought with a universal skillset outside of a few like in previous souls games, boss battles in Elden Ring have now become rhythm & memorization games with the skill portion largely based around the capacity to have quick reaction timing to their attack patterns. In Elden Ring, outside the basic premise of timing your rolls, what you learn from one boss rarely carries over to the next since each boss is a memory-rhythm game where learning to dodge their specific patterns is the key to victory and that must be relearned over and over again with each new boss.

This made Elden Ring not fun to engage with (to me). Additionally and equally important, Enemies in Elden Ring have every cancer thing from previous souls games cranked up to 11 alongside new mechanics to make them as frustrating as possible. Here is a list of the issues with Elden Ring enemy design that are largely absent in previous Souls:
---- Bosses no longer play on a equal field as the player. Examples include Bosses having insane tracking to the point where they can just suspend the laws of physics and redirect their attack or entire movement trajectory just to catch you and some Bosses & normal enemies being able to animation cancel out of attacks while you have to commit to yours.
---- Bosses have tons of cheap moves that have little telegraphing of what they actually do and you can only know after it happens, alongside literal "snap-moves" that are so fast it's nearly impossible to dodge them unless you knew they were coming beforehand.
---- Mix-ups in boss patterns that are designed to catch you in a roll after your iframes end & confuse you are now a universal standard instead of a rarity and the large majority of boss battles in elden ring have them. Likewise, attacks being overly delayed just to throw you off is universal throughout the game as well.
---- Instead of phases being a rarity reserved for big/important bosses, in elden ring they begin to become a universal thing given to most bosses. Not only does this make the mechanic less unique & special, only reserved for certain bosses previously to make them really memorable fights, it also just artificially prolongs many fights & makes them tedious.
---- AOE instead of being reasonable and telegraphed during boss fights & a rarity outside of them are now spammed incessantly during said boss fights and many enemies throughout the world have them for little reason. Additionally AOE attacks in elden ring rarely make sense and were clearly just added for artificial difficulty; many attacks create nonsensical artillery-explosion-esque shockwaves for no reason, AOE screams/roars being a thing now that are spammed across many enemies and which can kill you for some reason, magical explosions hitboxes being overly large, etc.
---- Many boss attack patterns & their combos starting in the late-game and through the entirety of the DLC (the DLC having broke even many in the cultish git gud crowd apon release) become overly-long and full of visual clutter that makes them hard to keep up with, alongside the DLC bosses (and DLC normal enemies) dealing insane amounts of damage. These fights along with the above, as previously said, turns Elden Ring's gameplay during boss battles into just a rhythm game of dodgeroll memorization so you can get a single hit in before dodging the pattern all over again, maybe 2-3 if you've mastered that particular boss fight.


Other issues i have with the game;
---- The souls camera starts to show its limit when confronted with with all of these large bosses & more importantly extremely fast moving bosses that often jump high up
---- The open world is good & nice as a first-time experience but overall i feel like it hurts the game more than helps it, once you learn the game you can really abuse it with it's open world and after playing it once or twice most people just speed through the open world, skipping past the large majority of enemies & environments to get specific items for their build. The open world also makes the order of things feel disjointed with many encounters not playing off the way the developers expected them to because they didn't take into account the freedom of the open world, the level & power variance a player may have apon meeting the encounter and especially the speed capabilities of the horse in said encounters. Overall though, i would say the open-world does add to the first-time experience majorly even with it's flaws during and after.
---- Following up on that, bosses are reused excessively throughout Elden Ring in various ways from dungeons to those phantom versions, far more than any souls game before it. This is primarily due to the nature of it being a open world game.
---- The decision to not include Covenants in this game & abandon them can only be described as a negative as it provides no benefits while taking away alot of the Multiplayer interaction (as well as singleplayer).
---- Speaking on the above, Cooperative play is implemented poorly and requires modding to be made tolerable and in general the invader & phantom experience is a noticeable downgrade from previous entries.
---- Personally speaking, i am not a fan of the characters in this game or the lore (i don't like anything martin writes). I would definitely grab Marika by the hair and drag her to my room though.
---- Armor feels like paper and is mostly for the aesthetic, coming from DSII this feels particularly bad.

For positives, of course, the game is beautiful, the music is dark souls music so 10/10 typically, as previously said while i believe the Open World to be deeply flawed, on a first-time playthrough i think it definitely adds alot to the experience & is worth the inclusion over it being absent. And, still, despite the souls system of combat being massively overburdened in this game due to the bosses pushing the limits of what this system can handle (in a bad way), it's still souls combat, which i love and i think has been positively ingrained into many people at this point. Predictably the build variety is also insane in this game, potentially surpassing even Dark Souls II in this field. Lastly, as much as i have to complain about the bosses and as much as many of them are reused, the boss roster overall is highly unique.
If Elden Ring is your very first proper Souls game then i can see why the experience can feel magical.

Overall, i simply don't find Elden Ring to be fun to engage with both for it's flaws and my personal preference (i'm not a fan of very fast-paced combat games period, even though i can of course play them). Maybe i would like it more if i abandoned my old-souls mindset and abused things like spirit ashes, phantoms & cheese builds constantly. Regardless, that is my analysis & thoughts on Elden Ring.

(written april 2026, recently tried giving the game another chance again after defeating the final boss on Nightreign, which while that game has the same issues it's more fun in a friendslop sense)

comment:
not saying this game didnt do amazing things or that they didnt put a lot of good work into it, but this game is not for everyone, regardless of how much you think it would be. I'm someone that's been playing dungeons and dragons for a LOOOONG time. started with 3.5, but i've also played AD&D, 4e, 5e, as well as a load of other tabletop rpg's. i've played loads of rpg video games too. some of my favorite games are rpg's of one flavor or another. that being said, i cant stand baldur's gate 3. i've tried so many times, i've tried vanilla, i've tried with mods, i've tried solo, i've tried with friends, but the game just cannot keep my interest past the beginning of the second act. i've watched videos about the story of the characters i cared about, and i've seen countless speedruns, but i just cant be bothered to play the game myself. the encounter gameplay is insanely picky about positioning, breaks or does unexpected things like letting enemies fire through floors/walls, or making you miss out on just a smidge of movement in enough places that you then cant complete the action you were moving for, etc etc. also, while rolling dice is something i'm very accustomed to, i despise rng on this level in video games. i dont feel like i'm being skilled or lacking skill, i feel like i'm being cheated.
some of the characters are actually terrible too. like, most are just annoying or barely memorable at all, with only a very small handful of characters actually having good stories. some characters have good stories, but terrible personalities that just grate me in every conversation. some character's logic is not logical at all, some story telling elements are frustratingly railroaded, and the max level of 12 really brings the game down. 
obviously, there's plenty of people that love this game, and it has great reviews, but its seriously not for everyone, and with a AAA price tag, its very difficult to recommend the game to people. with my experience with rpgs both analog or digital, you'd think this would be a great title to add to my library, but i honestly regret the purchase. also because of the nature of the game, i wasnt able to get a good feel for how i'd like the game before the refund period expired too, so now its just an expensive plaque on the back shelf of my steam library.

comment: Imagine making a game buggier and perform worse 10 years after its release and after the mess that was Cyberpunk. Yes, there is a way to play the old version on Steam. That does not solve three glaring issues. First, the Remaster has noteworthy accessibility improvements that you can't get otherwise. Second, if you overwrote your old save post-patch, it officially won't work with older versions again (tbf, the game explicitly tells you so when you go to the save screen). Third, the Remaster is a requirement to play the upcoming DLC as far as I'm aware, so just pretending it doesn't exist is not a sensible option for fans of Witcher 3. In any case, this really needed more time in the oven and there was no apparent need to release it now. Personally, I don't even think the game looks "better", just more realistic perhaps. For instance, I believe the more strongly saturated warm color scheme of the original, among other elements, were a key part of its art style, which contributed to it feeling like a playable, illustrated compilation of fairy tales. In addition, some of the gameplay improvements aren't nearly as impactful as they were suggested to be. On top of that, they raised the price of the game on all platforms, even on sale, so this "upgrade" is not free for everyone. All in all, I think this is quite disappointing.

comment:
Performance is just fine, running around 70–80 FPS on Ultra+ (no RT) at 1440p, but this is the kind of FPS I was getting back then with my GTX 1070 at 1080p Ultra with the HD Rework mod. Don't get me wrong, I appreciate the remaster, but for an 11-year-old game to run like that when other games like Cyberpunk run at 100+ FPS at 1440p, it seems disappointing.

The lack of anti-aliasing choices is also an issue. You only have two options: upscaling or FXAA. There's no TSR, and for older generation GPUs (amd 6000 series), the upscaling is stuck on FSR 2, which is the worst one right now. If you have an AMD 7000 or 9000 series card, you're good since you have FSR 4, but they could have at least given the choice for FSR 3.

Anyway, the game itself is great, but we are in 2026 and optimization feels like a must, especially when the game with the current GPU market. I will update my review later if changes are made.

comment:
As someone who loves DND, and enjoys games that are influenced or based on it, I can't say I can recommend this game. 

Cons:
Gameplay is clunky
Unintuitive UI
Clunky controls
Too many skill checks - not everything needs to be a skill check, too many times you'll have multiple over the course of a single conversation.
unbalanced comebat - gets too hard to fast, and very easy to wander into areas that you're way underleveled for.
It does what a lot of dialogue-choice driven games does, and often gives you a list of very bad dialogue options to choose from, punishes you for exploring dialogue options in ways that don't really feel right for the characters, etc.
Uneven writing with the dialogue in general.

Pros:
Visually gorgeous game
Excellent voice acting
Does more or less faithfully translate many of the mechanics of 5e DND, though could have done a better job with it.


Solasta just does this much better in my mind, though it doesn't look nearly as pretty as this game. For the price and the budge that went into this game, it should be a much better product.

comment:
If I could give a mixed recommendation, I would, including for Liberty City.
Summary for folks who want the brief - the main game plot is supposed to be a ticking time bomb where the MC have a limited time to save themselves, despite the worldbuilding and the core gameplay design contradicting it.
That's it, now for a more critical reflection below.

Unlike previous Witcher projects, the main storyline is relatively quick (20-30 hours). For people who defends the game with all the side quests and Phantom Liberty DLC, the gameplay doesn't reflect the ticking time bomb. There is no timer for quests, and since you are somewhat expected to reach multiple endings by playing through branching side quests, you actually lose the plot and momentum by doing everything else.

Imagine if you play Red Dead 2, but on the last arc - you feel like something is missing if you didn't experience the freedom and glorious adventures in the previous arcs. CPK have this issue, and it's terribly rushed with some characters' arc being noticably trimmed down. You either have to forgo the mentality of a ticking time bomb, or you get the worst and more unrewarding main story content if you choose to focus on it.

I play main as female V because she, like Kassandra from AC: Odyssey, have the better VA. V's background honestly feels underwhelming and only affects some of the choices you will make, like getting more money. For a corpo, she doesn't feel like it, and the decision to age her down from 28 to 23 does affect your believability of her. 
The game also over-balanced itself after patch 1.6, removing many fun previous mechanics like shooting through walls, hacking through walls, putting silencers on other guns besides pistols, and more customizability. Now, it kinda forces you to balance your character and build, which isn't as fun.

Everything else besides the main plot, including the characters, world, and combat, are all very fun. It is basically the Witcher gameplay with sci-fi elements. You can feel the project is rushed before the scope of their destination is reached, and I love the world so much I feel like it ruins part of the experience for me.
Hell, I'd argue the overbalanced nature of later patches was because the overall game, including sidequests, are maybe 80-100 hours in total content and it isn't nearly enough to have a bigger and more complex skill tree.

I also gave it a bad review because, like many cultured players, the decision to not add romance for both Aurore and So Mi cripples me for days and I had to install mods to regain small parts of my sanity. Despite this game promising a lot, the romance and a few quests felt short of, well, being short. There is something amazing here if they choose to tap into more, and I hope their Orion project sequel will deliver.

comment:
I wish Steam had a "meh" option. This game is the epitome of wasted potential. If you liked Fallout 4, this game shares a lot of similar quirks. Wide as an ocean, shallow as a puddle. Strong atmosphere and unique aesthetic, weak story with marginally more interesting side quests, and a flood of repetitive grinding. An RPG that doesn't actually give you meaningful choices for affecting the world around you or shaping your own unique path (take a shot every time you hear "Wrong city, wrong people" used as a cliche to avoid confronting this criticism. Or any quote from Pondsmith, really, as if Pondsmith's intentions are an excuse for poor storytelling and video game quality.) 

Like fallout 4, 2077 is a decently fun sandbox that has a lot of modding potential, but you also just need mods to fix this buggy and incomplete game. If you like a game where you can ignore the story (a story that tells you you're on an urgent quest but has no meaning to the gameplay,) then this is a decently interesting sandbox to roam about in and just do whatever strikes your fancy, like an amusement park. If you want an RPG where you can actually choose the role you play, a rather crucial part of an RPG in my opinion, and help tip the scales and meaningfully change a living world as a part of your journey, I recommend looking elsewhere.

So this is where I am somewhat conflicted, Act 1 I rate a solid 7/10, by no means perfect but a very slid start to a DND adventure, no complaints really there. Act 2 I would rate a good 9/10, the -1 point being towards Dame Aylin and the store locking around her existence, on top of if your doing multiplayer you can't actively have ShadowHeart in your party to do the related quest which promptly drops her from the party permanently for the rest of the game.
Act 3 is the the problem, I would give it a 2/10 at best, from poor writing, unfinished quest lines, gutted dialogues or arcs, it is an unfinished mess. You are best ending the game at the end of Act 2
Big Negatives
The game actively lies and fights you depending your actions
Pathfinding is difficult at times and deceptive at worst
Some characters feel poorly written and conversations with them are stiff at best bad at worst
Some combats are so poorly balanced and/or designed its not even funny
Dayme Aylin is a liability in every saying of the word, Unkillable if you don't have shadowheart with you but Easily downable against Ketheric, summons angels against you and Lorroaken but is killable if you side with her aginst Lorroaken
Camera angle and viewing is a nightmare and not user friendly especially if multiple floors are available
The sheer amount of instant game over events is absurd
Follow up to that how easy it is to backtrack against characters and plot against them not even five minutes after siding with them, I.E Emperor and Raphaels little deal and Gortash and Orin
Personally I will never recommend this game to anyone, how it won Game of the Year is beyond me

comment:
Buy this on a super deep sale for good story and characters, but otherwise the gameplay is disappointing.
- The world feels far more Ubisoft than Bethesda in design (go to the clearly labeled POIs and ignore everything else, much more a checklist of tasks than an immersive open world).
- Many systems are fundamentally clunky, such as driving control being complete ass and menus being hidden within menus which can be easy to miss.
- Combat is nothing special, with gunplay feeling very standard and hacking feeling like a poor man's slower more shallow magic system (though hacking is quite useful out of combat, such as for stealth approaches).
- Character builds are not interesting.  I had like 20 unspent talent points at the end of my playthrough because I just didn't want any of what was available since it didn't help my playstyle.  Same goes for the DLC talent system - only one of the four options was interesting to me so I was not incentivized to go find the rest of the points.

No issues with crashing or performance in about 40 hours of gameplay, which was enough to do the main quest, and much of the side content until I got bored of it.

comment:
It's been 2 years and nobody cares about my opinion, but this is the most overrated game in history. It's fine. It's not a bad game, but I'd recommend Divinity Original Sin 2 instead to anyone who want a good gaming experience. The only reason to play this game (unless you're really into the deeply intertwined settings and can put aside the terrible combat that makes up most of the game, in which case Larian will not disappoint) is if you have absolutely no friends and absolutely NEED to experience Dungeons and Dragons 5e as close as possible to the original RAW. Otherwise skip it. 

This game strikes me as the sort of thing people played because it was hugely popular at the time, and not because people actually want gaming experiences like this. 

It's virtual DnD. Sounds great except they kept all the terrible parts of Dnd that are only there to make mental calculations and in person description faster/more fluid. The combat is slow, like holy hell it is SLOOOOOW. Why is a computer game taking this long? 150 hours for one playthrough? No thanks. It's also really badly done (not Larian's fault). Dnd combat isn't good. It has never been good. It is functional. 
In actual TTRPG play, most of the excitement happens in your imagination and the combat rules are just there to provide tactical decisions. Computer games have been doing better turn based combat than this for decades. Dice are real life random number generators that allow you to quickly add a bit of chance to your game without consulting electronics. Computers have been capable of better deeper RNG since videogames were invented. Why go back to d20?
Because it's d20 based instead of having any actually inventive systems, the lowest percentile you can affect an action by is 5%, which means unless you have a 100% chance of clearing the roll, at least 1 in 20 attempts will fail. In TTRPG play that's fine because your GM can take the content you would have missed and put it behind a different check, but in BG3 you either have to save-scum or accept you don't get that content. (or slog through another playthough). 

Larian is amazing and if Wizards of the Coast wasn't involved, this game probably would have been 10x better and 100x less popular. Hopefully all the money goes to making the next one actually good.

comment:
I do not like the direction this game and company is traveling lately.
Elden Ring is good, duh, I won't argue with that. However, there's a lot of issues that are baffling.

The Enemies:
There's maybe... 10 or so enemies in the game, with a few area distinct enemy types. It seems that without a linear world to hinge on, Fromsoftware forgot how to design challenging encounters. Expect seemingly random enemy placements outside of the legacy dungeons and catacombs and caves.
On the topic of dungeons, what a pathetic excuse for content are the copy-pasted catacombs. If you don't enjoy spirit summons, there's practically no reason to explore defeat the boss at the end of the majority of catacombs. You get shafted out of practically a third of the game's content being exciting.
Oh, also you can parry every basic weapon wielding enemy in the game for an easy victory.

The World:
The Lands Between is... beautiful. Until you get bored of the big tree and the grass that is. There is a lot of grass and very little reason to traverse it. It seems that Fromsoftware was too afraid to place weapons and armour out in the open world except in a few specific cases, perhaps concerned people wouldn't find it. Expect to find 2 dollars and a pile of crab eggs for killing a giant bear.
Legacy dungeons. These initially solved my fear that Elden Ring would be a big empty world, the prospect of exploring actual castles dotting the landscape sounds incredible! There is one castle in the base game. There is a manor with minorly hot water dyed to look like lava, an academy with one classroom in total, a city with enough housing for maybe one thousand people, and a bunch of forts claiming to be unique.
Shoutout to Redmane Castle though, definitely the best part of the game in my opinion. Too bad most people don't even fight through it, as a certain trigger caused by playing the game deletes all of the enemies in the castle and locks the doors to treasure to give players a red carpet to fighting Radahn.

The Bosses:
The best parts of the game. Well, I mean the rememberance bosses! The normal bosses are typically copy and pasted enemies from other more high level parts of the game. Shoutout to Tree Sentinel though. Most bosses are uninteresting to fight and have the same issue as the lack of enemy variety. Also, bafflingly, the least enjoyable enemies in the game are the ones repeated the most often amongst the world. The gargoyles, nights calvalry, the black knives, demi-human queens, large stone imps, erdtree avatars, putrid avatars, hero of Zamor, leonine misbegotten and those snake tree avatars. Big health pools, selective stagger response on hit, one-shot attacks, and enemy overwhelm are typical.

Rememberance Bosses:
There aren't enough of them. Its clear that Miyazaki was hands on in the construction of most if not all the Rememberance bosses in lore and gameplay.

Lore:
Its bad. Fromsoftware took the approach of item descriptions conveying lore vaguely and made it even more vague. Cool spell, who made it? No one in specific, probably some unnamed dude. Cool armour, why is it fat? Idk. Every NPC either dies or ♥♥♥♥♥ off from the game world forever or becomes just a vendor.
It seems obvious to me that Mr. Game of Thrones deeply influenced the development of the game and artstyle. Elden Ring leans heavily into the epic story of a hero conquering the world and thinks nothing deeper than that. Kill Marika's kids and then marry her or her kid, mend whatever the Elden Ring is. I have no idea what the Elden Ring is actually, I know there are great runes and they come from the Elden Ring but what a great rune itself is really quite vague. Am I holding it? or is it etched onto my soul? is it getting tattooed on my belly?

Character customization:
Good character creator. There is no personality in your character unfortunately. You stand the exact same way as every other member of whatever body type you chose. Your face is closer to a mask, an in-depth porcelain doll. You are also short, 5ft 7in. I get the issue with creating character models needing to be the same size for balance but I don't like being 5'7" frankly. All of the armour in the game makes me look fat or even shorter.

Armour:
Do you want to look like a hobo or a freak? Even when wearing high tier armour? Then this game is right for you. The metal of the world is all in different qualities or shades or glossy, hardly able to mix and match. Most armour clips with itself even just during a basic walking cycle. Capes clip consistently through sheathes with no option to hide sheathes. All armour sets are too eccentric to feel like your armour or too bland to be desireable. Most armour makes you look wide and short, leading to a oversized fit from the outside. Much like a child wearing a strainer on their head and hockey pads.

Skills and Weapons:
Medium shields are just better than light shields once you find carian retaliation or storm wall. Any weapon with innate bleed is simply better than ones that don't. Split damage still sucks. Just spam ranged weapon skills, you'll be fine. Kill a jar for one of the best talismans in the game, kill a disabled and terminally ill woman for one of the best talismans in the game, kill a masked man with a funny accent for a pair of balls strong enough to kill god easily. Kill people for their clothes? sure! its how you get the highest poise armour in the game. Kill your friends for their weapons, kill homeless people for their bell bearings (you are actually encouraged to do this, there is no penalty.) Thy kind are all of a piece... Pillagers...
Weapons are unfortunately too easy to swap and mix attributes and skills, leading to objectively better weapons than others. Like with the bleed I mentioned. Also, please make bows and crossbows stronger and faster.

Spells:
Spam em, there is no penalty for doing this. Its actually faster and better depending on the spell. Charging spells is a welcome addition, but not being able to cancel them is a poor choice. Spells are impossible to free aim properly and do not track enough to be usable in an open environment. Not to mention that most enemies past soldiers dodge the moment you cast. True PvP warriors.

Endings:
Bad. Boring. Evil. Feed a serial killer your "seed" and then take his "ring" to curse everyone and their children forevermore.

The DLC:
Bad. All of the same issues as the base game except the rememberance bosses suck too now, genuinely unfair, use a shield. At least its super pretty and the lore is interesting enough to be worthy of thought. Messmer my beloved. Thou art... Tarnished, it seems. Laggy as hell. Water will ruin your fps instantly for some reason. Did you know that you're actually supposed to kill the furnace face golems? I had no idea. 

Tarnished Edition:
Hmmm, microtransactions... the armour genuinely looks it was made by a modder. Torrent skins should have been in the game from the start, and access to a heavy armour set without murdering someone should also have been in the game from the start. A paid band-aid fix for things that should have been in an update about 4 years ago.

Final thoughts:
This review is messy, but one I've been meaning to get around to for a while. I love this game, but its flaws are very... very hard to ignore. I have very mixed feelings. The messy style of this review reflects my own conflicted thoughts on the matter.

comment:
Elden Ring is probably the worst FromSoft / Souls game I have played. Its not a *bad* game by any means but compared to the other main line Souls / FromSoft games it is. 

Before getting into what I don't like about this game, I will say a few positive things. The game looks beautiful and runs pretty well all things considered. The voice acting, characters, verity of enemies, locations, etc... are also all well done, and even though I don't like open world games because they are usually slop filled with nothing, Elden Ring somehow manages to make it feel more alive and actually have things to discover and do. Thats about all the compliments I can give it though. 

For the things I don't like, for starters, its a painfully easy game. I have no idea how people are saying its the hardest souls like game or harder than Sekiro, both I hear quite a bit in the spaces I am in online or the videos I watch. Granted I have not yet finished the game yet, I cannot bring myself to do so, it feels like im forcing myself to play this game. But I still do have (I think) enough playtime to form some sort of opinion based on what I have played. From the bosses and enemies I have had to fight, none of them were difficult, and most only took 1-2 tries. I know there are probably harder enemies and bosses in the rest of the base game, and DLC (from what ive heard) but thats not the main problem I have with this game. I do plan on eventually completing the game and DLC, but until I do that my review will stay as is and I doubt it will change. 

The main issue I have with this game is that for most of my time playing its straight up riding on horseback going from one castle or cave to the next while having to fight pathetically easy ass enemies in between. At first it was really cool riding a horse and exploring the world, but eventually it got boring and tedious. I know one of my compliments was that there were things to discover and explore, and that is true, once you found a new castle or cave or whatever to get into THAT was fun, but for the other majority of the game, you are just left riding on a horse until you get to those fun parts, and even then they don't last very long sadly. Maybe I just prefer the more "linear" (I don't think Dark Souls 1 is linear) Dark Souls games, but for most of the time, it never felt dull, repetitive, or felt like I was simply waiting for there to be a fun moment like I do with this game. I get its an open world game, but its still. The reason I don't have this issue with RDR or RDR2 is because the combat while on your horse in those games is actually fun, and there's more you can do with your companion, even having a bonding level with the horse and various other mechanics. I think they dropped the ball not making the 1 animal your around for 99% of the game have more mechanics than just feeding them when they have low HP. 

Another thing is that at least for me there was almost nothing rememberable about this game compared to the other ones. I can think of several moments, enemies, characters, etc... from the other souls games, sekiro, bloodborne, that have stuck with me off the top of my head. The only cool thing I can remember is when you are about to fight Radahn you can see other characters in the game at the Castle ready to be summoned and fight alongside you. As far as im aware its the first time you could summon this many people and it felt very cinematic and cool. Again, something really cool that happens because its a main boss / castle. Another L for the rest of the open world area. I just find it extremely funny that even though its an open world game, the best parts is when you aren't in the open world, like in a castle, cave, etc... 

I think this game would have benefited from being not open world, or at the very least having a smaller world. Again, I do plan to finish this game eventually, and change my review accordingly, but until then all I can say is that as a game itself it is fun somewhat, but compared to the other Souls games or From Soft games, its the weakest one. 

I do expect alot of criticism / hate and I suppose theres nothing I can do about that, but these are just my opinions and if you enjoyed the game I'm happy that you did. 

7/10 (review will change eventually).

I play through, wreck havoc on bosses, and more, but eventually, I hit the mid-late game area's and I'm ♥♥♥♥♥♥. Not because the enemies are tough, which they are, but because I'm kinda under leveled. That isn't really how I like to play RPG's. I love my Claymore sure, but I want to try out other weapons on bosses, different builds, constantly. And this game makes it very hard to do that. I always end up with incredibly evenly spread out stats, because I wanted to try out a certain weapon effectively, and it blisters my supposed build. comment:
Given how hyped this game is, I would like to give you an in-depth analysis of both its positive and negative aspects and explain to you why I don’t recommend Baldur’s Gate 3 for most players. I will break this review down into the Good, the Bad and the Ugly:

The Good:
Let’s start with what makes this game truly shine.
Characters. You’ll get up to 10 recruitable companions with lots of unique dialogues and (for the most part) their own personal quests, some of which fantastically written, revealing rich origin stories including deep character development. Add stellar voice acting on top of all that and you get a highly immersive and memorable experience! 
Motion capture animations. Another reason why this game and its characters are so immersive is the motion capture animations. I think I’ve never experienced so many characters in a single video game coming so vividly and iconically to life as in bg3. Again, the voice acting adds massively to that.
Adjusting Dungeons & Dragons rules. For those of you who are unfamiliar with the original pen and paper game, it’s extremely unbalanced, especially when comparing the different classes to play. In the community, it’s widely known that there is a huge power gap between spellcaster and martial classes which gradually widens from middle to late levels. Larian studios apparently learned from DnD players homebrewing and elegantly solved this by cutting the maximum level down to 12 (which is btw how most tabletop DnD campaigns are being played) and redesigning certain classes.
Soundtrack. It’s all you could ask for in an RPG: epic during intense moments, soft during emotional moments, dreamy during exploration and overall fantastical.

The Bad:
As cool and amazing as the good stuff sounds, there is a lot of bad stuff we need to address here.
Tutorial is very lackluster for gamers with zero DnD experience. If you’re completely new to DnD, you should probably stop here because this game won’t even teach you the basics properly. Fortunately, I have DnD experience and know the rules of 5th edition, upon which this game is based, so it was no problem for me. However, I can see a newbie getting steam rolled repeatedly without knowing why simply because they haven’t been taught well.
Difficulty is all over the place in this game. I’ve only played on balanced difficulty so perhaps this doesn’t apply as much to other difficulty levels but don’t expect a linear increase of difficulty overall. Act 1 (Char level 1-6) felt to me like walking through a minefield. Act 2 (Char level 6-10) on the other hand felt like your usual gaming experience. Most battles were moderately challenging with a few boss battles that demanded more strategic thinking. Finally, in act 3 (Char level 10-12), most battles became trivial with combatants at much lower levels than your party and subpar gear you could already loot/buy in act 1. Even some boss battles didn’t impose that much of a challenge.
Just one bad decision could screw up your whole playthrough which is devastating in an extremely long game like this (more on that later). I had to basically start over after 35 hours because I realized after a quick internet research that due to one single misjudgment I’ve completely locked myself out of recruiting Karlach, the companion who I was looking forward to the most and wanted to romance, although I haven’t even met her yet. And that's just one of many examples of how you can unknowingly and irreversibly maneuver yourself into a very unpleasant situation, which is why I advise against approaching this game blindly, as I did and as is usually the case for me with RPGs.
Mini games with mechanics not to expect in an RPG game. There have been a few occasions when I wondered whether I purchased the wrong game because it suddenly deviated from its turn based RPG formula and turned into a completely different game with completely different gameplay mechanics and those are NOT skippable. Maybe this is a me thing but when I purchase a game I expect it to be what the description says and not surprise me with in built mandatory mini games that stop the momentum and force a different gaming experience upon me.
This game is fricking looooooooooooong! It took me 220+ hours to finish it, NOT including the 35 hours I replayed. Moreover, I skipped some content at the very end of the game, just to get over with it faster. Now you might be thinking: if there’s a lot of exploration and story to dive into then that kind of length would be natural. However, about half of my playtime went into sometimes boring, sometimes infuriating downtime that could have been greatly reduced if it wasn’t for bad game design. More on that in the “Ugly”- part.

The Ugly:
The ugly parts aren’t nearly as buzzkill as the bad ones but annoying to say the least.
Level design is counter intuitive and unnecessarily prolongs the game with confusion. Most of the larger buildings like palaces, temples and forts look as if a drunk architect built them. There is close to zero consistency in terms of layout and some pathways and connections look completely out of place. I guess they tried to avoid sameness while providing intriguing playgrounds for specific battles but in the end, they just turned out confusing. I’ve lost count of how many times I got lost in a place I’ve walked past several times before because of this goofy design.
Inventory management is clunky. RPG veterans know all too well how much stuff is piling up over the course of a full playthrough when there is loot literally everywhere and it’s no different in bg3. Some games offer you search and filter options for easier management but not this game. Although you have separate pouches for alchemy, keys and food, if you want any sort of order in your inventory, you have to drag and drop every single item at a time. The “add to wares” - function isn’t helpful either because you’d still have to click on every single item in order to use it. May as well drag and drop when you’re trading. Far from elegant and again, something that unnecessarily prolongs the game.
Lootable vessels are everywhere! Why is that bad, you may ask? Because almost all of them are empty. I started this game looking into every single lootable vessel I laid eyes upon until I realized I haven’t found anything, even after opening the 100th or so. However, I still occasionally opened “unimportant” vessels out of boredom and to my surprise I found an important key in act 2 in one of those. So not only does the game drown you in loot spaces of which most are empty but also it misleads you in falsely believing you could save time by ignoring them and focusing on the “important stuff”! Yet another way you can waste hours and hours of playtime in a frustrating way.
Traps. It seems like traps in bg3 serve the sole purpose of wasting your time and resources. They’re not puzzles as you might think, they’re simply hindrances that require you to pass an ability check. Otherwise, you’ll have to suck up the damage. Line of sight isn’t always clear. Maybe the programming is a bit clunky here or I missed something but if it’s the latter, they could have at least highlighted the object that gets in my way for better understanding. Also, for some reason ranged spells that deal damage in a straight line don’t work over stairs. Can someone explain to me why I can’t aim my spell slightly upwards/downwards?

If you made it this far, congratulations and thank you very much for your attention!

comment:
I don't want to be that annoying guy or downplay the great work CD Projekt Red did in giving us some free improvements. I played the Witcher for a long time, and it was always great to revisit the landscapes, the unique experiences, and that feeling only TW3 can deliver. Sometimes I’d just ride aimlessly with the HUD turned off, simply to enjoy the journey. It’s no wonder some scenes in The Witcher rival those in Red Dead 2.

That said, I wanted to start a fresh playthrough on "Death March" difficulty to get the last three Steam achievements I was missing. Right from the start, I noticed quite a few things, specifically:

Cons

#1 Missing textures: one instance occurred at Vizima Castle after speaking with Emhyr the chessboard and the wall were invisible.
#2 The colors have definitely changed, they look a bit more washed out, almost pastel. I noticed that nights with a full moon are practically as bright as day. I can see distant trees illuminated by the moonlight.
#3 I have to talk a bit about the new interface, I think they tried to modernize the UI to make it more intuitive but... seeing 30 separate notifications for every piece of silver or iron I crafted doesn't exactly keep the interface clean.
#4 Honestly I don't see a huge difference in gameplay between the previous version and this one. The things I noticed that actually helped were dynamic combat camera and new target-locking options (which made combat easier, I’d say)
#5 I’ve run into the occasional bug here and there while playing like seeing Geralt in a Tpose while in inventory.
#6 This is just my personal opinion but the updates to graphics, lighting, and color reminded me of Crimson Desert. Nothing against it but I vastly preferred the colors in the previous version.
#7 Having played with mods for a long time I was happy that CD decided to add official mod support, including for consoles. But I really missed basic features that should have been implemented already, like using a torch while riding Roach
#8 Well, basically now if you dive underwater you can see absolutely everything.
#9 Character cutscenes look almost pitch black, you can only see the lifeless glint in their eyes, haha. 
But seriously, it looks scary now.

Pros:
#1 It supports mods now. Apparently, there are already some working, hehe
#2 I was eager to see the skill trees! Honestly, I’ll keep playing just to see how I can craft my Witcher builds.
#3 It’s easier to notice certain skill tree "powers" in action now like the perfectly timed dodge that makes the sword glow blue.

I love The Witcher because every game offered a unique experience. With mods, the game turned into a cinematic masterpiece. Unfortunately, with this update, I’m noticing some visual glitches, bugs, and issues that need fixing. And to top it off, it’s a 40GB update.

I preferred the previous version. Don't get me wrong, I appreciate the upgrade. But a bit of the essence has been lost

comment:
I understand why a lot of people love Baldur’s Gate 3. The writing, voice acting, world reactivity, companion interactions, and freedom of choice are impressive. There is clearly a massive amount of work in this game.

That said, I do not enjoy playing it.

The game feels painfully slow. Movement feels like power walking everywhere, combat encounters take way too long, and the pacing constantly drags. I like turn-based games and JRPGs, so the issue is not simply that it is turn-based. The issue is that this feels more like a slow tabletop rules simulator than a smooth video game.

The dice rolls are also constantly in your face. Everything feels like a roll: dialogue, combat, perception, traps, attacks, checks, saving throws, and more. I understand that this is based on Dungeons & Dragons, but as a video game experience, it makes too many moments feel like RNG rather than satisfying player skill. In JRPGs, RNG exists in the background. Here, the game keeps shoving it directly in front of you.

The gear and stat systems are also not explained clearly enough. It is often hard to tell whether one weapon or armor piece is actually better than another because the bonuses, conditions, and mechanics are not intuitive. The game gives you a lot of options, but not enough clarity.

For hardcore D&D fans or players who love slow, tactical CRPGs, this may be a masterpiece. For me, it feels clunky, overcomplicated, slow, and frustrating. I respect the ambition, but (well I realize I am in the minority here,) I do not think it is fun to actually play.

EDIT: Steam currently shows that I have only played this game for around three hours, but that is not accurate. I usually play offline, and Steam does not appear to be counting all of that time correctly. I have put at least 20+ hours into the game because I genuinely tried to give it a fair chance and understand why so many people love it. This review is not based on a quick first impression.

I'm not surprised.  I hated the Divinity series too, but I bought the unbelievable hype around this game being good.  Huge mistake.  Maybe I'll put some more time on it in the future.  But more than likely I'll just uninstall, perhaps delete from my Steam library, and blacklist anything from Larian from now on.  Their design ethos just isn't me.

comment:
I absolutely cannot recommend this game. Don’t buy into the hype, this is not a great game, and it’s nowhere near the masterpiece people pretend it is.

If you want to play real CRPGs, go play Divinity: Original Sin 2 or Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader. Those games actually give you meaningful freedom, real build variety, and choices that let you shape your own path instead of constantly funneling you into scripted outcomes.

TL;DR:

Dating simulator: 7/10

Graphics: 8/10

Voice acting: 10/10

CRPG: 3/10

Story: 4/10

Gameplay: 5/10

Music: 4/10

Baldur's Gate 3 is basically an F5 / F8 simulator disguised as an RPG. The dice system dictates the outcome of major decisions, and a ridiculous number of those outcomes lead directly to instant failure, unfair fights, or outright game over screens. The game literally rolls dice to decide whether you’re allowed to continue without reloading... that’s not depth, that’s bad design dressed up as innovation.

A huge portion of the so-called “choices” are fake. Pick the wrong dialogue, fail one arbitrary roll, and suddenly you’re trapped in an unwinnable encounter or punished with a game over. That’s not player freedom... that’s trial-and-error with extra steps.

They sold this game as some gigantic RPG with unmatched scope, but that claim falls apart the moment you actually play it. Most quests are effectively mandatory, either because the game artificially locks progression or because stepping outside the intended route gets you instantly destroyed by enemies far above your level. The result is constant paranoia: spam quicksave every few minutes because the game loves punishing exploration with cheap deaths.

And if you want proof of what this game’s audience actually values, just look at Nexus Mods. The most downloaded mods tell the whole story: most are adult mods expanding romance and sex options, and another big chunk are cheats.

A huge part of the praise comes from people who don’t care much about CRPG systems at all, they just wanted a polished fantasy dating simulator with cinematic dialogue and party members to sleep with.

comment:
[h1]ABSOLUTELY TERRIBLE GAME[/h1]

I really don't understand the hype around GTA V.

The map is way too big.

There are too many cars.

Too many weapons.

Too many missions.

Too many things to do.

Sometimes I just want to drive peacefully and suddenly the game expects me to commit several crimes.

Completely unreasonable.

The police are also extremely rude.

I accidentally stole one car and suddenly they act like I did something wrong.

Then they chase me.

With helicopters.

Very toxic community behavior from the NPCs.

The driving is also ridiculous.

You crash at 200 km/h and somehow survive.

But when I lightly touch a pole, my car sometimes decides it has seen enough of this world.

The physics clearly need therapy.

And don't even get me started on Trevor.

I refuse to elaborate.

[h1]THE ONLINE MODE IS EVEN WORSE[/h1]

I joined GTA Online and immediately discovered something horrifying:

Other players exist.

Some of them even shoot at you.

Completely unacceptable in a game about crime.

Then I found out people have been playing this game for YEARS.

Some players have businesses, flying vehicles, bunkers, submarines and enough money to personally fund a small country.

Meanwhile I was standing outside a convenience store with $37 wondering where my car went.

Terrible new-player experience.

Also, Rockstar keeps adding things.

At some point a game should simply stop having content.

I have a life.

[h1]THE STORY IS ALSO BAD[/h1]

Three protagonists?

Why?

I can barely manage one personality in real life.

Now I am expected to keep track of Michael, Franklin AND Trevor?

This is basically unpaid management work.

The characters are also way too memorable.

Very bad design.

I still remember them years later.

[h1]GRAPHICS[/h1]

Game came out in 2013.

Still looks good.

Suspicious.

[h1]FINAL VERDICT[/h1]

Enhanced: 80 hours.

Legacy: 454 hours.

Total: 534 hours.

Clearly I hated every second.

[h1]0/10[/h1]

Absolutely horrible.

Would never recommend.

...

[b]Just kidding. :D[/b]

[b]Recommended.[/b]

comment:
So if it was a separate title I would recommend the original game and not comment on remastered version. But here we are...
 
TLDR I basically can't run the remastered game. It replaced my og copy and I had no say in it, only could revert it with issues, so remastered gets thumbs down.

1) They changed the game to "remastered" instead of making the remaster a standalone installation. My potato could run the OG on ultra just fine, but the remastered can't keep 20fps on low while standing still and not moving the camera. You have to switch the game version to "classic" in Steam settings if you want to play the original.

2) When I switched back to "classic," the RED launcher couldn't initialize the game. File verification (which the launcher asks you to do) didn't help. You have to go to \\bin\\x64\\ in the game folder and run witcher3.exe directly.

3) Saves made on the Next-Gen/Remastered build got converted to the new format on update, instead of doing it when you load the save, or ideally only making new saves use the new format. My 1.32 saves were untouched, but my NG+ saves (made on 4.0) got converted to 4.04 and won't load in classic which is 1.32. To fix this, hex-edit the save file (located in Documents on your system drive. Make a backup first tho). Find the line at offset 00000C10 — don't get confused by the bunch of 00 entries before you find the right line. In the 6th or 7th column of that line, you'll see 1B. Change that entry to 13, don't touch anything else, save the file, and the save will load in classic just fine. Credit to Maxizera's guide.

comment:
A beautiful, open-world Souls Like that most will probably enjoy, especially if they are new to the genre. Technically it's the entry with the most new gameplay mechanics and stunning graphics as well as amount of bosses and areas to explore/clear out, however, aside from that it doesn't have much else better from previous titles.

I played through DS2 and all the DLCs as well as NG+, it's my only experience with the series but it was a really good one. So when I entered the world of Elden Ring I had similar expectations of the bosses and enemies and general ideea of exploration, except they couldn't be applied. ER takes such a inbetween position of gameplay that it utterly annoys me how disrespectful it is to the player, it tries to stay on two stools, one which is Dark Soul's movement/dodge based wait out with punishment to the boss after their combo, and to the Sekiro's/Bloodborne aggressiveness of the enemies/the player...? 

Most notably the only real mobility change the player gets in combat is jumping, which would have been a nice addition if it wasn't for how ridiculously inertialess it feels. Finding the actual gap where you can attack the enemies and bosses freely or at least even just trade with them - is extremely tiring. The recovery time for the combo's are so short your gameplay will be 95% of the time just seeing someone's body and a bunch of metal sounds and bright flashes while constantly spamming dodge. Dark Souls at least had you use your actual positioning/walking/running and not just dodge rolling at the correct time so you had  a more balanced type of gameplay between the boss and yourself.

Horseback fighting is also extremely clunky and unsatisfying, most enemies that were designed around it are really not entertaining to fight against because they are so much easier when using the horse. It should have stayed as a mode of transportation since the springstream mechanic is quite fun and the world is already pretty big. To continue - the world being big doesnt necessarily mean it's shallow as a puddle, but I would have definetely preffered if they condensed the world by 2x and not made the curious player feel like they waste time 90% of the time. Dark Souls while linear would always reward curious players, so when i came over to ER and started looking over each nook and cranny only to get useless crafting materials - well it's just discouraging and feels like the developer trying to take out as much time out of you as possible.

Ashes of War are perhaps the only good mechanic that came out of this entry and even then from the little use that I did have with them, it seems most are extremely niche and likely to never be used in favor of other objectively better ones leaving 90% of them to never be used and be clutter. Take this with a grain of salt as I didn't use them all that much.

Overall, while the game is good and many new players will enjoy it - I wouldn't buy it if you are self respecting Dark Souls fan. The game caters rather hardly to the hardcore players and I say this as a DS2 fan which had the same allegations thrown against it. Elden Ring is through and through made to break your patience and test just how much are you ready to adapt to it's bosses and new mechanics constantly. God forbid you are a UGS user in this game, good-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥-luck, you will need it.

comment:
I really wanted to like this game. Spent so long with my friends trying to get a campaign going. We tried with 4 people and after months and months of aligning schedules and starting multiple campaigns I decided it just is not meant to be played with more than 2 people on your first run.

So I tried it solo and for the first couple hours it was so much better. I tried tactical difficulty and after dying a few times it felt like my decisions in character specs and party config actually mattered. But after failing repeatedly in a couple fights against higher-level opponents I realized a lot of the time, winning and losing was less about skill and more about going back and gaining experience to buff your crew.

It's an RPG and some grind to beef up your characters is totally expected. The problem is that for me, the story elements were so slow and not rewarding. The little amount of strategy sprinkled in was too few and far between bland dialogue trees. So many story beat payoffs felt like just edgy sex jokes involving fantasy creatures.

The conversation around this game is so positive and I've never heard anyone talk about the downsides of multiplayer in this game so I'm very disappointed with it. Even solo I got only a few hours of entertaining game play, but I believe the right people would enjoy it solo. I imagine for those who play it solo, you could then have fun playing with others who have already beaten the game. But starting fresh with multiple people ruins the experience. If players wander to different places, they start and end quests independently, and trying to enforce your party staying together is extremely difficult because listening to every conversation and waiting for the speaker to choose their dialogue is tedious. comment:
The game is still so average all this time later.

Even with heavy modding, the game just feels so dead. Story is pretty average, and there's still so many bugs after all this time. It's also crazy that there are just so many low quality/missing features. GTA Online had callable cars that actually drove to you on release, whereas even after however many years, Cyberpunk's best effort is "spawn it instantly behind you and sometimes it won't glitch out".

An example of the poor story writing is Jackie: gets introduced, doesn't mind that you "ruined" a massive heist, suddenly best friends, "fast forward 4 months" trope, do one job, anti climactic death. Builds literally zero attachment to the character that's supposed to be your best friend, and kills him off immediately.

And the AI car guy: why tf would an AI car be doing you favours? The whole point of an AI is that it's supposed to be cold and efficient, which is what they paint it out to be when it's introduced. "No I can't deviate from the route, blah blah blah", 2 minutes later, "yes, I can go out of my way to come out of the city where I explicitly don't operate without guarantee of payment, that makes sense for a sophisticated AI with no connection to your character".

There is no sense of scale in the game, because the area design is so bad. The main city itself is pretty tiny for a AAA game, especially when so much of it is just empty filler. I was expecting to be wowed with a massive futuristic city that felt alive, but it's the complete opposite. You can really tell it's very much a patch job from the botched release, as still nothing that they promised before release is actually possible with exploration.

I still remember the E3 trailers, and it looked completely different to what they eventually slopped out.

The only really good feature I like is the ability to fast forward through the endless dialogue; no, I do not want to stand in a hallway for 30 seconds listening to small talk whilst in the middle of a mission that completely breaks the immersion of a high-stakes stealth mission ffs. Oh, and on the topic of stealth missions, I love how your companions will just run through enemies and their line of sights because their pathing is so bad.
