comment:
A legendary masterpiece that lived long enough to become a hyper-inflated casino.

It’s been over a decade, spanning three entire console generations, and Rockstar is still milking Grand Theft Auto V harder than a dairy farmer trying to pay off a mortgage. What started as a groundbreaking open-world experience has slowly morphed into an exhausting grind-fest. The single-player story remains iconic, but GTA Online is a relentless machine where everything from a basic sports car to a flying motorcycle costs tens of millions of in-game dollars. The economy is so aggressively inflated that it feels entirely designed to push you into buying Shark Cards just to exist in the same zip code as the fun stuff.

If the digital inflation doesn't break your spirit, the public lobbies absolutely will. Trying to progress your criminal empire or complete a heist as a legitimate player feels like a medieval punishment. You're constantly trying to coordinate with randoms who mysteriously disconnect halfway through a setup mission, all while navigating an endless plague of modders and cheaters. It is a daily occurrence to spawn in, immediately get blown up by an invisible hacker, and have a literal UFO dropped onto your character's head.

GTA V is a beautiful relic of gaming history that has massively overstayed its welcome. If you want to experience the phenomenal single-player campaign, it’s still worth picking up on sale. But if you’re hoping to jump into GTA Online today without a dedicated group of friends or a bottomless real-world bank account, you’re essentially just signing up to be target practice for a 12-year-old on an Oppressor Mk II.

- Music and sounds are generally great.
- Quite enjoyable single player campaign.
- Graphics are good in most areas. Some are rather ugly or even disgusting, but this might be expected from a horror RPG.

Cons:
- Outdated combat system copied from earlier games without much revision. Every major flaw that existed in game mechanics over 17 years ago are still present in Elden Ring.
- Game consists mostly of combat with very little other RPG elements. This might not be a bad thing if the combat system was better.
- Worst co-op game of all time. Very little options and PVP cannot be disabled.
- No real reason to play this more than once. The world is always the same, and you can do everything that's worth doing with just one character.

comment:
The best save-scumming simulator since Pathfinder: Kingmaker.

Baldur's Gate 3 looks fantastic and has all the ingredients of a great RPG: an excellent story, incredible voice acting, cinematic scenes, interesting classes, and plenty of quests. Unfortunately, the dice-based gameplay completely kills the experience for me.

So much of what you do comes down to dice rolls that even characters who are supposed to be good at something can constantly fail at it. What's the point of making a decision or building a character around certain strengths when the game can just decide that your character is suddenly incompetent?

Pros:

- Great story, graphics, and cinematic scenes that make you want to keep playing.
Probably the best voice acting I've ever heard in a game.
- Extensive and interesting class and character building.
- Lots of well-designed and memorable quests.
- The game encourages multiple playthroughs if you want to see everything.
- The amount of choices and possible outcomes is genuinely impressive.

Cons:

-The heavy reliance on dice rolls can make your character choices feel meaningless. Even with a high chance of success, you can still fail at something that should be routine.
-The constant failed rolls can turn serious situations into a comedy show. At some point you could put circus music under almost every encounter and it would fit.
-Some characters and dialogue feel more like edgy teenagers than actual adults, which can really hurt the immersion for me.
-The constant save-scumming becomes almost mandatory if you don't want important situations decided by an unlucky roll. This reminds me a lot of Pathfinder: Kingmaker.
-Loading saves repeatedly gets especially annoying when you already know that a failed roll was the only reason something went wrong.

Overall:

I understand why so many people consider Baldur's Gate 3 one of the best RPGs ever made. The production quality, voice acting, visuals, story, and character building are absolutely top-tier.

But personally, the dice system ruins too much of it for me. I prefer RPGs where character progression actually makes you reliably good at something. If my character has the skills for a task, I want that to matter instead of constantly watching him trip over his own feet because the game rolled a 1.

For me, Dragon Age: Origins and Dragon Age II are still much closer to what I want from an RPG. Baldur's Gate 3 is incredibly well-made, but the core gameplay philosophy simply isn't for me.

comment:
I've beaten it and I've spent over 600 hours with it (probably double that if you count the GOG version as well), but the percent of that time was actually fun is not that high. It's also full of so many frustrating design decisions.
For example:
1. Alert is a top tier feat in normal D&D 5 already, but with a d4 for initiative it's just ridiculous. If they were doing that, it should give only +1 to iniative (and it would still be a powerful feat). Meanwhile, the mess they made of the action economy made the "use your shield to shove as a bonus action" you can get through the feat completely useless.
2. They made a complete mess of the action economy by letting you cast two spells in one turn, jumping is an action for some reason, and they made shove a bonus action instead of an attack (but they also nerfed it so you can't use it to knock someone prone). There's other examples, but that's enough.
3. "Weapon actions" OK, at first glance this makes sense, could be fun. If I have a spear maybe I can rush someone down and... I can only do that once per day? Why is there even a limit to a completely mundane non-magical action?
4. The conversations: There's a distinct lack of options to disagree with a lot of people. Rather it's 3 options like "I agree" or "I agree and apologize" or "Maybe you're right after all" or "Get defensive but don't disagree".
5: The culture in game: There's no consistency at all, and people that are human and look like they belong in that part of the world is a very small minority. I think there *should* be exotic races and species present, especially in the city or in the extraplanar journeys, but not everyone should be an exotic, because then nobody is. It just makes the world building feel flat. Speaking of flat, why does Viconia, a relatively young full-blooded elf look so old?
6: The party members. All the males are completely unlikable. Not "charmingly annoying" or "gets under your skin, so you want to see what bad things can happen to them" (the old version of Wyll was a bit like that). No, you just want them to go home and leave you alone.
7: Character creation: Shield Dwarf should get a +2 to Str and Con. That's what makes them so good at doing dwarfy stuff. But no, someone at Larian has something against dwarfs (that would explain why so many of them in game look nothing like a dwarf apart from their stature too), and every race has the same bonuses. The same thing screwed over humans too, who lose their stat bonuses and their level 1 feat, instead getting weapon and armor proficiencies because every human (and half elf) has miilitary training I guess?
8. Perhaps the most annoying feature, but I almost forgot it, is The Controls: Casting a spell with one character then switching to another often has you clicking 3-4 or more times on the portrait you're trying to switch to before it actually does, and the camera often refuses to follow you "upstairs" when you're trying to get a character to move there. Also, rather than a simple drag to select multiple interface like in the infinity engine games or many RTS games, or Owlcat's Pathfinder games, there's a needlessly cumbersom e "chain" system which makes positioning a complete pain when accuracy or speed matters (which it usually doesn't, but still), especially since if you decouple them, switching between them can take multiple clicks. Using the function keys to switch usually works on the first try, so I don't know why they screwed up the mouse controls so bad.

That's just 8 things - there's dozens upon dozens of large, small and tiny annoyances that collect until there's just a feeling of fatigue trying to play the game.

Luckily, there's mods that fix almost ALL of these annoyances (doesn't fix the controls or the camera, and Realms Restored is a pain to install on Linux), but playing the game without mods is just not a good time.

comment:
A mile wide and an inch deep perfectly describes this game. To call it an RPG is, which technically true, feels wrong given that it makes the same cardinal sin that FO4 mad and has a voiced PC that completely kills most immersion the second they start talking, not to mention it also hilariously makes the same mistake of dialogue options being vague and sometimes completely different to what the PC actually says.

 The world LOOKS nice, they did a fantastic job making it look like a complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥(I'm not being sarcastic, its a well made ♥♥♥♥♥♥ American city), but that's the only thing I can really say was good about it. The inhabitants might as well not exist, they either do nothing(civvies) or are the horde of mindless npcs to kill with no consequences. The police are a nonissue(which has always been a running theme in these kinds of games) and become even more so after finishing the DLC. Gangs in general feel like an after thought and set dressing than anything substantial besides from giving the fixer related to them a basic personality. 

Missions are another problem in that outside of the story ones, its almost always just "GO here, kill these people, get item/person" Sure there's SOME good ones, but the VAST majority are copy paste kill this variety of goons, move on to next set. It tries to give you interesting non-combat stuff but fails when it becomes so obvious they put so little effort into the non-combat stuff. Non-lethal take downs and hacks feel pointless then there's no consequences for killing when I can easily avoid all consequences. I'm sure that's a message but it falls flat after the 100th (except for the cyber psycho quest obviously, and the reward is just another ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gun.)

The story itself was ok, predictable admittedly, but it wore its inspiration on its sleeve unabashed so I cant fault them for that.  Johnny was an ok character, a bit on the nose at times and his and V's relationship felt jumbled at times like the game forgot I was on good terms with him and randomly have V act like he suddenly hates him. NPC romances were a joke, but that's because they were NPC romances, no one but loosers take those seriously.

The DLC was surprisingly good story wise, gameplay wise was more of the same. At least it felt like my actions actually mattered this time rather than not.

Oh and the bugs ARE still there, they just arent game breaking anymore, just funny, like Bethesda bugs.

a solid 4/10, horribly disappointing for what they promised.

comment:
As other reviews note: BG3 is excellent... mostly. But it's so fundamentally broken in critical areas that I cannot recommend it — especially not to players who want to roleplay beyond the devs' intended path.

Three years after release, this game still has game-breaking bugs. But this isn't a random glitch — this is quest design failure.

Here's what happened: To progress through the Shadow-Cursed Lands, you need a working Moonlantern. I made two valid story choices the game explicitly offers:

The game provides zero working lanterns through this combination of legitimate choices. No warning. No alternative path. Just: your save is worthless now.

I didn't cheat. I didn't exploit. I didn't do anything "wrong." I played the game exactly as designed, made roleplay choices the quest system clearly didn't account for, and the game simply... broke.

This isn't a soft-lock. This is a hard lock. Game over. The end. Hours of gameplay gone unless you install third-party mods to fix the developer's mistake.

A €70 AAA title should not require third-party mods to fix progression bugs that shouldn't exist. A €70 AAA title should definitely not hard-lock players for making valid story choices.

If you like linear, heavily railroaded RPGs where every decision is pre-approved: you'll probably love this.

If you want actual roleplaying freedom: be warned. The game punishes you for stepping outside the intended path."

[h1]UPDATE[/h1] after more hours playing

[b]I now have 3 broken Moonlanterns and one that works. The working one I found deep into the area that can only be reached with a working Moonlantern.[/b] This is like selling concert tickets in front of the stage — a virtual game over. [b]Must be fixed with mods.[/b]


[h2]The Good[/h2]

The battles are genuinely fun and motivating. Losing a fight makes me want to retry, not quit. That's rare and well done.

[h2]The Bad[/h2]

[b]Zero tutorial.[/b] You either know D&D 5e like the inside of your nose, or you'll spend hours googling what your spells actually do. For a 70 euro AAA game? Unacceptable.

[b]Inventory management is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ PITA.[/b] Sorting, moving, identifying — all unnecessarily clunky.

[b]Bugs and annoyances.[/b] Party members suddenly stop following because they randomly didn't make a jump they've done 100 times without issues. Clicking through doors (on the ground behind them) to walk through them closes them 80% of the time. The whole interaction with the game feels extremely clunky. The camera often makes you wanna pull you hair out. I've had fights that took forever because it was so extremely hard to even find the enemies because the cam just doesn't work properly (especially true for enemies on higher ground). I could make this review at least 10 times as long as it already is by just writing about all the bugs that Larian obviously didn't care to fix in those 3 years since release.... WTF?

[b]Open world is marketing fiction.[/b] As one player perfectly put it: Somehow this game deluded everyone into thinking it was open world when it has more obvious rails than Railroad Tycoon.

[h2]The Game-Breaking[/h2]

[b]Gale's explosion mechanic is catastrophically opaque.[/b] The game can end with zero warning and zero explanation. You load your last save, camp again, same explosion. No clue what triggered it. No way to fix it.

[b]Shadowheart's pivotal story moment[/b] has essentially ONE continuing branch. Knock her out instead of killing her? She becomes a lawn ornament forever. No story, no consequence, nothing.

[h2]Verdict[/h2]
It's not Baldur's Gate 3. It's [b]Baldur's Rail 3[/b]. No open gates to be seen.

Still fun despite itself. But the your choices matter marketing should come with an asterisk: as long as they match the flowchart.

I'd say... if turn-based combat is what you're here for... you will enjoy this (if you can live with the bugs, some of them extremely annoying!). If you're after good roleplaying with lots of open branches... look somewhere else.

comment:
Sadly, The Witcher 3 Remastered is running pretty poorly, even on a high-end PC. I honestly don’t know what went wrong here or who they outsourced this to, but the optimization really needs some work.

I’m getting around 40–55 FPS at 4K DLSS Quality with Ray Tracing and Path Tracing, and it can dip into the 30s in crowded areas. What really confuses me is that even if I turn Path Tracing off, the FPS barely changes. It literally stays around the same. Even switching DLSS to Balanced doesn’t seem to give me any noticeable performance boost. Like… how does that make sense?

The game looks great, don't get me wrong but the poor optimization was enough to make me turn it off.

I absolutely love The Witcher and CDPR, but I have to say, I’m thoroughly disappointed with the performance right now. Hopefully they can sort this out soon because this game deserves better. 

If you really wanna enjoy the masterpiece that is The Witcher 3, play the older version not this heap of a mess.

comment:
I'm not the target demo. I thought I could get into this game considering that I kind of like fantasy stories and magic and stuff. I'm just so bored with this game. I can't get past the slog of the combat system. Every fight is just so slow and tedious. The characters seem cool I guess. The world seems very cool and well made. The colors and the landscapes seem well made and all that. I never have played DnD so I didn't really know what I was getting into. I didn't think I had to watch a review before buying a game that's overwhelmingly praised but I guess I should have. 

You'll probably really enjoy this game if you like learning about in-depth systems for everything you can think of. But like I just wanna like play the game and not read a 50 page guide explaining the basic combat or fundamentals of the game. I don't wanna watch a YouTube video explaining the best kits or ways to build your character or whatever. 

I don't have the time or energy to invest into learning every single like thing in this game. Or interacting with everything I see. I don't even know what 90% of the UI I'm looking at does (even with the little explanations when you hover over them). I'm just so overwhelmed with what I'm looking at with every aspect of this game. It feels so incredibly complex and just tedious to do every little thing. 

TLDR: I'm not a nerd, so the game is not for me. You'll probably enjoy it though if you like super nerdy boring combat systems that take an eternity to get though.

comment:
After 232 hours, here is my honest take.

The maps feel small and confined compared to true open-world RPGs like Skyrim or Fallout. Too many invisible walls masquerading as 'strategic terrain.'
There is no real RPG depth. The branching narrative is reactive, sure — but the underlying systems like economy, crafting and faction reputation are basically non-existent.
The dialogue system feels dated, possibly as a nod to Baldur's Gate 1 & 2. Respect the heritage, but someone should have cut 40% of the banter.
The D&D mechanics are faithful to a fault — low hit rates, binary spells and constant save-scumming. This isn't hardcore difficulty, it's just friction.

No clear feedback when actions are blocked in restricted zones. The UI tells you WHAT is blocked but never WHY.

In 2026, with modern AI tools, a solo developer could vibe-code a more polished experience. Just kidding of course but this game deserved better! :(

Not recommended — unless you are 40+ and grew up with Baldur's Gate 1 & 2.

comment:
This is undeniably a fun game, but it's not perfect and has quite a few prominent flaws people seem to rarely talk about.
This is one of if not the best attempts at integrating the most fun aspects of DnD into a video game, but it does it without isolating people who have no prior experience and/or interest in DnD. The game has a lot of different environments that differ enough to keep you interested. Though I cant say you can bask in the view of it that much due to the fixed eagle eye view of the game (unless you use the photo mode in which the camera is adjustable). In my opinion that makes it a little harder to navigate, but its not a big deal. 

People seem to really like the character creation in BG3, its praised so much that I think most people may know BG3 as the game people like making intricately designed sexy elves in. It's true, the character creator is really fun to play with (with the added countless mods the game has, which is another thing I like about it, it makes a lot of mods very accessible). I like that you can choose a backstory that will affect your stats and I like that one of them makes you really evil. I have to mention that some races dont have nearly as much extra content as others do, so thats something you should take into account if you decide to make a human, gnome, halfling or dwarf. But the classes make up for it. Unfortunately you cant really customize the face of your characters that much as you're stuck with pre-made base ones, and I cant say they're very diverce. You can choose between a selection of shaven or non shaven ♥♥♥♥♥ and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for your characters though so thats fun I guess.

The biggest issue I have with this game is the writing. In my opinion it's not it's strongest suit. Which wouldn't matter that much if this were a simple strategy or fighting game where the lore would feel like a bonus, but the story is crucial to the game and takes up a lot of it. It has a lot of "some races are inherently bad" tropes that I hate in media. There is no better example of this than the fact that one can (if not encouraged as it makes the combat easier) kill the goblin children with no consequences (even Halsin, the contradictory guy who claims to love all of natures creatures, can maul them to death). This weird fantasy racism affects other less popular races as well, including the gnomes, which we can play as. Astarion will often be cruel to your character if you do, and its very apparent that his prejudices affect his worldview (of course he will face no consequences regarding this because when does he ever). This sorta ties into my next point and major complaint; the game has very explicit and violent animal cruelty on several occasions. Blood and violence is one thing, but adding unnecessary animal gore is another. This really jarred me the first time I saw it, and as far as im aware there were no warnings given for this in the game. You're even encouraged to crush the animal's skull with your foot to kill it faster in one of these mentioned scenes. This is out of pocket and adds nothing to the game. I would argue that if the depicted animal were to be, for example, a dog, a lot more people would find issue with these scenes. Due to it being a disliked and often demonized animal, this slips under the radar. Whether you want to admit it or not falsely labeling any kind of animal as evil or "not as important" leads to harm and disruption. Id like this trope gone from all media, not to mention from big games with a lot of reach. 

Steam reviews are sometimes too restrictive, as I dont want to leave a "recommended" on a game I have several issues with. I was quite disappointed in it. However Im not saying this game is entirely bad, clearly a lot of effort has been put into it and despite all of its flaws I still think it's enjoyable. And I like that you can ♥♥♥♥ the alien squid.

comment:
Elden Ring was a disappointment for me because it tries to combine an open world with the soulslike formula, yet never fully excels at either.

As a soulslike, it relies too heavily on systems and ideas that FromSoftware has been using since Dark Souls 1. After dozens of hours, I often felt like I was playing another variation of familiar mechanics rather than a true evolution of the genre. The combat lacks enough fresh ideas to justify the massive time investment the game demands.

As an open-world game, it also falls short of the best examples of the genre. The world is huge, but much of the content feels repetitive. Similar enemies, repeated dungeon layouts, recycled bosses, and familiar activities create the impression that quantity often takes priority over quality. Instead of being excited to explore, I frequently felt like I was simply crossing another section of the map to find a slightly different version of something I had already seen before.

My biggest issue is that the combination of an open world and a soulslike structure does not work particularly well. What I love most about soulslike games is focused level design, interconnected areas, meaningful shortcuts, and a strong sense of progression through carefully crafted environments. Elden Ring sacrifices much of that focus in favor of scale, and the result is a game that often feels diluted compared to the tighter experiences that came before it.

I cannot say that Elden Ring is a bad game. Its production values, scope, and ambition are impressive. However, as a long-time soulslike fan, it failed to deliver what I personally look for in the genre. It did not meet my standards as a soulslike, and it did not meet my standards as an open-world RPG either.

For that reason, I would not recommend it to players who prefer more focused and replayable experiences such as Bloodborne, Mortal Shell, or Lies of P.

comment:
World building and exploration: 4/5
Few games have locales and lore as evocative as this game, but the From formula for half-baked lore might be beginning to wear thin. The world is often also too large, and the level design of the open world is... lacking.
Visuals and art direction: 5/5
Every frame a painting. The DLC especially is amazing, visually.
Build variety: 5/5
Never has a From game offered such variety, and it's hard to think of many other games that offer this much, either. Tens of weapon classes, spell schools, lots of armor and talismans, different buffs and synergies to build on - it's great. It's too bad that so much isn't viable in the late game without cheese, but it's difficult to balance so many options.
Dungeons: 3/5
Some legacy dungeons are very good, like Stormveil and Leyndell. But many are incredibly linear, like Farum Azula, and devolve into straight lines.
Enemy variety and quality: 3/5
Enemies are recycled ad-nauseum to fill out the large world, and enemies are often poorly balanced and the over-use of delayed attacks where an enemy (misbegotten, I'm looking at you) will hold their weapons up for 6-7 seconds before finally attacking is just comical, the only way to know what to anticipate is to be subjected to it a few times first. Game design in general is very akin to arcades, where you would have to memorize a pattern, not hone your pattern recoginition and reactions, so that you would die as much as possible and put another coin in. More on this on the bosses.
Bosses: 2/5
Most bosses are bad. Margit, Morgot, Mohg, Godrick, Rellana, Messmer are examples of good bosses that are worth your time to learn, but in a roster with 100+ that's a very poor crop. Input reading is rampant, delayed attacks and 10-hit combos that can only be avoided by failing over and over until you memorize them (or looking up guides) feature in every boss, bosses in general do massive damage, especially towards the end of the game, and their health pools balloon. The end result is that you will spend 90% of the boss fights just watching the boss have fun, before you might be able to get a hit or two in, rinse and repeat. A boss like Malenia is actually really well designed besides two moves, but the moves are telegraphed really poorly and can come out at any time, and if the player's positioning isn't optimal when she decides to do it a non-streamer without 1k hours learning the fight will die and have to try again. But she could also just never do those attacks, you could be lucky. Then you'll beat her since the rest of the toolset is very fair and managable. And Malenia is not alone in this. Radagon is not a particularly fun fight, Elden Beast outright sucks, Fire Giant is absolute bottom tier of From's bosses ever, PCR phase 1 is too basic and phase 2 turns your screen into a white smear where you can't see what he does, Malekith phase 2 spends 80% of his time airborne and untouchable, Metyr is garbage tier, bosses are recycled again and again - even remembrance bosses like the Ancient Spirit, Godrick and Astel. In short it's difficult to say much positive about the bosses as a whole. In previous games, like Bloodborne and DS3, bosses were difficult but fair. There were few gotcha mechanics. The developers did not try to waste your time. Here you should probably look up boss guides before you touch the golden walls since that's a much better use of your time. There's gigantic crutches that a player can whip out to avoid all of the above, like strong spirit ashes or the mimic tear, but they trivialize the boss encounters so much that saying that it is intended to fight them that way just can't be true.

Overall, a good game brought down very low by what has been the highlight of From's previous work: The bosses. They are mostly very bad. Considering how much of the game is centred around overcoming bosses and how much time you will spend fighting them, it's difficult to recommend the game on its merits as a whole. Many players will build their character around a fun use of weaponry and spells they discover as they explore, only to find their build useless against a big chunk of bosses, demanding either a respec or the use of spirit ashes.

Most likely, a new player going in with the viewpoint of bosses as necessary speed bumps filled with visual spectacle that should be overcome with spirit ashes, rather than the absolute highlights of their journey, will have a much better time than most.

comment:
This game is really ... overhyped and overestimated.
More specifically I am talking about the gameplay.
It is true that the graphics, quests/dialogues, music, are amazing.
But the most important thing - gameplay - is not.
The combat especially is my main problem.
It is just soo random in a way. You basically only spam left click and dodge. There is no weight to dodging/blocking; when fighting vs multiple enemies they will constantly attack you from different directions, and the only thing you can do is spam dodge > fast attack > dodge > fast attack. There is no depth to the combat, it is annoying and repetitive. Yes it is definitely serviceable but ... from a game so revered, which I just now am playing for the first time ever, I was tremendously disappointed.
Bad/unenjoyable combat can suck all the fun out of a game like this, even if every other aspect is perfect.
The signs(spells) are not fun and also not very useful.
The talent tree is the worst I have ever seen in an RPG, honestly.
I am looking at all the talent trees - alchemy, signs, swords, general - and I can not find a SINGLE talent where I want to invest my skill points. Everything is bad in the talent tree, every skill/talent looks weak/pointless/boring. This in combination with the combat makes the gameplay very unfun for me.
Also Geralt controls are JANK - there is no better word to describe it. The horse also. Many many modern games suffer from jank controls though, but things like this are something I was not expecting from what is considered to be one of the best games of all time. Too much mediocrity and jank in the gameplay here which I find very hard to tolerate.

Many of this game's developers made one of my new favorite games - Blood of Dawnwalker - and you can see some of the jank that's in the Witcher from 2015 can also be found in Dawnwalker from 2026 ... 
But the gameplay and systems and talents and combat are much more to my liking in Dawnwalker. It is truly an amazing game and combat there is weighty and if you are skilled you will see it, feel it, and when you lose in that game you can see where you made a mistake and what you need to improve.
In the Witcher 3 however is not the same, I am repeating myself but the combat is just so random, every fight whether I win or lose, I do not at all feel if I improved my skill or if I failed; dying seems like bad RNG as opposed to a skill issue on my end; and winning a tough fight also feels like I managed to "cheese" the fight somehow, as opposed to me becoming better at the game. And not to mention fights vs 4+ ghouls/drowners or similar fast creatures, the game is just terribly designed for a combat against multiple enemies.

So yeah TLDR 80% of my problems with this game are with the combat, and the other 20% with its controls/systems/menu/vendor navigation and stuff like that.
Even though I am a graphics junkie, and this game looks phenomenal, I am finding it veeery hard to enjoy it. And this is my favorite type of game - open world fantasy world with big focus on story. And this game does so many things much worse than almost any other game I've played in similar genres.

comment:
DISCLAIMER:
The game is definitely worth buying if you can get it at a massive discount, as in: single-digit price, being that one cannot deny that it is not a complete miss after the massive overhaul and fixes which polished what they could from the infamous initial version.

PROS:
The game obviously had a AAA budget and a fairly long story.
Someone poured their love for the Cyberpunk lore into the concepts and the pre-release marketing promised to deliver it.
If you want to end up with a mindless time-skip in the form of a semi-idle walk-and-click in your Library, this is a good choice. But again: only and only at a massive discount.

CONS:
1. Before anything else, the first thing that destroys the fun in this are the *unskippable* segments.
[spoiler] After Chapter 1 , you are thrown into an unskippable walking simulator with horrendous overeasy gameplay, that suffocates you with hopes of ending every time there is a fade-to-black, but no! At several points you have to literaly press the forward button several times to (!)crawl forward [/spoiler].
And the dialogue skip option is intentionally taken away at instances where you just sit and look at a character the developers deemed to be so important that you cannot skip.
Do you have choices? None that affect the gameplay.

And this can eat up to 15+ minutes of your life at several instances.

2. The gameplay is a an enormous tease and a letdown. You grow powerful incredibly fast and are given such a vast array of ways to combat that I had stopped upgrading my character a tad bit into chapter 2 because I couldn't find a reason to. The enemy AI is atrociously bad and unchallenging, the weapon classes are a gimmick (one even removes the need to aim at all, scoring instant headshots at a click of a mouse) and at first I thought the driving physics were some sort of an in-game joke.

3. The "cyberpunk" starts and ends with cosmetics in an illogical world that is simply any GTA-like space of copy-paste design, but you get to have a universal remote in your eyes.
The characters are unbelievable and the dialogues are cringe-inducing, with propaganda and forced perspectives infused with varying subtlety.

4. The game-breaking bugs that made it infamous are largely removed, but still present. At certain points the loading screen will shut down the game, there are untested spaces where you can get trapped and have to reload, the physics quirks are still present although rare, etc.

I really wanted to like the game and read online review promising the gameplay to get better as time progresses, but even this much time invested in it later, I cannot say that it is a win.
Unless, I repeat, you are to get it at a *large* discount.

comment:
elden ring is flawed, very flawed.
a confusing mess of gameplay systems that don't come together as more than the sum of their parts.

you run around on your horse for 15 minutes to do a 5 minute long "dungeon" before running around on your horse for 15 more minutes.
collect this weapon, collect this bell bearing, collect this spell, collect a truly ridiculous quantity of materials in an increasingly longer list of stupendous locations to upgrade anything you have.
all in the pursuit of minimizing a difficulty that doesn't exist. the vast majority of the game is trivialized by at least 12 different mechanics. heavy attacks, jump attacks, ashes of war, spells, pots, spirits, twohanding, torrent, great runes, somber weapons, talismans, status effects.

the "longer" areas are a bitter memory of a studio that used to try. the world design of dark souls 3 looks like a masterpiece in comparison. and that game is not stunning either.
at least in that game, you (generally) Can't just sprint to the end of the biggest dungeon in the entire game in about 5 minutes.

don't get me started on the story. from has lost their touch on that front since ds2.

there are brief moments where the game shows it may do something interesting, but that's all they are, moments.
because the fundamental problem is that most of the game is running.
hurray for open world.

comment:
Great story.  Have read FR since the 80s with Salvatore etc.  The game itself should be much better and only fully succeeds because of the voice casting and the already present lore of FR.  Constant trip wires put in place by Larian who let themselves down by trying to be clever showing the combat log being visible for each action.  I scrutinise every single action in the combat log and often find apparent errors, which are clearly meant for players to not notice and take Larian at their word.  Every game has this in the background but to show it openly is where it breaks down how Larian manipulate the mechanics.  Many tooltip differences where such as  Swashy with rakish bonus skill tooltip where I have to pass my own ac to knock the weapon from the enemies hands.  Reverse arcane synergy on myself (tooltip stated this,) where I received disadvantage on all attacks across all my party.  Skills ignored such as athletics not even registering in the combat log but still taking the bonus action.  A lot of this may be down to honour mode as Larian appear to abuse HM to justify changing the mechanics which you cannot see as they do not update any tooltips.  
And the dice rolls are rigged to a degree.  Many times I set myself up to be needing 4's and 5's only, yet find I miss almost as often as hitting.  It hovers around 2,3 & 4 which are the most popular of my dice rolls.  But this will suit the narrative as it restricts the player accordingly.  Nobody spends $100m on a game to have it all come down to a 1d20 roll.  And certainly nobody would honestly show this in a combat log for all to see.  I wouldn't do it, you wouldn't do it and the next person wouldn't do it either.
The game is a relative breeze, honour mode or not.  Shame Larian feel the need to manipulate the mechanics and the combat log via the rigged die rolls.
Should be a 5/5 without question.  Instead a solid 2/5.

comment:
So I was misled as to what this game is. Let me jump straight to the point: It's a glorified walking simulator, not an RPG, with piss-poor gunplay and lots of bugginess. I bought this deliberately years after it initially came out because it was allegedly so bugged. But there's still so much lack of polish that it just strikes me as ridiculously poor craftsmanship from CDPR's side.

The whole city feels empty and lifeless. Most of the doors do not register as interactable, i.e., they're just plain props. This makes it difficult to know how to get from A to B because many paths are not available. The pathfinding itself is super bad, often telling you the wrong way then, when you actually walk that way, deciding midway through that you should rather go back. Ridiculous. The whole city is constucted like a maze, something out of System Shock. That's just stupid. Environment traveral is annoying and painful.

Gunplay also just feels weird. Reloading is super slow, mag size of shotguns and sniper rifles is ridiculously small (4 shots!). There is also very few guns, like 20 different weapon types probably. They're all the same but different "tiers". Disappointing.

Inventory management is HELL. Mark something as "favorite" but that mark gets lost as soon as you transfer to your stash. Unequip of attachments sometimes not possible with meaningless error message "ACTION BLOCKED". Auto-compare is weird (e.g., it compares a shotgun with the currently equipped sniper rifle which makes ZERO sense). No marking weapons as trash functionality. All in all way worse inventory management than Borderlands 1. Sorting is weird too. Somewhere in the middle of my attachments is suddenly "Evenlyn's Purse", a non-interactable, non-removable story item.

Game is buggy at times. Random physics glitches all the time (cars flipping/hanging/jumping). Sometimes a weapon shows it is not fully reloaded, "R" does nothing, switch to a different weapon and back and you see it is fully reloaded. Sometimes when stealing a car the car goes into rampage auto-drive mode that cannot be deactivated (apparently a known bug that just isn't getting fixed).

Some things just feel dumb. Like I shoot the driver of a car, the window is busted open. Yet to actually STEAL the car I need more strength than I currently have. Like, what STRENGTH is needed to open a car though the busted window and removing the deceased body from within? Exactly: none. I can call my own vehicle but sometimes when roads intersect verticaly it spawns on the wrong road (let's say I'm under a bridge it'll spawn on top of that bridge so that I cannot reach it).

In a game that plays in a city of crime, why is the ONE THING I cannot do mug people? Geeze it is SO OBVIOUS that I want to mug people yet I can't. I want to mug everyone so badly and yet I can't how come this super obvious feature was not implemented?

And the story, don't get me started on the story. It is so unbelievably stupid. So I play this absolute 1000% certified a-hole. Like, I have literally zero remorse, zero conciousness. You know how many people I have shot point blank in the head with my sniper rifle? No remorse WHAT-SO-EVER, sleeping like a baby. And yet, when it's my own life on the line because imaginary Keanu Reeves magically appears in my head and wants to "overwrite" my brain (yeah don't ask) I cry like a little bytch about how awful this all is and how unfair and that I WANT TO LIVE. You stinking turd, do you know who also wanted to live? That cop that I shot that one time because I got confused about the gray and yellow pathfinding and thought I was meant to shoot him (spoiler alert wasn't meant to sorry honest mistake). Like, I have absolute zero sympathy with that character of mine with that cringy name "V" as a cherry on top and you want me to feel sorry with that dude? LOL! By all means overwrite his brain, nothing of value would be lost like AT ALL.

On the topic of cringe, sheeeeeeesh let's talk bizzzzzzz. Can we please at least acknowledge how preeeeem cringy everyone talks in this game, dawg? If this is the future then Jesus I really don't want to grow that old. "You got some iron" effing hell man just talk like a normal person and not how Boomers imagine the future by poorly imitating Gen-Z speak. This is ridiculous.

The characters are also just so dumb. Jane or whatever her stupid name is think's I'm a "really good person". BWAHAHAHAHAHAHA! HAVE YOU EVER TALKED TO ME, DUMBASS JANE? You don't know the FIRST thing about me, quite obviously! Clearly, I'm rotten to the core because of all the stuff I have done. I'd shoot you in a heartbeat for those juicy Tier 1 Components, you better believe it. Also, why does every Tom ♥♥♥♥ and Harry keep calling me? I wish I could just mute you all, blacklist your calls. That also means you, stupid Panam. I don't want you annoying me! What we did was PURELY transactional, I do not like you, you do not like me, so stop effing calling me you stalker!

The missions, man, some missions are so stupid. This one mission you help a robot taxi operator find its lost taxis. Some TAXIS are depressed. Some TAXIS are afraid of speed. One imitates GLaDOS. It's not funny, it's effing stupid. And annoying. One of the taxis is suicidal and our "hero" V just mocks it for it. Like, what the hell. Zero effing empathy yet a ♥♥♥♥♥ crybaby when something remotely bad happens to him. 

And why do I have to get to some location to get paid for some missions. Like, can't you just wire transfer me the money? You clearly can since some missions do. Walking simulator, I tell you, walking simulator!

Enemies. Most are super easy to defeat. Like one shot. Others do not take damage when hit in the head with the sniper rifle. I have no idea why but clearly this is just piss poor balancing. And the AI pathfinding of enemies, it is teeeeerrible! Instead of hopping over a small fence which I can easily do they need to walk all the way around it. "I'm gonna flank em'" they scream yet, spoiler alert, they do not flank me but show me their pretty little heads for me to pop with my rifle.

Clothing, do you have any idea what I look like? Let me tell you: since pants without positive attributes (found none so far) are just dead weight (count towards your carry limit), the better option is just to omit them. So now I wear sunglasses (gives some zoom stat), a life vest (give some other stat) and my rifle. Do you know how stupid I look as the pantsless avenger with my micro penis hanging out for the world to see? What a great choice of the devs to let us choose the size of our junk in character development. The sound of my bare feet flopping on the streets as I slaughter waves of enemies makes my day. But you know what bothers me? When I sit on my motorcycle I suddenly wear shorts! HOW COME? How can I be the pantsless avenger when I wear shorts? Not fair. You give me the option to go commando, you better let me go full commando. Even on that stupid ugly motorcycle of that stupid dead "friend" of mine.

Dialogs, on top of being cringy, change NOTHING of the outcome. Like, no decisions matter at all. Most of the dialog is just side knowledge which is useless, the first option only makes the story progress. Usually I skip through the whole ordeal if I can because blah blah blah I don't care this is too dumb and meaningless and I really, REALLY do not care about that character or their "friends" or about his imaginary friend Keanu. You can all DIAF for all I care.

I even get dialogs when talking to NPC vendors, which just feels artificial and stupid. Like I want to buy a gun, sorry, I want to buy "some iron", then I have to endure something like this masterpiece: "Looking for some new iron, got some?" - "Oh this city yes it is a city of crime indeed and a weapon for defense is a really good idea, you should carry some, yes what a brilliant idea of yours why do you not have a small peek at my grand selection?" (shows 3 guns, all identical) Just WHY.

comment:
If you are expecting a fun D&D adventure, this is not it.

I tried this game late last year, a co-op playthrough with my wife. All our D&D friends hyped it, so we figured it had to be good (we were waiting for her to get a machine good enough to run it, she finally did after Black Friday).

It did not come close to even our lowest expectations. To start, the pathing in the game is so incredibly broken. It is incredibly aggravating when your character walks through lava or uses extra movement walking along a path you didn't designate. Especially in D&D - map placement is like the most basic thing I can think of, and they can't get that right?

About the companions - they are flat at best and tired tropes at worst. We killed Astarion after he ambushed us and admitted to murdering others the same way; the devs act like it is a real D&D table and you HAVE to role play with these people whether you like it or not, or you will die. (I was a Rogue so we didn't get locked out of anything fortunately.) There isn't even continuity with the hunter looking for Astarion, you can't tell him you killed him, no reaction even if you dump Astarion's corpse on the ground in front of him. Idiotic and lazy design - they didn't anticipate players would kill a character who is trying to gank them on the road, and include that interaction option later?

The controls are incredibly confusing too. Soooooo many reloads because of UI misclicks, even after 80 hours into the game. It is so incredibly unintuitive that I honestly can't understand why people rave about this game.

I could go on about all the minor unexpected differences between BG3 and either 2014 or 2024, like the differences in spells, rest mechanics, etc. Yeah, this is NOT 5e D&D. 

(I will say the one nice thing was that Silence actually did work on the hag. Made the fight a breeze even at level 4. But the fact that I'm celebrating such a basic thing really tells you how poor the rest of the game is.)

comment:
I don't expect this to be seen by someone legitimately wondering if this game is worth picking up or not. I don't even expect this to be seen by anyone really but to begin: Elden Ring is at best a mid game and at worst a terrible one.

You will frequently be put in situations where you have to hope for RNG that the enemies don't move in a way that locks you into unavoidable death, bosses that deal ridiculous damage while you deal nothing, enemies that have ridiculous stats despite what they are (e,g, archers with large health pools and ridiculous damage reduction on top of that). You will get to experience the constant cycle of having to guess when an attack is going to happen because the enemy has 3 different versions of the same attack that are all identical in start-up but come out at different speeds that deal high damage. Not to mention the FromSoft special of lingering hitboxes or hitboxes that just plain make no sense, almost always to the detriment of you! Another FromSoft classic too of enemies having grabs that inflict bleed so they will 99% of the time kill you. On top of all that, enemies just plain do not follow the same rules you do, they will not run out of FP, they do not have to stop their combos at any fixed point and can string as many attacks together as they want (this is mild hyperbole, they genuinely can string together their hardest to avoid moves in one combo and I've had enemies that forced me to wait dodging through 7 attacks before I could even attempt to poke them) and speaking of stats:

Poise does next to nothing relevant in this game. It will help your attack not get interrupted if you get hit by something while charging a heavy attack but god forbid you don't want to be staggered by every pebble that hits you regardless of what you're wearing.

Level design where traps, hidden doors, and enemies are just thrown at you in ways where you'd think you'd get a grace after running low on healing despite having 10 flasks and, oops no sorry. Did you die? Make that entire slog again, bud. Oh that hole you need to dodge a trap? It's a small enemy that you're going to end up either dying to the trap trying to hit the enemy or die from the enemy somehow almost instantly proccing bleed or some other status effect on you. The Haligtree is a perfect example of another issue with the level design: Elden Ring does not do platforming well, at all. You will be put in situations where you will wonder if it's even what the devs intended before realizing, yes, they did in fact and- oh sorry you stood on the wrong part of the branch bud you will not be punished for the bad game design with death.

I think FromSoft games were what made me fully realize there is nothing more infuriating than a game over that takes way too long to get you back in the game. Ironically, for as quick as your health drains it's actually fairly long to die in this game. You get your choice of a quick death where the game still sits before finally going to the loading screen or on the opposite end: an animation that takes what feels like a full minute before you even get to the 5 second needless linger part that boots you to the loading screen.

TL;DR Elden Ring is mid at best and bad at worst. Play Dragon's Dogma or Hollow Knight for games that do the "challenging but fair" approach (in Hollow Knight's case) or the open-world medieval approach in DD's case

comment:
I should've written this a long time ago, but oh, well.

I do really think that this game deserved some of its praise back in the day (mostly 'cause of lack of competition, honestly), but finishing it left such a bittersweet taste in my mouth that i can't truly call it a „masterpiece for ages“.

I think i do understand the core vision of developers. Larian tried to ensure that this game will translate pure, chaotic DnD experience: and, I'll be frank, they somewhat did it with the outstanding turn-based combat system and all the possibilities that comes with it. Unfortunately, they failed on the other aspect that makes TTRPG have it's own renown: freedom of choice, being whoever you like to be and the consequences of it.

Storyline, and thus the choices that this game is kindly offering, have been written in such a straightforward and dichotomical way that you are either Mr. Goody-Two-Shoes or a pure offspring of Satan (wink-wink) with no real choices in between. The problem is not with the idea itself, but with it realization: whatever you choose, you'll ride on the same railroad over and over again with no differences that really matters on a global, narrative scale. Moreover, this game simply punishes you for picking granted conventionally evil choices and robs you out of possible content with nothing in return. The only consequences is, sadly, the amount of XP you'll gain and alive characters that you'll meet as the main quest goes on, i'm afraid. 

The overall quality of writing dissatisfies as well, granting a generally promising, albeit not without flaws, Act One and delving deeper into mediocrity as the story progresses further in Act Two and Three, with the second being a strange, linear filler and third an unpolished disappointment with big chunks of planned content removed in a hurry. 

And the characters? Sadly, with some exceptions they all seem more like humanized, basic fantasy archetypes/alignment charts put on screen rather than living persons with interesting, properly designed backstories and character depth/development (i'm talking about you, Wyll). And if the Act One tries to keep that a little secret, enriching the game with a bunch of popping out of nowhere party banter, interactions, random events and intrigue, well... later all of it slowly starts to disappear as you'll come closer to Baldur's Gate itself. 

But does that REALLY matter in the case of enjoying that game? No, i think not. To be honest, I've enjoyed every last bit of it, playing all day and night long in search of fun that this game perfectly delivers. What saddens me the most is the possibilities of what would've been if the game was delayed for a couple of years for extra polishing, and if the cut Early Access content/story hadn't been cut so unwisely. 

Alas, it is what it is, and despite the fact that I left a negative review, I do think that's up to you to try BG3 out and decide everything for yourself, although you should severely lower your expectations if you're looking for role-playing experience and an interesting story: you'll have nothing of that. But you'll have Minthara.

comment:
6 years later and on patch 2.31, a lot of people like to say they've "fixed" the game now.
Well, you can patch the bugs, you can rework your god-awful skill tree, inventory and crafting mechanics.
You can add police that actually chase you, quests that actually function and cars that actually handle like cars.
They did all that in an attempt to "make things right", which I'll acknowledge.
But one thing you can't patch is the terrible, TERRIBLE writing.
They don't even give you the ability to skip dialogue until you've gone through the motions of a completely rail-roaded THREE HOUR LONG prologue every time you want to replay the game (or pick a premade character to start at Phantom Liberty, but doing so hamstrings you if you aren't playing a hacker). 
WHY can't you skip dialogue in the prologue? ♥♥♥♥ you, I guess.
The main plotline with the engram is just plain bad. It saps so much player choice out of V's character, and of course there's tolerating Johnny Silverhand.
My God, Johnny Silverhand. With Michael Pondsmith's tabletop character they actually managed to make Keanu Reaves not just unlikable, but insufferable.
You might even find yourself asking just how much of the time CDPR spent consulting with Pondsmith was concerning the game world and how much was spent on faithfully recreating his annoying rockerboy avatar in the video game, complete with a soundtrack that makes you question how this rockerboy ever had a fan base in the first place. Seriously, if SAMURAI were a real band that had to stand on their own merit independent of the game they'd struggle to break 100 views on youtube. "Chippin' In" is one of the worst songs I've ever heard in my life.
And if you thought Silverhand was bad enough they somehow lower the bar further in Phantom Liberty with Songbird, the Mary-Sue the DLC revolves around, who the game treats as a tragic heroine who can do no wrong despite her being another generally awful self-insert and the architect of all her own problems.
Gameplay wise the game is fine.
Combat is engaging with a decent amount of depth once you've gotten yourself a loadout of weapons and cyberware you like, but if you're playing a hacker the gameplay loop is extremely boring and tedious (scan a guy -> dump hacks -> he dies -> scan next guy -> repeat until entire room is dead and you didn't even need to draw any of those guns you went to the trouble of getting).
The voice acting is broadly competent. There are some stand out characters that are well voiced, but again the material they're working with is not ideal. Male V's voice is fine. Competent, unremarkable but not annoying either. Female V's  voice however is just bad. The voice actress they chose for her has two modes: "Make my voice quiver a bit and ham it up" for any scene that is even vaguely dramatic and "sassy girl boss" for anything else. This can get quite annoying given that this is the character your stuck with for the entire game.
Itemization is still all over the place, with certain paths giving objectively superior rewards which further limits replayability (for example siding with Songbird in the DLC gets you the single most overpowered piece of cyberware in the game, while siding with Solomon gets you an ok pistol and a mediocre cyberdeck).
As for role playing, this is not a role playing game.
V is a fixed character, you can choose whether they're male or female and you can make some morality choices here and there but generally your decisions don't have a huge amount of impact on the game.
The stock endings are all quite unsatisfying, Phantom Liberty adds some new ones in what seems to be an attempt to address this, but they're not much better.
I'd give it a 6.5/10 in it's current state, which is unlikely to change as CDPR seem to consider the myriad problems the game still has to be resolved now and they've long since moved on to botching their next game. I shan't be trusting CDPR again, the people who were responsible for the quality of their previous titles are either long gone or simple don't care anymore.
Does Cyberpunk 2077 now deliver what was originally promised, all those years ago?
♥♥♥♥ no.

comment:
I've been trying to give this game a fair chance because I'd heard so many good things about it, but honestly, I just don't think it's that good. To me, it feels like one of those massively hyped games that ended up being far more impressive in reputation than in reality.

The story has been surprisingly difficult to follow and stay invested in, while the mechanics often feel clunky and frustrating. Too many times I've had the game do something I never intended, forcing me to reload a save and replay sections just because the controls or interface got in the way. Instead of feeling smooth and intuitive, it often feels like I'm fighting the game itself.

The characters haven't helped much either. Most of the companions and NPCs are forgettable, and I honestly don't understand the popularity of some of the fan favorites. Astarion feels incredibly overrated and irritating, while Lae'zel spends most of her time coming across as obnoxious and unpleasant. I know a lot of people love these characters, but they simply didn't click with me.

As someone who genuinely loves D&D and runs two games a week, I was expecting something that captured the spirit of the tabletop experience. Instead, this often feels like a game wearing a D&D costume rather than actually embodying what makes D&D special. So many mechanics and design choices just feel off, and the overall experience rarely captures that freedom and excitement that make the tabletop game so enjoyable.

Considering the price, I don't think it's worth paying full price for. If you can pick it up during a major sale, then maybe it's worth giving a shot. Otherwise, I personally wouldn't recommend it at its current cost.

Oh how i wish there was a "mid" option, because oh boy as fun as this can be, there are a LOT of problems...

Oh and the game is borderline unplayable in a traditional sense without modding the game... what do i mean by that exactly?

Well the game just blatantly cheats, like... extremely hard... how?

The gunplay; without mods to force the game to stop messing with your aim (especially if you're like me and rather have manual aiming skills over smart weapon aiming for you) makes gunplay borderline impossible at anything further than close range... snipers, rifles, SMGs, shotguns, pistols and melee... only 3 of which are actually viable because the game makes all of your shots, even ones fired while aiming down your sights, have extreme bloom (thank you to the sniper i bought after a quicksave for revealing that actual garbage 'mechanic' to me, and the mod i found shortly after to completely remove it from the game, then proceeded to have my guns actually shooting straight, and proceeded to land a sweet flickshot on an NCPD as they were turning the corner in their car)

Enemies have blatant aimbot, full stop... the only reason i know this is because peeking out of cover, running erratically and dodging seem to do literally nothing against the absurdly-stupid aim these rainbow 6 rejects seem to have... and they can instantly reduce your health from 100% to 0% in a matter of *milliseconds*, getting to the point that 90% of my deaths weren't from my own mistakes, but because i happened to pop out of cover and instantly got sent to the death animation before i could even process who was shooting at me to cause it... of course, there's another mod that reworks this terrible system into something more reasonable... not perfect, but reasonable... indirectly also making the quickhacks that affect enemies in combat actually *DO* something, rather than quickhacks being 90% pointless outside of damaging directly or stealth centered...

Gun customization feels mid at best; seemingly caused by them trying to stop people from just stripping guns of attachments judging from my research, but in reality just causes the system to feel like wasted potential... of course, there's mods to remove this restriction and make phasing out your guns for new ones not feel like a cyberpunk borderlands game with worse systems... notice a running theme yet?

Just because a game can be a narrative experience does not mean the gameplay needs to be so lacking and mid, the gameplay with mods feels much more fun and reasonable, and apparently these problems have existed for actual years and they just haven't bothered to fix them... that's the thing though, the *community* should not be the ones fixing your game, and you shouldn't *require* mods to make a game both actually function somewhat properly, and be enjoyable to play...

I swear, if it wasn't for modders and getting this game on sale, i'd be furious that i bought a game this poorly made, both in stability and in gameplay... just another perfect example of why you never get things full price and why modders need to exist...

comment:
The more I play this game, the more I don't like it. For a game so complete, it's missing so much. 
There's the small things, like the Dash action being the only action you can't cancel, to having no confirmation on whether or not you want to end your turn (I've accidentally hit "end turn" a lot and f-cked myself over).. and nonsensical errors, like being told "you can't fast travel" when you try to long rest while a party member's dead body is out in the open. (Why can't it just say "you can't rest while a party member's body is in the open?")

Then, there's the continuity issues. At the very first settlement in the game, I talk to a friendly tiefling because a rat led me into a storage room. The tiefling is content with my presence, but another one walks by and sentences me to prison for trespassing! 
Another time, I was accused of stealing immediately as I entered the settlement when I did no such thing. I was forced to battle enemies much too strong because of it, and essentially resulted in a forced loss. 

Next, if you don't bring some of the game's offerings of party members with you as soon as possible, you will get trampled with way too many enemies and have no chance. That wouldn't be so bad if the options weren't all so boring! None of them are fun or interesting, and some of them are a chore to have around, like Gale. 

It's also way too easy to agro people! I have to save every 2 minutes because any random conversation will end up triggering a massive battle with 20 people! 

Controls are confusing. If you click on a health potion in your action menu for example, it doesn't give you options for what to do with it. It just drinks it. You have to click 'throw item' first, then select the health potion.. that's backwards. So many times I've wasted health potions, poison, etc. because of this. 

Lastly, the battling itself is just so boring. It goes so slowly! Although it moves faster than real D&D, it just feels so flat and uneventful. And get ready for enemies to have 1HP left and every PC you have to miss miss miss miss miss miss. On enemies at the start of the game.

If you're looking for a D&D-like experience, this isn't it. This is so boring compared to D&D. It fundamentally isn't fun.

comment:
Played both Divinity games so have experience with these type of Larian games. Those games were complex, but BG3 dials it up with an absurd amount of RNG. I'm no stranger to turn-based rpgs, but not super familiar with the DnD rule set. So I guess it appeals to the randomness of the tabletop. But from an actual RPG gameplay experience, I find all the extra RNG extremely tedious. So much so that the game, unfortunately, feels like a crawl to play. Setting/story draws you in well, but this game will trigger anyone with analysis paralysis. That's why this ~20 hr review is what it is. Initial impressions of the game are not great and the game doesn't seem warranted of it's crazy run time so far. However, I am willing to go back here and there and see if my experience improves. If things click better, perhaps i'll update my review. Clearly this game has an audience, just maybe not for me.

FINAL THOUGHTS: put in another 10+ hours, think i'm spent. The game is beautifully put together, it's just a shame that the actual gameplay/mechanics are so subpar. Even down right bad in areas. Maybe it's because I've played my fair share of other RPG/CRPGs, maybe it's just that I don't gel with the DnD ruleset present, but there isn't really anything that revolutionary here that hasn't been done in other games. Overall wanted more RPG, less RNG.

If you're looking for a bit of shallow fun, go for it. It's essentially a hybrid of Farcry games and a GTA style open world with a sci-fi noir theme. Something about the story/writing is a bit too edgy for me so that hasn't drawn me in. The graphics are nice but Night City is 99% set dressing with a bunch of meaninless filler slaped around. On normal dificulty,  you're essentially a god from the get-go and can run and gun your way out of most situations. The RPG mechanics are pretty surface level too. Don't expect a well crafted progressoin curve. Most perks and chrome are just a few percentage points, though you can unlock things like double jump etc. though it still feels a bit empty to me. 

The gameplay loops is going from mission to mission. Don't expect an intriocate world like Skyrim. While there are a few forks in the quests, it's nothing like what you might find in Obsidian titles. Most of the decisions you make are pretty unimportant.

comment:
Okay so I'm rewriting this review after having played several more hours, and beaten the first 3 main boss fights. Of course, all opinions are my own, and it's very subjective as to what a "good" playstyle is. 

     My biggest problem with the game is the combat, which obviously significantly hinders my experience with such a combat-focused game/genre. It feels generally "clunky" to me, not smooth and intuitive. Not to say that the motions aren't smooth, they are, it's more so that you can't adapt as frequently as I think you should be able to during a battle. 

     So for example, in the first main boss battle with a guy named Margit, I would like to run in when there's an opening, get a few strikes in, and then dodge out of the way when he's about to strike. However, one thing that this game doesn't do that I think it really should is give command priority. So I might strike 3 times, but right after I try to strike for the 3rd time, I realize Margit is about to strike and my hit won't land, so I need to doge early and cancel my strike. But because you already pressed the attack button, you can't doge until the game finishes that strike. So what happened is I ended up playing very conservatively, only risking a maximum of two hits before running away. Having to play that reserved makes the fight drag on and isn't necessarily overly difficult, it just feels boring to me. 

     Another thing I found very infuriating, especially with Margit, is the insane amount of variability in the time between the start and execution of an attack. Sometimes Margit raises his weapon and strikes immediately, the next try he raises it and strikes 3 seconds after holding in the air doing nothing, the next attempt he does it for 5 seconds. Again this contributes to only getting one or two hits in when sometimes you could get 5 or 6 in, but because you don't know, you have to play conservatively instead. 

     Now the second boss's attack pattern was actually much more intuitive for me. He had the right amount of variability. Not the exact same script, which would be too easy, but not the insane range of variance that Margit had. Sadly, the third boss, felt exactly like Margit all over again. Just a frick ton of attacks, then a short window to get a few hits in, then back to dodge city. 

     Which leads me to my next point: repetitiveness. See, all three of these bosses have felt extremely similar, just each one having subsequently faster attacks. Godrick's (the second boss) pattern differed, for the better, but it still followed the same principal of needed to overuse dodge's a bunch, be very conservative, and keep doing the same thing for 5 minutes. I found it boring. Essentially, up to the third boss anyways, the game's battles felt very "same-y". 

     Now, the last big thing I'll point out is the game's exploration. It doesn't make me want to go explore the world at all, and when I have gone exploring, the world feels very "empty" to me, to say the least. Most of the people you encounter are either enemies (which are trivially easy and repetitive), and the NPCs you encounter, at least by 10 hours into the game still, are few and far between. Plus they're just not very interesting. 

     I also think the entire UI, specifically the Inventory and Equipment menus etc., are overly complicated but that's a nitpick, once you get used to them they aren't that bad. 

     Overall, I just think the game's combat is too repetitive, clunky, and the exploration is very lackluster. Even if the game gets a lot more interesting as it progresses, I still feel confident leaving this review now, as a game shouldn't need more than 10 hours to hook you. Steam's refund policy even suggests that Valve believes hours should be plenty of time to understand if a game is good or not, but at the same time, I do understand the appeal, after all I've played for 10 hours now.

comment: I am a big fan of RPGs; basically every single one of my favorite games is an RPG. So when I heard about a new critically acclaimed RPG that was released, I immediately bought it. In retrospect, that was obviously a bad decision. I am someone who cares first and foremost about gameplay and consistently doesn’t like games whose main selling point is their story. I don’t like the D&D system; I love roleplaying, but the mechanics D&D uses to simulate roleplay and combat make it actively less fun than just roleplaying with no rules at all. If I thought about it for even a moment, I would have realized this wasn’t going to be a game for me. But I didn’t. I had two playthroughs, the first I quit after completing Act 1, and the second I managed to finish the game  On the surface this game has all the things you’d want from an RPG, exploring areas, filling out your map, beating enemies, collecting items, completing quests; lots of little hits of dopamine that make it easy to keep going. But when I really think of the quality of each of these aspects, they aren’t very good. First, and the only one I don’t mind, exploring the world is enjoyable. There are lots of hidden items to find and areas to explore. My only complaint would be that it got a bit overwhelming at times with how much exploring and options I was given. Next, beating enemies, my second least favorite part of the game. As stated, I don’t like the D&D’s combat system. I feel it does a bad job of simulating real time combat and the combat isn’t very fun. BG3 is a video game though, so turn-based combat is normal. However, I personally don’t like the initiative order system; initiative is easily the biggest determiner of how well you’ll do in a fight, so it’s annoying that something that important is random. There’s a reason why most RPGs either have you and the enemy alternating attacks, or have everyone’s attacks refresh on timers, it makes the combat much more strategy based, which is what you want for turn based combat. In general though, BG3’s combat is way too random, with how likely you are to hit and how much damage you do. You could replay the same fight with the same strategy over and over again and get vastly different results. Yes, you do want some randomness in a combat system so that it isn’t a solved game, but BG3 has just way too much randomness for my liking. In general, enemies don’t really have weaknesses or special attacks; most combats feel very similar to each other, boiling every fight down to just draining the collective HP pool, and once you figure out the best ways to do that, you’ve basically trivialized the whole combat system. I have more gripes with the combat system, but I don’t want this review to run too long, just know it is easily the worst RPG combat system I’ve experienced and is not fun. As for my least favorite part about the game, it’s collecting items, which might just be a thing only I care about. Typically, RPGs do one of two things. Either they have a bunch of basic loot scattered about, or have lots of unique loot across the map with in-game ways of helping you find it, both are completely valid ways of doing loot. BG3 on the other hand had a crap ton of unique loot all over the place with no built-in way of helping you find it. I am a loot goblin, and I enjoy picking up everything, but there is no good way of tracking loot you’ve gotten and finding loot that you’ve missed. You either have to heavily explore every area when you enter it or use a guide, otherwise you will miss a lot of stuff and have no way of knowing what you missed. For example, I was doing a thrower build for Karlach, and there was a weapon that I wanted to get. I ended up having to reload a save because the guy who sells that weapon leaves if Shadowheart is your party, which she was. Like, I didn’t even know that guy was a vendor. It’s way too easy to miss loot in this game. Also, I hate how so much of the best loot are from shopkeepers; I want to find the really cool loot, I don’t want to just buy it off some guy. BG3 is clearly made for people to only find some of the loot, which sucks for people who enjoy collecting loot like me. I mean, so many games feature collectathons for a reason. Anywho, BG3’s lack of care for loot goblins like me made exploring feel like a real chore. And finally there are the quests, which I personally wasn’t a big fan of, but I can see why people are. I was never able to get invested in the world, and while I enjoyed the characters well enough, the slight joy I got from these characters was vastly offset by how little I enjoyed the gameplay. Whenever I dislike the gameplay in a game, it makes it hard for me to care about the game’s other aspects, and BG3 is no exception. Although, I do have a couple of actual complaints about the quests. First is that in Act 1 nothing you did really progressed the story at all, heck you can just walk up to the mountains and pretty much skip the whole thing, it made the first few dozens hours of the game feel like it had little momentum. Second is that Act 3 has way too many quests, like I only got through half of Baldur’s Gate and I already have like 20 side quests, some of which would require me to go into the second half of the city and pick up even more side quests, I just got way too overwhelmed. I feel like they could’ve paced the quests better so that you’re finishing some as you get new ones. Overall, I don’t have much to say about the quests, I’ve experienced far better and far worse. And finally, in terms of the story, which everyone seems to adore, I don’t really see what’s so great about it. It’s overall a pretty simple story, with you just travelling from place to place, helping random people, killing bad guys, until you eventually get to the ending. It was a pretty standard RPG story. And in terms of choices you can make, there almost always two options, one good one and one evil one. Sometimes the choices you are given are more morally ambiguous, but for the most part if you are doing a good or evil playthrough, you only really have one choice. And of course, the majority of the game is exploring, fighting, side quests, etc. So even if you did a second playthrough of the game, the vast majority of the game would be identical, with only minor things changing. Of course, this isn’t a problem, most RPGs don’t have branching stories, but with how much emphasis this game puts on roleplaying, I expected a bit more options to make the character feel like my own. So overall, the exploration was enjoyable, but collecting loot wasn’t fun, the combat is boring and has way too much randomness, the quests and characters are alright but nothing to right home about, and the story is pretty standard. As always with games critically acclaimed for their story, I fail to see the hype. 6.5/10
