comment:
Well, I played it all the way through based on the overwhelming praise, it certainly had its moments, but the bad outweighs the good for me.

The good:
The characters are excellent.
Leveling is a significant event, like it should be in a D&D game.
Good boss fights.

The bad:
Fiddly goofy game engine STILL riddled with bugs.
The game can't even tell you if you will be able to hit a character after moving, it just lies.
Goofy animations in cutscenes and awkward character movement spoils many of the moments.
Had to install a mod to double walking speed to make the pace of the game tolerable. I think without it I would have stopped playing after 6 hours.
Combat is extremely and unnecessarily slow.
Just an absolute metric ton of JUNK items to sort through, and poor inventory management options.
The camera is absolutely awful, especially when dealing with multiple levels of elevation.
The game is like half focused around jumping puzzles and ordering your party around is like herding cats.

comment:
I genuinely tried to like Baldur’s Gate 3. I loved the first two games, and after hearing so much praise for this one, I gave it 27 hours across two separate playthroughs. Unfortunately, I think I am finished with it.

The presentation is excellent. The graphics, music and voice acting are all top quality. Almost everything surrounding the actual experience of playing the game, however, feels unnecessarily awkward.

The user interface is horrendous. I repeatedly clicked on companions or other characters while simply trying to move around, triggering conversations and interactions I never intended to start. The inventory system is cluttered and tedious, and even basic actions, such as entering stealth and positioning a character for a backstab, feel more cumbersome than they should.

Exploration is equally frustrating. Holding the Alt key only reveals interactable objects within a very limited radius, making it easy to overlook important items or routes. On my first playthrough, I reached the Underdark but eventually gave up because I could not work out how to progress through it.

I was not expecting the game to hold my hand, but Baldur’s Gate 3 often seems designed around the assumption that players have endless time to consult online guides, tutorials and walkthroughs. A game should provide enough information for players to understand its systems and make meaningful progress without repeatedly leaving it to search the internet.

The balancing also feels badly uneven. I frequently found my party completely outmatched, and combat rarely felt satisfying enough to justify the preparation, inventory management and repeated reloading surrounding it. Rather than tactical and rewarding, it often felt crude, slow and lacklustre.

There is clearly an impressive amount of work in Baldur’s Gate 3, and I understand why many people love it. For me, though, the beautiful presentation cannot compensate for an interface that constantly fights the player, frustrating navigation and progression that too often feels dependent on outside resources.

Perhaps I am simply no longer the target audience for games like this. Baldur’s Gate 3 was my final attempt to become invested in a widely acclaimed modern PC game, but instead of feeling entertained, I mostly felt exhausted.

comment:
TL;DR: I am pretty bad at the game but that's not the reason I dislike it.

Now that I finally got to really playing through Elden Ring, I must sadly say that my initial opinion did not change. I know it is a hot take and contrary to the overall opinion, but this has to be the worst FromSoft game I've played (granted I've never played Bloodborne or any of the Armored Core games so those are out of the count). For me, soulslikes are closer to dungeon crawlers than the anime boss rush that they've become. That's why I think that even though Dark Souls 3 is my favorite overall, none of the games have come close to the feeling of DS1.

While the base combat still feels good and far more fluent than any Dark Souls has ever done, the issue is that they've gone head first into the idea that you wait for a combo, then hit once or twice, rinse and repeat. To me, that has become a tedious way to fight, considering how well games like Monster Hunter have perfected the idea that you can take control of the fight and play more aggressive. Yeah, I know that you can do that in most soulslikes too but the difference is that even when I've learned a boss so well that I know almost all the spots, it never feels like I am in control. The only FromSoft game that made me feel like that is Sekiro. The reason this wasn't an issue in DS1 for example is because bosses actually died after a reasonable amount of hits.

And that's the key point, these games focus too much on bosses and with Elden Ring, the idea of visual clutter to make things look cool instead of engaging to fight has been overutilized. There is so many flashy moves that are 100% dodged only with iframes, which to me signals incredibly lazy boss design. When I practically have to analyze the moves like I go through some SDVX charts, I just feel like rather focusing on a game where studying things on paper is actually fun. In my entire playthrough, the only boss I actually felt was fun and I'd like to go through again was Placidusax. Maybe Maliketh too, if we exclude the first phase. Not a huge fan of it but that's mostly just because I suck at it. Radahn was nice as a concept with all the summons and it being a sort of a brawl but the fight itself was pretty meh. Other than that, the bosses were pretty lame.

As for story, I can't help but feel like they just took the original story of Dark Souls, gave it to Martin and told him to just reimagine it with them and then they called it a day. This is almost a carbon-copy clone. And with most NPC's dying and that being a trend of FromSoft's games, I feel far more surprised when someone lives but I find it hard to care for the questlines when they're just "go talk to someone, quit to menu or sit at site of grace, go talk to them again + maybe a summon/invade at the end." It just feels lazy that this formula is still repeated for almost every quest, even after all these years. FromSoft should really come up with something new.

The world design was great though. Places like Stormveil and Leyndell felt really fun to explore. But the open areas and the open world was bad. For me it just doesn't work in a soulslike setting. It is too open and when everything respawns, there's no permanent impact on your actions, which to me is a key point of open world games. Plus when the entire world is practically dead and almost everyone is hostile, I feel like the sense of exploration is pretty watered down.

It just doesn't feel like there's really a need for the open world setup, especially when you realize how linear the game actually is. It's not like you can approach Leyndell from several areas, since the map is extremely linear and there are places blocking your progress further. It is a good thing in this game but makes the open world feel pointless. I feel like it only exists for the same reason that Monster Hunter Wilds is "open world", which is just to fill a marketing tickbox because open world games are trending. You need to sell the concept of the game being massive, not so much the actual amount of unique content being there, so what's an easier way to do that than making your game open world.

All that being said, it is not necessarily a bad game. I just think that it is mediocre when compared to FromSoft's previous products. I started with DS2 then DS3 > DS1 > Sekiro > Nightreign > Elden Ring and before playing Elden Ring, I considered DS2 the worst FromSoft game, which is why I find it hard to believe it would be just nostalgia talking.

comment:
This game is overrated, overhyped, boring slop. 

Open world sucks. Nothing to do or much to really interact with. Since the devs spent so long just making environment decorations to make this world feel ""alive"", there's almost nothing to do in terms of gameplay. This also affects the structure of the world, level design, and general combat. This game is full of details that are so unnecessary and lead to alot of extra development overtime and it adds nothing to the gameplay. Which is pretty bog-standard. 

People praise this game's "build variety" and think being able to triple jump, dash, or home in on people with swords for arms is somehow enough to justify how stiff the general combat feels in this game. Which you won't even get to that point where you get to play around with fun stuff until the end-game anyways. Guns have no impact, have weird diagonal recoil patterns that are difficult to control, and the base gunplay feels rigid, stiff, and lacks any satisfying weapon animations. The weapons themselves are so impractically designed and cartoonish, not to mention being bulky, ugly, and unwieldy. This even transfers over to gameplay where it feels like you're carrying weapons that weight like 50 plus pounds. 

The story is also so boring. Games like this are praised unanimously but most scenes are just characters sitting around talking, and of course you never get to see your character so it makes me wonder why there is even a character creator to begin with when there's like one cutscene you see them in and mirrored surfaces. Action sequences are heavily scripted, railroaded, and downright awful to play because of the stiff gunplay. 

This game has great visuals, but the graphics being so impressive comes at a cost of the game itself being weak. I'm sick of people praising this game, jerking it off, and calling it a masterpiece. I played it on PS5 ages ago, and got it again on PC after I sold the PS5, and the game was just as boring as I remembered. If you people like this game, you're subhuman and deserve all the remake slop we've been getting because your standards for video games are so low. I bet you think God of War Ragnarok is a masterpiece too.

0/10 — Completely Unplayable. False Advertising.

I bought this game expecting a masterpiece, and what do I get? An absolute disaster.

I booted it up, spent 30 minutes in the character creator trying to find the sliders to turn my tarnished warrior into a 2D anime waifu. Nothing. Not a single pink hair option that defies the laws of physics. No oversized cat ears. Absolutely zero cell-shaded graphics.

Where are the visual novel segments? Where are the beach DLC outfits? Where is the NSFW content that I specifically browse Steam late at night to find? Instead, all I got was depression, grey rocks, and a giant tree that looks like it hasn't seen a drop of water in a millennia.

I looked everywhere for a swimsuit skin for Malenia, but apparently, the only thing she exposes is my total lack of gaming skill.

Thankfully, Steam support understood my profound grief and approved the refund. I will be taking my $60 back to where it belongs: buying high-quality, 99-cent anime puzzle games that actually respect my cultural needs.

Avoid this garbage unless you actually like "gameplay" and "challenges." Disgusting.

comment:
This review is about the Remastered version.
For me, the original game is one of the best ever made. The writing and script are among the very few in video games that can boast novel quality book perfection. The art and environments are equally impressive. The original had only one major (though forgivable, given the quality of the rest) flaw: the gameplay. It wasn't THAT bad, but it had significant issues.

The Remastered:
Graphics:
It looks like they simply threw in ray/path tracing without any real tweaking or optimization. The result is that the game still looks beautiful, but the lighting behaves very strangely broken at times.

Gameplay:
I watched a long livestream where the developers emphasized that there would be many small changes, which together would ensure a better gameplay experience. That turned out to be completely untrue; unless it's a bug issue, I think they actually made the gameplay worse.
I had to disable the new dynamic camera; it gives me a headache.
Enemy behavior is atrocious. I can't tell if it's just buggy, but if it's intentional, it's unforgivable. I tend to think it's just buggy, given how poorly they behave.
It seems like the distance calculations are completely broken.

Geralt's movement is terrible and feels stiff/locked-in. It’s just like the original, back in 2015, the developers justified it by calling it "realistic," but in reality, a fat a** like me can turn, move, and sprint with far more grace, speed, and precision than Geralt.
In the remaster, it actually seems even worse somehow.
Perhaps this is linked to the fact that everything is buggy,I hope so, at least could be fixed. 
Combatting enemies has become far more frustrating than in the original.
As previously mentioned, the spacing "feels" broken, as do the hitboxes. Enemies move and behave as if they never know what to do, and not in a "tactically unpredictable" way; they just seem genuinely buggy and broken.

Audio.
The audio was generally excellent in the original, save for two issues that haven't been addressed at all here.
1. The music is wonderful overall, but after dozens of hours, it becomes truly repetitive and annoying during exploration because it is essentially a single track on an endless loop. It would have been so easy to include an option to pause the continuous music; instead, I’m forced to mute it entirely.

2. When the Witcher uses his swords, the impact sound is the same regardless of what you hit, armor, wood, or flesh. Instead of sounding like a sword strike, it sounds like a pinprick in every instance. You can't feel the impact, which significantly detracts from the gameplay experience.

Honestly, even though it’s free, I expected more care, love and polish from CDPR. I am very disappointed and hope they fix it.

comment:
So this is it. The Holy Grail of gaming. The Second Coming of RPGs.

Let me tell you about my combat experience. I see an enemy. I have a bow. He’s on a roof. Simple, right? WRONG. The camera said “absolutely not” and locked itself into a position that let me admire some really nice brick textures instead. I died staring at architecture. Immersive.

The turn-based combat is an incredible innovation for people who think chess is too fast-paced. There’s a goblin three inches from my face. I have a sword. I have murder in my heart. But I have zero action points because I had the AUDACITY to walk here. So I just… stand there. Menacingly. The goblin and I share an awkward moment. He’s probably thinking about his family. I’m thinking about uninstalling.

And god forbid you don’t have a PhD in D&D mechanics. Every ability has a description longer than my apartment lease. “Roll a d20, add your modifier, subtract your will to live, consult the moon phase chart…” I just want to hit things. Why is there homework?

Yes, you can do “anything.” You can talk to animals. Betray everyone. Push people into chasms. Very impressive. But between those five minutes of chaos, there are seven hours of moving at the speed of bureaucracy.

This game is overhyped. I genuinely refuse to believe this gameplay resonates with so many people. We’re living in a simulation and this is a glitch in the Matrix.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

comment:
Stay on the path...  I was looking for an enjoyable romp through an open D&D world.  This was not it.  This game is a slog on rails along paths with only scripted encounters.

Let's start with the main reason I can't  recommend this game.  It is a game on rails.  There are no random encounters, no open world, just paths.  Lots and lots of paths that make getting around harder than it should be.  It is incredibly boring.  If you traveled a path once there is nothing new, no enemies, no random events, just a slog to and from your destination.  Want to train up your part early by grinding some levels?  Too bad.  Want to challenge yourself in an area with tougher creatures?  Nope.  Follow the path loser.  How is it that the old 16 bit D&D games got this right, but this game fails miserably.
Then there are the choices that impact your party relationships.  You have 2 options, have sex with everyone or treat them like they are cancer.  It is incredibly shallow and kinda feels gross at times.
My favorite quirk of all is when I was walking through a settlement and accidently clicked a mushroom instead of an empty space only to turn the entire settlement aggressive.  That's fun...
I wanted to love this game, but it is just not fun.

comment:
This game is like a company directed a team of skilled artists to make a giant mural of a piece of doggie doo-doo on a lawn. All that modeling and animation and voice acting, and the result is a game world that's unpleasant to be in and poorly-written.

You also can't say it's a satire or warning, because:
1) it was fundamentally made to be a $70 power fantasy
2) which means the player character always wins and rises to the top of the garbage pile
3) it doesn't have the insights to be a satire or prediction

Also, the writing is just incoherent. For example:
The memory level with Silverhand nuking a tower and then surviving being on it (?) was so illogical that I looked up fan theories, and apparently the consensus is "well if you read the books and the tabletop RPG stuff, actually the nuke was carried by a different guy, it was a Militech funded operation, the memory that you SAW IN FULL DETAIL and PLAYED THROUGH was just Silverhand's delusion".
And then there are just vague hints about that in the game but no real clarification.
The vast majority of players won't get that. It's not sophisticated storytelling, it's just bad communication. Basically the "haha joke's on you I was only pretending to be retarded" meme.

Good storytelling would do things like:
- introduce Silverhand before he gets in the player's head
- have gameplay interactions from the player's situation
- explain why Silverhand hated Arasaka so much and why he had a nuke
- give some justification for people following Silverhand when all he does is make bad assumptions and insult people

The game could've had a cool character instead of Silverhand that made people feel conflicted about "killing" them, but no, as your forced companion, you get a stupid ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who spends his time being annoying in pointless ways.

Maybe save some time and just watch the anime instead.

comment:
Game looks stunning, music is obviously awesome and well, everything is fun. Until you spend a few hours playing the game, and start encountering the same bosses over, and over, and over again. Sometimes two of them, sometimes four, sometimes six, sometimes eight. Yep. Bosses that were initially only meant to be encountered once and individually, you will face in ridiculous numbers over and over again because this game's release was rushed. Also I despise how unfair the difficulty spikes are. "It's a souls game" shut the ♥♥♥♥ up. One moment I find a very easy to kill mob, two steps later I feel like I'm in a bossfight, and I have to kill the bloody bastard because otherwise I won't be able to progress past him. I also hate the RPG elements of this game, because you need to farm enemies to even stand a chance in many areas. So kill a few weak enemies, get to a site of lost grace, get back up, restart. Very fun, in a game about explorating incredibly cool looking environments. Staying in a box and mindlessly killing the same enemies over and over again. Oh and, I almost forgot the absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ enemy attacks and hitboxes. Sometimes you get killed through walls, or through other enemies. Which is not supposed to happen, in case you didn't know. And sometimes you blatantly dodge an attack, it lands past you, but somehow it still deals you 999 damage. So truly, if you want to play this game, install mods to make it more fun. Unfortunately that means you'll have to play offline so you won't get the cool teammates and messages nor the invasions, but otherwise it's basically just not fun.

Almost forgot to mention that you lose all of your runes, the game's money that you use to purchase anything and level up, everytime you die. So good luck leveling up and finally being able to progress through the game. Again, that can be fixed with a mod. This game does not have native mod support so you'll have to look it up, it's not that difficult. Anyway, probably buy it expecting heavy frustration and at a high discount. It's truly unmatched in the artistic aspects, but that's it. Most overhyped game of 2022 by FAR.


Edit : the game is an open world yet expects you to go to certain locations in a certain order, every enemy is balanced that way. So if you have the misfortune of going somewhere because "yeah that looks cool" and the devs labeled it as "late game" (though you won't ever figure out on your own) well you're screwed. Instead, you're meant to go to area x, then y, then z, then so on. Like a linear game. Though it's OPEN WORLD. There is nothing open about the way this game's progression system. So somehow figure out where the ♥♥♥♥ you need to go, look it up, still don't understand, try again, and again, and of course again. Not having fun ? Skill issue.

It should also be noted that to progress through the game you need to find some random ass item in the middle of nowhere, then somehow guess that you're supposed to emote with that item in your inventory and equipped to your left hand and do a backflip in front of a hidden bookshelf. I am exaggerating, but trust me, barely. This happens way too often. The game calls those "puzzles", they're more like time-wasting sadistic chores.

Also I have to talk about how this game's community just doesn't take criticism at all, you criticize their holy game and you're a dumbass, a noob, someone whose opinion doesn't matter. Every player's opinion matters.

NOW, onto the good stuff, as I've said :
1 : very cool looking environments
2 : game runs at 60 fps at all times for me (but can never go beyond)
3 : combat, when it works, is very fun
4 : summoning other players and writing messages to other people in real time is incredible
5 : no text or voice chat for once, only emotes and premade messages, which heavily limits toxicity (at least in game lmao)
6 : the soundtrack
7 : the replayability, you just love to come back to finally beat the ♥♥♥♥ out of everything with overpowered gear (though that'll take you 3 billions years, probably)

comment:
I've played only a little over 8 hours by the point I began writing this review. Here are my thoughts:

Pros:
This game looks amazing, it has a great voice acting, sfx and music. Character customization is unbelievably vast and really thought through. The setting is interesting, some of the mechanics I've come across so far are also good (like different origin stories for your character, etc.). There seems to be a lot of things you can do, but I can't really judge that, since I've only played it a little and couldn't properly explore the entire game. Story overall also looks promising, although I can't really judge that either with 8 hours of gameplay.

Cons:
Now to the cons, which for me are currently overweighting the cons. The game feels clunky. The driving is awful, it is probably the worst driving I've seen so far, feeling even worse than FC3, which already was a pain in the ass for me. The gunplay is massively underwhelming in my opinion. Like how the hell am I dumping 3 shotgun mags into someone's head and they are still alive? Enemies are extreme bullet sponges and that just ruins the experience for me. Also, the guns feel really unresponsive and the melee is just sliding around the room, slashing at people without much depth. The dialogues are really long and "draggy". The quests so far have not really felt rewarding and were rather boring. Some of the mechanics, like braindancing, were just straight up immersion-breaking for me. It took so long to finish the first braindance quest that I straight up don't want to ever experience it again. It was an interesting idea, I don't deny that, but overall it just feels dull. 

With that being said, I currently can't recommend the game. I wish I could give it a neutral score, especially since I can see the good things it has to offer. I really wanted to give it a shot and like the game, but I currently don't have enough time on my hands to force myself into playing a game that doesn't really entertain me, hoping it gets better soon. It is my personal preference though and I can deffinitely see why some people love this game so much. For me, it just didn't feel worth to continue.

I am a huge CDPR fan, especially because of The Witcher games, in which I've invested hunderds of hours across different platforms, but these games just felt rewarding, the story was gripping, the setting was even better (for me personally) and I didn't mind spending so much time on it. With Cyberpunk2077 I can't really say the same. Chances are that I will eventually change my review later, if I ever get to a point of giving it another shot, in the future, but currently I will just leave it be.

comment:
[b]Summary[/b]
[hr][/hr] 
I've had people recommend this game to me for years; now that I've played it I'm just utterly confused as to how anyone can find fun in this title.  It runs like it has congestive heart failure even if you have the hardware, and the gameplay is so hands-off you may as well just watch the anime.


[b]Performance[/b]
[hr][/hr] 
Short version, it's terribly optimized and getting consistent performance (60+fps) is impossible.  I've spent 4 hours in the actual game, the rest of my 'play time' has been benchmarking performance and trying to fine tune the controls so they aren't fighting me.  I just cannot find a way to stop the game from randomly cratering into the 20fps range.  The assumption at this point is that I'm on an i7700k (above mininum, below recommended) and that's the bottleneck.  The GPU is a 3070 (above recommended) and there's 32gb of RAM.  Even without any ray/path tracing enabled the game will never stay above 60fps for more than a few seconds.  With DLSS enabled there is brutal artifacting and ghosting, whether in the benchmark or the game proper, so that's not an option.  Basically, the system requirements mean nothing.

The game can go higher than 60fps, but it will regularly tank into the 20s regardless of settings without warning.  I set everything in the options to either off or low - even the level of detail and crowd density - at 1080p and it will still randomly tank into the 20s.  It'll hang in the 20-30s for a couple seconds, spend another 5-10s in the 40s, before 'stabilizing' between 50-60fps.  After a few minutes it will randomly hang again and struggle to recover.

The benchmark says I'm not dropping below 60fps at minimum everything settings, but the actual game experience is very different.  I get the same benchmark result at 720p with medium texture resolution as I do 1440p with high texture resolution (my 4K display maxes out at 60hz and i have the game capped at 65fps).  This is the biggest indicator of a CPU limitation.  Unfortunately, there are no settings for this outside of 'Level of Detail' and 'Crowd Density'.  In other words, I either live with it or move onto something else in my backlog.  Pretty easy choice.


[b]Controls[/b]
[hr][/hr] 
This was actually the most disappointing part of the entire experience.  Even if this game could get to a minimum 60fps I have my doubts about it would ever feel good to navigate.  The movement and controls are somewhere between non-functional at worst and feeling like you're under water at best.  

Walking is slow, running is slow, carrying a body gives you plenty of time to consider how you could be better spending your time.  Dashing by default is an absolute mess, and driving by default is worse than that.  In fact, driving is so bad there's an auto-drive option.  Also, it's pretty much the first thing you do after character creation.  When you're at 60fps the game feels decent, but it's usually bouncing between 50 and 60 or tanking entirely.  That variability isn't helping the controls, but even when the game is hitting that 60fps they still don't feel great by any means..


[b]Gameplay[/b]
[hr][/hr] 
The play experience is more akin to a visual novel than an FPS.  I know it's supposed to have RPG elements but I was really unprepared for how little game there is to play.  You mostly listen to other people talk, which can't be skipped and more frustratingly is broken up where characters will expect you to say something.  Sometimes you don't have to, other times they'll pester you until you respond (quips such as 'are you listening?' and the like).  You can't even walk down the street without hearing some random NPC polluting your ears with useless drek.  It all becomes noise very fast.

When you do get to do something other than respond to dialogue, it feels like executing a checklist.  Remember how people hated always having to go into detective mode in Arkham Asylum?  Here it's called scan mode and it's equally annoying.  Want to open a door?  You'll probably have to scan it and do something else first.  It's easier to steal a car - which hilariously also involves opening a door - but doing that would involve driving.  It rarely feels like you can just do something, there always seems to be a process attached to it.

The combat is fine, which is as much a criticism as much as it is a compliment.  You have guns and can shoot stuff.  The game really expects you to employ a variety of stealth and hacking techniques to overcome a lot of the challenges.  Once again, that's a process and it is rarely as simple or quick as violence.  This is probably why the combat feels so tepid.

A feature that's oddly missing is a custom radio channel.  You need a mod to have a custom radio channel, which is a feature indie companies with a fraction of the budget have integrated without issue.  I guess they really want to make sure all the money spent on copyrighted music was worth it (music is subjective, but I feel they wasted their money).

My big critique - outside of some more options to ease the strain on the CPU - is the field of view slider maxing out at 100.  This is unacceptable and makes the game feel claustrophobic regardless of where you set it.  


[b]The Good:[/b]
[hr][/hr] 
The game does have its positive elements; they simply don't matter when the overall experience is so poor.  The graphics are nice, even at low details, and I particularly really like all of the neon colours.  The character models are nice (especially with the graphics kicked up to high), and the voice work is quite well done for them.  I wish more games had an options menu as extensive as this, it's generally quite comprehensive.  At this point I don't think any amount of tweaking will ever make this game feel good to play, but I really do appreciate the vast options.  


[b]Conclusion:[/b]
[hr][/hr] 
Ultimately then, I guess there are two things that this game accomplished.  The first is that I spent enough time trying to get stable performance and proper controls that I'm no longer eligible for a refund - something I wasn't even thinking about initially as I was expecting to enjoy this title.  

The second accomplishment is that freeing up 70gb of hard drive space means I can install some games that aren't fighting me every step of the way to do the most basic of things.  They might even be fun.

comment:
The Witcher 3 is one of my all-time favourite games, but I'll leave this negative review for now, even if that sounds like a wild reaction to a free update.
Unfortunately the remaster is in such a messed-up state, that I can't really recommend playing it until they (hopefully) fix it up. 
I like the visual update itself, but there's no world where it should run like that. 
Trying to get this thing into a stable state for 4k, without sacrificing nearly every setting in sight, is basically impossible on a 5080. I get 60-80 FPS with Balanced DLSS and 2x Frame Gen. This frame rate fluctuates so hard and comes with so much random input delay, it basically makes the game unplayable. Or at least VERY hard to stomach.
As if that wasn't enough, the game completely starts choking to near-death at random times. Often after exiting some kind of menu, but sometimes at random, sometimes mid-combat etc. When that happens, the GPU gets stuck at 100% utilization while the game drops to 20 FPS. Presumably some kind of Frame-Gen choke, but who knows. This sometimes gets fixed by switching resolution back and forth. Otherwise it's a restart. Get unlucky and the game chokes again after 15 minutes.
Turning off DLSS isn't even a viable option anymore apparently, since the game just sacrifices half its pixels or something. I honestly have no idea what's going on there.
Other than that I've had audio issues where characters were suddenly at what feels like 20% volume. Happened right before the long post-White Orchard cutscene sequence too. 
Had NPCs glitch in and out of existence, enemies freeze in place after being hit by finishers, and many many similar glitches that aren't a big deal alone, but really stand out when you're already annoyed at the bad performance.
Being unable to get an uninterrupted hour of gameplay without running into major bugs and having to restart is simply not very fun or immersive. It wasn't actually quite as bad when I started the game, maybe because of the smaller tutorial area, but it's a fact that it no longer runs well, even if I go back to that area.

In theory I'm very happy that CDPR decided to give this game another makeover. In practice this is NOT it and I hope they properly fix it up soon-ish. Especially considering that they want us to buy and play the upcoming DLC.

comment:
[h1]GTA ONLINE: THE KORTZ CENTER HEIST[/h1]

[hr][/hr]

I've seen some sorry-ass sights in my time, y'all. I've seen a rattlesnake eat its own tail out of spite. I've seen a man try to saddle a bull after a fifth of whiskey. I've sat through games so broke and so dumb they oughta be tried for horse thievin'. But nothin' — and I mean [b]nothin'[/b] — prepared this old cowboy's boots for what Rockstar just drug in off the highway and called an update.

Welcome to GTA Online, a game that went from "Cowboys from Hell" to just plain [b]hell[/b] in one ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ day. The culprit's got a name, and it's [b]The Kortz Center Heist[/b].

I'll admit it — I was fixin' to be excited. I saddled up, tuned my guitar down to drop-C, and waited on this update like it was the second coming of Dimebag. What I got instead was a bull that bucked me straight into a cactus patch and then took a piss on me for good measure.

[h2]The Bugs[/h2]
Lord almighty, the bugs. Stacked on bugs, stacked on more bugs, like a pileup on I-35 in a Texas ice storm. I couldn't list 'em all if you gave me till Judgment Day. And the heist itself? It wants your whole damn ranch just to walk through the front door — a mountain of cash, hours of your life you ain't never gettin' back, and a mansion you'll only own if you've grinded so hard you've worn the treads clean off your boots.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]The Nerf Massacre[/h2]
But that ain't even the real crime here, partner. The real crime — the one that oughta get Rockstar run outta town on a rail — is the [u]total, wall-to-wall nerfin' of every other heist in the game[/u].

[b]Casino Heist?[/b] Nerfed.
[b]The Doomsday Heist?[/b] Nerfed.
[b]Dr. Dre's Contract?[/b] [u]NERFED.[/u]
[b]Vincent?[/b] [u]NERFED.[/u]
[b]KnoWay?[/b] [u]NERFED, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥![/u]

Nerfed across the board, for no reason 'cept "'cause we felt like it." That's the whole explanation you get. That's Southern hospitality Rockstar-style — smile at ya while they empty your wallet.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Cayo Perico Got Gutted[/h2]
And they saved the worst for my favorite, [b]Cayo Perico[/b]. These sumbitches took a hacksaw to it till the most common loot in the whole operation — the Sinsimito Tequila, bottom-shelf swill if there ever was one — drops [b]80%[/b] of the time and sells for a measly [b]300 GRAND[/b]. Three hundred thousand dollars, y'all. I remember — hell, my buddies remember — when that same bottle of rotgut fetched a cool [b]million[/b] minimum. Now it's worth about as much as a busted spur. Where in the hell is this game headed?

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Rockstar Don't Give a Damn[/h2]
And naturally, Rockstar don't care. Support's deader than a Texas jackrabbit on a summer highway. Feedback goes into a canyon and never echoes back. We've been hollerin' for years for fair prices and gear that actually matters — a proper police uniform, full duty belt, rank insignia and all — and what do we get instead? Another overpriced, nobody-asked-for-it vehicle priced like it's made of solid silver, over and over, same song different verse.

They ain't lowerin' prices. They don't care.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Shark Cards: The Original Sin[/h2]
What they [i]do[/i] care about is the fat stack of cash rollin' in off [b]Shark Cards[/b] — which, somehow, people keep buyin'. And let me tell you somethin': Shark Cards are the original sin of this whole rodeo. See, back in the early days, players figured out the [b]BAWSAQ stock market[/b] and started makin' real money the honest way — smart trades, sharp instincts, no plastic required. Rockstar didn't care for that one bit, on account of it not puttin' a dime in their pocket. So they shut the exchange down and rolled out this two-bit monstrosity instead, priced like they're sellin' you back one of your own kidneys.

[hr][/hr]

I'm done. I ground my boots down to nubs tryin' to earn somethin' that'd make the grind a little easier, and these sons of the highway spit in my face and called it an update.

Much obliged, Rockstar. May you choke on your own greed.

[h1]SCORE: −∞/10[/h1]

Givin' this pile a flat zero would be an act of charity so generous it oughta be tax-deductible.

[b]If you're still playin' this mess — saddle down, quit, and delete it. There ain't no savin' this one, partner.[/b]

comment:
For as much fun as I had with this game, there was a lot to criticise and complain about. When you're fighting enemies and sneaking through enemy forts, this game is really good, like a proper successor to Deus Ex. But most of the game is not doing this, you'll spend much more of your time travelling to these locations and watching a lot of cutscenes (braindances are also supremely boring after the first time).

To rub salt into the wound, the story has an interesting premise and good characters but falls flat due to a lack of story/gameplay integration and the story is really short and really one sided. I get that this is called cyberPUNK, but for a role-playing game, you don't get a lot of choice in how you want to play the role of V in this story. If you don't want to be a punk, sorry, V is going to be one whether you like it or not. The story insists on having everything be a grey moral to the point that it lost all of its meaning, but puts its foot down and insists that choosing to side with a Corpo is a bad thing, despite dedicating one third of the story to a Corpo member trying to win you over (his story missions also had the best setpieces). All of the endings fall flat because of this insistence that no ending can be happy, but especially the Corpo ending since, despite all of the endings/routes following a theme of sacrificing something for your survival, that ending has you sacrifice the MOST things to receive the LEAST rewarding, most downer ending of them all. The double standard would be funny if it weren't sad.

I have also found the game to still be somewhat buggy, one I remember a lot is that if you save the story quests for last and level up on the exploration content, you end up with quests not triggering because the game tries to space them out but doesn't have anything to trigger them with. There is also a bad bug with pop-in, maybe due to low RAM allocation. Vehicles don't load in quickly enough, meaning you can't drive until they do, and several times during races I fell through the ground due to the map not loading in quick enough. On another note, it's also really annoying how you NEED a cyberdeck to do any hacking, whereas the Sandevistan is really fun for stealth builds, but having one means not being able to do really basic things like opening doors, especially after they nerfed quick hacks into the dirt.

Overall, get this on a sale. It is a passable looter-shooter/immersive sim hybrid but is bogged down a lot by not having enough cool levels to play through and too much time spent on a weak story with a forced moral message. Otherwise this game costs way too much for what it is.

comment:
Beware, this game is nothing like Baldur's Gate, TOSC, Shadows of Amn or Throne of Bhaal.
So far it seems like nothing is remotely similar except that the city of Baldur's gate is supposed to feature in it at some point. I'm not trying to say this is a bad game, it is AFAIK keeping quite true to D&D and appears as though it's a very high quality crpg of D&D fifth edition( ...? I think it's the fifth edition, it did say but I wasn't really paying attention). 
My problem is that it isn't remotely true to Baldur's Gate games in a gameplay sense. It is turn based, combat is very slow, you have to wait for everyone to take their turns. I don't like this.
You have no party formations, although that doesn't actually matter anyway. 
You constantly have to roll things and watch a picture of a dice to see if you can: open a chest; persuade a character; scratch your balls etc. etc....

Oh and btw, for some reason Larian have felt the need to include removable underwear and fully rendered genitals. IDK wtf for exactly, maybe at some point in the game you get to roll your luck with someone and have a full cut scene D&D porno, but I digress. Some people really like this sort of thing and it's not for me to disparage them (nor is it my intention, I just find it curious that they spent the time to render all those ♥♥♥♥♥).

I'm not really that far into the game ATM, the story I've come across is well done and well thought out and the 3d world is very impressively detailed, it is somewhat challenged in terms of scale compared to previous games in the series as far as I can see though. Not that some of the previous games didn't squash a bit too much in here and there, but I'm still in the first region you get to and already the scales of time and distance seem horrendously warped. 
A character I picked up (easily missed btw) has just said how much they trust me after we've been travelling together for a few days. This occurred the first time I went to camp for a full rest. Which is also weird, that I have a camp set up for a bunch of people to stay at because for some reason nobody can travel in a group larger than four and also, I JUST GOT HERE, when did I go and set up this camp, when did I find this remarkable hideaway, seemingly safe from/for all....?

Honestly I believe it would have been better if they'd kept expanding on Siege of Dragonspears' method: Keep making what people have loved for twenty odd years.

comment:
A "neutral" opinion review
A very expansive but underwhelming game, D:OS and D:OS2 are some of my favorite games of all time and I kickstarted them. This game somehow felt like a step back in a lot of regards compared to their previous games. 
The scale is bigger and if you're the type of person to find more cinematics=better presentation you'll probably prefer this game as an adventure rpg to the previous ones. In my opinion though, the pacing is horrendous and it's not helped by the fact that I don't think that the story is particularly cohesive or the world more interesting, it is partially mitigated by Larian's efforts to allow the players to tackle it in differents ways. 
Add all of that to the objective fact that the combat/customization is a huge downgrade from their previous games and personnally, I couldn't help but be disappointed. 
There's not really any memorable area in this game or an encounter that really stood out, might have to do with the game being quite easy coming from D:OS & D:OS2 though.

comment:
[H1] Cyberpunk is wide as an ocean and deep as a puddle. [/H1]

Even that is a hyberpole as to how wide it is. 
The premise and the atmosphere of this game are top notch. The city [i] looks [/i] great, every time you turn there's a high chance you would get a background screenshot and it does have one of the best cyberpunk worlds out there. Corporations are prevalent and suppressive as they should and the premise of the blackwall and the AI's is intriguing to say the least but that's it.
Once you look past the surface the veil drops as quick as the disappointment hits you because there's hints of greatness everywhere, however the story as a whole, the little moments, the world and the gameplay just don't live up to the potential. 

Buckle up because there's A LOT to say. 

The game is BUGGY. Not in an obvlivion haha look at this funny NPC exchange way, just [i] embarrassingly so. [/i]
Tons of visual bugs, flashbangs exiting menus, physics bugs, unlootable enemies, NPC's phasing through walls or spawning in and out of nowhere and the game even softlocking me a few times with unkillable enemies and that's all on the latest "2.0 comeback" patch. 
[url=https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLv4LBJ7ubTUXF34qf_S6HSCKK7Ijc0kLX] Here you can find some of the bugs I encountered [/url] (I will be adding more clips as time goes on) 

Even if that weren't the case:

The city, while pretty as I said, is empty. There's nothing to do. Only three types of activities. 
- Main and side missions, which usually are a big chain of zones to clear after listening to uninteresting dialogue for 10+ minutes. 
- Side gigs, which are usually just a big zone with enemies to clear and get -item/person- of interest.
- Police scanner missions, which are usually small zones of enemies to clear and a lootbox. 

The activities are all the same, scale being the only differentiating factor and a great part of the stories (especially in side content) is told through logs / mails which is extremely lazy and makes everything feel samey. 
The only deviation here are the races (only 4 in total) which are a joke and a repeatable fetch quest they added in the DLC. 

When it comes to the gameplay itself... again there's glimpses of greatness, it can be VERY satisfying at times, hacking away and causing mayhem but there just isn't anything to it. Whether an enemy is an "elite" or not only changes how tanky they are. Sometimes they dash around and sometimes they don't. They don't work together, they don't have any synergies between them. There's no reason to prioritize one enemy over another besides snipers. 
At some point I was going around causing everyone to suicide without lifting a finger. At first it was funny, then it just became boring, not that shooting tanky enemies over and over is all that much more exciting. 
The bosses are all lackluster, tanky and just run at you in a straight line. 
What's funny is the tankier the enemies are the more it highlights all the animation and feedback issues with the combat and I don't even know why ammo is a thing since you never run out.  
Also stealth is a joke, as in it makes every encounter trivial, even more so than it already was. 
To add to all of that, there is no reason to use anything other than Iconic weapons. You get tons of those so the vast majority of the loot you get is rendered useless besides crafting mats. Apparel barely gives stats, so you can forget about that mattering too. 

Would have been serviceable for a great story... but yeah the game is lacking there too. Besides Johnny and Panaam there's no memorable characters to speak of.  Most plotlines and character archetypes have been done better in superior sci fi stories. 
Johnny is a foil to V and only reacts to things and characters happening around V, so his character can only do so much to stay interesting. V is a non-character which only exists to ask stupid questions, everyone talks so slow as if they are mentally handicapped and / or like a angsty 15 year old. The main story contradicts the mission design. You are supposed to be dying but you can spend endless hours not only clearing the map of busy work but dabbling in the side missions which CAN affect the main stories choices. Except that side content... takes time, time you don't have yet V is completely chill just going on random misadventures with whoever asks something of him. 
Credit where credit is due, there are some decent choices in some missions but it doesn't matter when you find none of it interesting. 
This isn't even approaching how interesting and intricate the dialogue in Witcher was.

Also to add to my frustrations, ♥♥♥♥ the advertismenets. World building my ass, there's no way to turn off TV's and Radios and you are constantly bombarded by at least 5 different sources of sound blasting the same 4-5 ads over and over and over. 

I haven't even gotten to how terrible the skill tree is but alas, the review is getting long as it is. I could go in great detail about a lot of things and honestly no other game has made me want  to write a video essay as much as this due to the insane amount of undeserved glazing it receives online I'm going to leave it here. 

Would I recommend this game to someone else? 
Despite my 100+ hours, hell no.

comment:
A Legendary Franchise Reduced to Shock Value

Let’s be honest: this game is obsessed with sex to a point that feels embarrassing.

Instead of delivering a mature, lore-driven Dungeons & Dragons epic, it constantly drags the player through intrusive sexual tension, unsolicited advances, and dialogue trees that feel engineered to funnel toward sexual outcomes. You can barely interact with companions without conversations bending toward flirtation or outright propositions. It doesn’t feel natural. It feels compulsive.

And when one of the first defining choices in character creation is genital size, that tells you exactly where the priorities were. In a universe built on decades of rich lore, layered politics, divine conflict, philosophical depth, and complex moral choices, this is what they decided to emphasize? It’s juvenile. It’s unnecessary. It cheapens what should feel epic.

The problem isn’t that sexuality exists. The problem is how intrusive and persistent it is. Dialogues corner you. Emotional beats derail into awkward intimacy. Instead of earning connection through storytelling, the game repeatedly defaults to sexual provocation as if that’s the most compelling form of character writing available.

What makes it worse is the generational disconnect.

I started my Dungeons & Dragons journey at 12 years old with Baldur’s Gate I. That game sparked imagination, strategy, moral dilemmas, and a lifelong appreciation for RPGs. Now my own son is 12 — the same age I was when I fell in love with this universe — and I would genuinely feel uncomfortable introducing him to this as his entry point into role-playing games.

Not because fantasy should be sanitized. But because this feels excessive and unfocused. It feels like shock value over substance. Instead of welcoming a new generation into a vast and intelligent fantasy world, the game risks pushing them away with its constant emphasis on genitals and sexual encounters.

And that’s the real wasted potential. This could have been the bridge between generations of players. Instead, it feels like it slammed the door shut.

To be clear: the technical achievement is undeniable. The combat is deep and satisfying. The production quality is extraordinary. The voice acting and cinematic presentation are top-tier. There are moments of brilliance throughout.

Which only makes it more frustrating.

The talent was there. The budget was there. The lore was there.

Restraint wasn’t.

comment:
They forgot to put the game in Cyberpunk.

I've been playing through the story for about six hours now, and I think I've seen half an hour of actual gameplay.
The rest of the time has been spent on the intro, endless dialogues, tutorials, driving sequences (which can run on autopilot — no interaction required), and a “Braindance” — which basically means dragging sliders until the game tells you you've done it right.

At times, it feels like you’re playing a one-button game where you’re constantly pressing the “Next” button. This is often the highlighted dialogue option, opening a menu, walking into a trigger, or buying an item. Considering that you’re basically just pressing “Next” the whole time, the key bindings are absolutely bonkers. For example, there are three different buttons for drawing/holstering your weapon on foot and in a vehicle. Why this isn’t just a simple toggle key is beyond me.

You’re constantly forced to wait: Wait for dialogue, wait for the scanner, wait for a cutscene, wait for an elevator, wait until the NPC has walked somewhere. Think I’m exaggerating? Pay attention to how often the current task says something like “wait for … to happen” or how often you’re presented with a progress bar. The only progress bar I expect to see in games Is the loading screen and that should be as quick as possible.

Combat feels both overloaded and one-dimensional at the same time: You’re shown all kinds of stealth and melee mechanics, but you don’t need them at all — you just end up shooting everyone in the face. If you’re playing stealth, the loop goes: Kill, quicksave, kill, quicksave, quickload if you’re spotted, repeat. And then there’s this thing where the game teases you in the intro that you could perform a simultaneous takedown with your companion. Turns out it’s not part of the missions — it only happens when it’s scripted.

The gunplay is somewhat reminiscent of loot shooters like Borderlands, where enemies are bullet sponges and headshots aren’t lethal. Instead, you end up grinding just to get that one upgrade that lets you reload 20% faster—something you should have from the start, so the gameplay isn’t so terribly sluggish. If you can’t take out an enemy from a distance, you just run right up to them and blast them in the face with the shotgun. In any serious shooter, you’d be dead in seconds. But not in Cyberpunk. And this is on Hard. It’s topped off with a bit of hacking, which means you can make enemies explode or stun them just by clicking on them.

Unfortunately, the story hasn't really grabbed me so far either. There are a lot of people who want to hurt you. You die twice. There's a heist, and they implant some stuff in your brain. That's mainly because of the uninteresting characters. We've got Hispano B.J. Blazkovicz and a handful of other plastic buddies, all of whom are way to talkative and never get to the point. If the dialogue options have serious consequences, the game doesn’t convey that very well.
I experienced a bunch of soft locks already where a npc just would not enter his trigger and the mission would not continue.
[Edit ~20h] In the mission "Never Fade Away" I experienced frequent crashes.

It’s all a real shame, because I thought The Witcher 3 was absolutely fantastic.
The lighting is nice, though. Just like the sound design. It can get a little busy at times. But overall, the technical aspects are pretty good.

I’ll keep on playing. If people say the story is good, there must be something to it. Maybe I’ll find the fun at some point. Maybe John Wick will cheer me up. But then again why does it take a game like this 6 hours to present something interesting? I could have played an entire other game with actual interaction at that time.

[Edit at 10 hours]
I found a scene that’s symptomatic of cyberpunk:
In a brothel, you have a conversation with a prostitute. The goal is to get some information. During this conversation, you’re bombarded with calendar quotes:
“You’re scared because you have given up on your dreams.”
“Not a single thing in this world isn’t in the process of becoming something else.”
“Fear is our weapon in the fight against death.”
"But everything has its end."
The conversation is so generic: if you replace V with $Name and Night City with $Location, you could insert it into any series or game. I suspect you’re supposed to learn something about V’s character, but you don’t. What makes this even more absurd is that you can bypass the scene from the very beginning by saying the safeword (even though you are not in an extreme situation). 
What some might call “building atmosphere,” I consider a waste of time. There are so many games that manage to portray deep characters and atmosphere without trapping you in hours of fluff dialogue.
This scene lasts 5 or 6 minutes. After that, you have to move on to the next cutscene.

[Edit at 32 hours]
The final mission does not have any gameplay either. [spoiler] You can just decide to kill yourself. V probably should have done that right at the start, That would have been a lot less painful. [/spoiler]

comment:
Game is good if you make it quick. Because the more you play, the more flaws and inconsistencies you'll notice.

- Still filled with bugs, most of it are physics and visual related( random flares after exiting map view, falling through the map, bosses/enemies stuck in invisible terrain, animation loop, civilian cars randomly blow up when nothing is happening, etc...) while none are game-breaking, it's simply incompetence for a game to have this many bugs considering it been out for more than half a decade, people says it's a lot better now compared to at launch, but it was a hot mess of garbage back then, which is a very low bar to pass. If you are someone who likes to mod your games and stuff, expect even more bugs.

- Throughout the game you will encounter a plethora of dialogue choices, some will affect the outcome of the mission, your relationship with certain NPCs, and even the ending of the game. Sadly, these instances are only the minority and 95% of the time these choices are meaningless, A/B/C/D simply bring you to the same outcome, they even hit you with these when there's only one option available. Instead of just let the conversation flow smoothly and represent you the options when it really matters, they constantly hit you with the illusion of choice and leave you wonder whether your decision have any weight to it or simply just a mean to an end.

- A massive amount of side quests, similar to dialogue choices, some of these will affect NPCs relationship and endings while the rest are straight up boring, have zero substances and just a reason for you to explore the map, level up and get some gears, and the open world aspect amplify this further, ignore the pointless quests, and suddenly the map looks empty, at least the views are good.

- Gameplay overall is fine except for close up combat which feel unpolished and unresponsive, like a random game in its alpha state and again, the game been out for years, there's no excuses for this. Looting is also buggy, some items can only be picked up at a certain angles, same thing with interacting with objects and scanning.

- Etc... and the DLC also have all of this problems.

Still worth it if on sale I suppose. And if you want to level up or get certain equipment, just get it from CET and stick to the main and related side quests. Again, the more you play, the worse it gets.

This game sucks. I rushed my way through the campaign just to say I gave it a try, and its horrible. 1/10.

comment:
centrist cyberpunk is kind of a non-starter for me. i was really hoping this game had anything interesting to say about our world (given it has cyberpunk in its title), but it's so much about its characters that society isn't allowed to exist. quests have dynamic combat encounters that provide quite a bit of flexibility with how you complete them, that allow for a lot of player expression, but they're connected by a story in which the momentum inevitably grinds to a halt every other mission.

if you're inclined to actively seek out side content, to do literally everything possible in games before completing the main quest, then you'll probably have a lot more fun with this than i did. frankly, the late game missions are designed around having done a whole bunch of side quests, upgrading gear, getting new passive abilities, etc. so the game is much more for you. personally, i think this game's big issue is that it's too difficult to discover side quests, to stumble into the fun; if the main quest is going to force you to wait potentially multiple in-game days before you're allowed to continue, you shouldn't be able to drive for five minutes without something catching your eye. i only really like doing side content if it seems immediately interesting, but since the interesting parts of side content are only in their twists, i spend 90% of the quest line waiting for the cool stuff and then the quest is over before i get to do anything interesting or unique.

im gonna be annoying. sorry. if fallout new vegas looked anywhere near as good as this game and didn't require modding to be playable on modern systems, i'd have given up on this before the end of act one. this isn't a bad game, and it's pretty, but its gameplay is mogged by games that came out 10+ years before it, and that alone makes it hard to recommend to anyone in good conscience.

comment:
If you are reading this, then you probably already know the positives of Baldur’s Gate 3: freedom of choice, great voice acting, strong quest design, memorable companions, and the ridiculous amount of ways you can solve problems. I'm not going to sit here and pretend those things are not impressive, because they are.

But because those parts have already been praised to death, I want to focus on what, in my opinion, makes the game overrated.

Baldur’s Gate 3 is clearly a good game, but I don’t think it is the flawless masterpiece people make it out to be. To me, it is also bloated, clunky, awkward, weirdly horny, and surprisingly weak when it comes to the feeling of progression. I will address each of those in the following sections.

[h2]Weak Progression[/h2]

One of my biggest problems with BG3 is progression. For such a huge RPG, I rarely felt genuinely excited about my character becoming stronger.

The story moves forward, the stakes get bigger, and the locations become more dramatic, but my actual character build often felt weirdly static. Gear progression especially felt underwhelming. It is very possible to find strong equipment in Act 1 and keep using it through Act 2 and even into Act 3.

I understand that this is probably good for balance, as it avoids the usual RPG problem where every item becomes useless after two hours. But from a player perspective, it can feel boring. You defeat major enemies, explore dangerous areas, open some impressive-looking chest, and then the reward is something you instantly send to camp because your old gear is still better.

I mean there is clearly something wrong when I'm deep into Act 3 and still wearing gear from Act 1 without feeling much reason to replace it. Loot should be exciting. I should look at a new weapon, armour piece, ring, or cloak and think, "Oh, this changes my build." But too often in BG3, loot just feels like mildly interesting clutter.

[h2]Underwhelming Level-Ups[/h2]

Leveling up has a similar problem. Because BG3 follows Dungeons & Dragons 5e, progression is more restrained. Yeah, I get that it is faithful to the tabletop rules. But as a video game RPG, it can feel really underwhelming. There is no proper skill tree, no big long-term upgrade path, and not many future unlocks that made me excited.

Some classes get fun powers, but plenty of level-ups feel minor. You get one spell, a passive, a feat, or some practical option that feels fine but not exciting. Many of the coolest choices can be taken early, and after that you often just pick whatever is left or whatever seems vaguely fitting.

A skill tree would have helped. Not some bloated mess with 300 meaningless icons, but something that gives a stronger sense of direction. Something that lets you look ahead and think, “Oh wow! I cannot wait to unlock that!” In BG3, I often didn't feel like I was building towards some powerful fantasy version of my character. I felt like I was just selecting from a small menu of practical options.

[h2]Combat: Great Ideas, Clunky Execution[/h2]

Combat is a mixed bag for me. When it works, it can be genuinely great. Positioning matters, height matters, surfaces matter, spells matter, and the environment can completely change a fight. You can push enemies off ledges, block routes, set traps, summon creatures, buff allies, debuff enemies, and turn the battlefield into complete chaos.

But when combat does not work, it becomes slow and clunky. The camera is often terrible, especially in multi-level areas. Trying to click the right enemy, floor tile, ledge, ladder, or doorway can feel harder than the actual fight.

Pathfinding can also be stupid. Characters walk through fire, acid, traps, or other hazards like they are trying to speedrun natural selection. You finish a fight, relax for half a second, and then someone casually strolls through burning ground because why the hell not.

The hit chance system can also feel awful. I know missing high-chance attacks is part of D&D. But that does not mean it always feels good in a video game. Nothing kills the heroic fantasy faster than watching your trained warrior miss a point-blank attack while some goblin with the posture of a wet sock crits you from across the room.

[h2]Inventory Management: Fantasy Warehouse Simulator[/h2]

Then there is the inventory system, and oh boy, it honestly deserves its own prison sentence.

By mid-game, your bags are full of scrolls, potions, arrows, keys, books, notes, quest items, food, rings, amulets, dyes, tools, random bones, and 46 pieces of equipment you are keeping "just in case." Managing all of it becomes a chore.

The game gives you so many items, but sorting through them is tedious. You constantly move things between characters, send things to camp, compare gear, check whether some random note still matters, and try to remember which companion has the potion you need.

Somewhere in your backpack there is probably a useful item. Good luck finding it.

[h2]Act 3: Too Much of Everything[/h2]

The pacing also becomes a problem, especially in Act 3. Act 1 is strong because it has mystery, danger, discovery, and a good balance between freedom and direction. Act 2 has a strong atmosphere and feels more focused. But Act 3 is where the game starts drowning in its own ambition.

The city is impressive, don't get me wrong. There is a lot to do. But sometimes there is just too much. Every building has secrets. Every NPC has a problem. Every street corner threatens to become a side quest. You can’t walk 20 metres without someone asking you to solve a murder, uncover a conspiracy, rescue someone, investigate a basement, enter a portal, or confront a god. 

The amount of content is impressive, sure, but this density hurts the pacing.

[h2]Romance Writing: Too Fast, Too Easy, Too Awkward[/h2]

The romance writing is another big issue for me.

The issue is not just that the companions are bisexual. That alone I can survive. The problem is that nearly every companion feels player-sexual in the same way. Instead of feeling like complex adults with different preferences, boundaries, and emotional pacing, the party often feels like they all joined the same fantasy dating app and instantly matched with the player.

You meet these people, survive a few fights, avoid being completely evil, and suddenly half the camp starts acting like you are the most desirable person in Faerûn. Ridiculous.

The romance feels too easy and too fast. It does not feel like trust is properly earned. It feels like romance unlocks because you picked enough polite dialogue options. I even had scenes that felt weirdly romantic when I was not trying to romance that character at all. I was just choosing normal polite or supportive options, but the game seemed to assume I was interested.

The silent protagonist makes it even more awkward. A companion pours their heart out, becomes vulnerable, or expresses attraction, and your character mostly communicates through silent staring and vague hand gestures. Instead of two people building chemistry, it can feel like one fully acted character falling in love with a mute wax figure.

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]

That is why I cannot see Baldur’s Gate 3 as the flawless masterpiece people make it out to be. It is ambitious, reactive, and impressive, but also bloated, clunky, awkwardly paced, and surprisingly weak as a progression-based RPG.

I respect the game a lot, and I understand why people love it. But for me, the weak progression, messy Act 3 pacing, clunky combat moments, silent protagonist, and weirdly rushed romance writing hold it back too much.

What most reviews fail to mention is the game's problems.  The fundamental gameplay basics of the game are just, bad.  Not the game balance; the problems are even more basic than that.  Controls, camera, environmental collision, pathing, physics, ui problems.  Not to mention crashing.  The basic fundamentals of a game which should be ironclad before a game dev has barely done work on graphics or writing a story.

The game is extremely polished, but at core functionality level, the game might as well be a pre-alpha build.

Most people are okay with that, and there are lots of mods that exist that fix some of these problems, several of which I installed.  But I've always been of the opinion that mods should add to a game, not fix the game's code for the developers.

And it leaves a very sour taste in my mouth when I encounter minor glitches every few minutes, in what is otherwise a good game with a good story and compelling characters.

comment:
**Overrated as f****

Let me get this straight. This is definitely not a game for a broad audience. This game is for D&D lovers. If you've never played D&D, just skip it. Now, let's go through some specific points.

**1. The game is slow**

And when I say it's slow, I'm not talking about the kind of slow that builds atmosphere, like in *Red Dead Redemption 2*, where you're riding your horse and actually feel like a real cowboy. No. *Baldur's Gate 3* is slow in a negative sense.

Every time you fight, you have to move from point A to point B, then wait while all the AI on the map does the same thing, and then you press the "Attack" button only for your opponent to dodge. These fights are long, and they're not interesting at all.

When you finish a fight, you start looting bodies and containers, and believe me, you'll spend HOURS of your playthrough managing your inventory. In most RPGs, you often find valuable loot that helps your progression, but in BG3 you can spend hours without finding a single useful weapon for your main character (or you find the same weapon with +1 damage).

Progression and combat are not rewarding at all.

But the biggest source of "slowness" is the D&D dice system. Believe me, you'll reload your save file a lot. Like... A LOT. You'll spend hours staring at loading screens.

This brings me to my second point. Also, whenever you want to do anything in combat, you need to press a button and then click on a target. Sometimes I click a skill, miss the target by a little bit, and hit empty space instead. That can literally cost me the fight. Guess what you have to do then? Reload your save.

The game has a lot of randomness because of the D&D mechanics. You have 10 Intelligence, need to pass an Intelligence check, and the required roll is 12. You roll a 1. Nice. Guess what? Reload your save. And you do it hundreds, if not thousands, of times.

**2. The game is overwhelming**

You don't have one character who progresses through the game and upgrades their gear. You have an entire party.

Unlike *Clair Obscur*, for example, where you start with one character and gradually recruit others, BG3 fills your four party slots very quickly.

And if you have at least one mage or cleric—good luck. These classes have tons of skills. You need to spend so much time reading and remembering everything that it starts to feel like a second job.

You also have four separate inventories to manage. Inventory management is a huge pain. You find an item, read its description, transfer it to the right character, equip it, and then sometimes realize you can't even use it.

**3. The writing and style are just mid**

I'm talking about two things here: the writing and the world design.

I'm not talking about the story because I dropped the game during Act 1, so I can't really judge it. But from what I saw, it felt like very basic fantasy without anything special. The dialogue is on the same level as Marvel movies—simple writing with occasional jokes.

As for the style, the game doesn't really have one. If you look at *Disco Elysium*, for example, you can immediately tell there's nothing else quite like it. If you look at other top-tier fantasy franchises, they usually have a unique visual identity and a distinctive world.

*Baldur's Gate 3* just feels generic to me.

I don't have much else to say about that.

9/3/26 Review edit at 34.4 Hours

I wish Steam had a mixed review option. After a few days I tried again and managed to get more invested in the game and get to the end of Act I. But the main problem of my original review never went away. Combat never stopped feeling tedious and slow, and the pacing of the game really just feels off to me. 34 hours in and I feel like no actual plot developments have happened, I don't really know any more that I did at hour 10, and the slow and wifely spaced out side quests become a slog. It just gets repetitive after a while. I'm still going to attempt finishing it but overall I'm disappointed. I feel like a lot of the tiresome aspects of the gameplay were solved by other RPGs a long time ago and the tabletop RNG turn based system is a downgrade for nostalgia's sake.

Characters--Generally ok but sometimes intolerably cringeworthy, especially in romance scenes. I thought the character writing for some characters are one of the stronger aspects of the game, but some companions definitely are not as well done as others

Setting--I found I generally dislike the DND setting, which was surprising. It just feels so generic and tired and like a mismash of a thousand tropes that are more interesting in other games. Somehow this game really made me wish I was playing Dragon Age or the Witcher instead

OST--The main motif is catchy at first but it becomes SO ANNOYING after a while

Class building/ customization/ other PC elements: The DND chains are so aggravating and one of the bigger frustrations of the gameplay. Generally speaking I feel like there is a good reason video games have moved away from strict class systems in RPGs. Even the multiclass options feel restrictive because you miss out on so many high level perks. And the levelling itself is so slow, and unless you're a spellcaster, levelling gives you so few new options for abilities or customization. I know I said I was only in Act I, but why are my 2 main melee fighters still using the same 3 moves every turn they were using at level 1 after 34 hours? Very unrewarding IMO

comment:
I made a stealth runner, stealth and magic, methodically crawling through dungeons, taking my time to not be seen, and by level 12 I was pretty good at it. Then for the next 31 levels nothing changed. When i turned to the internet to figure out why the downtime in my gameplay loop hadn't improved in 30 levels. I found that there were more efficient combos and perk choices that I could be making. So after some research and spending some of my in-game money, I improved my build. Or so I though. The downtime had gotten shorter, but not significantly so. So little, in fact, that I would argue that it hadn't changed. Then after more research, I found that certain resource-recovery perks were intentionally disconnected from the most popular stealth quickhack combos, without it being mentioned anywhere in the game. I can only assume this was done for marketing purposes? Because the first version of the game was such a failure (not that I had invested a lot of time into it back then, and personally dont have an opinion about early CyberPunk77) that they decided to allow only fast paced action builds to shine so that they could redeem themselves more quickly through paid youtube shillery.

Ok, fine. So i put together a Damage over Time build that used the whip to detonate the debuffs. But I found that the interaction between the skills was rarely happening and that fights would only be explosively fast. With yet more research I found that the whip's hit scan function was bugged and ultra thin, so when you were attempting to hit the also bugged hitboxes of mobs who were displaying debuff animations. So my whip attacks were hitting less than 20% of the time and enemies were dying slowly to the DoT's alone.

From my experience alone, it can be surmised that, either on purpose or on accident, no single part of this game actually works. Certainly if you don't want to play sandevistan/katana build you shouldn't spend money on it either.

The narrative is irritating. I get that V is a headstrung, insecure, dumbass, but how many story hooks can start with my character being forced by the game to do something dangerously stupid? Am I expected to believe that she grew up in night city? I've been here 15 minutes and can tell you those jerks are going to do something jerky.

Also as an accomplished netrunner, V constantly praising Songbird and "needing" her for hacking jobs felt bad. Luckily my V was a weak nerd though, because if i was a sandevistan using katana wielder, I would have been pissed that the game required me to constantly ask the help of a geriatric woman to open all the doors in that intro.

Ultimately I think I'm done with CDprokect Red for a while. Maybe they'll get their act together eventually, but at this point in time I think we can safely say that the constant development issues over there are a feature, not a bug.
