comment:
A friend of mine finally peer-pressured me into playing this. Oh boy, here we go.

The character customisation is strange. It’s unfortunately basic for the most part and apparently, any race can have any skin-tone because “why not?”. With equally out of place brightly coloured hair dye (and...fully modelled privates?). What do you mean it’s established the races didn’t look like that? I should have taken the quality-warning and refunded it.

A lot, and I mean a lot, of stuff will be thrown at the player with little or no explanation. Confusing as all heck, but looks exciting. I feel really sorry for people that haven’t played Dungeons and Dragons. I’ve played enough of the tabletop game to understand most of it, but oh boy, new players will be very confused. Good luck with things like Action, Bonus Action, Opportunity Attack and Disengage. And that was just the tutorial.

I really like that all your Actions and Bonus Actions for each character are laid out to you during combat. It’s given me a whole new appreciation of what classes can do in a turn. Especially since it took me about six months of regular sessions of the tabletop version to understand the terms.

Controlling your character to move and interact with the world is really complicated. There are so many buttons to push, interaction options and wheels to pick from. And that’s outside of combat with one character. Things can get really overwhelming.

In my fourth hour of playing, I got my whole party killed. I’m not sure why the combat-difficulty spiked so suddenly, but it did. Every combat encounter in that area was suddenly four times harder. I guess Bethesda isn’t the only company that have no idea what game balance is. It’s the first area of the open world. Calm down.

Combat can be really annoying with how difficult the camera is to use. If there are walls or multiple levels in the area, the camera doesn’t know what to do. And the movement cursor can get very confused when there are multiple objects you can interact with next to the spot you want to move to.

I am sick of how badly ranged attacks work in this game. You try to target an enemy and “sometimes” the game will suggest moving to a good position. Unfortunately, sometimes it suggests “run to the target and fire at point-blank”. When just moving a little closer does the same job. And sometimes the game can’t figure out a clear shot, when manually moving to a good position is easy. I cannot stress enough how irritating the targeting can be and hoping you don’t run out of movement while you reposition.

I didn’t expect almost all of my party members to talk about jumping my bones so quickly in this game. Like, wow. There was the option to accept advances for almost all of them. That was sudden. Even weirder when it felt like they were getting jealous of each other after I accepted with one of them. My goodness, I’ve known you people for three days and we’ve hardly conversed.

This game makes everything feel long. Bloating simple things like moving from place to place. It took me about 30 minutes to find the door to a building with a stupid number of floors, balconies and rooftops. With lots of little containers and items all over it. I’m just looking for the door. It’s so slow-paced that it felt like I barely did anything after an hour.

And that was just Act 1. “The good part” that received “a lot of polish”, according to the community.

Be aware that sometimes set-pieces will break themselves. I’ve had that many scenes that were supposed to start with dialogue, but instead started with combat. I know this because I talk to my friend about this game and he’s informed me about a lot of scenes I’ve accidentally sequence-broke.

Anytime a really cool character is temporarily fighting on your side, you should assume they aren’t good at fighting. This is a reoccurring thing. Oops, the cool character forgot how to fight. Oops, they ran from the boss for random enemies on the opposite side. Oops, they’re down. Oops, they did it all over again every time you attempt the fight. Useless! This game is confusing.

The writing is, well, not the worst thing ever. At least it’s better than what you might see in a more recent Bethesda game. But there has been a lot of “What is even going on?”, “You guys are really stupid” and “Oh, who saw that coming? Everyone” moments.

There is a serious problem with the combat in the late-game. You see, you should be leveling-up to become stronger, gain new combat powers and keep up with enemies. Problem. To keep the game challenging, the devs had the genius idea to make the stronger abilities not reliable against the harder enemies and you’ll end up relying on the weaker attacks. This is really dumb. I feel like I’m playing the game backwards. What’s the point of all these cool abilities if the really hard enemies have very small hit-chances or immunity? I’m either garbage at this game (which I am) or these devs figured this was good enough.

I think I’m starting to understand the weirdness of Balanced (standard) difficulty. I often share stories of my playthrough to because the reactions are humorous and I learn what I missed. I’ve heard just how easy it can be to cheese the heck out of this game. In fact, another friend has also told me similar things. Problem. I don’t know how to do any of those. It’s my first playthrough and I don’t know any overpowered exploits. I can’t do 1000 damage by launching an owlbear or filling a room with grease to burn everything. I guess the default difficulty is so high because the devs expected you to exploit it. Um, hi, regular player, here. I don’t know how to cheat everything! This game is harsh to new players. That is my current understanding of why the difficulty feels so hard.

I made it to the final part of the game. I would say with my sanity, but that wasn’t be for long. It is...awful. It’s awful. It’s the bad combat on steroids. It’s a clusterf*ck of unknown status effects, enemies spawning, random spells, the camera bouncing around while going black, tight time-limits, confusing terrain, game mechanics keep breaking, your dead allies’ rag dolling, and to top it all off, being cut-off from your camp for an hour or two. Wow. I am so mentally fatigued from this game that I went to a guide pretty quickly. When will it end? End the game already, please. Which sucks, since the visuals and plot are meant to be pretty serious at this part. But I couldn’t take it seriously because I was so bored at that point.

Credit where credit is due. I didn’t think they could pull it off. The ending wasn’t awful. It was done in such a way that it was really satisfying. I kept thinking about a Nicholas Cage movie when a guy explained that if you have a bad story, you needs to at least nail the ending. And they did. They nailed a satisfying ending. It was a first run and I didn’t know what I was doing, but I could end this trash on a high note.

Okay, I’ll dial it back. I did have fun while I played. There were a lot of fun moments with colourful characters in it. But man, the game was rough, long and had serious priority issues. Too much effort on making it huge and pretty. Not enough of ironing out controls and explaining things. Welcome to Bad Game 3 by Lame Studios - it’s a quite a doozy (that joke was awful, but it was too funny at the time to not use it).

comment:
Writing this is say that on release the Remaster visually feels like a downgrade from Next Gen.

The lighting in the game I think focuses on realism over visual aesthetic and clarity: contrast in the game is muted, certain areas like the castle in skellige turned grey and muddy in comparisons next gen's warm lights and cool shadows. Holding up a torch washes out Geralt into a dusty yellow with even lower contrast.... the bloom and harsh lighting and details hidden due to distance or shadows has been removed. Sometimes shadows obscuring things is good! Lets you focus on the characters and creates beleivable depth.

Upon opening the game, the sensitivity that I had in Next-Gen became dizzyinng in the Remaster. This might be due to the fact Geralt is now smaller and closer to the center of the screen. In my opinion, the closer "over the shoulder"-like camera felt more immersive and was easier to see with, but that absolutely is a to each their own thing.

Finally, I was super excited for all the new features added to camera-mode, but the scroll to zoom-in doesnt work for now, and I find the mouse working on the camera more disorienting than anything. While you can add characteers and props, I didnt see an option to moving around characters on XYZ to fit into where I pointed the camera. Its probably just a learning curb, but with the whole lighting, contrast and color grading situation, I'd rather downgrade back to next-gen to take photos and run around in the game.

I dont have much to say about gameplay, I didn't get far enough into the remaster to play as the stuff I stated above was enough to have me back out. Hopefully the upcoming DLC will be Next Gen friendly but I doubt it..

I enjoy playing the Witcher 3, but ATM I cant reccomend the Remaster in terms of visuals ( and my fan getting louder ) ... Theres probably things I can do to adjust controls, but nothings going to change that color grading fn so yeah.

comment:
Well this was somethin, but not what I was expecting. Cyberpunk was a very VERY ok game, but I just cant recommend it. I will point out things i liked and the ones i didnt:

PROS:
- Graphics. Night city looked phenomenal. City is very well planned out and feels alive. 
- Character outfits and looks. They are very detailed and look awesome
- There are a lot of ways to upgrade your character abilities, skills etc
- A few characters (like Johnny) are nice
- Loading screens are a bit unique
- A lot of ways to customize your character looks.

CONS:
- Gameplay is very mediocre, could even say its just bad, not very fun to play, which is the biggest minus for me
- Whole game feels more like just a movie. 
- There is a lot of DEI things in the game (which makes sense its cyberpunk afterall). But still at sometimes these things are too much shoved into your face.
- Some characters are just put in the game for the case of DEI it feels like, which makes them unnecessary, not needed, not fittin.
- There is a LOT of bloated dialogue in the game. At some moments there is just too much talkin and made me almost fall asleep at times.
- Npcs and object keep on bugging, glitching, destroying them selfes even after all this patches the game got.
- Enemies AI is on brainded level. They just standin sometimes waiting for you to shot them. 
- Bosses are a complete joke. First one I encountered was like a DEI final boss and almost made me vomit. Their mechanics were also underwhelming.
- Driving mechanics are not too bad, but could have been much better.
- Sometimes some cutscenes during them missions just hit you out of the rythm of the game. Characters randomly start talking about their feelings while sitting next to each other in between some heavy action focused segments. Just pacing could have been better.
- Story was decent, good enough at times. But still it felt like it was missing something.
- You dont earn much in game money from the main story missions, all that money is hidden behind side missions, objectives, which is kinda annoying because you want to upgrade your character and cant because it needs money.
- Feels like the game is so much automated that at times it can play itself. You just need to hold W key and hold your left mouse button and you occasionally press space.
- Difficulty scalling is pretty bad. At highier difficulty than normal enemies become a big bullet sponges and at lower difficulty they just die too quickly.

Overall I was expecting much more and got dissapointed. I can only recommend this game for "movie games" enthusiasts.  It was ok but not good enough for my gaming taste.

Now Im kinda worried of The Witcher 3 third dlc and Witcher 4 after seeing what they did with this game.

I can understand that this is a fantastic game. Great characters, well written story, awesome soundtrack, strong graphics, and just a fantastic time all around. But the reason I do not recommend this game is simple: every single thing you do is essentially a dice roll. And let me tell you, when you have Guidance, Deft hands, dexterity, and like 2 other things to give you a bonus and STILL fail 4 rolls to pick a 15 skill lock...... understand the game is the epitome of a gamble. While I also understand that's a facet of DnD as a whole, it is an aspect I cannot stand in this game. It seems to go out of its way to push your use of Inspiration if you've had 4 for too long. Or to ensure your roll fails if you're skipping dialogue. I understand that the program is exactly that, a program. It randomly generates your roll. But it somehow feels malicious in some cases.

Look, if you're not gonna mind the constant gamble of everything you do outside of walking or are a DnD player yourself, this game is going to be one of the best RPG's you play. However, if you're anything like me and hate the randomness of your rolls even if you have all the advantages in the world, then do not get this game.

comment:
To be fair, I'd recommend checking this game out on a deep deep sale, as it's more like "an interesting phenomenon". I don't think it's a good game in traditional sense.

The whole thing is rather barebones and janky, but it poses as something much bigger, using smoke and mirrors, and the good old bluff. The facade of beautiful environments, film set lighting, and great music hides a non-reactive world, poorly re-cut (version 2.0) dialogue, and illusion of choice and consequence, where all the major decisions and relationships can be turned around in the last mission (depending on who you choose to help you). Stealth is janky, as is climbing and driving. RPG systems are poorly explained, crafting and upgrading is meaningless, as differences in tiers are in tenths of a percent. Some things, like quickhack vendors, aren't explained at all.

By the way, fans who are trying to frame the DLC and fixes as similar to No Man's Sky comeback story are kidding themselves. Hello Games actually sat down and wrote the systems they lied about prior release. CDPR fixed missing assets, added a few minor features like multiple apartments, and that's mostly it. You can see a shadow of collosal ambition of the creators here, in both the scale of the open world, art direction, and the themes within the narrative. Remember, at some point CDPR said they should be capable of reaching RDR2 level of quality. Maybe that's why it is interesting phenomenon, more as a record of collective delusion, an internal (and possibly mid-life) crisis in CDPR ranks.

As a game, it will leave you frustrated, more often than not, because you'll be tricked into thinking that you can do much more, and have much more choice than you actually have.

comment:
Elden Ring is obviously not a bad game. With such an overwhelmingly positive reception, it is clear that it works incredibly well for a lot of people.

But taste is subjective, and after 73 hours and several attempts to get properly into it, I think I can fairly say that this game is not for me.

I enjoyed the Dark Souls games in the past, but at some point I think I grew tired of this style of gameplay. Elden Ring takes that formula and expands it into a huge open world, which is both its greatest strength and one of its biggest weaknesses for me. If you love difficult exploration, environmental storytelling, build experimentation, and discovering things with minimal guidance, this could be an amazing experience. If you enjoy using interactive maps, wikis, and progression guides on a second monitor, it may also fit you well.

For me though, I prefer games where the story, characters, and quests actively pulls me forward. My biggest issue with FromSoftware’s Souls-style games has always been that they do not feel like RPGs in the way I personally enjoy RPGs. There is lore, atmosphere, and worldbuilding, but the storytelling is very indirect and cryptic. If you mainly want a character-driven RPG with story choices and clear quest progression, Elden Ring may disappoint you.

There are absolutely things I like about the game. The atmosphere is excellent, the world feels oppressive, and defeating a difficult boss after learning its patterns can be very satisfying. I also understand why the lack of difficulty settings appeals to many players, because it makes those victories feel more earned.

But many of the same things that make the game rewarding for others make it frustrating for me. The game often feels like it does not respect my time: there is no normal pause function, death can mean losing resources, some runbacks are tedious, and questlines can be so obscure that I often felt pushed toward using a wiki. I do not mind difficulty, but I do mind feeling like I need external guides just to understand how to follow certain quests or avoid missing major content.

The game has lore and atmosphere, but very little of what I personally consider satisfying storytelling: proper dialogue, clear character motivations, narrative agency, and quests that are understandable without a guide.

Ultimately, every time I try to play Elden Ring, I end up feeling bored, frustrated, or like I have to push myself to continue. I can admire parts of it, and I understand why so many people love it, but I do not personally enjoy the overall experience.

If you are an exploration-first or gameplay-first player, this may be one of the best games ever made for you. But if you are like me and prefer structured quests, stronger narrative direction, character-driven storytelling, actual roleplaying and narrative agency, I would advise skipping it.

Not recommended.

While Phantom Liberty was a great expansion, the update that was released alongside it absolutely ruined the game. 
They made all skill checks and areas scale with your character. The idea was to remove early level restrictions from the map and open up the entire city from the start. Which was just never a problem. The idea as a whole is just counterintuitive. It's basic game logic that the areas closer to big bads should be higher tier. And progressing towards them is half the fun of these types of open world games. Plus, it wasn't like leveling to keep up while exploring was remotely difficult or problematic in any way.
This change wasn't just unnecessary, it also ruins the experience as a whole. Your character now feels less competent the more you level, actively punishing you for exploration, and it restricts your character building by FORCING you into specialized builds.
Now this can be fixed with a mod and the game is still great otherwise, but I could never recommend a game that requires a mod to feel playable. 

TLDR: 2.0 ruined the game by punishing exploration and forcing character specialization, this is fixable through mods, but screw the developers for doing this to begin with.

comment:
This is obviouly a staggering accomplishment that most will love, but I don't know if it's a fun game for me.

DnD is just not a great system for computer games. The gear is too boring, the consequences of luck swings too arbitrary when there's not a DM to improvise a correction. I personally  can't handle entire arms of the games  story being locked away from a coin flip, and having save scumming be a core mechanic sits wrong with me. They made a lot of cool improvements but as many mistakes; like jumping being a bonus action.

Gear  management in Original Sin was so godawful I found those games unplayable and bg3 just barely manages to be bearable. Still the inventory is a beast, specifically on controller.  If items can freely teleport between character inventories, why  even have separate inventories? Why allow you to pick up  junk with no value or utility (looking at you, Rope).    Why put thousands of lootable empty vases?! Empty containers should be unlootable. Checking every box in every storage room is degenerate gameplay for the most pathetic of dopamine goblins.

I loathe the camera, you can't look anywhere but straight down. The sense of exploration is totally missing. You just stare at dirt patch or cobbled floor over and over as you navigate the a webbed railroad. I need to see things in the distance and have there be any number of ways to get there. I need geography.  The whole great forge area of the underdark was a nightmare with this camera.

The few puzzles are terrible, every corpse i was actually curious to talk to had nothing to say (like all the ones lying dead in the mouth of a dungeon, apparently placed only as scenery like an empty vase). As mentioned rope is useless.  The inability to talk to enemies or negotiate combats, that no one ever fled or plead, this game is a dating simulator + combat.

I just got bored of mindflayers very quickly. Having a worm in my brain for the entirety of the game put me in a constant state of discontent that prevented me from every really embracing the world. The villains in general weren't compelling, one-note cartoonishly evil.

My favorite companion was karlach who had the least story it seemed.

they try and make the worm bottles sound like they're dangerous and will have a negative side effect so I completely avoided using them. Turns out the game spends the entire story lying to you about how permanent and dangerous they are for your character. There's no consequences, no callback, not even a steam achievement for consuming 0 worms. The game constantly suffers from poor communication around the impact of choices you can make. It's really great that several points in the game have irreversible affects with basically no warning.

Because the narrative insists there's urgency, as a sign of my competence, and  attempt to actually role play  the situation, I took as few long rests as possible, which actually just meant I missed out on tons of camp story. This same problem happens in ME2, where I skipped every sidequest because of the "urgency" and everyone died.

Frequent freezes, often half an hour  into a long combat.

With how buggy movement is (errors in swash buckler sneak attack forecasting, jumping characters clipping invisible hitboxes and getting suck on corners midair), combat needs a "restart turn" button. This is the kind of ♥♥♥♥ that ruins the immersion for me, not lack of cutscene volume. I inhabit a character with my actions, they should feel like an effortless extension of myself. Any friction, reloading because my character threw himself off a cliff because of a misiclick, ruins the illusion.

There's never been a good game with bad music and never been a bad game with good music, and overall the music here is forgettable.


In the end it's just too railroady for me. Divine Divinity (2002) remains my favorite Larian game.

comment:
The game offers plenty of scenarios, lots of fun, and countless hours of playtime. Unfortunately, its core is still in beta and hasn't really changed since the launch of CS2 (which was supposed to be a fresh start). While the new mechanics and the game itself are wonderful and refreshing, my personal verdict is negative. Despite the time spent and the fond memories this game gave us (my friends and me), I ultimately cannot recommend it. It is far too competitive; playing frequently can lead to far more negative memories, and some of your friends might even end up playing in a way that harms them—turning into masochists, so to speak.

Игра предлагает множество сценариев, массу удовольствия и бесконечные часы геймплея. К сожалению, её основа всё ещё находится в стадии бета-тестирования и практически не изменилась с момента выхода CS2 (который должен был стать «новым началом»). И хотя новые механики и сама игра — замечательные и свежие, мой личный вердикт — отрицательный. Несмотря на потраченное время и приятные воспоминания, которые подарила нам эта игра (мне и моим друзьям), в конечном счёте я не могу её рекомендовать. Она слишком уж ориентирована на соревнование: частая игра может принести куда больше негативных эмоций, а некоторые ваши друзья могут даже начать играть себе во вред — превратившись, так сказать, в мазохистов.

El juego ofrece una gran variedad de escenarios, mucha diversión e incontables horas de juego. Por desgracia, su núcleo sigue en fase beta y no ha cambiado realmente desde el lanzamiento de CS2 (que se suponía iba a ser un nuevo comienzo). Aunque las nuevas mecánicas y el juego en sí son maravillosos y refrescantes, mi veredicto personal es negativo. A pesar del tiempo invertido y de los buenos recuerdos que este juego nos brindó (a mis amigos y a mí), al final no puedo recomendarlo. Es demasiado competitivo; jugar con frecuencia puede generar muchos más recuerdos negativos, e incluso algunos de tus amigos podrían acabar jugando de una forma que les perjudica, convirtiéndose en masoquistas

Le jeu offre une multitude de scénarios, énormément de plaisir et des heures de jeu infinies. Malheureusement, sa base technique est encore au stade de la bêta et n'a pratiquement pas évolué depuis la sortie de CS2 (qui était censé marquer un « nouveau départ »). Bien que les nouvelles mécaniques et le jeu lui-même soient excellents et novateurs, mon verdict personnel est négatif. Malgré le temps passé et les bons souvenirs que ce jeu nous a offerts (à mes amis et à moi), je ne peux finalement pas le recommander. Il est bien trop axé sur la compétition : une pratique fréquente peut générer bien plus d'émotions négatives, et certains de vos amis pourraient même finir par jouer à leurs dépens, se transformant pour ainsi dire en masochistes.

comment:
I must say; if you buy it on sale it's going to feel less bad than if you do it for a full price.

The game itself is alright. Just alright. For an AAA title from people that made Witcher series this doesn't quite cut it, now does it? The original release of this game was a total mess, so I waited and waited till everything was done and patched to even try it. I like cyberpunky aesthetic and feel, if nothing else, experiencing that vibe in this game would be alright.

I must say, the strong suits of this title are the. . . Segments with Johnny. Stealth approach trying to not alert the enemies and using your 'magic' (quickhacks) to manipulate stuff in game.

The weak suits are the combat itself (it's too easy and not challenging at all), stories that don't involve johnny or his insights (he's a colorful character that while crude, has a proper main character energy), driving (it feels off), bugs that are still in the game - there are a lot.

While bugs themselves don't outright softlock you and aren't game breaking, there's a ton of them. From bad rendering, to enemies phasing through stairs and catwalks, to vehicles spawning and despawning while you look, vehicles with enemies falling out of the sky and exploding on impact with the ground because you walked out a bit too far from their rendering , the vehicle you own spawning in unreachable places or places it can't leave from. . . There's a ton. I played a 'vanilla' experience naively thinking I wouldn't see all that mess. I was wrong. Perhaps there are mods improving those aspects, there should be some at this point anyway. 

The game itself is rather boring. The moment you realize your build you locked yourself into doesn't utilize quickhacks but has to rely on some other cyberware (part of equipment you 'wear') it becomes extremely straightforward and frankly, way too easy. I couldn't for the love of me sit through all the extra side content. I would physically die of boredom, so to leave an honest review, I rushed to the ending.

It's a blessing I could stick with the game for 117hrs but that's just because of my willpower to see it through and perhaps find something that's suddenly making this 6/10 game into 8 or 9. Sadly, in my case there was nothing of the sort.

Play if you must or otherwise feel compelled to, but only after getting it on sale. Don't have regrets for wasting money on something that was hyped out of the orbit and underdelivers.

comment:
Will update this review once problems are solved. In its current remastered state, I can't really recommend it FOR PLAY ON THE STEAM DECK, which is my main modality of play. 

On PC, with decent specs, it runs perfectly fine no issues with the remastered. If anything, the remastered edition looks a lot better, textures are less washed out, contrast is better, and the systems overhaul is pretty nice. However, playing it on the steam deck LCD is a different story. 

Pre-update I was able to play either locked 40fps native stable, or 30fps upscaled to 60fps with LSFG-VK 2.0 and have minimal input lag and smooth frametimes. Played like a dream to where I was (middle of Velen questlines). Post-update with the remastered, this is no longer possible. Running things at absolute lowest settings possible (lower than steam deck preset) WITHOUT LSFG feels like there's about 250ms of input lag and frametimes spike from 20-80ms, very unstable. With LSFG-VK 2.0 at 2x, optimized settings, input lag feels about 150-200ms but artifacts and tearing are a huge problem, no real improvements to frametimes either. Deck runs at about a constant 85-90C, so there's small room for graphical improvements, but none that would matter for stability or performance. This is what I consider unplayable. It's not LSFG producing the issues, the game literally cannot maintain stable 30fps in medium intensity areas, even at 1280x800 resolution, much less Novigrad. Yes, you can revert the game to pre-update status, but then why do the remastered update in the first place?

I don't doubt that they'll make performance updates over time, but in its current state, I cannot recommend it for the modality I play the game on. As with everything, YMMV, though.

comment:
Yet another generic open-world game, good game if it's the first open-world game you ever played
6/10

Pros: Graphics

Cons: 
1) BUGS: Still has multiple bugs after almost 6 years after release, MOSTLY VISUAL bugs, on one occasion wasn't able to pick an item to proceed with a side quest, found the exact same issue from a post 5 years ago - still isn't fixed.
2) Side Quests: 
A) 90% of them are kill/steal/grab a person or body and leave. Generic objectives = generic story. 
B) Side quests are spawned in a weird manner, coming in trickles, instead of spawning all of the options at once. While more "realistic", wastes the time to drive and teleport between cities one time after another to the same street.
C) SPAM: Too much spam in speeches, phone calls and SMS - even if there was something interesting in the 5% of them, I am not gonna read all of it because most of it are fillers.

Side activities except driving: none
PARKOUR: only jumping. so many body modifications but can only upgrade jump height - disappointing.
CYBERWARE ("hacker abilities"): not many options to choose from, and the ones you do own aren't very interesting in their usage - disappointing.
DIFFICULTY: Easy on "very hard" difficulty.
ECONOMY: Finished the game with 1.3M dollars because there is nothing to spend it on except body upgrades. No way of obtaining them for free, higher tiers are locked behind your level, making you to buy newer tier and sell the lower tier and wasting extra money instead of buying the higher tier (even though it's an RPG, it makes less sense when you can higher tier just appear out of nowhere just because you level up)
DRIVING: of the cars I have used, only cars that I received from quests don't have oily wheels. No chance of obtaining and driving an Air Vehicle? disappointing.
COMBAT: as simple as it gets, some enemies look differently but don't require drastic change of measures  to deal with them, simply shooting anywhere them will do. No thermal vision in 2077? too bad
AUTO-SAVES: on the face.

Summary:
Questionable game design, flat story (even the main story feels short), basic combat and gameplay. all budget went into graphics

comment:
I went into this open-minded, and with no spoilers. Big mistake. 14 hours into the game, I feel like I would have had more fun watching someone else on their second playthrough, rather than experiencing it myself for the first time.

Great writing and characters, but it's not a fun game.

The game wants you to explore the world and characters, but actually railroads you. Step 2 feet off the invisible "intended" path because the game suggests that you should? Have fun reloading after getting melted by a single frog or whatever + being forced to reload your save.

The good:
- The decisions you make, and the story itself is very malleable and impressively adaptive. 
- The characters are interesting. 
- The story is fun and engaging.

The bad:
- It's actually railroaded, despite how adaptive and free it may appear. You must follow exactly whatever the developers intended, in some way or another, and the illusion of choice is frustrating. 
- If you don't know how to deal with an encounter, you're screwed. The game doesn't teach you how to play, what's dangerous, or what's important. Have fun reloading your saves multiple times because you didn't know that a fight was coming, or realising that an enemy being 1 level above you stops you from progressing AT ALL, and then being forced to go and do something else. Combat is absolutely trial and error.

The ugly:
- Inventory management is not fun.
- Unless you've played DND before, you're basically guessing what everything does. 
- Tutorial pop-ups are sparse.

comment:
After the so-called “Remaster,” which basically forcefully slapped a bunch of mods onto the game, my opinion of the game itself has changed.

Let’s start with the fact that this isn’t really a remaster. It’s just a collection of forced mods that, as a player, I never asked for. The game worked perfectly fine for me as it was. If I wanted to replace or improve something, I could simply go to Nexus Mods and download whatever I needed myself.

But the developers decided that I needed exactly what they thought I needed.

Adding post-processing effects and volumetric lighting doesn’t make the game look better. It just highlights how outdated and angular the vegetation sprites actually are.

If you want to make a remaster, then make a proper, completely reworked version as a separate edition, like Dead Space. Don’t forcefully slap a bunch of mods onto something that was already working perfectly fine.

And if CD Projekt Red ever tries to pull something like this with Cyberpunk, I’ll simply start pirating all of their future projects. Because why should I pay for something when the developers might eventually ruin it because they decided that’s what I needed?

comment:
I've tried completing this game twice now, and I just can't get through it. 

It looks gorgeous, the world is interesting and the options for combat and story all seem cool. But after you dive a little deeper I always feel like its so, so shallow. 

I've tried smart weapons. It feels cool for a while but then you realise you've just trivialised everything because smart sniper just kills everyone from a safe distance. I was doing quests way above my level and killing cyber psychos I shouldnt be able to easily. So next attempt I tried a melee build and upped the difficulty, go the opposite way right? Again it felt initially cool and fun, but eventually I realised I can just walk or dash up to everyone, blocking bullets and then smash the attack key. Blocking, parrying, strong attacks? Waste of effort, just run up to people and quick attack. Job done. 

So many people to talk to, so many quests, until I realised that again, shallow. Everyone you try to talk to in the streets have one line they say and it has absolutely nothing to do with you or your story.  Conversations with NPC's it felt like no matter what option I chose it didnt matter hugely. 

Lots of gangs, lots of options and allegiances right? No, everyone just attacks you as soon as you go close to them. No story there, just mindless mobs. 

Even the weapons, there's so many but then eventually you realise theres almost no variety in how they make you play or what they really do. 

I don't get the love for this game, it feels like a nice picture you look at and then move on because that's all there is to it.

comment:
The Witcher 3 is one of my favorite games of all time and I've been looking forward to this remaster ever since they announced it for a full PC playthrough. Unfortunately, I have to say The Witcher 3 : Remastered on PC at the moment, is an absolute disaster of a release with many features either broken or not working at all. 

No amount of cutting edge hardware can brute force bad optimization and this release is the perfect example of it. Getting the same performance with and without Path Tracing Lol. Anyone who understands tech will tell you how absurd that sounds. My performance should have tripled without Path Tracing but instead I am getting the exact same performance for two drastically different looking graphics setting. Relying on frame gen to wheelchair you past 60fps on an RTX 4090 is crazy business.  They basically took an 11 year old game that looked perfectly fine in the first place, and made it so it doesn't run on the latest hardware 11 years later. I guess now it really is a modern game since modern games don't run well either.

The only copium/hopium I can gather from this is that at least CDPR are ditching this engine for good after next year's DLC. But it's not like Unreal Engine 5 is the gold standard for game optimization either 😂

Can't complain much about a FREE upgrade but you know you've ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up real bad when people are mad about something you gave them for FREE.

The fix for me was force-disabling the Easy Anti Cheat, which made me unable to play online. Smoothed out the open world frame drops. Still bad in dragon fights and other particle heavy fights though.

This game has its ups and downs. Exploration is the main draw of this game for me, something that didn't feel boring for even a minute. The reuse got a bit much at times, after having found almost every dungeon I must've fought 8 or so Erdtree Watchdogs. At some point it feels like you are better off not having seen all the game has to offer. Bosses are hit and miss. A lot are just overtuned. Some also have attacks that come out without any warning like Godrick's whirlwhind and Beast Clergyman's dual swipe. You must just learn to predict when these come out. I even did Malenia with no bleed and no spirit ashes/summons, took me maybe 80 or so attempts but at the end I was just glad it was over.

comment:
Look, I REALLY wanted to like this game, I love D&D but... This game just isn't it for me... The character customization is surprisingly limited, spell casters are useless, I get that level 1 spells and stuff need spell slots, but it feels like "Well, just had a hard combat, and I can't do anything anymore for the next hard one!" which really sucks cause I love spell casters in D&D, but what is the point of Minor Illusion or Disguise Self? When will I use them when I just have one combat after the other and no opportunity for shenanigans? The characters are annoying, I'm sure they're well written, I just don't like them. I really hate how the game rolls for me in combat. I get that makes the gameplay more streamlined, but I don't get the feeling that you get when you roll high in D&D, in this game it's just "Oh, the enemy took ___ damage, cool." And also the setting is just not it for me. I like having more low stakes, and I get that's not what the game is going for, but like there aren't any other D&D games so I don't have a choice??? And finally, there's like no player agency. So far all it feels like I can do is either: "You're cool." or "♥♥♥♥ you." and with some special differences like: "You're cool. [Roll Persuasion]" or "♥♥♥♥ you. [Roll Intimidation]" like I want to be able to do funny stuff, not just be forced to do the same things over and over... Oh yeah also cause the setting is so serious, I can't play as a goofy little guy, and I can't choose my characters backstory or like, anything?? I know it wouldn't be useful, just add it as an option???

Again, I'm sure this game is great later on, it just doesn't do it for me and I can't bother getting further in, which is sad, cause I was really hopeful it would be fun, and I can't refund it anymore. I just really wish this was more of a D&D game than a D&D inspired game.

comment:
The name is Baldur’s Gate. Show some respect for the name.

The game consists of three acts; the beginning is great, the middle is so-so... the final act and the ending are a total letdown. By the time you reach the third act, if you’ve done the side quests, you’re screwed: you hit the level cap. You end up playing the final 33% of the story without leveling up.

Whether weapons are +1, +2, or +3 doesn’t make much of a difference—they deal the same damage regardless of class or race, which is super ridiculous.

There are simplifications stemming from the 5th edition, like the removal of THAC0 and changes to AC calculations—they’ve simplified it way too much so even kids can play.

This simplification has really taken the fun out of the game: there’s not a single boss you can’t just slice and dice. You can take down a boss with the crappy sword you find at the start of the game? In BG and BG2, you’d have to agonize over “what the hell isn’t immune to this? Which item should we use to deal damage?”

Speaking of bosses, there were only two (2) dragon fights in the entire game.

One of these dragons is an undead dragon and the other is a red dragon—you can even cut them down with a plain old knife. Damn it, Larian, what a waste...

Under the guise of LGBT inclusivity, everyone can romance everyone else. This could have stayed an option, but it’s gone way beyond that. All your party members (yes, everyone—men, women, gay—everyone) are hitting on you at every rest stop, for ♥♥♥♥’s sake. Even the boss you defeat toward the end of the game (the Emperor) wants to have sex with you...

comment:
Let me start off by saying that objectively speaking this is a phenomenal game, but for someone who grew up playing Dark Souls 3 and Bloodborne as one of their first major gaming experiences ever it doesn't hit the same spot.

My main gripe with this is the open world. Coming from Dark Souls 3 and Bloodborne I was sceptical about this being open world, because I feared that the quality of level design and unique encounters would suffer as a result and unfortunately I was right. The few legacy dungeons that this game has don't even come close to the quality of other FromSoftware entries and they are ruined by the fact that you have to traverse a beautiful but empty open world to get there. Where other FromSoftware games' levels felt coherent and rewarding and respectful to the time you spent in them, this game puts too much emphasis on the space between them. There is no big AHA moments, where you would see a new area conncet back to an old one like in other games and ultimately those are the moments I love in FromSoftware games.

As I was saying in the beginning, this is by no means a bad game, it just feels like a punch in the face for anyone who loved the aspects of other FromSoftware games that this one is missing. As much as I like how them going open world to appeal to a wider audience made more people fall in love with their games, I really hope they go back to a more linear and interconnected design for their next main singleplayer entry.

comment:
1/10 — The Hackers Have Better Anti-Cheat Than the Developers
This game somehow managed to achieve an incredibly impressive feat – the actual enemy team isn’t the biggest problem here. The real monster is the anti-cheat.
Every single match is a competition of cheaters to see who can cheat more – wallhacks, aimbots, impossible tracking, headshots through walls – you name it, and at this point, I’m not even surprised. I’m not asking “how can they do this?” – I’m begging “how long are they going to let this happen?”
The very fact that the game’s “developers” allow this to happen is part of the issue, though
It’s wild how fast they could implement new skins, bundles, battle passes, events and other assorted cash grabs, but apparently, detecting a player who can spin around 5 times per second and wipe out an entire team while invisible through walls is too hard for their tiny team of developers to handle.
I can spend hours upon hours upon hours upon hours dedicated to improving my aim, learning the map, discovering new strategies and playing the game as it is supposed to be played – only for someone with a fresh account and a cheat to come into my lobby and turn it into a glorified target practice. I will report them, receive my prize of an empty “report received” message and pray that the next match won’t be another round of Hackerman Simulator 2026.
But what’s worse is that cheating in this game – and the lack of anti-cheat measures – destroy the game from the inside. The very premise of a competitive FPS is ruined when it’s possible to simply install a better cheat. Why would players invest time and money into the game if they can simply “download miracle cheat 3.0” and become the best player in the world?
The developers could have solved this problem in the past, but instead, they give us empty speeches about “community reports” and “dedicated servers”, giving us the same tired answers over and over again:
Hackers appear → players complain → devs promise action → nothing meaningful changes → hackers come back.
 It’s not funny anymore. The competitive FPS genre revolves around trust – and this single fact has been understood by cheat creators from day one. This development team, however, apparently does not have a brain, and that is a serious problem. The enemy team isn’t even the problem.At this point, the hackers aren’t cheating – they’re testing the quality of the anti-cheat and the dedication of the developers. Good gunplay, potentially fun gameplay, ruined by the feeling that I am playing the game against not opponents, but an army of script Kiddies who enjoy cheating. Will not be purchasing any time or items from this dev team until they show some dedication to fixing the game.

comment:
A great D&D adaptation, but a frustrating game

Baldur’s Gate 3 does an impressive job of translating D&D rules into a video game. Character classes, spells, abilities, dice rolls and many other mechanics are remarkably well implemented.

Unfortunately, I increasingly dislike the actual game built around those mechanics.

The biggest problem is the combat design. Especially in Act 3, major encounters constantly introduce enemies with special abilities that are poorly explained or completely unexpected. Enemies become invisible, stun characters, move without provoking opportunity attacks, apply multiple status effects, create darkness, and use combinations of actions that are difficult to understand from the player's perspective.

The problem isn't difficulty. **The problem is a lack of information.**

A good D&D encounter gives you enough information to make tactical decisions. BG3 too often makes you discover the rules by getting hit by them first. Eventually combat starts feeling less like *“How do I outsmart these enemies?”* and more like *“What ridiculous special ability did the game just pull out of nowhere?”*

Large encounters are another problem. Watching 15–20 enemies take their turns one after another makes fights incredibly slow. Combine that with all the status effects, animations and special abilities, and some battles become an exhausting exercise in waiting.

The camp system also becomes increasingly annoying. Wanting to take a long rest can turn into another cutscene, companion conversation, romance scene, dream sequence or even a fight. The companions are interesting, but the game sometimes feels like **group therapy with occasional adventuring in between**.

Loot has the opposite problem. In BG1 and BG2, finding a magical item was exciting. In Act 3 of BG3, I constantly find supposedly powerful items and think: *“What am I supposed to do with this?”* Many are so build-specific that they immediately become vendor trash.

And then there are the technical and UI problems: unclear mechanics, missing or misleading indicators, awkward camera behavior, and situations where the game behaves differently from what its descriptions suggest.

I actually like the D&D rules in BG3 a lot.

**It's the game built around them that increasingly frustrates me.**

I enjoyed BG1, BG2, Icewind Dale and Neverwinter Nights much more. They had fewer systems, smaller encounters and less spectacle, but they generally **let me play instead of constantly getting in my way**.

At this point, I frequently find myself asking:

**“How do I beat this?”**

followed by:

**“Do I really want to spend another hour doing this?”**

That's a disappointing place for a Baldur's Gate game to leave me.

**Excellent D&D implementation. Increasingly frustrating game design.**

comment:
The story mode is very fun and the graphics are still very pretty in 2026, however as good as the premise of the story is, it still has some minor plot holes. More importantly, the story mode has remained the same since the game's release in 2013, it has received 0 DLC's. 
Every update the online mode gets more and more unplayable. Sessions crash unreliably when playing with friends, and the game can crash even on powerful hardware. The online mode has memory leak issues, causing longer sessions to have progressively worse performance until you join another session. Not to mention how Rockstar strategically engineered the progression and focus of this mode specifically so that players are incentivised on buying Shark Cards (using real money to get in-game currency). More specifically, the introduction of unrealistic sci-fi vehicles such as the Deluxo or Oppressor MK1 and MK2, essentially founded a toxic playerbase, which annoyed new players, causing them to want to get those vehicles too, and the cycle continues. I hate to say this, but this is still a good game mode. The simple nature of this online mode being based off a story game, means there is little for the developers to get wrong. Even if the game is the most cash-grabby piece of media in the last decade, it will still be fun.

comment:
I was positive I'd love this game, I mean look at the accolades and Steam rating.  I bought it once when it came out and got a refund.  Then, just this week I was convinced I just bought it at the wrong time the first time, and that now I'd really dig into it.

That didn't happen, I still think it is just plain overrated.  It has some positive aspects, not a complete waste of time but overall I just can't recommend it.  The main problem I have as a Keyboard and Mouse PC user is that the controls JUST PLAIN SUCK!  It's not just me, this is a  well known issue.  The target lock is broken, yes I know you can choose to not use it but let's be honest at this price and this far along in the game features that are in the game should just plain work.  This is what happens when a console title is ported to PC . . . poorly.  That alone is a deal breaker for me.

Another thing I just didn't care for are the enemies.  Not so much the bosses, but the regular enemies you encounter along the way.  They just seem so . . . "synthetic".  They remind me of automatons, like robots very strange looking and moving.  Yes the world is huge, but it seemed like I was just running around killing time looking for something useful to do, and at the  same time any threat that I came across was more than likely something that would just outright kill me.  The avatar you play in the game is just plain weak.  Not looking for easy mode here, I like a challenge but my "Hero" should have some better combat ability, especially when encountering enemies straight out of the gate in "newbie" areas.

The combat is pretty lame IMO, again mostly because of the horrendous controls and targeting.  Just kind of repetitive and uninteresting to me.  And the gear progression leaves not much to look forward to.  I start my Samurai with a weapon and armor set that I will be using pretty much the whole game.  Yes I can add +1, +2, +3, +4 to my Sword but wow, not much to look forward to or work for.  The armor I start with is pretty much it, and the Katana I start with is one of the best in game...so no progression to work towards there.

I'm certainly in the minority, as most folks LOVE this game.  But, I bought it once early on . . . got a refund.  Bought it again later on and walked away from it, again.  This time I had enough hours so that there was no refund option, so they got my money.

Bought Dark Souls II after uninstalling Elden Ring . . . WOW, now this is something special.  Wish I'd have bought this first!

comment:
First off, Elden Ring is not a bad game. The boss fights, visuals and world building are all cool, and while I finished the game and then some, its just... a drag. 

The world is massive, and you can really feel it. Exploration is a key to Elden Ring, and that can be fun at times. What is not fun, is the absurd scale of the game combined with a complete lack of non-filler content. Useless crafting materials, random ashes (another whole topic on its own) and grave glovewort being treated like "rewards" for exploring far off corners of the world, same one enemies in every dungeon, and half of the boss fights being "what if we did it again... but now there's two of them". Same one tree sentinel. Same one tree spirit.

With enemies scattered all over with nothing to gain from killing them, the game heavily encourages you to not fight, and just explore in the open world. What's that? John Knight patroling a random road drops a unique item, but you ignored him as he's literally a generic enemy found all over elsewhere? Oh well, thats unfortunate. Better luck next time. 

Souls games inherently will never be possible to mostly complete on a first run without some sort of guide, and quest chains even more so as they're intended to be done over multiple playthroughs, but the insane amount of NOTHING in this game that is just recycled over and over and over that you CANNOT skip without a guide because guess what, that one dungeon you chose to skip, missed or forgot was the one dungeon that didnt just have useless ashes in them. That one hill over there might have a key item for your build or quest chain, so you better go explore it thoroughly, but wait... there was nothing. Again.

As I started with, the game isnt bad. The game is mostly enjoyable. It has some crazy fights, its weapons and various forms of incantations/sorceries are very cool, but there's just too much in this game that has no place, or is recycled adding nothing but filler, for me to reccomend it before literally any other fromsoft souls game. If part of the enjoyment in these games for you is trying to explore and find as much as possible without help, the world is filled with far too much nothing, but hey, at least it will look pretty and the main boss fights will be cool.

comment:
I've put off buying this game since release. The reason: the original teaser showed a very gritty very brutal and harsh world. The first gameplay trailer showed it to be "GTA but reskinned to future tech".

But due to a deep sale I gave it a shot.

It's alright. It's definitely entertaining. But it's not the game I was hoping it would be. It's not the "Blade Runner" dark dystopian vibes. It's more "GTA meets Saints Row" vibes. "haha d*ck implants malfunction" vibes. The characters are all caricatures, stereotypes, blown to the extremes. Voice lines sometimes feel like they recorded them out of order over several sessions with no cohesion or flow. You are constantly being slammed by messages and calls and side information but there really isn't that much reason to read it all because there's very little substance to the world building and it feels tedious. It also doesn't feel like you actually change the course of the game at all as often your dialog options are the same but just worded differently. 

If we look at gameplay: the main missions offer a bunch of ways to get the objective done. That's cool. Outside of that there's no dialog options to talk your way out of things. Stealth is not really rewarded and a lot of it is just combat. The combat in itself is pretty alright but at higher difficulty enemies just become spongy and your weapons generally feel quite weak making a human take as many bullets to the head as a full on robot. For a Saints Row game that's what I'd expect. I was hoping for something a little better here.

Overall with the expectation of an immersive dystopian RPG I can't give it more than a 6/10. It's fun. It works well as 'mindless entertainment' (although admittedly there's to much in the sense of unskipable cutscenes / dialog in the game to be purely that.... just the 'intro' to the game took me 4 hours while not doing that much besides getting to the title screen. Dialog where you don't really have options aside from saying the same thing 2 different ways which in the end doesn't matter).

I think the framework for this game is solid. The art direction is very cool. The music is solid. The factions and stuff that's all good. If they every make a part 2 I hope they invest more into it being an actual RPG more akin to Deus Ex or Mass Effect (although... well controversial ending... but that aside) and that they make it a bit more grounded and gritty.

comment:
This is a very difficult review for me and I cannot show all my motivations in this section, after all if you are reading this you want a quick opinion before you buy the game.

First of all, I’m sure that most of this reviews here are from genuinely honest people that enjoyed this game, and I can see why. The mechanics are impressive, the implementation of powers, spells, skills it’s a breath of innovation; for the most part the game feels alive with interaction of NPC, great voice acting, choices and consequences. 
If this game was called something like “Legends of Forgotten Realms” or “Heroes of the Sword Coast” and wasn’t connected in any way from the previous Baldur’s Gate saga I would love this game 100%.
But sadly it is not.

The fact is, in my opinion, Baldur’s Gate 2 Throne of Bhaal was the perfect ending for the saga, maybe a little rushed  (the developers they were hurrying due to the upcoming shutting down of the company).
A book also from those years established the canon ending, clearly stating the fate of most of the notable characters, even the Bhaal Spawn.
I played dozens of time BG and BG2 plus the expansions, I shared those moments with the community of the time and we appreciate the character’s arch and stories of each one. 

 Then Wizard of the Coast released the modules Descent to Avernus and Murder in Baldur’s Gate, compromising the endings from the awesome series by reintroducing PNG that were supposed to be elsewhere or not existing. 
And probably Larian’s writers did even worst, [spoiler]by no respecting the few good canonic elements and reconnecting the main plot to the previous BG chapters.[/spoiler] 
All because they want to grab more income by squeezing a well loved brand that most people out there do not remember so well anymore. 
Larian had the resource  to write an all new story, a new brand for a spectacular title. Instead they lacked courage by playing safe.
Also I want to mention the impressive presence of bugs related to sub quest, graphical errors that breaks the immersion  especially in the last chapter of the game. Considering the game was in early access for a very long time (full price around 60 bucks) and the use of AI during the last period of develop this is a very reprehensible conduct. 
I do not reported the bugs and errors I encountered during my experience.

My only hope is in the newer generation of player. Who may enjoy good stories, who may discover the first games and who wants to appreciate the old adventures and perfect ending… do not stop on the surface and find out how the game industry was different back then. 

I know we are not so many anymore and maybe this message is not important; but if YOU are like me, a real fan of BG, do not buy this game. It’s an insult to all the original BG’s writers and the gamers who loved the series.

comment:
I've debated with myself a lot if I should give this game a good or bad review, because in many ways it's a really great game, but the issues I have with the game is so core to the experience that I simply can't justify a good review.

The bad:
 - When you do an attack it attacks in the direction of your last movement input. I believe it should attack in the direction of where you're looking.
 - Dodge and run on the same key. This makes a lot of the dodging so inconsistent since it's very obvious that starting to run is very delayed, and if you're already running it suddenly require you to unclick + click to dodge.
 - Action buffering seems *very* inconsistant. I've have yet to figure out the exact rules for when an action buffers, and when it doesn't. Because of this most often the action buffering will get me killed, because my char will do unpredicable actions I didn't expect.
 - Poisen/rot/etc. swamps seems to only make you stand in a corner and wait and waste your IRL time mostly.
 - Hotbar and menus in general just seem so badly designed. Hotbar/weapon swaps require you as a mouse user to let go of your mouse to do the swaps.
 - Many bosses 2nd stage seems to use *spam particles on players screen so he can't see* as a difficulty mechanic.
 - Area denial attacks from many bosses seems to have very bad hurt boxes.

The good:
 - Stunning game.
 - Great and rewarding boss design.
 - Insane amount of hours of content (granted 75% of that is dying fighting bosses).

Overall:
I really enjoyed the game in general, but because the attack/movement mechanics is just such a core part of the game, the frustration with the bad control design in the end means I'll be giving the game a negative review.

comment:
I've played through the game several times, and every time I complete the game I like it a little less. I've played more hours on another account, I have completed the game three or four times. I will be concise.

It is scripted to all hell, cutscenes galore, actual roleplaying opportunities are few and far between without impactful consequences. I cannot in good faith call this game a good RPG, this is just Skyrim with a different setting. I found it very hard to care about any of the characters - everyone was just a different brand of weird ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I had no attachments to any of the characters when I reached the end of the game. I would have rather had them all killed.

The best part of the game by far is combat, specifically melee combat. Again, the CD Project Red has laid another dung pie that scales with player level with level equipment. Maybe there are people who enjoy the life of a homeless person with a horde of garbage in a shopping cart, but I certainly don't. I have no tolerance for having to sift through all the corpses to find an item that is 5% better. And there is crafting for some reason? Yes, pick up even more ♥♥♥♥ and turn it into other ♥♥♥♥. It's just busywork. The game is at its best when you get a legendary weapon so you don't have to look for another one and just start cutting people into pieces after acquiring the necessary skills and cyberware. The game is much better if you completely ignore the meager RPG components and just play it as an action game.

So, in conclusion, it's a very bad RPG. If you are looking for a true RPG experience, don't play it. The plot is okay, the combat is okay. You will get some enjoyment out of playing this game, but it's not worth it.

comment:
Lots of good things to say about the game but at the end of the day I'm not really having fun. Other games (including its predecessors) reward you for immediately responding to the move an enemy is making. Elden Ring, however, has basically all enemies bait your reaction so that you end up getting hit as you're dodging. Now this is fine when you're in a 1v1, but it's really far from fine when lots of encounters involve multiple opponents. To avoid this you need to apply cheese, lure enemies into hallways, etc. It's frankly not fun.

Co-op is fun as long as you're not encountering invaders, who will have cleared the entire game already while invading lvl 20 players and 1-shotting the host and all the other phantoms. Profoundly un-fun.

All pvp revolves around creating a build that just stunlocks someone or 1-shots someone so the moment you're hit you're already dead or in an unstoppable process of dying.

Other developers would be adding free content to the game to reward loyal players, but this company decides to charge €5 for some overpowered weapon(s).

If you like the other souls games I genuinely cannot guarantee at all that you'll enjoy this one.

comment:
The Death of The Cayo Perico Heist: How Rockstar Methodically Killed the Only Fair Content in GTA Online
When The Cayo Perico Heist dropped in December 2020, GTA Online players felt like they could finally breathe. After years of forced cooperative misery, mental breakdowns caused by unreliable random players, and outrageously overpriced properties, Rockstar finally delivered something that felt too good to be true: a highly lucrative heist that could be played entirely solo.

Cayo Perico was the ultimate symbol of freedom in Los Santos. You didn’t have to beg anyone to join, and you didn’t have to waste hours on tedious setups. You could jump in, pull off a slick stealth run, and pocket $1.3 to $1.8 million in just over an hour.

But then, Rockstar realized that players were actually having fun, and—more importantly in their eyes—they weren’t buying Shark Cards anymore. That’s when the methodical, ruthless, and shameless nerfing of the heist began, turning El Rubio's island into a frustrating, low-paying chore.

The Rap Sheet: How a Jackpot Was Turned into Spare Change
1. The Desecration of the Pink Diamond and Primary Targets
We used to cheer when we saw the pink diamond on the security cameras, knowing we were in for a massive payday. Today, Rockstar has practically stripped these targets of their value. Slashing the value of the Pink Diamond—sometimes dragging the total payout of a solo run down toward the $900k mark—is a massive slap in the face to the player's time. Why risk your neck against a private army when you walk away with barely more than what a basic VIP contract used to pay?

2. The Systematic Punishment of Solo Players (The Cooldown Terror)
The most hostile move was the execution of the solo playstyle. If you complete the heist alone, the game now forces a brutal 3-game-day cooldown (approx. 2 hours and 24 minutes) before you can start it again. Meanwhile, team play has a much shorter cooldown. This isn’t "game balance"; it's blatant extortion: “Play with others (who will take a cut of your money), or wait hours to play again.”

3. Guards Suddenly Became Mind-Reading Geniuses (Wallhack AI)
Stealth was the beating heart of Cayo Perico. You followed your memorized route, quietly took out the guards, and slipped away unnoticed. But Rockstar rolled out an update where guards now detect dead bodies. While this sounds good on paper, GTA Online’s notoriously buggy, decade-old AI turned it into a disaster. Guards now frequently see through solid walls or spot corpses on the completely opposite side of the map. Precise stealth has been replaced by a frustrating, unpredictable gamble.

4. Jacked-Up Setup Fees
Just to make absolutely sure you don’t keep too much of your hard-earned cash, they quadrupled the heist setup fee from $25,000 to $100,000. Before you even set foot on the island to scout, you start in the negatives, all while your final payout is actively being gutted.

Verdict: A Monument to Corporate Greed
The current state of the Cayo Perico Heist is a perfect mirror of what GTA Online has become: a game that is no longer designed to entertain you, but to frustrate you into opening your real-world wallet.

They took away the freedom, they took away the fair pay, and they replaced it with a buggy, soul-crushing grind. Rockstar didn't just ruin El Rubio's island; they sabotaged their relationship with their own community. This isn't game development—it's highway robbery.

sluggish and unpolished mess that admittedly becomes very fun with the introduction of a complete deflection system. i will never play this game without the fantastic deflection mod, i struggle to understand how anyone could consider this games combat a fun or engaging evolution of the priorly perfected souls combat of bloodborne, dark souls 3, and sekiro. major bosses with the aggression and combo complexity of sekiro and dark souls 3, but with the unresponsive and sluggish mobility of ds1/ds2. 

elden ring is significantly carried by its worldbuilding, narrative, and characters. in the absence of such good writing, elden ring is a very obviously unfinished game. i will appeal to the flippant asset reuse as evidence that supports my theory that elden ring was never finished. with some notable exceptions such as morgott, midra, messmer, and mohg, elden ring has the second weakest and most unpolished roster of humanoid bosses in the series. 

a very confused and disorganized development team made this game. its almost as if this was a collaborative project, with no succinct and comprehensible vision, developed by many people who may not have ever even met other members of the development team. there is unfortunately no defense for such inconsistency, no matter how fervent elden ring defenders become. this game is monolithically flawed in ways prior souls games were not. elden ring should not have been an open world rpg, maybe then it wouldn't be the bloated and unpolished mess it is 

the deflection mod fundamentally fixes malenia though, which is pretty epic. fighting a sekiro boss with no ability to deflect and with no mobility is pretty unpleasant. ♥♥♥♥ boss made extremely good by the introduction of deflections.

mid game, overrated game, unpolished game, not terrible game, not great game, the third worst souls game, still much better than ds2

comment:
This review is NOT how I would rate the game. If it was, I'd give it a 11/10. Great gameplay, story, art, everything! This review is if I would recommend this game to other people who are looking through Elden Ring steam reviews, and If you aren't sure on whether to get this game or not, please listen to what I have to say.

If you are looking for a game with amazing... Everything... get this game. It is allows thousands of different playstyles with thousands of great weapons and armor. Even better with the DLC! HOWEVER... this game does not hold your hand whatsoever, and that is partially why I don't recommend it to newer souls players or people who want to have a laid back time. Before you flame me or tell me I'm wrong, I beat the game with 120 hours with no guide or help whatsoever, so although some things might be wrong, I have a good amount of experience with this game. Regarding this "hand holding" issue, I have two major concerns. 

1. This game is extremely vague with where you are supposed to go.
Sights of Graces are helpful and tell you where to be to some extent, but in some instances, it doesn't help you outright and you are forced to look up where to go or what to do. There is a great example around 1/4-1/3 of the way into the game that I constantly find people looking up where to go.

2. Quest and Items can be extremely hard to find and are locked behind dialogue options, choices, bosses killed etc. Which gets rid of the desire to pursue it in the first place.
This kinda goes with my first reason, but this is such a large issue that it should be mentioned. All of my friends who have played this game struggled to level up or find items, which led them to look up where to go, defeating basically the entire purpose of this game of discovery. I know this game is supposed to be extremely difficult, (I have played other fromsoftware games like sekiro) but for a game as large and expansive as Elden ring, I feel that there should be some sort of way to at least track quests or give you a hint of where to go.

In conclusion, if you skipped everything else, If you are a die hard FromSoftware fan 100% get this game, it is peak. But if you are not familiar with how FromSoftware does it, Elden Ring should not be the first game you play. It overwhelms many beginners and causes them to quit early.

comment:
Regarding prevailing evaluations, I contend that BG3 is an exceptionally well-crafted game, yet ultimately constrained by excessive structural rigidity.

While the game offers substantial exposure to the practical mechanics of DnD, it falls short of delivering the degree of agency typically associated with the genre. Although such restriction may be justified as a compromise to accommodate novice players or to streamline development, the resulting experience is overly prescriptive and limits genuine player autonomy.

The narrative architecture is predominantly linear and unidirectional. Consequently, players are confronted with a dilemma: either compromise immersion—an essential expectation in CRPGs—by exhaustively completing side content despite the urgent narrative premise of a mind flayer parasite, or engage in repeated playthroughs with alternative characters. In the latter case, players are compelled to enact decisions that may contradict prior moral alignments or emotional investments, thereby undermining narrative coherence and experiential continuity.

The core design deficiency lies in the absence of a meaningful post-narrative state. Unlike The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, which permits continued exploration in a decompressed, post-resolution environment, or Red Dead Redemption 2, where narrative succession is achieved through a character such as John Marston, BG3 terminates the player’s progression abruptly upon completion of the main storyline. This design choice is neither sufficiently foreshadowed nor mitigated.

As a result, the relational bonds formed with companions, along with the accumulated value of equipment and progression systems, are rendered functionally obsolete. The player’s sustained investment—both affective and strategic—is effectively nullified at the moment of narrative closure. What remains is a diminished incentive structure, wherein the only recourse is to re-engage with previously unexperienced content through repetition rather than organic continuation.

This structural limitation significantly attenuates the game’s long-term experiential depth and undermines the durability of player engagement.
