comment:
[b]tl;dr[/b] - Many times I've regretted giving Baldur's Gate 3 chances. Turn back now.

Buy only at deep discount if you're a CRPG/D&D fan. Accolades and rampant Stockholm syndrome aside, this is a painfully flawed game three years after release, still unacceptably janky. If you're even slightly bothered by poor UX or bugs, prepare to suffer death by a thousand little cuts.

Let's begin...

[h2][b]The UI - frenemy at best, always pressing its thumb on the scale against you:[/b][/h2]

*  The default camera constantly gets in the way, obstructing free views of the battlefield. At times it's so disorienting you'll struggle to tell what's going on. Just to attack somebody the game keeps obscuring, you'll have to click this over here... then that over there... then that up there...(By Act 2 I had to install a mod just to make it playable).

* In a game where every other threat triggers turn based mode, when you encounter traps that do damage based on time, does it pause? Nope. Experience low level parties perishing on the clock as you frantically try to button-press your way out of it. Worse - press wrong, and it's possible to initiate dialogue between characters _as they burn in real time_. Like some dark comedy, your party is locked behind a text based UI, discussing whatever plot point Larian decided was more important than their gradually cooking into charcoal briquettes, screams punctuating your mouse clicks.

*  Try to shoot a pesky goblin who hit you just a moment before and it'll reply 'it's not possible', beginning a new mini-game: line-of-sight-wackamole. Spend many mouse clicks sleuthing which spot will allow you to return fire without yourself stumbling through acid, poison, or fire. Don't worry, if you give up, the auto-aim is always there to masochistically drag you through things that hurt.

[h2][b]Bugs - so many still awkward or outright broken features:[/b][/h2]

*  Group pathing is excellent... at doing exactly the wrong thing. Click to go around or even jump over that obviously dangerous acid pool, and your party members follow you... stumbling through it like idiots anyway. Break group to avoid this? Enjoy 4x the number of keystrokes and mouse clicks. There's no undo function for inevitable clicking mistakes - hope you don't mind frequently reloading from saves.

*  Quests glitch, incompletable due to some decision you made hours ago, or not starting at all. You can try to hide finished items in your bloated quest log but that feature will turn itself off every new session.

*  Items for summoning assistance in tough battles... activate in the wrong place and your mercenary ogres just stand there, their AI pathing unable to navigate a giant room (looking at you, Goblin Boss fight). Then afterwards, they'll demand 500 gold for literally doing nothing.

[h2][b]Annoyances - plenty to go around...[/b][/h2]

*  Enemies react utterly inconsistently, sometimes ignoring combat right in front of them (the realtime->turn-based transitional logic deserves its own post). Today a battle 'ended' within obvious view of an enemy who'd not yet aggro'd. Then, instead of giving back control, said non-combatant enemy suddenly 'woke up,' beginning a brand new fight! ...Cancelling all my prior-battle consumables and yanking me back to turn-based mode... despite neither pressing a button nor anybody moving. Oh goodie... guess I'll have to re-bless... and spend another charge of barbarian rage... and...

*  Don't you dare keep characters together for mutual support. Most people in the Baldur's Gate universe seems to carry acid bottles in their pocket, AoE so rampant it makes the previously mentioned line of sight problems even worse. D:OS2 explodium barrels(tm) return for several guest appearances too. Stand in the wrong place and... boom, sweep up your character's residue~

*  Action bars change without your consent and the logic for placing new buttons is poor at best, dumping icons haphazardly. Hope you like futzing with everything over and over again if you're remotely interested in customizing. Every level. Every new weapon type.

[h2][b]And the rest...[/b][/h2]

How does Larian compensate for some of these problems? By shoving at you small mountains of consumables and vendor trash items until your bags nearly burst, becoming a tedious inventory. Rewards are oddly paced, progression just mildly interesting. Resources go out of wack once you recognize camp supplies are basically limitless, allowing you to long rest after every battle, far more than any D&D campaign would allow.

Too easy? Turn up the difficulty so UI flaws become downright hostile. You'll struggle to get characters to do what you want, a single mis-click frequently ending battle in catastrophe. Eventually saving before every battle round isn't cheesing - it becomes... necessary.

Sigh.

On the plus side, the story is remarkable for its many paths - no other title I've tried goes to these lengths (though expect cliche and forced moments - Shadowheart... I just met you and you're trying to jump my bones). And the many lines of dialogue, well acted, making you feel like you're part of an actual world? Solid.

But even when the best parts rise to the surface, starting to immerse you, the jank buzzes back into your face like some aggravating fly you can't waive off, reminding you're just playing a messy CRPG that will never get the polish it desperately needs. There might be a good game... buried... under all this... somewhere... but it's tiring to look. If you're not familiar with D&D 5e, it'll be twice as hard.

"Okay, relax, you're just being picky..."

"It's just a game, reload and start again..."

"...This is fun..."

<<Game Lucy-Footballs me with some new issue>>

"..."

Not sure I'll ever reach Act 3. Quit more than once, then blown the dust off months later while bored and had no other games to play. Do I hate myself? Guess so. Will I continue to fall for it? Probably - that's on me. Do I believe in this negative review? With all my heart.

Thank you for reading. /rant

comment:
Divinity: Original Gate 3 is an impressive game in some aspects. The scale, visuals and how some quests have multiple ways to complete them - the amount of work put into it is truly amazing.

But my god is this game boring. I've tried playing it several times and I could not bring myself to playing it longer than the first act. If not for my friends - I would not be able to finish the game.
Some say that this is THE best RPG of all times. Well, in last 5-7 years, yeah, maybe. But this speaks of overall RPG games quality of the last years, and does not make BG3 "the best of all times".
- The writing in the game is between mediocre and just plain bad, with plenty of stupid motivations and illogical outcomes/dialogues.
- I still don't understand what this game has to do with the Baldur's Gate name. It's Divinity Original Sin that just references "Baldur's Gate" quite often.
- The worst enemy in the game is the camera itself. One of the worst if not the worst camera I've experienced.
- The main story is uninteresting at best.
- I like when player is being introduced to a world that lives by itself, having it's own rules, logic, factions etc. In BG3 the world revolves around the player. You're the best, the finest, the strongest, your allies are demigods and EVERYONE wants to f**k you eventually, whether you've romanced the NPC or not. It's like a power fantasy for little kids, not a "real world" that was and will be just fine without the player.
- It maybe has something to do with me being old and grumpy, but I hate almost every companion NPC in this game, they are so annoying.
- The fact that you hit level cap long before the end of the game is just... why?
- Bugs. Well known bugs still, after all this time.

In my opinion the best Larian game is still Divinity: Original Sin 1. Enjoyed it much more than BG3.

comment:
I genuinely don't understand how you take one of the greatest games ever made and somehow manage to make it feel this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ disappointing.

The Witcher 3 is a game that has aged remarkably well, even by today's standards. Its world, atmosphere, environmental storytelling and art direction were already phenomenal. The next-gen update was supposed to take all of that to another level, but instead, at least on my system, it feels like a downgrade disguised as a graphical upgrade.

Let's talk about the graphics first. Without ray tracing, the game looks surprisingly flat. The lighting lacks the depth and natural feel that made the original experience so immersive. Shadows, ambient lighting and environmental details often look inconsistent, and the overall image just doesn't have the visual richness you'd expect from a so-called next-gen update. And the worst part? Turning on ray tracing doesn't exactly solve the problem either. Instead, it absolutely chokes the GPU, turning what should be a visually enhanced experience into a frustrating performance nightmare. For a mid-range GPU, the optimization is genuinely atrocious. The performance cost is simply absurd for what you're getting in return.

And then there are the graphical glitches. Clothes flicker, textures don't always seem to match their surroundings, and certain environmental elements look completely out of place. The weather effects can look inconsistent, and the lighting sometimes feels disconnected from the environment. There are moments when the entire world looks gorgeous, followed by moments where everything just falls apart visually. The inconsistency is infuriating, especially when the game's original art direction was already so damn good.

The whole experience gives me serious pre-Cyberpunk 2077-release vibes. The kind of technical mess where the ambition is clearly there, but the execution leaves you wondering whether anyone actually tested the experience properly across different hardware configurations. It's frustrating to see a game with such an incredible legacy suffer from technical issues that take away from the very atmosphere that made it special in the first place.

And honestly, that's what pisses me off the most. This isn't some mediocre game that needed a complete visual overhaul to become relevant again. This was The Witcher 3. A masterpiece that didn't need to sacrifice its stability and visual consistency just to chase modern graphical features. A proper optimization pass, consistent lighting, stable textures and reliable performance should have been the bare minimum.

I'm not against graphical upgrades. Ray tracing can look incredible when implemented properly, and I'm all for pushing visual fidelity forward. But when the game feels noticeably worse without it and becomes a performance disaster with it, something has clearly gone wrong with the overall experience.

For now, I'm putting this game aside. I would much rather revisit the original experience than keep fighting with graphical inconsistencies, flickering textures, questionable lighting and performance issues that completely ruin the immersion.

It's genuinely disappointing to see one of the greatest RPGs ever made brought down by technical problems that should never have overshadowed the experience in the first place.

An absolute masterpiece of a game, let down by an update that feels like it needed a lot more time, testing and optimization. I'll be coming back when this mess is actually worth playing again.

comment:
The game has a lot to offer, but in it's current state, 2 years after release, if you want to roleplay as anything but what the intended path is: don't bother.

For multiple hours I've been trying to tolerate many sequence breaks, buggy triggers and wonky fights, but the breaking point is how the game punished me for having the one race that doesn't let me gain an inspiration event... let me explain:

Spoilers for Act 1:
[spoiler]So I'm Dark Urge as a Female Drow, I'm trying to roleplay as an evil character. I'm on the "goblin temple" where Gut is. So I go to the torture chamber to get a Dark Urge inspiration. The goblin tortures see me and I say to step aside and let me handle it. They obey and decide to leave the place... but I have no option to torture the prisoner. I can talk to the prisoner and get information about Halsin and the Nightsong, I can pick up the torture weapons, but I can't attack the prisoner or have a dialogue option that lets me torture him. No option as a drow allows me to torture the prisoner. So the work-around is to use Disguise Self, turn to another race and THEN the option will appear for me to torture... why? Why is this even a thing, considering Drows are basically the more intended-to-be evil aligned races in the entire game and THEY are the ones that miss out on one of the most evil actions on act 1? It's stupid on several ways, and this is a drow-exclusive interaction Larian Studios knowingly programmed without the option to torture.

And if we must point out other issues I have had so far with my playthroughs of this game: NPCs don't react to the bodies of their own kin on ground.... so basically I wanted to slaughter all the druids in the emerald grove, so I, one-by-one, sometimes two at a time, used Performance and Minor Illusion to guide them to some outside area, and repeatedly killed them outside of sight of other druids. And that way I was able to kill all druids with none of them suspecting a thing or reacting to the dead druid bodies.

I accepted to be on a romance with Lae'zel, but with no sex scene yet, it was just the flag to trigger the initial romance. When I went outside of camp, Shadowheart and Laezel were talking about how good we were on bed, even though we never did anything.

Another major issue: at night, Astarion confided to me about his vampiric nature, and I asked about Cazador and his backstory, so on... then, on the same night, the cutscene where Astarion tries to bite me plays out, and my character (and the game) act like this was a huge revelation and they did not know about it. The next morning, the same dialogue options about Cazador and his backstory were there as if I had not triggered them already, so the game got confused with flags.

It also happened that goblins have shot through walls with their arrows to hit my characters in some combat during the blighted village. And it wasn't through a window or crack, it was literal solid wood wall, a goblin was on the other side and Astarion on the other, they shot and hit me, and Astarion couldn't hit back with his bow.

I've also faced many wonky path-finding moments where my characters went through extremely long paths for something that was mere meters away from them, happened at least twice: in the goblin camp and in the dark cave below blighted village.

And there's no search option on the adventurer's chest, which can easily have over 100 items in just a few hours of exploring (which the game heavily encourages)

The game continuously makes several time-restricting scenarios/ideas in the earlygame, which would make you think you shouldn't long rest as that could mean events will happen while you sleep, but the truth is that next to nothing happens if you long rest, in fact you HAVE to if you want to progress character stories. My issue with the long rest system is that it is inversely proportional to the story's narrative and what you would think is going to happen or should happen, and the paranoia that events MIGHT happen if you long rest is completely broken when you realize they won't, such as the hyenas being pregnant with gnolls for several days or karlach being wounded and a few meters aways from her hunters for several long rests, just standing there.[/spoiler]

While I'd love to go on about every inconvenience, some minor and some major, steam has a text limit, so I'll drop here.

So, in summary, the roleplaying game has too many events and scenarios which absolutely break the roleplaying aspect of it, for too many times has my immersion been broken, and basically I can't properly play as an evil character because the game isn't built with that in mind, it's built with you being a helpful hand. I won't recommend you play it if you're as picky as I am. But otherwise it's an okay game to turn your brain off to.

comment:
Where to begin....

God I had such high hopes for this game..

Ok act one. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ what a world CD project ReD created!
You're dropped into this MASSIVE world that feels so alive your mind just experience a complete overload.
On top of that their path-tracing technology and general visual effects are so beyond anything else thats out there you can almost smell the humidity as it rains on the asphalt! 

Technologically speaking this game is surreal!

Then you start exploring, doing all the side gigs
Getting to know all the NPC and what they stand for.
It doesn't take long to realize that the science fiction aspect of this game is really mostly related to the medical implant aspect. It does not take long to realize this game pulls no punches when it comes to some of the ugliest things that humanity, or lake-thereof, has to offer.
Drugs, abuse, coercion, exploitation, murder, torture, suicide, mental illness, black-mail, violation of ones autonomy... this game doesn't just "NOT" shy away from it, it flat out embraces these topics.

By the time you reach the end of act 1 you are neck deep in corporate conspiracies, loss of any autonomy, and you find yourself in a landfill, thrown out discarded like trash, WITH trash, fully betrayed by the very city you've come to love.

Act one Cyberpunk 2077 is a 10/10... top shelve, nothing better out there, no doubt...



then comes act 2...

And all of a sudden the writers mediocrity becomes very clear VERY quickly..
The entire act 1 was designed to give you the chance to shape what kind of V you wanted to be.
-Stealthy
-honorable
-mass murdering ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
Take your pick!! it was all in your own hands.

Act 2 in contrast to that forcefully funnels your character, and all the side characters, down a very narrow trajectory that quit frankly is so poorly written it would make a cheap porno feel like an Oscar nominee by comparison!!! And that's NOT hyperbole!!!

Lets start with the obvious.
Almost nothing you do produces the degree of narrative consequence Act 1 taught me to expect.

Your choices have very little meaningful impact on the characters if at all.
What was a starting point for massive potential quickly comes crashing down hard as no one in this game learns anything, adapts, grows, or evolves. The only growth is your talent tree, and your arsenal of weapons/appartments/cars
But as far as actual emotional depth is concerned. NADA!


Relationships...
If you are the type of person who wants to solicit work from Joytoys and one night stands... then sure there is some material in this game that can tickle your fancy. But once again try to have anything of meaning and you will be horrible disappointed ESPECIALLY if you're playing a Male-lead protagonist and you're choosing to have straight orientation... because your ONLY option is Panam...
An alcoholic, impulsive, short-tempered, foulmouthed, nomad with the body of a porn-star, who only gets excited when she's committing mass-murder followed by socializing with you over the bottom of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ bottle. 
To add insult to injury, the only time you can be intimate with this bloodthirsty phsycho, is when you're driving a billion dollar tank called a baselisk, blowing everything to ♥♥♥♥, and getting electrically high with her like its a rave-lazer show...
It's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ pathetic. 


And then... there is Evelyn... 
Evelyn is very real. If you've ever worked in trauma departments anywhere you will recognize Evelyn immediately! And not just in act 1, but harrowingly enough you will recognize her in act 2!
Evelyn is a over-confident attractive woman who's intellect is above average. She's not a genius, but she's ok. She is also wildly attractive and has learned to survive by utilizing her sexuality.
Like any woman in such an industry she desperately wants to get out, and tries to use her connections, her charm, and her smarts to organize a heist that would be her ticket to a better life.
This goes horrible wrong, which is unfortunately also a very real-world parallel.
After having been brutally violated for an entire week by several parties, you manage to safe her in the worst state possible... but she is alive...
Anyone who has worked with people like Evelyne recoil during this scene, and her respons to being saved is what you would expect from someone in her shoes. 
So now comes the very interesting question.: How do we help Evelyn recover, how do we get her back on her feet? 
Had CD project red actually given us a proper route for that, it would have been infinitely better... but what did project red do????
They made Judy leave Evelyn A LONE (everyone knows you NEVER leave someone like that a lone!) Followed by Evelyn getting into a bathtube and ending her life.
ARE YOU ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ KIDDING ME!!!!!

You can save Barry the cop by going to the graveyard and figuring out Andrew was a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ tortoise, but EVELYNE is a scripted un-changeable suicide!!?


Peralez 
Someone is remotely modifying a mayoral candidate's memories and personality. V discovers it. You tell the victim.
And then the game ends the storyline.
You cannot investigate the perpetrators, devise countermeasures, help Jefferson fight them, or discover what's happening. The provocative premise is the payoff.


Cyberpunk 2077 repeatedly mistakes provocation for profundity.

It raises fascinating questions about trauma, consciousness, autonomy, sexuality, religion and identity—
BUT!! it treats asking the question, and producing a shocking image itself as an answer. It's not!
None of the imagery or questions posed make a work profound. It's how you engage with that material that counts, and Cyberpunk skips that step altogether! It's a complete cop-out!

But hey... enjoy driving your supercar through Night City while geeking out over its reflection in the rain-drenched asphalt.
Words are not enough to describe how terrible this game truly is.

And I, for one, will never play another game by CD PROJEKT RED.

comment:
When you see the negative reviews from people like me with hundreds and thousands of hours of playtime, that's your signal that something happened. Something went wrong. 
Elden Ring is a masterpiece of a game with excellent story telling and visuals. It's a piece of art that I intend to continue to share with as many people as I can because good art deserves to be seen. So why the negative. 
FromSoftwares parent company recently had a shift in power via a stock buy from a company who has shown anticonsumer interests in the past. Now I'm not going to lie to you about the contents of the 5$ addon. It's something like 5 sets of armor, 2 npc encounters, and 3 cosmetic skins for your steed. These may not be the exact details, and in any other game this would be not the most egregious addon on offer. But this is the first of it's kind in a fromsoft title. It's a canary so to speak. What is more important to me is the history of the addon itself. The addon was a way to move copies for the switch 2. This extra content was exclusive to the switch 2 for a period and is now being allowed to branch out to the other versions. Which is fine, that's how business works. The problem, however, is that the switch 2 copy of elden ring is the exact same price as the shadow of the erdtree bundle. Meaning switch 2 has the new addon content, the dlc, and the base game for 79.99. Everyone else is the ONLY ONES footing the "bill" for this addon content. 
Recently a "community quest" went live. It doesn't matter what the challenges are, the rewards are artwork and twitch badges which irrelevant to the game. This is a blatant bid to boost player count. The company that bought the controlling interest is a hedge fund, more players means higher share price. I'm not fooled and neither should you be. Participate in the quests, there's no harm in playing the game you love. But don't buy the horse armor. It's a trap, a crack in the ice, the first of many needles.

comment:
This isn't a good Souls game.

Firstly, let's get this out of the way: Souls fans, this review is not for you. You already bought the game, completed it six times and are busily posting a long rant nobody will read about why whatever weapon is underrated/overpowered. 

For the rest of us, who might dip in and out of Souls games from time to time: this is just a Souls game but worse. The only thing that makes it any different from Dark Souls 1, 2, 3 or any other Fromsoft game is the open world - and the open world makes literally everything worse. 

Don't get me wrong - it was the correct decision to put an open world in. The game isn't for me, it's for the Souls fans who've played every game FromSoft release a dozen times over and just need something new. For those people, the open world is the least harmful breath of fresh air possible. 

If you're not sick of the sight of Souls games, though, the open world is a terrible addition. Pacing is dead and buried, the usually stellar map design is relegated to only existing in dungeons, and you have no idea where you're supposed to go next. If you don't look it up you can guarantee you'll miss a region entirely, then have to choose between never experiencing it or doing it while horribly overlevelled. Speaking of which, if you like to explore and find everything, you'll be overlevelled anyway; I didn't grind once and yet was 30+ levels ahead of where I should be for virtually the entire game simply because I refused to skip content.

The worst thing, though, is the bosses. Bosses are FromSoft's selling point, and they're usually both well-designed encounters and also very visually impressive. In this game, however, thanks to the open world they have to put 300 more of them into the game than there should be - gotta put SOMETHING in the open world after all. They can't design 300+ unique bosses, so that means reprints. A LOT of reprints. By the time I gave up on the game I'd fought an estimated six Crucible Knight versions, dozens of lesser versions thereof, half a dozen gargoyles, seven (I think) Ulcerated Tree Spirits, over a dozen Watchdog Statues... the list goes on. The anticipation and impact Dark Souls usually has with its bosses is entirely eliminated because nine times out of ten you'll see the boss health bar pop up and realise it's the same thing you've already fought before. Repeatedly.

To conclude, if you're NOT someone who plays every Souls game relentlessly, do yourself a favour - buy Dark Souls 3 instead. Hell, buy ANY Dark Souls game. If you already own one, play that instead. They'll have proper gameplay pacing, proper map design, and most of the bosses you fight will be unique and interesting. 

They'll be better than this, in other words. This was legitimately a boring game.

comment:
So this review only concerns the Remastered version and the quirks with it, hence it's a 'not recommended'. Steam's reviews really need an overhaul as they don't allow for any nuance. The game is still really good as it always has been (base game less so, expansions are terrific).

Anyway the new version introduces a whole lot of issues that make you realise "yeah, makes sense they made it free". The graphics overhaul comes at a huge performance increase and the new ray tracing/path tracing makes the game just look off in a lot of areas, while in others it makes it look better. In other words, it's inconsistent and also not worth the performance hit. Worse are the visual glitches that are kinda numerous now which is a shame.

Then there's the updates to combat which... honestly, you barely feel. The devs had a selection of many great mods that tried to do something about this combat system that already felt dated upon release and instead they went for "let's add a few new finishers (that you won't notice in your first hours of playing anyway) and some new sign VFX. done!". The "visual" uplift of the combat isn't even as extensive as it could have been as there are other areas that could have deserved more attention, for example giving you more counterattack animations. The point is, them bragging about "enhanced combat" in this remaster is extremely, extremely generous and far from reality, unfortunately.  It's a shame because there's a lot of great combat mods out there that the devs could have been inspired by.

The new skill tree is... meh? I never liked TW3's character progression as I found the system of slotting skills before they can work to be unnecessarily limiting because you won't take a lot of skills that are just "fun", you'll just take the ones that are the most useful. Adding a lot more skills to the trees just doubles down on this problem and makes it worse, because now there's even more cool looking skills that I can't pick because I don't have the room for them. How can they not realise that a system where you LEVEL UP AND GET A NEW SKILL THAT YOU CAN'T USE BECAUSE YOU DON'T HAVE A SKILL SLOT FOR IT just feels terrible? This needed a Cyberpunk 2.0 esque overhaul, especially with the upcoming expansion it would have been very welcome. The very least they could have done is made it so some of the skills on each tree are "passive" and don't need to be put into a skill slot to work.

But the worst issue is the bugs. After 2 hours in I've already ran into a couple and it's just frustrating to play a 10+ year game and have its new edition feel even more buggy. What is this, a Bethesda game?

There's things that are nice and that I liked about this version though. Some UI changes are nice, the integration of an ingame mod library (and making them available on consoles by effect) is also really nice, though some mods shouldn't be there as they haven't been updated to work with this version.

So yeah, disappointing remaster overall, I should say. It just feels oddly rushed and undercooked which is very questionable since they didn't have to release it now, with the expansion still about a year away. Of course you already have a bunch of idiots on the internet going "iTS fReE wHy aRe yOu cOmPlaInInG" as if doing something for free gives you diplomatic immunity to criticism. But the more important counterargument is that I am pretty sure the new expansion will require you to play on this version, so if you don't like any of the changes but will want to play that, tough luck I guess.

Hopefully it will get patched and improved by then. And I hope that the expansion will get the polish it needs.

comment:
Baldur’s Gate 3 shines in its writing and characters. The narrative is well-crafted, and the world feels alive thanks to memorable personalities and engaging dialogue. It’s the kind of game I wanted to love, and the story alone almost carries it. However, the experience is held back by fundamental flaws in its combat and design. Flaws that make it hard to recommend wholeheartedly.
[h2] Combat: A Frustrating Power Fantasy [/h2]
I don’t oppose turn-based games by default, but BG3’s combat doesn’t deliver the power fantasy it promises. When facing 20 weak enemies in a single room, I should feel like an unstoppable force, clearing them in seconds, not gambling with accuracy rolls and damage dice for foes that should die to a stiff breeze. The game constantly throws overwhelming numbers at you (unless you save-scum, which shouldn’t be a core “feature”), and it feels like lazy design.
[b] SPOILERS FOR ACT 3 AND SHADOWHEARTS QUESTLINE IN THE BLOCK BELOW! [/b]

[spoiler] The basement in Act 3 during Shadowheart’s questline was the tipping point for me. I had to cheese my way through with a firewall on the stairs just to get past the relentless enemy spam. It’s not challenging; it’s tedious. [/spoiler]
[h2] Design Disconnect: Combat vs. Story [/h2] 
It’s clear the writing and combat design happened completely independent of each other. The game pretends to offer meaningful story choices, but in reality, most paths lead to minor dialogue tweaks or game-over screens. I played as a resist Durge sorcerer, expecting surrendering to the urge to open new narrative branches. Instead, I got a few lines of unique dialogue and some superficial changes. This isn’t Fallout: New Vegas, where choices ripple through the world! It’s a puddle compared to an ocean.
The disconnect extends to the game’s tone. BG3 forces you into a rigid D&D 5e simulation, complete with RNG and spreadsheet math, but it lacks the camaraderie and flexibility of a real tabletop session. As a DM, I know that level 1 goblins would cower or die in a funny, narratively satisfying way, not force the player to slog through every roll.
[h2] Industry Trends and Award Hype [/h2]
[b] Not really about the game, but important if you're considering getting the game because of it's critical acclaim. [/b]
BG3’s near-perfect scores and GOTY wins say more about the industry than the game itself. It’s not that Alan Wake 2 or other nominees are bad. It’s that awards, like movie Oscars, favor grand, cinematic experiences over smaller, tighter designs. BG3’s 96% “Overwhelmingly Positive” Steam rating is misleading (not really, but let me cook): only around a quarter of players have earned the “All’s Well That Ends Well” achievement (finishing the game). 
[h2] The Community and Criticism [/h2]
[b] Once again, not really related to the game, but still interesting imo [/b]
The most frustrating part isn’t the game, it’s the patronizing fanbase in my opinion. Criticizing BG3’s flaws invites vicious backlash. The fact that there’s a dedicated keybind for loading quicksaves speaks volumes: the developers know players are save-scumming to tolerate the combat. Yet, pointing this out gets you labeled as “not getting it” or worse. (This is not exclusive to BG3, just a flaw with CRPGs in general)
I suspect many positive reviews come from players who didn’t finish the game but don’t want to admit it. That may be out of fatigue or fear of being piled on by the community. Or maybe they just played the first act, enjoyed it but never touched the game again, which is probably the best way to experience it.
[h1] Final Verdict: A Flawed Gem [/h1]
Baldur’s Gate 3 is a game I wanted to love, and its story and characters almost make up for its flaws. But the combat is a slog, the choices are shallow, and the design feels disconnected. It’s a game most players haven’t even finished, yet it sits at near-perfect scores. That’s not a testament to BG3’s quality. It’s a sign of how low the bar has fallen.
If you’re here for the story, you’ll find a lot to enjoy. If you want satisfying combat or meaningful choices, you might leave as frustrated as I did.
Not Recommended (after one playthrough as a resist Durge sorcerer, reaching Act 3).

comment:
Honestly, I don't think I can describe a bigger disappointment for me than Cyberpunk 2077. I know it's considered one of the best RPGs by many people, but after about 5 hours, my experience has been almost the complete opposite.

Let's start with the positives. Night City is absolutely stunning. The graphics are easily one of the best I've ever seen, especially with ray tracing enabled. The attention to detail is incredible, the hacking mechanics are fun, and the main story has been interesting enough to keep me playing. If I had to rate those aspects alone, the graphics would be a 20/10 and the story, so far, around an 8/10.

Now for the parts that disappointed me.

Driving feels awful. Almost every vehicle I've driven feels like it's sliding on ice. Cars, bikes, vans—it doesn't really matter. Taking sharp corners often turns into either massive understeer or drifting when I didn't even want to drift. Traversing the city ended up being more frustrating than fun.

The gunplay also didn't click with me. The weapons look fantastic and have great animations, but actually using them feels bland. Damage numbers often feel strange, and combat never felt as satisfying as I expected.

Another thing that didn't appeal to me was how heavily the game leans into sexual themes. I understand it's part of the world's identity, but after a while it felt like it was everywhere—from advertisements to certain side quests—and it became more distracting than immersive. Some side missions also felt random and forgettable rather than meaningful.

Performance was... acceptable. On my RTX 5060 Laptop GPU at 1440p with max settings and low ray tracing, I averaged around 40-80 FPS, depending on the area. However, cinematic cutscenes occasionally became extremely laggy for me, dropping to what felt like single-digit FPS regardless of whether ray tracing was enabled. I'm not sure if that's a hardware issue or something on the game's side.

I also wasn't impressed with the NPC AI. I frequently saw civilians walking into walls, repeating strange behaviors, or panicking in unrealistic ways whenever combat started. It broke the immersion more than once.

Is the game worth buying for around $12-$15? I'd say yes. At that price, there's definitely enough content to justify the purchase, especially if you're interested in the story and exploring Night City.

Overall, I don't think Cyberpunk 2077 is a bad game—it just wasn't the game I expected. While the world, visuals, and main story are excellent, the driving, combat, AI, and some of the side content kept me from enjoying it as much as everyone else seems to.

Overall: 6.8/10

Graphics: 10/10 (20/10 if your GPU survives)

Story: 8/10 (so far)

Driving: 3/10

Combat: 5/10

Optimization: 7/10

NPC AI: 4/10

World Design: 10/10

comment:
This is a cool game to pick up on sale, but it's pretty shallow and the story is incredibly boring and forgettable. I have not played the Phantom Liberty DLC so I cannot comment on that. Worth picking up if it's cheap and you like the futuristic setting.

Pros:
- beautiful city that feels alive
- great graphics
- varied combat systems, with guns, swords and hacking
- skill trees for different playstyles
- runs well, short loading times and easy to jump in and out of
- plenty of content in the city. Lots of stories, side missions and collectables.

Cons:
- the story is boring and forgettable
- the entire game is 1st person and you never see your character which makes it hard to identify with them
- whilst the combat is varied, the actual gunplay is very basic. You soon become OP and there is no reason to use any of the guns you find instead of Iconic weapons
- dialogue is weird. There's a lot of futuristic colloquialisms but the actual dialogue is just odd and easy to miss key details
- the game expects you to know a lot about the setting and ignores the 'show don't tell' rule. There will be loads of times were you're like 'wait, who is that?' 'what is that?' 'why does my character know this when I don't?'
- stakes feel very low and attachment to characters is odd. Everyone is a stereotypical Cyberpunk resident. My character seems to care loads for people she's just met, or form deep relationships with people she doesn't know.

Overall it's a nice looking game if you like the Cyberpunk/Bladerunner vibe, but the story is very poor, the gunplay is basic and there's just not much to do outside of the pretty aesthetics. I'd give it 3/10 as a narrative RPG

comment:
Elden Ring is genuinely one of the best games I've ever played.

The exploration is incredible. You can pick a direction, wander off, and somehow end up finding an entire castle, underground city, or boss that you had absolutely no idea existed. The combat is satisfying, the build variety is ridiculous, and the feeling of finally beating a boss that's been kicking your ass for an hour is something very few games can replicate.

It's not perfect. Some bosses can be frustrating as hell, the PC performance has had its issues, and occasionally the game seems determined to remind you that you are, in fact, terrible at it.

But overall? Elden Ring is an incredible game and absolutely deserves the praise it gets.

Unfortunately, the Tarnished Pack is where FromSoftware and Bandai Namco completely lost me.

$5 for two starting classes, a handful of armor and weapons, some NPC invasions, and three cosmetic skins for Torrent is already pushing it. But the fact that some of the equipment can be obtained in-game anyway makes charging for this feel even more ridiculous.

And then they bundle this content with the new Switch 2 version while turning around and telling the people who already bought and supported the game on other platforms to pay extra for it.

Seriously?

This isn't a real expansion. This isn't Shadow of the Erdtree. Shadow of the Erdtree gave us an entire new world to explore, bosses, weapons, enemies, and dozens of hours of content. That was DLC worth paying for.

The Tarnished Pack feels like they looked at a small amount of bonus content that could have been a free update and decided, "Nah, let's charge them for it."

And before someone says, "It's only $5," I genuinely do not care. The price does not magically make bad DLC practices okay. If anything, it's the principle of it. Elden Ring has sold millions of copies. People have supported this game for years, bought Shadow of the Erdtree, and helped make it one of the biggest games of the last decade.

So rewarding those players by making them pay extra for a couple of starting classes and horse cosmetics while giving the content to new Switch 2 buyers as part of their edition is just insulting.

I still love Elden Ring. The actual game is phenomenal.

But I'm not going to pretend the Tarnished Pack isn't a blatant attempt to squeeze more money out of an already massively successful game.

comment:
Going to be an unpopular opinion here, but I've tried to get into Elden Ring several times and I just can't get over some of the negatives. I know, for many people, there are so many good things about this game and I can see the reasons why its regarded so highly, but maybe souls games just aren't for me so I'm giving this review from that perspective (as someone who wanted to dip my feet into this genre). 

This has nothing to do with the difficulty of the game. I couldn't wait to "git gud" at this game or grind my way to victory if I needed to. I just had a really hard time trying to get over:

The various menus/interfaces are clunky. 

The controls: The controls feel really bad to me. I get you don't dodge until you release the button and all that stuff but just mechanically it feels clunky to me. I much prefer the layouts and more responsive action of fighting Valkyries in God of War or Stellar Blade. I first tried with KB+M and it felt clunky trying to dodge, parry, etc. People told me to try a controller so I grabbed a PS Dual Sense and it's clunky to use potions etc especially in the heat of battle. With KB+M and Controller I'm struggling to control the camera and actually see what I'm fighting properly. 

The controls again: How are there no native PS glyphs for this game? Tell me to press triangle instead of Y. Yes, I can get over it but this is basic requirement of a game this big. 

The graphics: Nearly everyone seems to say this game has amazing graphics. I'll admit the art direction is great, but graphically this game does not look great. Yes, graphics aren't everything but I expect better graphical fidelity than this. When I bumped up things to 4k it started to look decent (but like on par with Tainted Grail or some other AA game). Never was I ever thinking "woah this is impressive graphically". It messed with my immersion. Too much fog. Low textures all over the place. When you kill enemies they just sort of ethereally fade away in an uninteresting way. I tried turning on HDR and after a few computer restarts it was finally working and that did help, but why does this game have so many technical problems still? 

I've been on plenty of corpse runs in various MMOs over the years. This is a boring/time-wasting mechanic for me in a single player game at this point. 

Lore/Atmosphere/Exploration/Mystery: This was very good/interesting. I just couldn't get over the clunky controls, bad camera, and lackluster graphics.

TLDR: This game is probably great for lots of people, but if you care about tight controls and good graphics this might not be it.

comment:
[h1]Baldur’s Gate 3 Review – The Horniest Camp in Faerûn[/h1]

Baldur’s Gate 3 is, from a technical standpoint, an achievement.
Full performance capture, cinematic dialogue, seamless co-op, and a level of polish most RPGs never reach. It feels like the new benchmark.

And the combat deserves the praise.
This is the best turn-based DnD implementation ever made. Encounters reward planning. Builds, rolls, and positioning matter. It finally feels like tabletop logic translated into a digital space without losing depth.

If this review were only about systems, it would end here on a high note.

[h2]The Story That Never Dares[/h2]

The problem is the narrative.

For a game this large and this celebrated, the story plays it remarkably safe. The structure is familiar, the twists are visible from miles away, and the moral conflicts rarely force you into uncomfortable territory. It wants to be epic, but it avoids being unsettling. It gestures toward boldness without fully committing to it.

The villains suffer most from this caution.

[spoiler]Ketheric Thorm is framed as a tragic, god-touched warlord whose presence should reshape the world around him. Instead, much of his impact is delivered through exposition and brooding speeches before culminating in a fairly conventional boss encounter. The supposed avatar of dread ends up feeling like a raid boss with a tragic backstory rather than a transformative force in the narrative.[/spoiler]

The scale is large. The risk is not.

[h2]Companions Built for Applause[/h2]

The companions are memorable, but often in a performative way. They are designed to stand out immediately. Big personalities. Strong aesthetics.

Yet over time, some arcs begin to feel predictable. Shadowheart’s internal conflict repeats familiar beats for long stretches. Astarion’s trauma-laced charm oscillates between vulnerability and theatrical sarcasm in ways that feel engineered for reaction rather than discovery. They are not shallow characters.

But they often feel curated for engagement rather than organically unfolding.

[h2]The Horniest Camp in Faerûn[/h2]

And then we arrive at camp. The emotional center of the story. The place where bonds should deepen naturally over shared struggle.

Instead, it often feels like the Forgotten Realms’ most efficient speed-dating retreat.

The world is on the brink of annihilation. You have a mind flayer tadpole in your skull. Gods are scheming. Empires are shaking. And somehow, within what feels like a long weekend, half your party is ready to discuss eternal devotion.

It stops feeling like chemistry and starts feeling like a triggered dialogue tree. Intimacy accelerates at a pace that undermines tension. Emotional payoff is replaced by availability. The result is tonal whiplash. Apocalypse outside the tent. Romance queue inside it.

[h2]An Ending That Should Have Roared[/h2]

After dozens of hours, the finale arrives with competence but not with weight. It resolves threads, it ties off arcs, but it rarely challenges the player in a way that feels transformative. For a narrative centered around identity, manipulation, and cosmic stakes, the conclusion feels restrained.

[h2]Buyer’s Regret Verdict[/h2]

Baldur’s Gate 3 is mechanically outstanding and technically industry-leading. As a systems-driven RPG, it deserves recognition. As a DnD combat experience, it sets a standard.

But story and companion writing undermine the atmosphere it tries to build. The ambition in presentation is not matched by ambition in narrative risk.

Full-price bucks demand bold storytelling.
Here, your bucks are safer on sale.

I went in expecting an open world action game and got a talking simulator instead.

The world looks great and the atmosphere is strong. I just wish there was more to do in it and less time spent watching and selecting.

Good game for the right player. Not for me.

comment:
TL;DR: Fun enough for cheap, but low effort development visible everywhere.
This game is shoddy. Too much to list, but some examples running the gamut from "negligible but annoying en masse" to "They're supposed to be professionals.": unskipable info at start, about 30 seconds EVERY TIME; TWO idle screens before the menue; all the crap that makes picture quality worse activated by default (and not only the crap that we've been fighting with for 20 years, vignette and stuff, but all the modern stuff, too. Frame generation is on and looks as ♥♥♥♥ as always, Raytracing is on and looks worse than the experimental stuff from 25 years ago.); obnoxious cutscenes that go on forever with plenty of wasting the players time and no way to save or speed them up; the sandbox stuff is much more fun than the story but ultimately meaningless as usual, character development and story are on the level of servicable visual novels (absolutely linear, can be good at times but just as often bad, usually mediocre moving-things-along stuff), the game is cobbled together (when leaving a mini game or loading a game or doing anything that triggers an animation the game takes ~1-2 seconds to catch up, long stretches of not being able to save because the game stays in cutscene mode for half an hour after the cutscene, safe zones take ALL features away except walking and looking around making you walk away for a minute to run, crouch, use items, mounts, EVERYTHING), input is strewn all over the Keyboard because they couldn't be asked to develop for the platform that'll give them the most sales.
That said, it is far from unplayable, not all that money wasn't all wasted. It looks pretty, the mechanics work more or less, the atmosphere is good, the story is annoying but servicable.
If you liked Deus Ex you can use this as a much worse but newer iteration; without any magic but maybe scratching the itch. Compared to the newer Deus Ex parts, it is a good deal worse but obviously not as much as compared to Deus Ex. Quality on the level of the Bioshocks, but much more fun. One of the weaker examples of the genre. Get it in a sale for at least 75% off (max 20€).

comment:
The irony is staggering, and it is easily one of the greatest examples of real-world corporate hypocrisy in gaming history. The developer became the exact villain they were warning us about.

CD Projekt Red spent years marketing a story about a dystopian future where greed destroys lives, workers are treated like garbage, and corporate executives lie to the public for a massive payday—and then they turned around and did it themselves.

1. The Corporate Exploitation of Workers (Crunch Culture)

The Promise: The studio’s leadership publicly promised their developers that they would not use forced "crunch" (mandatory, extreme overtime) to finish the game.

The Reality: As deadlines approached, corporate executives mandated six-day work weeks, with many developers working brutal 16-hour days for months on end just to patch a broken product. They literally ran a human-grinder corporate sweatshop to ship a game about human-grinder corporate sweatshops.

2. The Multi-Million Dollar Lie

The Corporate Gaslighting: To secure millions of pre-orders and protect their stock price, the executives actively lied to the public and their investors. They claimed the game ran "surprisingly well" on older consoles (PS4/Xbox One) when they knew it was completely unplayable.

Review Manipulation: In true corporate fashion, they heavily restricted review copies. They forbade reviewers from using their own gameplay footage on older consoles, forcing them to use pre-rendered corporate B-roll. It was a calculated, anti-consumer media blackout designed to milk the consumer before the truth came out.

3. Turning Rebellious Art into Corporate Slop

The True Irony: Johnny Silverhand is a character whose entire identity is about bombing a corporate headquarters to fight the system. CD Projekt Red turned that punk-rock anti-corporate icon into a marketing puppet used to sell limited-edition Porsche cars, branded energy drinks, and gaming chairs.

Night City isn't just a fictional warning anymore. The way Cyberpunk 2077 was handled proved that we already live in a cyberpunk world—where a massive company can package the idea of "rebellion," sell it to us for ₹4,000, break their workers in the process, and still walk away with a massive profit.

comment: It's a cool setting with cool vibes and a theoretically good story. However gameplay feels like a GTA5 clone but worse. Waited until bugs were fixed and reviews were high to give it a try because I really really wanted to like this game and have a good experience with it. Character creation was awesome and well detailed, started the game with one of three options that were pretty meaningless to me but resulted in all my early npc interactions being extremely hostile against me. Still, got through tutorial well enough after significant controller sensitivity adjustments and graphics settings adjustments. After finishing what was a pretty cool opening sequence, was thrown into an extended cutscene of honestly idk what involving my character, one npc I just met, and a whole bunch of setting I didn't know anything about as if it was a wild drunken rampage with limited memory flashbacks. Major problem here is that for the majority of the cutscene characters were T-posing and hovering around. Graphics drivers were up to date, settings were properly adjusted for my system, but still T-posing npc's and I think my character as well in 3rd person, but hard to tell because the model adjustments looked the same but the outfit didn't match at all. This brings me to the two final major issues. After completing multiple main story missions I wanted to start branching out into side missions to make sure I didn't miss anything. However side missions seem to have a money cost to progress that is waaaaay above income you receive while just playing the game. Usually you do side missions to earn extras, not find ways to earn extras to let you do side missions. At the same time I ran into multiple issues of my outfit and weapons not updating or equipping when I tried to apply them to my character from the inventory, no matter if I was in or out of combat, in a public space, or in my apartment. I really really wanted to like this game, but sadly I just can't enjoy it, or even give it the mark of a function/completed game, even after all of the improvements by the devs since release.

comment:
This is my third attempt to get into this game. I'm done.

I want to love it. I've played the previous Baldur's Gate titles, I enjoy the genre, and I'm not looking for hand-holding. What I do want is a narrative that gives me a reason to care about what I'm doing next.

BG3 mistakes "mysterious" for "unclear." There's a brain worm in my head that's supposed to be turning me into a monster — that's a genuinely compelling hook — but the game keeps forgetting to remind me that's the point. I'm following quest markers because the markers exist, not because the story is pulling me forward.

The world is reactive and beautifully constructed. The writing is sharp when it wants to be. But the moment-to-moment narrative momentum is weak. Conversations can collapse into combat without warning. The game withholds information under the guise of tension when it's actually just poor player communication. There's a difference between a mystery that feels earned and one that leaves you genuinely confused about basic decisions.

Three attempts. Uninstalled. The brain worm wins.

comment:
The Witcher 3 is a good game. It is the best game in the series. It has good writing, graphics, and stability. Hearts of Stone and Blood & Wine DLC are free now together with the Remaster. 

That being said, if you are thinking of checking out the game again since the remaster released a few days ago...then I'd say that'd be the equivalent of stapling your tongue to a clipboard to see if it sticks. Despite CPR's lengthy list of changes and 'improvements' made to the game in this version...there's really nothing different:

Upgraded visuals, Enhanced combat, Improved traversal & movement, New Witcher signs FX, Revamped mount handling, Enhanced monster behaviors, Skill tree revamp, Transmogrification and the list supposedly goes on and on and on...

0% difference. All the Remaster does is just reshade the game slightly and add some pretty skyboxes.

Combat is still clunky, slow, boring, and unimaginative. Dialouge is still tedious and lengthy - requiring you to slam the spacebar key over and over just to get through dialouge you've already heard before. Nothing's changed in the story. Picking up loot is still a pain in the a$$. Enemies still only spawn in set, non-random locations and don't respawn unless you leave the area. There aren't any new quests. No new spells. Levelling up is still as slow as ever. Geralt still dies after stubbing his toe or falling 50cm. Roach still handles like threading a sock through a needle. The skill tree still sucks fat butt and takes 4eva to get through.

I'm not sure if the Remaster was even needed or why they released it now of all times. The Witcher 4 isn't ready yet. Cyberpunk apparently only had enough shelf-life for 1 solitary DLC. Project Red doesn't even have any other projects lined up. 
 ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ I guess they really wanted those some 10,000 fans to really get keen again for the series and to buy their completely random new DLC early next year for a game that's a now decade old. 

I'll still never know why they thought of releasing an actual open world RPG witcher game set during the early days just after the first Conjunction of the Spheres where you can play as a customizable character fighting off a plethora of monsters in the woods, defending the disconnected human villages, learning and interacting with the early witcher schools and actually doing regular monster hunting contracts. So much room to work with and yet they just chose to stick with another boring looong audiobook with the usual cast of people. It's going to be more snoring stories involving "King Kaedwin allying with King Vizimir of Redania to assualt Queen Calenthae of Cintra so that the borders imposed by Emperator Emyr Var Emyrs of Nilfgaard will lead to increased trade taxes on the shipments of cattle from Tretogor". It's one of the most boring parts of the witcher series and it gets worse the longer they drag it on. Lady of the Lake and Witcher 3 were onlyfun because all of that silly political nonsense finally came to a close in BIG EPIC BATTLEZ at the end. 

Do people even care about all of the politics in the Viedzmin series or do they play video games just to kill monsters? I can just listen to an audiobook for better writing....What's even left with Ciri's story now that the fuggin' Wild Hunt, Nilfgaardian invasion, and White Frost are all dealt with? Geralt even fuggin' gets unalived in one of the endings...so wtf. All of the conflict and narrative importance has already concluded. 

Why couldn't they just do a proper remake of some other older RPG, like The World of Darkness series (i.e. the one with Vampire the Masquerade), like they did with Cyberpunk? Take some crappy old tabletop RPG from the 80s and make a fun action game. 

Hopefully CPR doesn't balls up Witcher 4 again like they did with Cyberpunk on release. 

Thanks. I'll just stick to Space Marine.

comment:
Do I love this game? Yes. Do I recommend this game? Hell no.

Take Karlach for example. You meet her and she’s just standing there all sexy, talking in that deep voice, and you’re like “okay cool companion,” but NO. It’s not that simple.

You recruit her.
You help her.
You fix her engine like some kind of j*b.

And suddenly it’s not about the quest anymore.

It’s about her.

You start picking dialogue options based on what she’d like. Not what’s smart. Not what’s good. What she would approve of. You start waiting after conversations like she might say something else if you just… stay there.

Then it gets weird.

You notice things.
The way she heart pulses.
The way she licks her lips.
The way she says your name so buttery smooth.

You reload saves. Not because you messed up. But because you want to see her react again. Slightly different. Slightly better. Maybe this time she’ll say something more.

Then it gets worse.

You start thinking about her when you’re not even playing.
Like what she’d be doing right now.
If she’d be a top or bottom.
If she’d look at you like you were more than just a player.

You start imagining conversations that never happened.
Moments that aren’t in the game.
Things she’d say. Things she’d do. Things you’d do to her.

No, it’s fine. It’s normal. Totally normal.

Until it isn’t.

Because now you’re staring at the screen a little too long.
You’re leaning in a little closer.
You’re saying stuff out loud like “yeah… yeah you would.”

And at some point you realize.
You don’t even care about the story anymore.

It’s just her.

Just Karlach.

And the way she moves her body.
And the way her chest bounces as she walks.
And the way you’d absolutely do her in until her infernal engine combusts.

Like if she was real you would probably never pull out.
And honestly? You’d do it again.
No hesitation. No regrets. Just you and Karlach and a bottle of "stuff".

Where was I going with this.
Oh yeah kicking the squirrel was really funny.
What a great game.

10/10.

comment:
This game is great, but it has been such an incredibly frustrating experience getting to the good parts of it. Baldur's Gate 3 is a buggy unstable mess of a game that reminds me of Skyrim. It lacks quality of life features all over and I find myself managing the tedium of multiple inventories, potions, broken pathfinding, etc more than actually enjoying the game. It also suffers greatly of the same problem most "high immersion" games suffer from: it has quips, reactions and dialogs for so many little things happening but when you find a MASSIVE plottwist about the game's story and suddenly nobody has anything to say or think about that, it completely ruins any of that immersion. It also seems to assume in many places you interact with story elements and NPCs in a certain order, meaning you can easily miss out on story or find someone referencing things you have absolutely zero context for quite easily. The combat is as repetitive and one-dimensional as you can expect from anything trying to be D&D, thankfully there's explorer mode to breeze past all that and get back to the good part:
The story, the voice acting and the choices you get to make are all great. At the time of writing I'm somewhere in act 2 and I have to admit it feels a lot like DOS2 with a faerune skin draped over it. But that's not bad because I loved DOS2.
It's a shame I might not see the conclusion of that story as a minor patch, over two and a half years after release, has screwed with one of the mods I donwloaded through the integrated mod marketplace and seems to have corrupted the last 4 hours of saves, so I'm going to put this down for a while.

comment:
Locking comments so the army of simp prepubescent sweats doesn't brigade this.  Anyway, it's an old game now.

It is a hard game.  That's fine by itself, but there are multiple ways a game can be hard.  This game is hard in some legitimate ways, but also is hard and/or tedious in ways that just plain suck.

The camera can easily get occluded indoors and you are fighting blind.  In a souls game that kills you.

The lock on handling with "nimble" opponents will cause your movement to become extremely unpredictable, forcing you to constantly lock/unlock.  Meanwhile, locking is very clunky, sometimes locking something in the next room or just snapping your camera to forward which makes it even harder to regain the lock and, again, this kills you in a souls game.

Affordance is terrible.  Fans call this a feature (i.e. you don't know what level stuff is, etc.).  It would be if you could judge opponents in any way other than facetanking and dying.  You'll end up with giants you slay easily, then that small mob with a reused skin you recall from the lowbie area spanks you.  When minibosses beat you, you have no idea when you should come back.  As a result, the vast majority of what would be fun/challenging encounters are either - (a) you die, leave and maybe come back later or (b) oh yeah, let me go back there and... oh I killed it easily because I'm 20 levels higher now.

Also on a similar note, the game doesn't explain extremely important topics like leveling a weapon is more important than stats.  Or when a weapon scales with some attribute as "B" or "D", what does that even mean?

You find a boss and it barely takes damage.  Is it resistant to your damage type or are you just not high enough level?  Who knows!  Hey let's sink a ton of smithing stones into a blunt weapon just to find out and I sure hope I didn't just waste them.

Poor affordance and esoteric drops basically gating progression gives you two choices in the game: spend 10s of hours banging your head against the game to figure out the special place you need to go, to kill the miniboss, to get a drop you didn't know it had, to then give the drop to another NPC on the other side of the map, which will cause them to then sell you Smithing Stone[2] so you don't have to spend 20 hours farming Limgrave mines with a drop rate so low you aren't even sure it drops there..... OR you go to YouTube, find the cheese/needed steps and you're done in 30 minutes.

While on YouTube, you then notice some "great start to ER" videos and you watch one.  It shows you how to run around picking up all the somber smithing stones, open tons of chests and finally cheese a dragon so you have an incredibly powerful character.  All with zero real combat.  But yeah, Elden Ring is "hard" and you need to "git gud" and totally not a poorly crafted unbalanced and clunky mess of a game.

I will probably beat it in anger.  But if you don't own it, don't buy it.

comment:
It's the Witcher 3... of course it's great but the remaster is a different story all together. I've never been one to complain about game performance because I have always had old hardware and understood that it's just what I get for not paying for the latest tech. 

Since then however, I have upgraded to a 9070 XT and can run demanding titles with 100fps on 34inch ultrawide 3440x1440 without any frame gen. This includes titles like GOW Ragnarock (stable above 300fps) and Ghost of Tsushima which are graphically stunning. 

When I heard about the remaster, I was excited to play one of the best games of all time on my new hardware but the performance means that I simply can't enjoy it at all. I can't get anything above a complete slideshow 20fps with pathtracing on. Without it, the best I can get is an unstable 55fps and that's with frame generation on..... 

I understand that the graphical improvements would make the game perform worse but this game, despite improvements, still looks worse (on account of still being over 10 years old) than almost all other games I can run at 100+ fps. 

For anyone considering buying the Witcher 3 now and playing it on PC, unless you have a literal data center at your disposal than wait a while because the performance might hurt your experience of what is for many the single best title ever made. 

Will definetely change to positive if and when these problems are resolved.

comment:
I wish I could give a neutral review, but as i cannot and because most reviews are positive, I'm selecting a thumbs down. I won't get into the positives as other reviews expound on those aplenty. I do not think it is a bad game, just not a very good one either.

First of all and most importantly, this game is often described as being open world and having a heavy emphasis on freedom and choice. This left me very disappointed. I've played through most of the game (did not finish it, more on why later) over 200+ hours,  and it's actually very linear. Unlike in BG1-2 especially 2 where you can explore anywhere, constant cliffs, walls, gorges and roadblocks that box you in. Sure, there's a couple of alternate paths with small new areas, but not much. And this gets only worse over time - Act 1 is the most open but really still isn't, and 2 in particular is very locked down.

Linearity aside, Act 2 started to pull a good story together but it fell off hard in Act 3, which takes place almost entirely in Baldur's Gate. It should have been the high point of the game, but the city is boring, samey, little of interest to do, and the story gets a lot more boring. It was so jarring, that I left Act 2 hopeful and excited for the story but stopped playing not long after. I played through Raphael's house and got too bored with the story to continue much more. I don't know what the ending is and don't care tbh. Act 3 also performs badly, even with the native build update for Steam Deck it performs well under 30 fps. That was disappointing.

The characters were also mostly medicore. Gale and Wyll are boring, Gale even being insufferable. Shadowheart has a cool story arc in Act 2 but she consistently remains unlikeable despite being the "I can fix her". Karlach feels very unserious, like an irl person playing in a dnd session rather than a real character (though this does make her a great choice as an origin character), and it's a bit immersion breaking. Very OOC. Lae'zel is another "I can fix her" but she is very abrasive, nasty and constantly racist which put me off hard. Halsin's entire appeal is him being a literal bear, he's hot but uninteresting. Jaheira and Minsc i can't say much about as I never got them in my party.

However, the drow (wont say the name for spoilers) has a really interesting hidden arc on a good playthrough and is well-done as a character. And I have nothing but praise for Astarion and his questline, which went places I didn't expect and revealed a lot of his character depth and who he is and made me really like him and want to care for him.

Overall, the game isn't bad but also isn't that great and is very overrated and overhyped. It's unfortunately linear, with a very disappointing Baldur's Gate itself (the city). The companions are mostly uninteresting and overpraised. Sleeping with Raphael's incubus was really hot though

comment:
It was a major disappointment for me. While on paper this game has everything that it needs to be crowned as a masterpiece DLC, and while the first impression upon entering into the DLC provides further merit to that sentiment, very quickly does it fall on its face. 

We have seen this before? This is just an extension of the vanilla late game. Sure a ton of weapons, a ton of bosses and enemies, but at this stage of the game its a bit redundant unless you are ready to reset your character. Its fine to do that but ultimately its just a different path up the same trajectory. 

This vast DLC is... largely empty. It feels like a copy-paste of the altus plateau with slightly darker shades. 

The story, same as in the vanilla, seems very irrelevant. And while this is a staple of From Soft Souls game, in ER it is getting a bit too tiring and not cohesive considering the scale of the game. 

The bosses are the worst offenders. While I'll be the first to admit that I am not a speed/challenge runner, I played all the previous games and enjoyed them vastly. Struggled, sure. But still the bosses were enjoyable. In Shadow of the Erdtree, and ER by and large, the bosses seem without vision or balance. From the peaks of Sekiro and DS3, to bosses here that simply spam attacks, are too large to properly track and read, and generally contain levels of unprecedented bull...  

I wanted to like this DLC and the game. I even gave it a long break, upgraded to fully modern hardware, and watched a bunch of videos about how to properly implement jumping, strafing, and unlocking the camera to better move around bosses and enemies. But putting aside the fact that I am not the best player, the game had failed for me at the simplest level. It had failed to be FUN. Trudging through ER late game and the DLC is a slog. And while the vistas are astonishing... the content and the mechanics fall far, far behind.

Is it a recommendation? Sure, on a technical level it is still a masterpiece that needs to be experienced. The scale of it (while also its downside) is alone a cause for celebration. But a more polished experience with better executed ideas lies in DS3 and Sekiro.

What an absolute buggy mess. I bought this game after waiting for years to play it in a later state of development and its depressing how buggy the game is. Tons of the bugs are not even visible until you've progressed several hours into the game only to find out 'X' never actually started tracking and you will not be able to do anything with that plotline now without reloading to a save. 

This is on top of tons of graphical issues like tooltips and icons going invisible, characters randomly dying from literally nothing, characters falling out of combat and gameplay bugs like floating players all of which only have one solution 'reload the game' or outright close the game and reload. 

The kicker though, tons of these bugs have *years* old posts about them, they just have never been addressed by the devs and when I see threads about these 3 year old bugs where the only solution is to rollback to a save from 5 hours earlier, I just cant support the game. 

Fun fact too, apparently a few of these bugs like the floating characters even existed in Divinity games according to my friends who played those, so the chance of it actually being fixed seems non existent. A sad excuse of game development for something trying to ride the Baldur's Gate coattails.

Worth adding that you can play through them, just do research before like doing anything and be hypervigilant. I cant get a refund and the bugs arnt bad enough that I will stop, but its a much less enjoyable experience when you have to keep redoing things because of random bugs.

comment:
This abomination has almost nothing in common with the original Baldur’s Gate titles and should never have been seriously considered for Game of the Year.

Black Isle Studios was an American company that understood what made Baldur’s Gate special. This modern entry comes out of Belgium, and it shows. It feels completely disconnected from the traditional spirit and tone of the series.

The deliberately debilitating camera limitations are a perfect example. You can’t even properly look up. In a modern RPG? Seriously? It feels less like a design decision and more like an artificial restriction that constantly reminds you that you’re fighting the interface instead of exploring the world.

Item and spell descriptions are vague and poorly explained, forcing players into endless trial-and-error loops. Instead of the satisfaction of figuring something out, you’re left repeating the same failures simply because the game couldn’t be bothered to communicate clearly.

And then there’s the lore. Goblins speaking perfect English? Really? Do the developers even know what a goblin is supposed to be in the Baldur’s Gate universe? The world feels like it was stitched together by people who skimmed a wiki instead of actually understanding the setting.

Where are the Gibberlings? Where’s the mad necromancer and his deranged halfling thief? Xzar and Montaron were iconic companions that gave the original games their strange charm. Instead we get characters that are forgettable at best and bizarre at worst.

And what exactly is a Githyanki doing here? It all feels less like faithful Forgotten Realms world-building and more like creative licensing run amok.

This feels less like Baldur’s Gate and more like some unrelated RPG wearing its name like a costume. It’s the equivalent of releasing a Gothic remake with no Shadowbeasts—technically you can do it, but you’ve completely missed the point.

What a waste of time and money.

Game of the Year?

Yeah… right.

comment:
Before I start, let me say that I've been a D&D Dungeon Master for 27 years. 3rd and 3.5e were my jam. 
I've gotten this game in early access. Played a lot of early versions, and got frustrated lots of times for loosing my savegames, but that's not the reason I can't recommend this game. 
First the good parts:
The Graphics are absolutely amazing. the voice acting is perfect, the adaption of the RPG system is convincing and smooth.
Sadly the game isn't enjoyable for me for 3 reasons, all of them almost breaking the fun of the game for me:
1. The core theme of the game, having a parasite in me, repulses me on such a deep level that I can't empathize with any main character I create, any story point or mechanic based on the parasite, repulses me also. 
2. Romance and friendship in this Game are immensely confusing, in my first and only complete run I did (as a fan of the BG series, and after early access buying a game that wasn't finished I wanted to at least finish the game once), I got confused by my intention to do Friendship quests, which then later were revealed to be romance building scenes, which, as a straight guy, was highly uncomfortable to me, I want to have more influence over it what kind of romantic signals my character sends and stop it earlier if it goes into the wrong way, a simple straight or non straight button in the settings would have done the trick.
3. The story is hollow, the characters and societies depicted in this game, and the cultures they come from and which should define their motivations, they all do not work for me, and then it's all laced with pseudoreligion and highly artificially written npcs everywhere. 

Written for evil characters?
I would like to know if the makers of this game intended it to be played on the evil corruption path fromt he start, because when I tried playing an evil drow that wanted to grasp power through the parasite, the game worked, and since my character wanted to dominate most of where he was going, characterbuilding of his victims didn't matter, the evil options in this game are fun, while playing a paladin for my first run (as I always do in Baldurs Gate games)  just doesn't work. but since I don't like D&D 5e in the slightest I'm already biased.

Sumup: If you don't look too closely at npcs outside of your group, and if you're fine with being infested by a literal worm parasite and can get your mind off that, and If you want to play an evil character embracing a dark and disgusting path to power, this game is for you. Sadly it isn't for me. And I don't think it's a true Baldurs Gate successor.
peace and all the best to everyone.
