comment:
Wow...where do I even begin?

I want to start by saying that I have nothing but love and respect for Larian.  Divinity: Original Sin 2 is one of my favorite video games of all time, easily top 10 and maybe even top 5, and every time traces of that game shine through in BG3, a genuine smile appears on my face.  Then a moment later I get reminded that this is a D&D game, based on D&D rules, and the smile vanishes, because I realize I could be playing DOSE2 for the 30th time instead and having much, much more fun.

Baldur's Gate 3 sucks, but not because BG3 itself sucks.  Rather, it sucks because only getting to cast 5 fireballs per long rest sucks.  It sucks because having 28 STR and still failing a STR check in act 1 on normal difficulty because the dice decided to f**k you sucks.  It sucks because utility spells like teleports still consume limited per-rest slots even when you cast them outside combat, which limits exploration hard.  BG3 sucks because it's a D&D game with D&D rules, and D&D rules absolutely, completely, and totally suck.  They suck all the fun out of what could have been, and should have been, the greatest game ever made.

And I know this because DOSE2 shows what happens when Larian doesn't have to stick to a D&D rulebook.  DOSE2 is an unequivocally better video game.  In DOSE2, cooldowns are turn-based, which translates to 1 second per turn outside combat.  Thus, when you want to teleport outside combat, then do it again, you just have to wait 8 seconds.  This is long enough to get caught by patrolling enemies, if you plan poorly or just get unlucky, but you can still do it.  Character stats are also made in a way that actually makes sense - if your character has 28 STR and the check only requires 20, you pass the check, period, full stop.  You only have a dice roll when you don't surpass the threshold - so if the check requires 30 STR, THEN you have a chance of failure, but EVEN THEN that chance is based on the difference between your stat and the check.  So in this example, your 28 STR would still give you a 93% chance of success.  In BG3, your odds would either be completely random or a 100% chance of failure, but in DOSE2, you can spend stat points such that even if you can't guarantee success, you can directly dictate what your odds are.

I know a lot of people have said "trust the dice."  Well, I don't.  I tried to.  I've completed Act 1 of this game 3 times now, including every single side quest.  And no less than seven times, my character with 30 in every core stat and advantage in several areas still somehow managed to fail a dice roll.  I'm sorry, but I cheated myself a god character and the game STILL found a way to f**k me over.  Any ruleset that allows a character with maximum stats to fail ANYTHING is an inherently flawed ruleset, whether I trust it or not.

So I'm done with this thing.  I don't regret buying it and won't ask for a refund, but only because I love Larian and I am confident that the next Divinity game will be absolutely, positively amazing.  But I will never play this again.  Never.  Why would I, when I could just play DOSE2 again and have a better experience all around?

comment:
In the way of Elden Ring itself. One of the best to ever do it. If you love Dark Souls and have never played Elden Ring somehow. Do yourself a favor and experience it!

FromSoftware is taking steps towards the ways of Ubisoft, Bethesda, Bioware, EA, ect. Is FromSoftware even close to the the best of these terrible companies? No, far from them. They are still for intents and purposes. A good company. They just happened to slip up and made a mistake here. And as the consumer, I have the right to voice my displeasure about it. 

This $5 microtransaction that adds in a variety of armors and NPCs to fight is the start of something I don't like to see. And yes The Tarnished edition IS a microtransaction. SOTE is a DLC. What's the difference? The sheer size of content and effort put into it. SOTE was a GOTY runner up as a DLC. Brand new map, a multitude of new items, plenty of new enemies, new bosses, and new NPC story lines. The Tarnished pack gives you a small handful of new armors, 2 new invaders, and 2 new starting classes. That is NOT a DLC. 

$40 for 50 hours of new content = DLC. 
$5 for not even 20 minutes of new content in-which mostly includes a few armor sets and horse armor = microtransaction. 
I mean, it's literally in the name. MICRO-TRANSACTION aka a small purchase.
Simple as that.

I will happily purchase DLC from you, but I will NEVER buy a microtransaction from you.
FromSoftware... Please do not do anything like this again. 

Remember, it takes years to build up a good reputation. It only takes one action reverse those years of work.

How the ♥♥♥♥ is this game overwhelmingly positive. How the hell is this ♥♥♥♥ getting this much praise, i cant fathom. Just to even the score, here is my review.

Wish I could play V's story as he first experiences Night City's underbelly alongside Jackie and ME. It's dissonant when your partner who you supposedly worked with for like 6 months in a minute long montage treats you like a brother from another mother YET you still cant wrap your head around how mercs work.) [/spoiler] I wish I could experience THAT.

This "open world" is more like an open shop window, a facade, an illusion, where you can look at stuff but cant interact with it. You dont matter, your lifepath dont matter, your choices dont matter, the world remains a static ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Gangs dont rise and fall, you dont work with gangs, you work for someone "neutral" and always against some gang. Territories dont change, neither does the world. You are so much not part of the world that you dont even have a reflection. They also havent kept like half of the promises they made during the development. The driving is mostly awful, its crazy how can they ♥♥♥♥ up something so bad that isnt even a creativity issue and has been done for a hundred times and a hundred times better. 

The skill trees are very nice. Lots of synergies and different playstyles available, you can easily redistribue your perkpoints.

Okay, here is something good, this game also has value after all. And it is extra good because you can enjoy it without even buying the game: the music is FIRE, it made its way to my playlist. I just wish i could have discovered this music scene without spending a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ dime on this overrated hot garbage of a game.

This game is the epitome of wasted potential. Idk how they ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up so bad. Its not that this is a bad game. Its a shallow game that looks and feels good on the surface but it is rotten at its core. Again, such an immersive experience from the developers.

comment:
It's fun, but it needs a lot of mods and it needed 4~5 years in the oven to be in the great state that it is I still gripe with the lack of polish in certain areas but overall it's a fun game. For example, ladders don't take into account V's shoe type (or lackthereof), it's a single SFX for everything. the same goes for sliding. I'm telling you, it's weird that heeled boots, sneakers and bare feet all make the same sliding sound and they sound like we're scraping a some sort of hard plastic against the pavement. It's the same issue with generic NPCs, they all have the same footsteps SFX whether they have high heels, slippers or are barefoot. It's not a huge issue in the grand scheme of things, but in a game where immersion is important, it's quite a downer.

My most critical issue tho is that I started the game 3 times in total (1.7, post 2.0 and a couple of months ago) and I have a decent amount of hours, yet somehow the game isn't compelling enough for me to finish it. I have fun when I play it, but I never feel like I want to finish it. It's lacking some sort of hook for me.

I do have an major issue, why do I need mod to have a good looking female V?  Male V has pretty good options but I'll say it, most females look ugly af. It's dystopian, blahblah, I'm aware, but if males can look good, females can as well, at least sometimes, come on. Plus the game has so many voice over, I shouldn't have to use a mod to have NPCs talk in their languages, we have lore in built translation programs, why would it be an issue? Why can't I pick the voice language for V as either? It's not game breaking, but CDPR already put so much time into having so many voicovers, it's silly that we can't select them. It could be a separate free DLC to save some space as well.

That's only my opinion anyway, I can't exactly recommend a game I don't want to finish, I'm not even half way throught the main story. But don't let my weird issue stop you guys from playing the game, if you didn't do it yet. Just an old man ranting.

comment:
Incredible production values, if you want a shiny D&D game, look no further! The game is also mostly good, but I do NOT recommend it.

When combat ends, the game automatically switches from turn-based to real-time. If one of your party members is down you now have as little as 6 seconds (depending on how which death saving throw they're on) to navigate the UI to revert to turn-based and/or navigate to the downed party member before they die.

If you use the controller, tooltips will cover the context menu randomly, but consistently.

The former problem was mentioned to Larian 5 years ago and they couldn't be bothered. The controller issue is well known, but they can't be bothered.

Oh, and there's a launcher for all 3 of your Larian games (skippable with an argument added to the executable) and an optional Larian account to link with, but it's not invasive and isn't a seperate launcher running at all times a la Ubi.

The apparent refusal to fix known bugs coupled with the wonky implementation of D&D death rolls makes me give a soft "recommend against". Oh, and you can only play this game by save-scumming, but that's ok, it decided to delete my last 4 hours of saves and earn itself an uninstall!

comment:
Look, I know it's an amazing game. But it's not without its faults. If I'm playing an RPG, what I care about is the narrative. This game has a stellar narrative, but the game design actively resists showing it to you. The narrative allows some choice, but it's mostly built on allowing failure and presenting consequences for failure. Sometimes it's off of a failed dice roll and very often it's based on conversation tree options that vague and don't communicate the weight attached to them. I'm not opposed to meaningful choices or hard choices, but... the way the game allows and punishes failure often leads to worse gameplay and a lower quality narrative than what the game has to offer.

This can be related to small things, like a combat encounter that becomes impossibly hard and frustrating because you missed a character's side conversation, failed a persuasion roll, or didn't realize that it'd be easier if you LET yourself be ambushed. This can be annoying but it's not a dealbreaker.

The dealbreaker is allowing failure on major plot points (losing characters, or even losing companions), then doing nothing to transition the story or character dynamics in response. I'm having to Google if certain things are bugged. The negative consequences often come on suddenly and they aren't followed up with conversations or narrator cues to unpack what happened and what comes next; nothing fills the void of what you missed or lost. I've had to repeatedly save scum and force the "good outcome" just to feel in touch with the narrative. I'll still dump a ton of hours into BG3, but I'll be frustrated for far too many of them.

comment:
[h1] If you value roleplaying consistency, do not play this [/h1]

I've since dropped this game but I would appreciate it if someone would read through this and tell me where i may have gone wrong. Genuine advice would be appreciated. I want to like this game.

Consistency is not really something that you are going to find much of in this game. Its weird to talk about because often times these inconsistencies are intentional like the combat RNG (although intentional does not mean its good). What I want to focus on here in this review however is the consistency of the roleplaying aspect of the game and why I dont think its very good. What really irks me about this game is how said inconsistency in certain places does not translate well to the roleplaying aspect and general content of the game, if you want an RPG that respects your intent in a well polished and consistent manner, this is ABSOLUTELY not it despite the appearance it gives off of being able to do things however you possibly could want. One example of this that is not exclusive and in fact is the largest sign I personally found of a broader issue not just limited to combat in this game is the ability to fight people and cause chaos constantly. You can fight whoever you want and the game allows it and even encourages it as an intended and described approach during certain sidequests, however a good portion of the time, if you want to fight people, you will get curbstomped, and thus might have to rethink your approach and do something you didnt want to do for an outcome you didnt want. My issue is not born of difficulty, its born of the idea that if you want to be a hyper-aggressive gremlin, you are going to be punished for it a lot instead of rewarded and it can make it feel as if certain roleplaying options are not viable (again, not exclusive to fighting everyone), although being "rewarded" in this game is quite a subjective thing for many people. For a game as broad and inclusive towards literally everything as this, it really does not do a good job at integrating every possible way for players to go about things in an equal manner. In fact this exact thing is exactly what made me drop the game at the nere fight in act 1. I prepared as much as I possibly could think I could've, stabbed certain enemies in the back multiple times and save scummed in order to get optimal rolls on the damage values, and still couldnt get past the fight despite wanting to take the route of killing everyone and nere himself in that fight. Its wide as an ocean (everything you can do) but deep as a lake (the polish and value of each approach to a given situation). I dont expect every approach to be equally easy or equally rewarding, but I do expect the game to treat each playstyle it explicitly describes or offers as an equally viable and intentional way to play the game based on its presentation and it just does not manage that in my opinion. On a personal note: I am 35 hours in on one save slot and I have yet to figure out why people love this game so much, but I certainly know that at least for me, this game's unholy amounts of inconsistency in its combat, its tone, its outcomes and the inconsistency in the "RP" in "RPG" is just not for me. If you value roleplaying consistency and viability of your intentions in games, this is not what you are going to find here. Unless you've played D&D a lot in which case I can't really comment because I don't play D&D

Future edit: With a clear mind, I think there are some things I do genuinely believe are flaws, even with the months since I've played this. For one, when I say that your choices are not respected, that doesn't entirely mean just the dice screwing you over, but also the results of either succeeding or failing a roll. From what I remember, there really isnt anything that changes much when you succeed or fail a dialogue or skill check, the most things that happened for me were companions changing their opinions of you ever so slightly on an invisible scale (which given the amount of dialogue there is is basically worthless), the character fighting you which is just an extra hassle, or worst yet, content and options for your playthrough literally being locked out thanks to a dice roll and from what I could tell, absolutely nothing being done to balance out said locked content. Also, to expand on the combat, the best way I can describe it is switching between getting ♥♥♥♥♥♥ consensually and non-consensually by a 20 sided die CONSTANTLY. There are many encounters I walked into in the early game (most notably the goblin fight with dror ragzlin, the lycans attacking the cargo crew, and the nere fight), that are grossly overtuned for reasons I cant understand, these encounters kicked my ass multiple times and it was mostly because my party could not for the life of them get good rolls, and what makes it worse is that you could go a few feet away from them and fight something else that is much easier. Its overtuned fights in an area where they shouldn't be overtuned (I was playing on regular difficulty btw), on top of that, the enemies themselves also have an absurd amount of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ they can pull out of their ass whenever they want. In fact, what made me quit the game entirely was a moment in the nere fight when I had progressed through a good portion of it, but suddenly the enemies ensnare arrows start hitting perfectly every single time unlike before, and most notably, an enemy was throwing a bomb at my feet and the throw does 3/4 damage to the bomb, not quite enough to blow it up, however, in the last attempt I did, that same bomb randomly decided to take 4 damage and completely blow up my entire party for no reason. The combat is not only dictated by the dice, but also by swen vincke's wrath. Also, as for getting stronger, unfortunately this game does not do the best job at that. Here's the thing, at least in act 1, this game does not serve that well as an open world game, even in its more linear design as compared to something like breath of the wild. What I mean by this is that some sidequests will give you xp, some wont, some activities will give you xp, some wont, and some stuff you do literally wont give you so much as a weapon or item you'll never use. Compare this to something like elden ring where wherever you go, even if you get something worthless, you are still gathering runes for levels, in this game, you sometimes get ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. 
And onto my last point, the character writing is questionable. (Spoilers ahead) I know everyone loves this game's writing, but at least in act 1, there is nothing encouraging you to give a single flying ♥♥♥♥ about any of your companions save for wyll and karlach. Their entire development early game is them just telling you "I ♥♥♥♥♥♥ a goddess and wanted her love", "My society is very brutish and hardcore", "I am part of a religion that keeps secrets", "I am a vampire and I dont like it", it is simple character dialogue with nothing to show for it, like I have no reason to care, this is not a book where you have to use your mind to fill in the blanks and create an image, I am literally looking at these people and this world, why do I not get anything to show me why I should care. This is why I say wyll and karlach are the only 2 I actually gave a single ♥♥♥♥ about because with wyll, there's a scene where mizora will come down and literally sprout horns on his head in front of you, something he finds shameful, and with karlach, after you kill the paladins, she will take out her anger on the surrounding environment. This is show dont tell, and the rest of the companions dont get much of it at all. Also, to add to this, everyone, and I mean everyone is trying to jump your bones every chance they get in the early game to the point where it becomes a hassle trying to dodge having sex with someone constantly, the game continuously puts you in situations where it gives you a nudge nudge and a wink and I keep having to say "No".

I went into this game with incredibly high expectations, and I can fully say that in terms of the combat, story and detail of the world, it easily surpassed them. While I understand that I can read the dialogue history, needless to say this is incredibly immersion breaking. I have submitted a bug report for this, but am not hopeful as to the issue being addressed any time soon, as I have seen reports of the same bug dating back to 2023. Its also worth mentioning that the issue persists regardless of game settings (My macbook M2 Max should, and does outside of cutscenes, run the game very well, even on very high settings). I am seriously considering a refund if there is no communication from the team that this issue is going to be addressed in the near future. 

Edit: It seems like the issue is mainly on Mac and PS5, so Larian please use this to fix your otherwise amazing game, and buyers on those platforms beware that you may not get the whole experience...

I love GTA V.

I love the GTA series.

I love Rockstar Games.

So naturally, when GTA 6 was announced, I was excited.

**PC players apparently don't exist.**

Apparently my gaming platform is too dangerous for Rockstar to release GTA 6 on at the same time.

Console players get GTA 6.

PC players get…

We buy Shark Cards.

We buy the same game approximately 47 times.

And our reward?

**“Coming to PC later.”**

Later™.

No exact date. No proper explanation. Just the classic Rockstar silence.

I know GTA 6 will probably be incredible.

That's exactly why this is so frustrating.

I WANT TO PLAY IT.

I don't want to buy another console just because Rockstar decided PC players can wait.

So yeah:

**Amazing franchise.
Amazing games.
Terrible treatment of PC players.**

I'll probably still buy GTA 6 on PC when it eventually arrives.

Because apparently I'm part of the problem.

**Rockstar: 1
PC players: 0**

See you in Los Santos…

**in 2028, apparently.**

comment:
Upvote or Downvote can mean either loving or hating a game. Few see anything inbetween.

This game is inbetween for me, but leans negatively.

The positives are the incredible level of visual polish. It's a very polished game. All the technical elements are well done. I'll say that.

The negatives, though, are quite numerous, but they aren't all equally negative. Let's start with the obvious. This game is oozing woke ideology. Even if it won't say it out right, it's there, for all to see. It starts when you create a character, and the gender is separated from the sex. Want to be a woman with a penis? Go right ahead. Nevermind that it makes no sense in the setting. Never mind that it's an example of going out of one's way to cater to a very vocal and insane minority of people at the expense of reason and sanity. 

The woke doesn't end there though. Every scene feels like a Disney movie poster. They have the perfect balance of "races". Black dwarves, black elves, black this black that. Does it matter that dwarves evolved to live underground where melanin is closer to a mineral than a pigment catalyst? Not to Larian or WotC. They care more about virtue signaling than they do creating cohesive and meaningful cultures. All they see is skin color. They don't see subtle cultural differences, the tendency of certain races to naturally share traits which make sense to be inherited by their environment and nature. They throw all of that away to make sure that every gender and racial make up of humans is represented in every "race" or species in the game. It's stupid, childish, and down right disturbing. 

Because their idea of "diversity" is to throw a paint bucket on one of every character type in the game, it is to be expected that the actual meaningful types of diversity, such as thought, personality, interests, passions etc were ignored. Instead, it's only surface deep. Vapid, vain , and superficial differences are all the wokesters care about because they are what they claim to hate. This leads to very mundane, stale, and underdeveloped characters.

It's so hard to take the setting seriously because of the ridiculous colorswap skin color focused , gender bending characters. They look, feel, and act more like caricatures of real people than real people. Feeling any connection for them is out the window, with the exception of maybe two in the whole game. 

Further still, every character is bi, and every character wants to have sex with you after even a single nice word is thrown their way. It's jarring to be talking to a clearly straight character, only to have the narrator suggest we start having sex with eachother in only two dialogue exchanges. This might not seem like a big deal, but it will totally ruin characters for you when they are presented one way, then instantaneously given an abrupt 180 personality shift. Many such instances of this happening soured my opinion of the character to the point I just don't like talking to them. Add in the ridiculous skin color swapping and gender bending, you end up with a cast of characters better suited for the looney troons than a semi-serious RPG.

Moving on from the blatant political bent, the rest of the game suffers from a similar lack of meaningful nuance. Abilities all feel very similarly. Spells more or less offer different colors of the same few effects. Spamming the same few spells over and over, because they're clearly the most effective, gets old pretty fast. Combat in general begins to feel the same after a while. Fights move along methodically and predictably. Occasionally someone will crit, but the fights feel stale and lifeless. Turn based combat is rigid, inflexible, and creates odd situations.

Effects lack conviction. Most everything is just a couple turns in length. The odds of spells being resisted is high. There's not much satisfaction to the spell system at all really. 

Overall, the game lacks a feeling of urgency and lethality that would make the moment to moment combat more exhilarating. Instead, Fights move along in predictable fashion, with predictable outcomes, and predictable rewards. 

Having to rest every other fight wouldn't be so bad if the player wasn't forced to return to camp, requiring a level load out of their area, where they must then get past a few animations before they can rest. The process to rest adds tedium which quickly gets old, but always forces you to to do it. How great it would be to click a button and instantly just be rested up, with no loss to the challenge or value of the experience. The old BG games worked that way. It was a much better and more streamlined system.

Unlike other great Crpgs, the handholding removes much of the mystery from the game. Virtually every trap is automatically discovered. Their effects are typically minor, and the ability to disarm them is almost guaranteed with a default party. There's hardly anything left to the player's imagination, nor their senses. Hidden switches are easily seen, chests easily opened, most fights easily won. There are few interesting puzzles, though they do exist. The original Baldur's Gate 1 and 2 had far more detailed hidden item searching, where player agency mattered as much as the character. Baldur's Gate 3 does not think highly enough of the player to expect them to overcome adversity, so they give very little of it. 

The camera sucks. Controlling the Camera is tedious. Being 3D, it requires constant re-orientation and positioning. Oftentimes it gets stuck on walls, ramps, doorways or any other background asset.  I can't remember the last time I played a CRPG where the Camera fought me as much as the enemies did. 

Most CRPGs allow for seamless and fast switching of characters. Due to the turn based nature, each character must be resolved in order. While splitting party members up is possible, it's problematic. Characters can't be group selected, so each character must be controlled individually when group  mode is deactivated. Furthermore, every character has their own inventory, which is completely disorganized. It's just one giant x by y grid of item slots. Trying to find a specific item, on a specific character is downright obnoxious. The low contrast, dark color of the UI does not help with this. I've gone hours without even wanting to go  looking for items. It's easier to simply not care.

Finally, my least favorite mechanic by far is the die rolling system. Ultimately, this is what stalled my playthrough more than anything else. The ridiculousness of forcing me to click on a 20 sided die to resolve virtually every in game challenge is unfathomable. The game will have you rolling a die every minute, on average. Some rooms are so full of traps and treasure, characters will be rolling dice for minutes. First, a screen pops up, interrupting your flow. You then have to determine which modifiers you want applied to the roll. Then you click the die to roll it. Now you wait for the die to finish its flashy roll animation. Once that ends, it starts another animation adding your mondifiers together one by one ( could be 5 or more often). After this ends, it gives the result in a final flashy animation and tells you either you succeeded or failed.... this happens every..single..time... you want to open a locked chest, disarm a trap, convince an npc, pull a stuck lever... etc etc. You'll watch this same animation 1000 times over dozens of hours. This should have, and could have been done behind the scenes without the player even knowing.

BG3,despite all of its polish, has only superficial depth in both the setting and gameplay. They cleaned and polished every speck of character out of whatever this game claims itself to be. Whether its the repetitive combat, or the vain, skin deep woke pandering, BG3 just feels bland. While I don't love it, I also don't feel enough about it to hate it.

comment:
Pros: Beautiful art design, particularly character and monster design. Architectural design can be a bit generic and repetitive but it fits the setting. Incredible world design. 

Cons: Combat is, at its heart, a knife fight simulator. Not a true RPG and would not recommend to other RPG gamers. The magic system is shallow and underbaked and fundamentally doesn't fit a combat system that wants to be a rhythm game. If you like casters, stay away.

The game occasionally stops being an RPG and confiscates your build. As an egregious example: Rykard gives my pure-Intelligence sorcerer a twelve-weight Strength weapon that ignores Intelligence entirely, then balances two enormous health bars around using a weapon you'll never touch again. 

Other complaints: 

1. The sorcerer's principal progression region, Raya Lucaria, heavily resists magic. If you rely purely on exploration and refuse to metagame and explore Caelid early to get Rock Sling you will suffer. 

2. Casting speed is governed by Dexterity, making magic the playstyle with the most awkward stat distribution and imposing an archetypally incoherent stat tax.

3. The already lackluster spell variety collapses under the FP economy. The first spells you get will likely remain among the most efficient throughout the game. Many of the spells are situational, redundant or boring, larger version of a previous one.  

4.  Weapon skills and Ashes of War frequently deliver the feel and look of 'magic' with far fewer downsides. Moonveil and Dark Moon Greatsword as the obvious examples here. 

5. The summoning system is heavily restricted by geography but is also the only broadly reliable way for casters to create the uninterrupted openings required by the game's longer and more elaborate spells. Where summoning is disabled, the caster is pushed back toward quick, close-range attacks like Carian Slicer. In practice you'll often spend a good chunk of your game outside boss arenas as a spellblade by necessity, whether that was your intended playstyle or not. 

6. Summoning is also so poorly balanced that roughly 90% of its enormous roster is not worth upgrading. A handful of durable generalists and exceptional group ashes are almost never the wrong choice, reducing most specialized summons to self-imposed novelty picks. 

7. Damage-type adaptation is locked behind obscure spell acquisition, hybrid stat requirements, or entirely different casting traditions. To “adapt” here often means abandoning the mage you built. Even respec is gated by play-time and a somewhat rare consumable so it's not an encounter-level solution here either. 

8. Bosses frequently erase the strategic advantage of range. There's no real magic, in an RPG sense, without it. 

The standard Souls player rebuttal “but mages can melt bosses” doesn’t counter any of this. Sorcery has enormous optimized peaks when the enemy stays still and the player stacks Terra Magica, a Physick, specialized headgear, talismans and a summon. But that does not show that it consistently supports experiencing the world as a caster. 

Given that I had to ask an AI model to heavily rewrite the magic system into something resembling an actual RPG, I can't in good conscience recommend this game to other RPG players in spite of hundreds of hours of playtime.

comment:
I typically don't write negative reviews but I was so disappointed in this expansion I had to share my thoughts. The writing, narrative and gameplay of this expansion are garbage. The game looks great, some voice acting is pretty good, but the overall story telling and what the game actually has you doing in-between dialogues is not good or fun.
  There is an immediate shift in mission design and tone upon reaching the DLC zone. The whole narrative pov doesn't make sense. Are the npcs talking to "we the player", who knows about future events in the story or is it "V the street kid with Keneau Reeves in his head"? The characters seems to constantly be breaking the forth wall and speaking to the player with knowledge that the character V wouldn't have any way of knowing and this makes it very difficult to get invested at all in what is happening and I felt like a passive observer of a bad tv show, not an active participant in an immersive story and world.
  To start, a mysterious caller tells you "The president is in danger"... uh ok. Aren't I a steetkid from Night City who has days left to live? Why would I remotely care about the president of this violent, evil, corpo-hellscape of a dystopia I live in? Oh, they are actually a really nice president in this world and not corrupt or cruel and her omni-present ai assistant somehow knew I had a special chip in my head and that only I can help save her... ok... Then 3 minutes later the mystery voice is telling me "Hurry to that ladder V, the yellow one over there, I know you can do this." WTF game am I playing?! The campaigns in a CoD are more original than this and the vibes are completely sanitized and weak. Vocal coaching the player from yellow paint marker to yellow paint marker is the laziest type of game design and completely out of tone of the world of Cyberpunk 2077 too. Just say "Go to there" or "Go to this person" and then let me figure it out like a puzzle using all my cyber enhancements, don't give me 20 progress updates and tell me in a cringe manner how well I'm climbing in a game supposed to be set in a unforgiving gritty world. Anytime you are given freedom you can just sprint and dodge past all the meaningless enemies to trigger the next scripted moment that will reset all of the npc's, unless you are forced into a scripted gunfight you will have to kill everything or a forced stealth part that ultimately devolves into you kill everything. the stakes feel meaningless with checkpoints every 30 seconds and your actions in the world mean nothing and neither do the dialogue options, which gives the game no immersion. 
 I'll keep playing and update if things change but I was super shocked and let down by this DLC and the quality of the writing and mission design.

I had been looking forward to playing this game after watching countless videos about it. The world, lore, and overall concept are exactly the kind of RPG I enjoy. Unfortunately, I couldn't get past the PC controls.

I don't mind difficult games, Elden Ring's tough enemies made the world feel more immersive.  What made the experience frustrating was the keyboard and mouse implementation. Many key bindings feel unintuitive and clunky. Difficulty should come from the game's mechanics and enemies, not from fighting the controls. Good quality-of-life features and intuitive controls don't make a game easier; they simply make it more enjoyable to play.

It's clear that Elden Ring was designed primarily with a controller in mind. I may revisit the game once I get a controller, because everything else about it genuinely appeals to me. But for now, the PC controls prevent me from enjoying what otherwise seems like an incredible game.

Title: A Masterpiece… but Missing One Simple Freedom

Baldur’s Gate 3 is easily one of the best RPGs ever made.
The world is rich, the characters are unforgettable, and the amount of freedom in quests and combat is incredible. Every fight feels tactical, every choice matters, and the replay value is huge. It’s a game that pulls you in and refuses to let go.

But there is one major limitation that holds it back for players like me:
you cannot freely customise your own full party.

For a game that celebrates freedom, it’s surprising that creating a full custom team is restricted. Many players enjoy building their own party of heroes — not because we dislike the companions, but because we love tactical synergy, role‑playing, and experimenting with different builds. Even creating just three custom characters makes the game harder, because the difficulty doesn’t scale down.

It feels like the game pushes you toward using Origin companions, even when you want to enjoy the story your own way.

Still, despite this limitation, BG3 remains an amazing experience.
The writing, combat, music, and world-building are top-tier.
I just hope that one day, Larian gives players the option to create a full custom party without workarounds.

A game this good deserves that extra freedom.

Disclaimer: This is a Remaster review. The Witcher 3 I played back on PS4 is still a masterpiece. 

As someone who has put over 1600 mods into Skyrim, this feels like a heavily modded version of TW3, not a true remaster. I know they already did a next-gen update, so they had to call this something different, but calling it a remaster was a mistake. It does not live up to the expectations that word sets.

This remaster has stripped away a lot of the magic by desaturating the color and making everything look more realistic. The original game looks like a beautiful painting. This game looks like an unreal tech demo where they think higher quality bushes and realistic lighting constitutes better art direction. It doesn't.

The lighting changes/additions are not well executed at all. Putting aside the complete loss of the original's brilliant color grading and art direction, ray tracing and path tracing look decent outdoors. However indoors is a different story. Ray tracing sometimes works indoors, but path tracing almost never works indoors. Half the huts in White Orchard are pitch black indoors, including ones with quest NPCs. I had to keep switching between PT and RT and raster to try and get the least bad lighting for the moment. Not best lighting, least bad. 

Menus are weirdly laggy and glitchy, and somehow the fps seems lower in them even those steam tells me I'm getting 100+ frames. Again, how did that get missed? 

Geralt attacks non-existent enemies instead of the one right in front of him. I'm sure that was a problem in the original game, but for a remaster that supposedly fixing the combat issues...they are still there, unfixed. 

After nearly completing White Orchard, I think I'm just going to roll back and play the original version of the game, or maybe the next-gen. From what I've researched it's generally more faithful to the original vision.

Again, I was going to give it a "meh", but after struggling with its problems for hours, I'm going to outright downgrade it.  It's not a good game.  And it absolutely IS NOT one of the greatest games ever made.  Probably isn't even in the top 10 of "D&D" games ever made.

Problems include:

*RNG Bullshi...  At a certain point it no longer becomes fun to watch your characters fail to roll above a 4.  As someone who has done alpha and beta testing on games before, I can tell you that there is something wrong with their dice rolling system.

*Camera Controls.  The way you can move and control the camera is janky as hell, and absolutely frustrating.

*Interface. It's just poorly designed.  If I'm using an item from someone's inventory, if I don't have the right character selected, it uses that item for a different character.  Absolutely asinine.

*D&D Rules.  Nevermind how it's not working how it's supposed to...  It's not working how it says it's supposed to.  For example, I've watched Karlach drop out of a rage and lose it MULTIPLE TIMES despite being attacked.

*Pathfinding.  I've never seen such poor pathfinding on a modern game.  Couple this with poor camera controls, and I've often sent people way off path because I clicked on invisible terrain that the camera couldn't see.  Which leads me to the next problem...

*Lack of a pause button.  Some of these problems could be tolerable if there was a pause button.  If I was able to stop a character running off into misfortune because of the bad interface and camera, it wouldn't be as infuriating.  


I'm off to investigate if there are any mods that fix the broken RNG of this game.  If there are, I'll try again.  But I'd rather catch a testicle in a zipper than watch the game pathologically keep my rolls under 5.

comment:
Slightly hypocritical review, as I have enjoyed The Witcher 3 in the Next-Gen version, and I still will after downgrading from the Remastered version to Next-Gen with DX11 (Next-Gen and Classic are still available under the Beta branches).

But what CD Project Red and the gaming industry as a whole is doing with these graphical "upgrades" is madness.

I have spent hours tweaking the graphical settings for the game to look as good as it did in the Next-Gen update while maintaining solid 60 FPS, with mixed results. I can get it to run on 1440p@60 FPS with ultra/high settings and no Ray Tracing, but the problem is that it doesn't look good [i]consistently[/i].

This is because they have somehow introduced dynamic color pallets and lighting, so that the colors and illumination changes in different areas. Sometimes interiors are dark, sometimes a very bright gray. Sometimes it switches between looking good or bad as the colors and lighting changes from one frame to the other.

On top of that there are a tons of graphical glitches, popping, broken distant models, shadows, etc. And worst of all constant crashes, but I believe that this is a Linux/Proton issue that will be eventually fixed.

The "old" Next-Gen version in DX11 runs super super smooth and consistent with lots of headroom with my hardware. And it looks absolutely gorgeous!

What also shocks me is how many official reviews praise the update for the Path Tracing. I'm happy for everyone owning a 1.5k+ GPU, and Ray/Path Tracing are fascinating technologies, but personally think that the price of the hardware doesn't remotely justify these "enhancements". And it would be completely fine to have the options present in the game, but the fact that a 11 year old game becomes so badly optimized for modern mid-end hardware even with all the high-end stuff turned off is not acceptable!

Also some users do run the game with RT/PT, but then heavily rely on upscaling and frame generation. It surely is a matter of taste, but I find the looks too blurry with heavy upscaling and the delay too "floaty" with frame generation. And as I said before, I'm not even a fan of the new color palette/lighting, even with Path Tracing enabled. Summarized, the industry introduces super demanding graphical features to justify insanely expensive hardware, while introducing other technologies to downgrade the image/delay but boost the perceived FPS. And then they slap it onto old games, preventing them to run properly on modern, mid-range hardware.

As for the other new Remastered features, I will miss some of them. I especially like the additional accessibility features and quest markers on the map. Other than that I didn't notice the other improvements much.

I hope the Remastered version gets a lot more polish and optimization when the new DLC drops, so I can jump back into it and hopefully have a decent experience with a mid-range rig.

Go to honor mode? Probably 20-30% global bonuses and penalties. Not MORE enemies, or higher level enemies that you can see and go "Woah, hey-those guys are level 5" or whatever. No, you see "Lvl 2 Kuo toa" and it will miss once in 5 swings against your level 5 monk with AC 19 and Patient Defense running, while you try and attack their level 2 ass with AC 15 and you will hit about 1 in 5.

comment:
Its ok. Story was interesting at first but towards the end I was just rushing through to get it over with. Gameplay was whatever. I mostly played with Katanas, maybe that was a bad idea but it was just fine. AI provides no challenge. I recall defeating one boss by circling around a pillar repeatedly while blasting it with headshots each time it froze to T-pose. Enough said there I think. Almost never engaged with the quickhack mechanics, it was easy enough just running up and slicing enemies with my katana. Tried to do a stealth build but I got bored because of the unintelligent AI so I switched to melee/shotguns, which made it less boring.

The world is very pretty and interesting to look at. I never felt particularly interested or encouraged to explore so I never did except to finish quests. I think the only optional content I finished was the Delamaine quest and part of the cyberpycho quests. Very forgettable.

I never felt like my dialogue choices made much difference, especially the skill checks. I don't think those options affected dialogue even a single time. Most irritating example was succeeding a "cool" check to ask a merchant for a discount. They immediately tell me to ♥♥♥♥ off. Why even waste my time?

 I did enjoy dressing up my character quite a bit. It was the only thing I ever spent my money on since the game throws guns at you and I never felt the need to buy a car. It was annoying though because I had to keep driving around to different clothing stores to find clothes I liked.

I expected a lot more from this game. It was all kind of forgettable and never particularly interesting. None of the characters made much of an impression on me except for the arasaka bodyguard (cant remember his name) but I didn't know I could save him so he just died. Modern games have trained me to assume I cant do anything that isn't explicitly told to me by the game, so good on them for having a hidden outcome, but it ended up removing the only character I cared about so R.I.P. I think I got the "good" ending (the aldecaldo ending), but it didn't leave me satisfied (partly because I screwed up hooking up with Panam, my fault). I'd say this game was about as enjoyable as Fallout 4, with a better story and much better character customization.

comment:
One of the most frustrating games I've played in recent times. I rather play Demon's Souls, Bloodborne or Elden Ring. 
For my current campaign I played for about 30-35 hours (almost finished Act 1), all the other hours of my total playing time when I bought this back in 2023. Played mainly as a Bard (College of Lore). A couple of hours before I entered the underground forge I finally got to level 5. At this level you can definitely expect a bump in your overall abilities, especially if you choose to increase your main "damage" stat so to speak (other viable choices are alert for example). I cleared the Spectator, Ethel, Bulette all with considerable ease. Oh right, make sure your main stat is an even number, not uneven. If that makes any sense whatsoever. But then all of a sudden you also encounter a gimmick boss. All your rolls do nothing at all. It all magically misses or it almost does no damage. You got Bless, Vow of Enmity (which should give you an attack roll advantage btw) or other buffs and debuffs? Doesn't make any difference whatsoever. Just pray and hope the rng will be in your favor.   
I never played a game that explains so little, has so incredibly bad pathing, has weird camera spams when the terrain gets complex vertically, can be so infuriatingly obtuse in its questing and has so many bugs. Game of the year 2023? What a joke.

comment:
Let me introduce myself so you will get the feeling who is this review coming from. I started playing Counter Strike probably in 2003 or 2004 on the school PCs and in the local internet cafes. When I finally got PC with DSL connection in June 2006 the first game I bought was Counter Strike: Source and this was the exact moment when I created this Steam account. Later on Steam had some big database outage and all my hours recorded back in the days are lost so what you can see in my account now doesn't represent how many hours I spent in the game before CS:GO times. And then of course when CS:GO arrived it had many flaws, I didn't really start to play it until November 2014. Since then I played all the time, if not on this account then on another where I have 1k+ hours just playing with lower rank friends. I was so excited for CS2 - it was anticipated that it will have much more frequent updates, new interesting content, operations, better mechanics with subtick and all that stuff. We were told that CS:GO was lacking new nice things because of the "spaghetti code" that always meant breaking stuff and creating bugs whenever you touch it. CS2 supposed to be refactored game that makes all that issues gone. Guess what - it was all a lie. Things only got worse content-wise, subtick is a trash randomness and everybody wishes that 128 tick servers come back, and now they implemented some chicken eggs instead of things that players ask for - it's a complete slap in the face. We don't know what this is all for and who gives requirements to the devs, but that Product Owner should be replaced ASAP, the game was in the better state 3-4 years ago and earlier.

But I didn't even mention the worst thing that makes playing completely pointless. CHEATERS. There is no full version of VAC enabled in this game. Some auto-inputs are detected in some cases, but VERY rarely, and cheating such as wallhacking is fully allowed with no consequences. I know it first hand from the colleagues who just got so annoyed that they tried cheating themselves. It just revealed that every time when we thought "huh, that guy knows a lot", it was really just the wallhack and not the gamesense-like-a-pro players all the time. Playing faceit is now senseless as well. Cheat devs somehow have access to live data of all matches and you can literally turn on radar of every game in the browser on the 2nd screen (ie on the smartphone or 2nd monitor). Installing anticheat doesn't even secure anything as "cheats" can run on another machine and display what they want in the browser. I am suspecting that Valve devs participate in the share for being payed by players who buy these cheats because otherwise I don't see the reason why they can't patch the leaking server information. Oh and outside of faceit - you don't need this browser thing as all the information, every detail about every player on the server is stored locally on your RAM. Premier cheats use it like an open book. This could be patched easily as well. So Valve devs must somehow benefit from it that they keep it like that.

I can't recommend this game to anyone at this point. I will not play it again until internet will be flood over with the information that cheating problem is fixed, which I guess will never happen. This is it for me, about 23 years of playing Counter Strike and I am done.

comment:
MONTONOUS AND UNFUN. 

>>>

This game teaches you to run away from/past all of the enemies you face, mostly, and even if you work hard to learn their patterns and use the sluggish and unkind combat controls to defeat them, your reward is next to nothing. 

Seriously, I have barely found any gear or weapons worth using, most stuff you DO find is worse than the gear you probably already have. 

Many enemies don't drop enough runes to justify fighting them at all, and again your reward is nothing. 

Levelling feels like nothing changed. No tutorials or explanations force you to turn to youtube ect, and even then it makes little difference.

They worked so hard to make these areas and enemies and you may as well just run right through them.

The story is completely un-follow-able I have no idea what is going on, who is who. 

Most online tutorials just suggest cheesing and game breaking mechanics.

When you do grind out a big fight, often you are rewarded with nothing, pretty much. Once you beat the mariner boss you can go visit some guy in 'dragonbaren'  and there each enemy drops 1000 runes and is easy to kill and stun lock. Meanwhile, the vast majority of other enemies dont drop anything close to that despite being MUCH harder to deal with. 

The game encourages hit and run tactics if you do fight, due to large crowds of enemies who will stun lock and kill you, which is boring. 

Plenty of collecting and hunting to do, but I do not know what for, I am near to level 30 and have never needed to use the crafting menu. 

Most mechanics are pure mystery, just check online. 

Now, you must ask yourself, is this person who is writing this review just bad at games? not used to boss fighting games? is he just a bit salty? I have nearly 100%'d cuphead. Enjoyed it despite some rage. I have ground out many hard games, and I enjoy achievement hunting, I love a challenge. Elden ring is a monotonous bore I have no idea how I have come this far. 

The game doesn't run nearly as well as it should, my computer isnt great but can run other similar games smoothly. 

The open world aspect is whatever, I use the fast travel as much as possible and just rush through new areas avoiding absolutely everything til i find the next grace. 

I WENT INTO THIS GAME BLIND, thinking it would be fun. Do not do that. It is far too much labour to try and figure ♥♥♥♥ out for yourself, find little things in a big world and so on. Just take the advice of better players. 

I think the combat is dog**** and the controls are obnoxious, there should be a separate button for sprinting and rolling. I am using PC controls, its annoying and feels bad.

ONTOP OF THAT there is ♥♥♥♥ tons of outrage about the DLCS that I do not own being A) too expensive, nearly the cost of the base game, B) Some are effectively microtransactions, and C) Many people say to play through the base game before getting the DLCS because they don't add enough to change much of your playthrough, just new weapons and bosses locked behind a £40 paywall. 

I do NOT understand the hype at all, Its a genuinely bad game, I just wanted to level up and fight cool bosses, yet you are encouraged constantly to run away ect, go grind to avoid being one hit, then fight the boss and by your 20th attempt you might do OK. 

I could appreciate that if there were big upgrades, gear and combat pace improvements. EVERYTHING is sluggish. I have refused to use ranged weapons and magic, because THEN you really can cheese. 

Your reward? 2000 runes or so. Maybe a talisman. You beat a boss and leave the same power level you were before the fight. 

Also, the dropping runes on death is just an inconvenience, not difficult to deal with, just another chore you have to drag yourself through. The game is already so slow why try to take away people's hard work? its unlikely but why, like in games like terraria no one plays the drop items on death difficulty, because it takes forever to get stuff and people dont like that or enjoy the challenge. I just get on the horse, get my runes, and leave. Spend your runes before boss fights you cant leave. 

Yep.

comment:
Look. I know a lot has been said about this game, both good and bad. I'm not breaking new ground here. The pros of this game are the immaculate vibes and graphics. Being locked in on a mission makes the game flow and can be, at times, fun. And if this game was just an on-the-rail story-driven FPS, then yeah, I wouldn't have much to complain about (besides the hard crashes and game-breaking bugs that are still rampant, even now). 

The thing is, I can't let what happened be excused. I know CDPR pulled a "NMS" here and spent the last few years fixing it up, and that's good. But to glaze this game now only excuses the absolute fact that not only did they sell me an unplayable mess at start, they also sold me a DIFFERENT GAME. I pre-ordered this game because the makers of TW3 promised me an OPEN WORLD RPG, just like TW3, but cyberpunk. That is not what this game is. Night City is empty, a vacuous window-dressing void of any and all content save for the rare "work for the police by killing some dudes" (in a "punk" game, you sure do spend a lot of time doing the police's dirty work). No factions, no meaningful choices, all the shops and doors are closed, I could go on and on. Walking around NC is fun for the vibes, but it gets incredibly boring, and then depressing. 

I wanted to love this game so much. I was ready to lose myself in it. But even after waiting years to get this game in a playable state, it's clear this game is not 'open world' in any meaningful sense. It's not a 'role playing game' beyond choosing your combat style. Nothing you do really matters. Hop in a car (which are still absurdly hard to control on mouse/keyboard) and all the lights turn green, all the traffic disappears. Nothing you do matters, in the open world or in the story missions, as everything leads to a single "pick your ending" moment. In some ways, I'm more disappointed now than I was on launch.

If you want to just hang out in a cool futuristic cyberpunk city, this is the game for that. If you love story-driven on-the-rails FPS games, this is a great game for that. But if you want an open world role playing game, I can assure you that this is not that game. Don't reward bad corpo behavior, choom. Stop glazing this still-buggy mess of a failed promise.

comment:
This isn't D&D.

Obviously, I knew this going in. I really didn't think that would be that big of a deal, but it is. This is a D&D 5e system... it's a D&D setting... but it is NOT D&D. It's in an unpleasant uncanny valley where, in the end, it just feels like the 5e rules got shoehorned into a game they're not written for. It's all the weaknesses of 5e (unbalanced classes, martial/caster divide) and none of the strengths (flexibility, application of real world ideas into a game system, smooth combat resolution). It's a chimera, with semi-simultaneous action resolution, really high/long jumping for some reason, stripped down leveling (max 12), and lower flexibility for spells (Polymorph).

As of writing, every companion/"origin character" I've met has been unlikeable. Still, they're expected to be the center of the story, as there's no mechanism for you to have a backstory in the game. You might as well have spawned in those pods for all the relevancy your character's history or possible history has. 

The high magic in the game is kind of absurd. You have access to multiple scrolls of revivify at level 1 for game reasons, and you're literally flying around in a giant interdimensional Mind Flayer spaceship that took a wrong turn at Waterdeep, got hit by some dragons, and ended up in Avernus (because everything in D&D seems to end up there). I was rolling my eyes the entire intro because it was just so absurd. Combat is neither good nor bad, but it's kind of unfortunate it doesn't show the dice rolls for anything. Rolling dice in any other setting is a full-screen popup.

Larian tried their best, but I think, frankly, they had an impossible task. You can't adapt D&D, a collaborative story game, into a video game. You can make a [i]sandbox[/i], but that's not the same thing (and it's also not what they did).

The game looks great until something moves in a way that isn't just walking. Nearly every character in every scene is wobbling with mocap awkwardness; nearly nothing looks actually natural. They even have it in the trailers.

If you want an experience somewhat closer to what I think Larian was trying to accomplish, I would recommend Kenshi. You really do feel like you're creating your own story there, not stumbling through railroaded cutscenes. 

If you want a compelling mystery in a game that is both funnier and more representative of how D&D is played at the table, play Esoteric Ebb.

But if you want my honest advice...

[b]JUST PLAY D&D[/b]. This game seems to take over 60 hours to complete. That's enough for [b]ten 6-hour sessions of D&D[/b]. Buy the PHB for half the price of this game and

[b]Just[/b]

[b]Play[/b]

[b]D&D[/b].

But here is the thing: Night City is dark, diry and moody in a way that clearly took effort and it works, it really does feel like the future has gone to hell. 
Problem is that same darkness makes some parts a pain to actually navigate.

And honestly the biggest thing that got to me was just how much talking there is. 
You spend more time sitting through conversations than actually playing the game. 

The city is stuffed with NPCs everywhere, but most of them do not really say anything worth hearing. 
Feels like padding more than substance.

Still, at the end of the day, I would call this an excellent game. Just one with some real rough edges.

comment:
I'm sure this game is very successful at what it sets out to do, but I bounced off it hard. It's supposedly an RPG, but you can really only play two types of character: Hack a Bunch of Stuff and Also Shoot a Bunch of People, or Shoot Everyone. There really doesn't seem to be any other approach you can take. My first character was a street kid, and I made him Black, inspired by one of the hairstyles. But there's only one male voice, and it's a dirtbag white voice, and it didn't fit the character at all. So I immediately restarted and created a female corporate character. The voice fit, but the prologue quest suggested a double-cross choice that I wanted to take but wasn't permitted to, after which the game thrusts the player into a bleak introductory mission that's pretty much entirely on rails. A training sequence suggests that nonlethal takedowns are a thing, but then the game basically tells you that they're a bad idea and that you should just kill everybody. I was hoping for Neuromancer, but it felt more like Grand Theft Auto.

Also, despite the fact that my character was supposed to have superb reflexes, I couldn't make the dodge controls work. I'm a piano player; if I can't press the right keys at the right time, that is not a well-designed key sequence. In short, it was shaping up to be a grim, frustrating experience that didn't allow me the kinds of choices I wanted to make and had been taught by other games to expect that I could make, so I bailed out and requested a refund. I guess I'll never learn whether or not it deserves the hype, because I wasn't excited by anything that happened in my first two hours of play.

Don't throw me into a dystopia and then not let me fight the Man.

comment:
The Persona 5 of Souls: Beautiful art and fluid movement can’t hide that deliberate combat mastery was traded for mass market spectacle, serving up hollow power fantasies disguised as punishing depth.

The 500-Hour Fallacy: Spare me the "you got your money's worth" routine. Thoroughly testing builds and exploring the map across hundreds of hours doesn't excuse a back third that collapses under recycled encounters and artificial stat bloat. Walking away before the credits wasn't an act of rage or burnout, it was realizing the game had completely run out of ideas and stopped respecting my time.

Refusal to Support PC: Still no native ultra-wide support out of the box for a flagship release. Rendering the extra viewport only to deliberately mask it with black bars on modern monitors is lazy.

Shallow Cashgrabs: I never planned on reviewing this game, but the Tarnished Pack sealed the deal. Even as a Dark Souls II defender, it's blatant, low effort nostalgia bait. Blaming Bandai Namco lets FromSoftware off the hook for building it, and buying into cosmetic nickel and diming signals to both that standards no longer matter.

comment:

I first thought that this might be because in PnP, you have to keep track of everything by yourself, but at some point it gets so vast that a normal human can’t keep track of it. Where do I even start?
The game doesn't bother to tell you anything about it's mechanics, luckily I had people I could ask.
Throws. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ throws. You have to throw a dice if you actually hit the enemy and if your attack has an effect, your target has a saving throw if this effect hits. This leads to situations where you shoot a fireball at an enemy but apparently miss the ground he stands on and the enemy is too intelligent to start burning. A buddy of mine got nearly instantly killed by two enemies, while I survived two turns being surrounded by four of them. From their 12 attacks, only four hit. I got areactive skill that charms (basically useless) enemies that attack me. I only need one hand to count the enemies that [i]failed[/i] the saving throw against being charmed. In a boss fight, a powerful NPC missed all her hits for two turns and the boss wiped as all. Reload, the NPC now hits critical and oneshots the boss. This makes the game feel less tactical and more like entirely RNG depended.
Character progression is very limited. Pick a class, pick a subclass later on, you can pick your skills at level up, that's it. No attribute growth, no trying out builds, no specific ways to play your character. Reaching a new level doesn't feel like something you look out for, but a meaningless thing that just happens.
Very limited loot. Items might give you +1 on rolls or a new skill, nothing more. In act 3, I'm still using some items from act 1, because there simply wasn't anything better.
There is no mana or cooldown to manage, skills are just limited to one use and can only be recharged by resting. This plus the throwing mentioned above made my play almost exclusively with standard attacks as an archer, because why risk wasting a Tier 3 skill that I can only get back with a long rest or a strong scroll when I can simply shoot my bow?
There is other stuff, like seemingly every skill having another status effect or the 10+ effects you can stack on characters or the endless sub-systems, but it should be enough for now.
- The story never hooked me. Names and events get thrown around like everyone playing this game has a deep knowledge of the lore. I lost interest in story before leaving act 1.
- The companions are boring at best, annoying at worst. I didn't care for a single one of them and the worst part is that the characters are tied to their classes. Like Karlach but don't want a barbarian in your party? Too bad. Want a cleric but don't like Shadowheart? Too bad. You either have to pick your companions based on their class or roll with whatever class they are, regardless of party synergy.
- Camera is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Often things don't turn transparent so instead of walking along the corridor, your characters turns around trying to find a way up the wall above the door frame. Talking about doors, click on the ground behind a door and your characters often wont walk through, but close them. The camera is also oddly level based, making it impossible to move it up or down every now and then
- Every skillcheck comes with a dice throw animation. Cool the first few times, but when you have to disarm ten traps in a room, the unskippable animation becomes really annoying.
- Dialogues are bad and buggy. Sometimes, talking to NPC gives every party member the same options, ignoring intel from previous dialogues of other party members, sometimes NPCs refuse to talk to other party members when someone else already talked to them. In multiplayer, dice throws and answers given by other players sometimes aren't shown, only the sound is played. Conversations are marked as private, even when the private conversation box is unchecked.

The first CRPG I played was DOS 2. I played it solo and with a group of friends, we always stuck together, discussed dialogue options and made combat strategies. With the same group in BG3, we are constantly split, everyone goes their own way in combat and I never felt like doing a solo run.
We never finish DOS 2 because a lack of time. I'm not sure if we will finish BG3, because, at least for me, the game stopped being anything close to fun many, many hours ago.

comment:
**Not Recommended: I waited six years for this game to work.**

I was a day-one buyer of Cyberpunk 2077. I was there for the launch, and I swear I encountered just about every bug that ended up documented online.

So I waited.

I saw what CD Projekt Red had done with The Witcher 3 over time, and I genuinely believed Cyberpunk would get the same treatment. I wanted to experience this game when it was finally ready, rather than ruin my first playthrough fighting through technical problems.

Six years later, I still can't play it.

For me, it's the infamous audio crackling/popping glitch. If you've searched for this problem, you already know the worst part: everyone seems to have a different "fix," which means there really isn't one.

I've changed audio refresh/sample rates. Updated and reinstalled drivers. Turned SFX down and completely off. Disabled spatial audio. Used Windows spatial audio. Tried Bluetooth headphones, wired headphones, laptop speakers, desktop speakers, and monitor speakers. I've verified the game files, uninstalled and reinstalled the entire game, restarted the computer, turned it off and back on, and done all the other obligatory troubleshooting steps. I've gone through forums, Reddit threads, videos, and troubleshooting guides.

Believe me, if you're about to suggest a fix, I've probably tried it.

And before someone points at my Steam playtime as proof that the game must have been playable, those hours are extremely misleading. A huge amount of that time was spent with the game running while I was trying to troubleshoot the problem, testing settings, restarting, loading back in, driving around to see if the crackling returned, and repeating the process. Yes, there were stretches where I actually got to play the game, but I'd estimate maybe 25% of my recorded hours were spent genuinely playing rather than trying to make the game work.

And that's what makes this so disappointing. I *want* to play Cyberpunk 2077. I bought it at launch, watched CDPR spend years rebuilding its reputation, watched the game receive major updates and an expansion, and deliberately waited to give it the experience I thought it deserved.

But I've never once been able to actually play through the game.

Six years of patches, updates, fixes, and second chances, and a game-breaking audio issue that has been reported by players for years still makes the game effectively unplayable for me.

So, for the final time, I'm uninstalling Cyberpunk 2077. At this point, I have to accept that I'm probably never going to finish what I genuinely wanted to be a superb game.

I'm sure Cyberpunk 2077 is a great game when it works. I genuinely wish I could have found out.

...what, you didn't know this game was based off a TTRPG?  That was the original concept of this game: a video game adaptation not unlike CRPG's like Baldur's Gate did for D&D.  That's why back in 2012, CDPR "promised" things like:
* a "mature RPG...set in a rich, futuristic world" 
* a "gripping non-linear story filled with life and detail"
* "advanced RPG mechanics based on pen & paper RPG system"
* "varied selection of different character classes"

If only.

Night City could have, and should have, been one of the most expansive interactive, raw, gut wrenching environments ever to exist in gaming history.  The TTRPG even says that Night City should basically be its own character with everything it has to offer.  But instead, you get city block after city block of empty buildings, non-functional store fronts and window dressing.  A detailed world of which very little can be interacted with.  Most NPC's barely have anything more to say than a zombie would, and blend in with the background.  

One of the fixers tells you not to spend all your money on "glitter and XBD's".  Which would be hilarious if it was not so sad already, because in this game there is no glitter or XBD that you can buy in any meaningful way, in contrast to what the TTRPG offers.

The world of Witcher 3, by comparison, offers far more of a "rich world" with "life and detail".  And then consider games like Deus Ex and Daggerfall which came out decades before Cyberpunk 2077 did, and yet had far more interactive worlds by comparison.

The game is basically GTA set in the future: loot, shoot and run.  Some of the new quests added in the expansion are literally just stealing a car and driving to the target destination, while escaping from the police and any other aggrieved parties.

Quests are still mostly linear and handheld with waypoints.  Only practical variation seems to be dialog choices which seem surface level at best.  One of the "new quests" added in this edition is literally just repeatable recycled dialogue and animations, not even updating as you progress in Phantom Liberty.

You have a choice of lifepath when you create your character, being either a nomad, street rat or corpo, but these only affect the first hour of the game, and then anything afterwards is just the occasional unique dialog choice.  There's no unique equipment, missions or endings based on your lifepath.  

There are no "classes" in the traditional RPG sense in this game.  There's a skill tree, and you can invest in different stats which come with different skills to specialize in specific weapons or playstyles, but there's no choosing a class at character creation like a solo, netrunner or fixer like the TTRPG.

The Phantom Liberty expansion adds a single new area: a previously inaccessible area of Pacifica called "Dogtown".  This place is a run down, almost post apocalyptic neighborhood, so it doesn't really add to the "cyberpunk" theme of this game.  If anything, it's almost poetic how reflective this is of the state of Night City: mostly empty and a shell of itself compared to what could have been.  Compare how much extra content The Witcher 3 expansions "Heart of Stone", and "Blood and Wine" added.

To give credit where it's due: the Phantom Liberty expansion does add one new ending to the base game, based on certain choices you make in the Phantom Liberty storyline.  But without regard to story choices made in that ending, there's no final mission, no final boss, or any build up; just your usual follow the waypoints, talk to characters, move on, maybe get some dialog choices, etc.  So it's very unrewarding.

While I'll admit this game is a bit of a guilty pleasure for me, there's just too many flaws to the game's design that no amount of expansion will solve.  CDPR knows how to make good RPG's with the Witcher series, and games like Baldur's Gate 1 and 2 perfected the CRPG genre decades ago with a tiny fraction of the technology available when this game was made, so there's no excuse.

comment:
I could write a long video essay on why I do not think this is a good follow up to the amazing souls trilogy. I'll break it down in a summary with bullet points.

The Good:
-The Story. Its fantastic. Far more fleshed out and more interesting than even an entire three games of Dark Souls story.
-The Views. There are some stunning sights in this game. Seeing Raya Lucaria across the Lakes is astonishing.

The Bad:
-Enemies. It feels basic enemies no longer have any real function in the game anymore except to be run past. They're so copy and pasted without consideration that it feels a chore to kill them. There's also usually no reward for the vast majority of them. A boss will give you more Runes than a thousand standard enemies can give.

-The Open World. Despite the sights being fantastic, the Open World kinda doesn't add anything. There's so many extra dungeons with random, copypasted bosses that the Open World feels more like it took away from development time that could have been put towards certain fight mechanics and enemies.

-Fight Mechanics. Look up Zullie the Witch's video on how the heal punishing is not technically input reading but is just as bad because of how poorly they designed it. Its one of many very disappointing combat decisions in this game that makes it feel much worse than many other Souls games including those that came before. 

Overall, alot of people like this game, I get I'm in the minority. I don't blame others for liking this game but after playing several Souls and Souls-likes, this one so doesn't click with me its made me not want to buy any other Fromsoft productions on release anymore. Now, I'll be looking elsewhere for Souls-like experiences like Lies of P.

If you enjoy Elden Ring, you are in the majority, and there's alot of Elden Ring to like. I, on the other hand, have given enough time and effort to like a game I simply do not like nor recommend.

comment:
I've played this game and seen other parts I missed through other videos online. Despite all the great dialogue, items and spells, there's just so much that really ruins the experience.

Let me start off by saying, I played Divinity: Original Sin 2 before this, which has way less RNG, so that also probably didn't help. 

To start off with, combat: It's more unfair than challenging. Enemy ranger, (even ones you encounter at low levels) always seem to have way better odds than you do. Even if you get a height advantage on enemies, enemy rangers on lower levels always have more consistent hits than you. That with a height advantage, when you're at the same level or lower, you might as well not even try to attack. And Sorcerers... they are a lot of fun, but there's an entire act that basically makes you worthless; The Shadow-Cursed Lands. Yes, it is  only an optional path, but pretty much every other class doesn't get screwed over. I switched my class to a barbarian and straight away I was doing far better than trying to be a Sorcerer in that act. The RNG for melee isn't much better. Once again, plenty of enemy melee can hit you way more than you can hit them. Even using items against enemies has odds stacked against you. The same goes for healing too. You have a certain numbers that you can heal between. Most of time, I couldn't get above 50% of the minimum. If a healing item was 8-20, I'd consistently hover around 9-13.

The exploration: This is so poorly done. You have all these cool areas, secret locations to find and neat loot. But if you want to actually explore them, you need to pass a dice roll. You can miss entire locations because of dice rolls. And i don't mean you lose an easier way to discover them or only lose one path, I mean if the dice roll fails you just straight up don't find it.

The dice rolls: I get this is essentially a DND game, but good lord. Dice rolls on speech, certain items, finding locations, traps, treasure, it's everywhere. Unlike D:OS2, you don't find secrets from being a certain level in something, here you just get slightly better odds in the dice roll. 

The story: This is one of the few good things in this game. The characters are well written and some of the more comedic moments are amusing. But that wasn't able to save the rest of this game for me.
