comment:
I was really hoping that Balder's Gate 3 was something worth playing.

I've put in about twice as many hours as I needed to decide that I probably won't play this game again any time soon but I wanted to push through the slump in case I was just feeling grumpy. I should have guessed what was in store, given how little I liked the Pathfinder games. At least Kingmaker had some memorable characters and something like a decent plot. I don't care what's beyond the 'save yourself' plot of the first act. The party characters are vapid, poorly developed and comically formulaic. That each of them that I've met so far is hiding some dark secret dilutes any mystery or intrigue that might have come from pursuing those story lines. Each of the party members takes the time to point out that they don't trust you, don't like you, and are only sticking around because they expect something out of you. 

I guess these are the 5e rules? How does being able to make a halfling just as strong as an orc aid role playing? With no constraints I guess it's fun to make characters that look different, but why?

The writing feels like the writers were all last employed by corporate diversity training courses and never loved anyone their entire lives. All points of view are valid? Everyone is trying to manipulate everyone else? How many dialog menus result in a neat little lesson about not making assumptions about someone's background? I'm not even that far in and it already feels like I've been tricked into watching some HR mandated training videos on diversity at the workplace.

Too many, too long cut scenes: if I wanted a voice drama I'd go to Audible and listen to a book.

This game is miserable to play, except for combat which is ok, but no decision feels like it has any weight. Kill the goblin princess? Sell her stuff to the vendor without raising suspicion. Make your way to one of her captains, get assigned an important task. Kill a couple of goblins in the corner? No one will ever find out that there are three bodies in the middle of a well lit hallway. Just boring and disengaging.

The graphics are good, the opening location is genuinely creepy. No complaints here. 

How did this mess win so many awards?

If you're in to glamour shots and moral relativism maybe this is for you.

The game can often be visually impressive, but that alone contributes very little to the actual enjoyment of the exploration itself.

And the legacy dungeons aren't that much better, to be honest. Excluding Farum Azula, I don't feel like any of them really tries to propose a distinctive or interesting way of exploring in the way almost every area of Dark Souls did. Stormveil is basically a castle, Raya Lucaria is a castle with mages, Volcano Manor is a castle with lava, Leyndell spends most of its time feeling like a traditional dungeon crawler, and the Haligtree is okay but ultimately forgettable.

This doesn't mean the game looks bad. Quite the opposite: very often it looks fantastic. But visuals are only part of the job in a medium built around interaction. It's crazy to me that, despite being the first entry with a dedicated jump button, this somehow feels like the Souls game where exploration is least enjoyable.

The reward structure makes things even worse. The game fills the world with useless items in an attempt to create the illusion that wandering around is worthwhile. Half the time you go out of your way to reach some distant corner of the map only to find a crafting material or recipe whose function you'll forget five seconds after picking it up.

And then there are the catacombs and mines.

I hope you really like those assets, because you're going to see them a lot. They feel almost procedurally assembled: repetitive, unimaginative, full of dead space and absurdly unrewarding considering how much of a slog many of them are.

The entire map could have been one quarter of its current size. If that smaller space had been properly filled and given more attention, I'd probably be the happiest Souls player alive.

But thank God there are the incredibly rewarding boss fights.

Yes, I absolutely love being input-read into an AoE, roll-catching, delayed one-shot attack during a seven-hit tracking true combo. At some point you genuinely start wondering whether having somebody punch you while you're playing would improve the experience, if only because the physical pain might distract you from the spiritual hassle of fighting yet another random boss.

And that's assuming the boss isn't recycled. Be prepared to fight the same ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ thing over and over again, or, even better, a normal enemy arbitrarily promoted to boss status for the occasion. It's lazy design taken to an absurd level. There isn't a single boss in the entire game that I genuinely look forward to fighting again. Maybe Malenia and Morgott.

Regular enemies aren't much better, although their biggest problem is less the movesets themselves and more the absurd damage numbers. After a certain point, even with a full tank build, almost everything can practically two-shot you.

That doesn't mean their movesets aren't filled with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, because they absolutely are, but the damage is so aggressively overtuned in an attempt to inflate difficulty that every other problem almost becomes secondary.

That constant feeling of unfairness, combined with some of the least rewarding exploration I've experienced in this kind of game, pushes the frustration to another level.

What keeps Elden Ring afloat is its build diversity and lore. In combat, you can use almost anything and create an enormous variety of viable builds, while the world and its mythology are genuinely compelling. The problem is that the experience surrounding those strengths is often so exhausting that eventually you stop caring about what is in front of you, because everything starts feeling like another chore.

Worst entry in the series, and overall an average to below-average game.

If I also judge it against the minimum level of progress one should reasonably expect from a later installment in an established series, I have to mention how unacceptable the state of the AI is. Enemies are frequently just braindead.

The environmental storytelling has also become strangely self-celebratory. It was one of the defining strengths of the earlier games, but an open world should have been the opportunity to expand that formula and communicate the setting in more organic ways: through cities, settlements, populated spaces, or basically anything that made the world feel more alive.

Instead, despite having exponentially more space to work with, the game often falls back on the exact same formula: empty ruins, cryptic environmental details and item descriptions carrying most of the narrative burden.

At that point it stops feeling elegant and starts feeling lazy.

Bad.

comment:
The first maybe 40 or so hours was some of the most fun I've ever had in any video game, and I realize I've been chasing that high ever since, and somehow it only got worse. 

Firstly, the most blatant weakness for me is the storytelling: it's a joke. I can tell there's some interesting lore and characters somewhere in there, but it's presented in a completely incomprehensible manner. 

"You must seek the Elden Ring and become Elden lord!" okay, cool. Why? You are given the vaguest of the vaguest motivations to do *anything* in this game. I meet random characters with absolutely no context or build-up, that apparently I'm supposed to care for.  I have no idea who am I fighting and why. There's barely any RP in this supposed RPG, as joining 'factions' and completing side-quests is completely inconsequential. Not to mention those aforementioned side-quests have incredibly obscure requirements to complete, some feel almost impossible without the wiki.

I understand FromSoft is known for indirect storytelling, but when you want to tell a classic, multilayered fantasy epic, this style simply does not work. It's a completely ridiculous proposition that I'm supposed to rely on vague item descriptions to understand major plot points. Again, this would be fine on some other game that wasn't heavily touted as "having a great narrative written by George RR Martin!!"

Once I realized the story was pretty much non-existent, my open world immersion and suspension of disbelief was irrecoverably shattered. I began to see cool ruins as nothing more than simple repeated 3D assets thrown randomly across the landscape. It's absolutely clear that the devs had no idea what the story behind most places in this game really was, they just expect the players to fill in the blanks. That is not even mentioning the INSANE amount of recycled areas, enemies and bosses in this game. 

Well, the story is kind of bad, at least the game can redeem itself with its gameplay right? Eh, sort of. Like I said in the beginning, I thoroughly enjoyed the early/midgame. The enemy variety was great, and I had tons of fun fighting the early bosses.

However, that's where much of my enjoyment ended. What I started realizing, is that the open world aspect of the game doesn't really work. Here's what happens in Elden Ring all the time: you stumble across a boss or a difficult area which feels way too hard and you think "okay, I'll just explore and come back later." You come back after some hours, realize you've grown vastly more powerful, and the fight becomes an unsatisfying cakewalk. It's such a shame too, because some of the coolest bosses visually were the exact ones I beat in one try. There were some bosses that I  didn't have to engage with, because I could just brute-force it by chugging down health potions. 

The other category of bosses and enemies is those that are wholly anti-fun, attacking so rapidly that you can't play in a proactive manner. There are bosses that legitimately feel like I was playing a turn-based game, since I could get in a hit safely once in a blue moon. There's so many cool skills and playstyles in this game, but it feels like you aren't allowed to experiment with any of them. My complaint has nothing to do with the difficulty, it's about the forced defensive and reactive playstyle.  

That is, if you don't use spirit summons, which are one of the most baffling design choices in this game. The spirits summons turn most fights into a joke, as they draw aggro from enemies and allow you to freely act as you wish. This is clearly meant to be an accessibility mechanic, but it almost feel like the devs designed certain encounters around them. It almost feels like the devs are constantly whispering my ears like "oh geez, this encounter sure is a bit difficult, are you sure you don't want to use the summons bro?"  

This all leads to an extremely unbalanced experience. If I died, it felt I got cheesed out. If I beat a difficult enemy, I felt I cheesed them, as opposed to feeling like a hero who has slain an epic monster. It all feels very...mechanical in nature, which is the absolute killer of my immersion.

comment:
This game was incredibly disappointing to play.
For starters, this game is absolutely beautiful. The set pieces, the enemies, the backgrounds, the game is gorgeous to an unbelievable degree. What I find a bit lacking, however, is that a lot of the enemies and levels can feel overdesigned and clunky to a degree where the deeper thoughts of the design are unreadable. While high gothic architecture is always appreciated, it can definitely feel eye glazing at times when the developers obviously didn't care as much about a location as others. The biggest problems I found with this being the numerous catacombs, caves, forts, and mines that are present throughout the game. Although they are at numerous locations, with very distinct landscapes, there's never anything visually interesting about them that wasn't done before. It makes it feel very video-gamey and copy and paste, when I felt that the worldbuilding of this game was incredibly interesting originally.

The difficulty of the game is far higher than previous souls titles, which in itself is not bad. However, there is a clear distinction between boss encounters. There's Margit, who feel very intentionally designed, while remaining difficult in a fair way, maintaining the "I died, what did I do wrong" mindset that many of the previous games seem to hold. Then there's Knight Ordovis, which is a boss encounter stapling two mini-bosses you have already fought, then taking to precautions to make it feel like a well-made duo boss. The first knight will always cover the second's punish windows, and if you're unlucky, they will attack at such intervals where it is impossible to not take damage. The vast majority of this game is a good boss fight, followed by 2 or 3 boring to bad ones (Some of these being repeat bosses that you have already fought plenty of times before). The difficulty, then, feels less like a natural result of the game attempting to challenge you in an interesting way, but devolves into feeling like it is overly punishing and unfair because they didn't take the extra second to ensure the encounter played smoothly. It doesn't help that your rune gain is decreased if you summon additional players, so it makes single bosses crammed into a duo fight feel even worse, since you are discouraged to summon others to help even the fight out (See gargoyles and godskin duo). 

The game itself and its grandness seems impressive at first, since the selling point of over 100 bosses appears incredible, but you soon realize that the game only has over 100 boss encounters because of how much they reuse and repurpose the same enemy over and over again. I personally would have preferred a smaller world, if it meant having less repeat encounters, but the game insists on reusing things that don't make sense. For example, the tree sentinel being a returning encounter makes sense. But having an Ancient Hero of Zamor be in a catacomb makes it feel very repetitive. Why is the boss here? Because you reached the end of the dungeon. Erdtree Avatars guarding the Minor Erdtrees makes sense. Having a named magma wyrm followed by a nameless magma wyrm in another unrelated cave is boring and repetitive. Ancient Dragon Lansseax was extremely cool to find, but now, one of the later game areas throws an identical copy of the fight, thus making it less impactful. The critique here is not that the individual encounter was bad, it's moreso that the individual encounter's overall effect and impact in the game is weakened since now there are just more enemies that act exactly like the boss.

I would suggest playing this game with an open mind and a guide. Playing guideless will cause you to miss many things that the game, and most players, would deem as "important" and "required." Do not be surprised if the open world leads you to having a weapon lacking upgrades for where you're supposed to be. Perhaps, had I started the game with a guide in hand, I would not have struggled as much, but I also deem myself to be a pretty experienced souls-like player and have always enjoyed the problem solving and natural progression of the game. Sadly, it seems that this game tried to be too big, but didn't have enough things to fill the huge map.

comment:
i haven't finished this game and i probably won't, i doubt it will end in any way that satisfies me.

story-wise the game is better than most videogames, but that's not exactly stiff competition.
the celebrity actor is interesting and all but if you do side content then the writing for johnny goes downhill pretty fast. he changes from friendly to hating you and back with a real quickness. very jarring.
your romance options are mostly just eyecandy. i don't care about them at all and i tried to.
chemistry-wise there's only one of four characters that makes sense because she's relevant to the actual main story and one of the endings.

the original cyberpunk 2013 is a tabletop RPG series. you need a lot of worldbuilding written just to get off the ground, and the books are rich for what they are. something which gets better with some of the later editions.
however, none of that seems to translate through to 2077. this feels like a totally different world with some similar terms and figureheads. genre-wise it's more like post-cyberpunk instead of just cyberpunk. 
which means it's not really "punk"

gameplay-wise the game is just, fine.
it's sloppy in a lot of areas but the systems are interesting enough to carry through to the point where the story's momentum starts breaking down, presumably capable of lasting to the end of a better told story.

a lot of people seem to enjoy the game, but i can't recommend it, it's not cyberpunk.

Balders gate 3 is a game I very much want to like... but I can't no matter how much I try. It's a very strange meld of larian studios doing an excellent and terrible job at the same time.

The gameplay is excellent, while not a 1:1 of the tabletop experience its about as close as you can get without just playing tabletop simulator. Combat is fun, the world is interactable, and you can approach things differently. It all well made.However this all gets bogged down by the characters, story, and mechanics. 

Starting with mechanics; There is one that absolutely bogs the game's pace down. If you've played other crpgs you'll be no stranger to dice rolls for dialog, interactions, etc. One thing youll notice however is that they do this automatically. I select the dialog, the computer will run the rng with the modifiers, get the number, compare it to the dc, and give the success or failure, plus give the rolls information in the log, all in the span of about .03 seconds. Balders gate 3 does away with the working formula, that their previos titles also used, so that you can sit there and watch digital dice roll (that doesnt matter because the animation is just there for you it still just uses a rng) At first this isn't so bad, some might even find it charming, but after a while it gets old. Ive played 40-50hrs of this game and probably a good 5 hours is just watching dice roll. And you cant even disable it, you can skip the animation but it still wastes more time than the game simply running it immediately. It honestly is just infuriating to me, it takes me out of the game so much and just wastes my time. 

If it was just that then I'd be irritated but fine I'd still play it. Unfortunately there's more: The characters. I'm not really sure how they messed this up so bad, though I have a theory, in their previous games theyve had little trouble making, mostly, well written and  interesting characters. While I wouldn't say every main character from divinity 2 is my favorite, they are all interesting. I don't find any of the main characters interesting in bg3. Honestly it feels like they made them "sex appeal" first (twink, goth girl, muscle mommy, etc) then gave a half assed story to them. I had zero interest in progressing almost any of their stories, let alone even recruiting them. (The hirelings from withers are usually more interesting...) About the only one that larian gets a pass on is the githyankee simply because their lore has always been trash so she was doomed from the start. Their dialog is ok and sometimes its cool that theyll have something unique to say about stuff but they pale in comparison to larians previous works. I could write a master's thesis on each character and why they suck/are not great. But I don't feel like doing that much writing, and it wouldn't help the review anymore than if I just said the characters are boring.

However the single most terrible design choice they made was the main story itself. I would say that from an objective stand point the main story's writing is lackluster. The clinical term being that its simply "eh". From a subjective standpoint however I find it to be incredibly boring. Mind flayers are probably one of the most boring/lame/uninteresting monsters in the dnd universe. (Honestly I'd rather die to a pack of goblins than have to admit I died to a mind flayer.) This is further compounded by the fact that they say the word "tadpole' so damn much that simply hearing the word in a normal conversation irritates me. If you played a drinking game where you took a half shot every time someone said tadpole you would be dead and in late stage liver failure before the 3 hr mark. Out of all the monsters/gods/driving forces for a campaign mindflayers are a terrible choice (and the other half to the mind flayers isn't great eirther but given the series I understand why they're there) Liches, vampires, celestials, demons, devils, etc. Would have made for a far more interesting story. 
Back to being more objective, the story carries little weight because if how its presented. The game constantly says "oh my god you have to hurry and rush to get the thing out of your head" But you can just wander around and do whatever with no consequences. Everyone you meet who shares your affliction is also doing fine whether they're looking for a cure or not. (unless they're dead I guess) so the main hook of "you need to hurry otherwise you'll die" seems more like a suggestion rather than something I really need to work on. The issue is only further exacerbated by the fact that you can't actually do anything about it even if you try. You can go talk to everyone under the sun about needing a cure or you can seek no help at all and it makes no difference till the story gets to a certain point and you're actually allowed to do something about it. Meaning that I am literally only talking to people for loot and xp instead of actually being invested in the story and learning. which at that point I could just play actual dnd witha mediocre dm.

Also the game has weird level limit... despite trying to be tabletop accurate where the level limit is higher, But more strangely while most things are very accurate to the tabletop they just gutted warlocks for some reason? I'm not even a big warlock fan who's like upset about that. I'm just confused. My friend who dm's says its likely because warlocks are stronger in the early levels so they'd be strong all game due to the level cap, to which I have to say ok...? thats just how a similarly leveled campaign would work out on the tabletop. 
Also I do want to clarify while I do mention larians other games, mainly divinity 2, Im not a giant divinity 2 fan. I think it was a good/alright game overall just in comparison it had a lot more thought, care, and general work put into the *important* parts of the game. (story, characters, etc.) instead of focusing on graphics and making me watch virtual dice as a selling point to make it feel more like the actual game. (if they wanted that they should've just made the enemy/allied ai take super long turns and give me virtual dice to stack/roll/play with while I wait for my turn) 

My point is that if you want to play a crpg called balders gate just go play 1 or 2, its crunchy and oldbut theres a reason people still play it to this day. This game is a waste of time and money (and sanity and tadpole will become a trigger word)

comment:
The game is well made, nothing to argue about that. The thing is that, at roughly 100 hours in, I was wayy too far from the end (just started chapter 3) and had to call it quits because I had grown increasingly bored with the plot.
I'm not the biggest fan of super-large-scope, light fantasy stories about the big bad evil getting ready to do some bad evil things, and the good guys fighting against it. I know you can also take different paths and play the villain, but the overall worldbuilding, tone and scope of the story seemed pretty unoriginal and bland to me.
Everybody likes talking about the characters but I really didn't find them that deep nor complex. They all fall within pretty banal stereotypes and don't offer a deep level of interaction beside their quests.
The story and characters were the sole reason why I kept going, since the combat didn't tickle my brain enough (I DO like turn based combat, but i consider the JRPG type to be more fun), so once that source of stimulus dried out i had to give up.
It's not a bad game, just not my cup of tea.

comment:
After trying the game for a second time, I still have no idea what is supposed to be fun about it.

I can't stand the graphics, character creation is terrible, dialogue is crap, most characters can be boiled down to "Look at me, I'm so edgy, isn't it cool how edgy I am?", the combat system is a complete slog, animation quality is one of the worst i ever saw, the UI design is the same as original sin... in other words annoying, and the story is just not that interesting

it's cool that people like this game I guess, but I finished hundreds of games and played thousands. If you want a cool rpg that lasts 50+ hours you're better off looking at pathfinder kingmaker / wrath of the righteous, xenoblade chronicles, digimon story cyber sleuth / time stranger, hundred line, crosscode, final fantasy (any of them), sea of stars, or disco elysium.

EDIT:
because some people have reading comprehension of a goldfish and are too butthurt when someone criticises their "perfect" game, let me expand on this review a lot more I guess.

The way to describe Baldur's Gate 3 would be that the game is very, very wide, but also incredibly shallow. And I honestly think if Larian had about half the budget and actually thought about what to do with the game, it could have been a lot better.

Now, let me expand on why "I can't stand the graphics."
Overall I despise most games that are trying to do photorealistic graphics, in 99% of cases it looks disgusting to me. Good graphics don't need to be anime or cartoony or some kind of vivid spectacle. But if you want photorealistic graphics I would heavily consider stylizing them around something, or make the graphics just insanely good. 
Like Alan wake 2 is photorealistic, but it puts insanely high focus on environments and it's very noisy in its presentation, plus it's horror and very high fidelity, so it looks good. Which is probably another point, remedy uses real actors and the characters looks not just photorealistic but real. Which most games fail to do and the fake photorealism is inherently wrong. 
That's a stance on graphic design I will die on. Almost every AAA game puts emphasis on graphics and pretty much all of them fail miserably. 

Animation in baldurs gate 3 is something you can't defend, it's utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Characters simply stand in place and talk, in a very rigid pose with almost no emotion. And then when they need to move they suddenly get into an animation that is incredibly choppy and then they go back to standing and talking. There is absolutely no fluidity or movement to it, no emotion behind character actions. 
Even the scene where if you play a bard you get to do a whole song, while the song itself is pretty nice and the narrative around it is actually kinda cool, watching your character do that song is taking you out of it. Which again, photorealistic graphics with very rigid 3d models is the fault at bad animation. 

Which also ties to character creation, where you can't complain much about DND choices, it's copying a system and the system itself is by my standard terrible. But the visual creation is bad... Which is still connected to graphics, but it's insanely difficult to make a character that looks pretty and there are no sliders or anything, there's like 8 preset faces and most of them are ugly as ♥♥♥♥. 
Hair selection is probably the only good thing there. And it's cool you can look at your ♥♥♥♥ but overall the game doesn't really do much with nudity anyway. If you give me an option to have a dangling penis between my legs then have a decency of letting me use it as well xD 
But another thing, some people will see a lot of races and subraces. They are all humans. Human with pointy ears. Short human with a beard. Even gith are just humans with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up faces. The only non humanoid option is dragonborn and the only reason it is an option is because larian already have lizard models from original sin. 
The beauty of playing a fantasy game is playing nonhuman fantasy races. The very least we could have gotten was tabaxi. But their photorealistic graphics don't allow for individuality. 

Everyone is edgy wasn't exactly the criticism, I didn't really specify it, so that's on me. But the criticism would be "overly edgy". You can have good edgy characters. But bg3 companions are incredibly shallow and one noted. 
I keep hearing they get a lot better and deeper once you get far enough and explore the dialogue options but that's not something I'm willing to discover. Wasting 30+ hours on finding out that the character is not an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is too much time. 
You can write mysterious and intriguing characters without making them obnoxious. 

Combat is something I didn't enjoy in original sin as well, and it's practically the same here. It is deceptively complex. You can in theory spend a lot of time optimizing and strategizing but in the end it's all just dice rng that can heavily make or break the entire combat. On higher difficulty it could be different and all, but it's not a type of game to play for difficult combat, the story and characters are the main drawing point, so playing on normal or even lower is fair. 
And there the combat just slogs through because you're given a lot of options for very little value, often to your own detriment actually when just clicking an enemy for normal attack is gonna do a lot more than anything else. And it just slogs in round after round. 
You might say that pathfinder is even worse but that's not true because pathfinder has that granular strategy that can heavily change outcomes of combats. Plus pathfinder does have real time with pause so you can fast forward through trash fights while focusing more tactically in turned based on boss fights. It's stupidly difficult and often also boiled down to ♥♥♥♥♥♥ dice rng. But it is a lot more complex and rewarding because of it. 
Slog doesn't mean it takes long, just that the amount of time taken is not satisfying. And BG3 combat is not satisfying in any way.

comment:
The game is... tedious. 

Let me explain : Exploration does not reward looking IN EVERY CONTAINER or going out of your way to find things. This is especially true in the last act ( city of Baldurs Gate ) where there is HUNDREDS of houses you can break into only to find rags, useless notes or plain equipment that isn't worth much... The loot itself is NOT RANDOMIZED therefore you will always find it in SPECIFIC places which is okay if you have LOADS of equipment... However BG3 has a dozen or so rare / legendary items. Plenty of "Blue / Green" rarity that are very similar to each other making most of them useless. 

I understand that not every game has to have RNG loot but at least put MORE and I mean MORE loot in the game so players are rewarded for exploring / making cool builds. 

Enemy NPC's are blatant CHEATERS. They can see you through WALLS and often then can HIT YOUR THROUGH WALLS TOO! I was inside 2nd story building and the enemy mage shot a fireball which wiped 2 of my characters! THROUGH A FLOOR. Players can't do that. 

There is a potential for subsequent playthroughs BUT I see no point since you can literally RE-SPEC your character at will. Playing as "evil" character doesn't have any appeal to me so after Once doing the campaign I'll be done. 

The game doesn't go on "good" sale despite being released years ago. Can't take my single player character to play with my friends.... instead I have to make a new character that is bound by my friend's save. Now I understand this would break balance and some quests... but I think it would have been possible to have only 1 person the HOST interact with quests / NPC's. 

Either way only recommend on deep sale... if it ever happens.

comment:
If you've played dark souls then you know what you're getting into. For the rest of us:
Yes it's a huge world, with gorgeous scenery. But the roleplaying elements are paltry. (Do you want to marry this woman you just met? Yes or no.) The music is barebones. What little story you get is cryptic and obtuse. While the open world is nice for progression at your own pace, it's not a crowded or lively world. The few NPCs seem more interested in insulting you, I suppose to mirror the relentless barrage of combat.

At the end of the day, it's just a dressed up game about boss fights. The other enemies are pathetic in comparison, and they don't train you for the boss fight. If you aren't willing to try a boss 5-20 times in a row then it will be frustrating. And then they ruin it by shoving you in a tiny room with multiple enemies. Not much beyond the basics is explained in detail so you will have to do too much research. I found the console interface to be lacking, the weapon and build choices to be irrelevant (They all have quite similar speed). The way animations lock your character(including flinching) just feels cumbersome and negated the fun of this game for me. If you play ~perfectly~, then it feels good-- it's an abusive style. The horseback combat did add a nice variety. None of the fancy weapons or modifiers or craftables matter as much as rolling at the correct time. It's just a game about rolling. Spare yourself the frustration and just watch someone else play for the scenery.

comment: I have given this game so, so many chances. I even convinced myself that I liked it for a time but there are just too many little issues that make this game frustratingly unplayable for me. Controller support is not very good and what's crazy is that it's *really* good in Divinity Original Sin II, so I know Larian can do it. But comparing the controller interface to the keyboard/mouse in this game is just infuriating. When using a keyboard everything is very organized and it's easy to separate different types of spells/powers which can help when deciding what to do on your turn, but on controller you only have a row of radials with no clear organization and minimal indicators as to the cost of using these powers. I would have to spend a lot of time manually organizing my radials into something usable whereas in Divinity, spells are placed on a hotbar where it's easy to arrange them and see exactly what they do. It's possible some of this comes from the unholy matrimony of D&D 5e mechanics and video game design limitations but it's so frustrating that I just play keyboard/mouse. I guess that's fine, but, like, this game is available (and more expensive) on consoles where controller is the only option. Now something that I know is 5e's fault, is that combat is not very fun. It's okay, but Divinity combat is INCREDIBLE to the extend in which I look forward to encounters. In BG3 I dread them, not because they're especially hard (Divinity is MUCH harder) but because they're just boring. On top of that there's very little reason to be careful with resources or spell slots because you can long rest pretty much whenever you want with no consequences. Now, of course, there are little quality of life changes that make BG3 a step above DOSII in some ways, and I'm not going to pretend like the cutscene animations aren't super cool, because they are. This game is beautiful, no doubt about that. But my biggest issue, which makes all the little improvements worthless, is that I just can't play the game. I have spent hours, literally HOURS  just trying to join multiplayer sessions. And even when I can finally get in, the game crashes so often that it feels like there's always an expiration date on any fun I'm having. Not to mention the MASSIVE file size which just feels so ridiculously bloated and makes file verification (which I'm constantly having to run) take forever. What's crazy is that the game was working a few months ago, consistently for the first time since I started playing, and then they released a patch which broke everything all over again???? Why, WHY is this game *almost* incredible but just incapable of fumbling at the last second!? I will probably continue to give this game more chances, because it just occupies that much of my soul, but I do not recommend this game to new players. It's too much of a headache. Also ♥♥♥♥ launchers, bro.

comment:
Highly Rated, But a Tedious and Punishing Trial-and-Error Experience
Rating: Not Recommended
If you are buying this game based on its glowing masterwork reviews, hoping for a smooth and immersive fantasy RPG adventure to relax with after work, you should think twice.
1. Extremely Vague and Frustrating Mission Guidance
The quest design offers little to no clear directional guidance. Instead of rewarding exploration, the system leaves you to blindly fumble around huge maps. This lack of structure leads to aimless wandering rather than any real sense of discovery.
2. Punishing Invisible Traps and Chain-Aggro Mechanics
What is often praised as "unrivaled freedom" is actually a hyper-fussy physical and rule simulator. Simply walking over to inspect an area can trigger beast aggression, call over guards, and sound alarm drums—instantly turning an entire encampment hostile and forcing a GAME OVER. A single misstep can wipe out tens of minutes or hours of progress, creating immense frustration.
3. Tedious Micro-Management and Fractured Combat
The combination of mandatory turn-based combat and complex D&D rules makes every action feel like solving a math problem. Party members frequently unlink or get stuck behind terrain, requiring constant, tedious micromanagement. The combat lacks fluid feedback and feels more like administrative homework than rewarding gameplay.
Summary:
This game may appeal to hardcore players who have endless free time to study tabletop rulebooks and enjoy trial-and-error reloading. However, for players seeking a fluid, enjoyable fantasy adventure with direct positive feedback, playing this is simply an exercise in frustration.

I adored this game during my first hundred hours—so much so that I purchased "The World of Cyberpunk 2077," a hardcover book that, now looking back at it, was probably released by Dark Horse as part of the public relations and marketing work of CD Projekt Red to increase hype and sales before launch in 2020. I hadn't been so smitten by a world since discovering Star Wars in early middle school. But somewhere after that 100 hour mark, the story and world began unraveling for me and I finished the game feeling rather hollow.

Cyberpunk appears to be a labor of love for the many involved in making it. Aesthetically, it's gorgeous. There were countless times where I stopped to take in and appreciate the models and textures that were around me. The artists and developers who made this are top tier, no question. Unfortunately, as I continued my time in Night City, I was struck with the feeling of just how massive an endeavor building this city was and just how many assets were reused in monotonous ways. Things began to feel imperfect and rushed, and those moments of awe that happened so frequently turned into me questioning just why the game had to be so big and why certain gigs had to exist. The game feels far too large to the point of feeling incredibly vapid. It made me yearn for smaller, more thoughtful stories and environments that are carefully tailored and handcrafted. You don't have to paint the entire world. Paint a few very interesting locations and allow the viewer to dream about the rest.

The story itself is at its strongest in the early main quests, when the player doesn't quite realize how terribly superficial all the endings will turn out to be. I felt like I had a stronger emotional connection to Jackie for four hours than compared to my 200+ hours with Johnny. I think this shows that CD Projekt Red tried to do far too much without a cohesive overarching narrative or goal. It left me feeling pushed and pulled in many different directions, confused, and frustrated that a game with this much potential could fall so flat. It's a good game and there are there are many things that I experienced while playing that will stick with me for the rest of my life, but I just wish that it was much smaller with more time and care put into crafting the details.

comment: I played finish Cyberpunk 2077 and I found the writing decent but also not outstanding. I feel that the game focuses more on the aesthetic of cyberpunk rather than the philosophical and psychological implications of society being in such a state towards humanity both on an individual and collective scale. The dialogue tends to resort to quoting philosophers in order to appear deep while hiding an inherent lack of depth. The world of Cyberpunk is really existentially empty. Those who are not elite live in extreme poverty and capitalism drains the life out of everyone and yet Cyberpunk ignores this sickening emptiness of existence. Johnny Silverhand is quite interesting at times but all he is is a walking talking ideology such that he appears shallow rather than complex. He appears to be just as dogmatic and narrow minded as those who accept the status quo. I would say the gameplay beats RDR2 but it is definitely has a much weaker story. Each character felt more like a trope, a kind of caricature rather than real. I don't believe anyone can live in the world of Cyberpunk without experiencing severe mental illness. It is a sick society and the game pushes colorful narratives upon us, beckoning us towards an adventure that is ultimately insignificant in the grand scheme of things. It just focuses on hype moment after hype moment rather than delving into the world which they have created which simply put is on the pinnacle of decadence. Disco Elysium is infinitely superior in writing about spiritual decay in relation to political ideology. However, the gameplay is highly addictive and the world is immersive and beautiful.

comment:
Yeah, yeah, I know, I must be crazy... But I just really didn't like it, OK? I'm sad to be this disappointed.

It's a well-made game for sure, no doubt about it. If it weren't for the great expectations, there might not have been such a great disappointment. I've enjoyed Larian's previous works, loved them even, but there was almost nothing about BG3 to inspire similar feelings.

The story was boilerplate D&D plot, stretched to 100+ hours. Meaningless, emotionless, drawn out tropes and cliches. Only Act 2 made me feel something. I put off wrapping up Act 3 for years from sheer boredom, and felt nothing but tedium by the end.

The characters were as uninteresting as they were horny, I couldn't care about them with the obvious exception of Karlach, who was an actually well-written character. Shadowheart and Astarion were ok-ish. The rest were forgettable. Couldn't decide if the late shoehorning of Jaheira and Minsc was welcome fanservice or a way to distract from the voidness Gale, Wyll and Halsin.

The 5e ruleset is not a good fit for such a game, and Larian's attempts at patching it, while valiant, were not sufficient. Some made it actively worse. The combat was plodding, the interface clunky and annoying, the abilities and items both overwhelming in number and underwhelming in the choices they presented. 5e was never meant to be a lootfest, but the magic items the game showered you with created perverse incentives and boring micromanagement. The gear-juggling was made so much worse by the abysmal stash and inventory system. That they were this bad really boggles the mind.

In the end, the game had nothing to say, nothing to offer but a fun romp that degraded into tedium by the end, Almost nothing about this game is truly memorable, artistically profound or genuinely touching. It was a 150 hour fast food meal served on a really nice and shiny plate. For all its bugs and failures, I will forever remember and cherish Owlcat's glorious mess that is Wrath of the Righteous over the slog that was BG3. Even Larian's own Original Sin games were superior.

Edit: I'm sorry for all the feelings I hurt.

comment:
I'm a new gamer, only played DOS2 and now BG3, so this is not from a seasoned gamer's perspective. While I have some grasp of turn-based combat, I don't know DnD rules -- but BG3 assumed that I did, and that made it hard to understand many mechanics for which there were no tutorials. I just wanted to jump in and have fun, not spend hours Googling tutorials and guide books or stumbling about clueless. It was not a great introduction to the game, especially since I'd set it to Explorer Mode and was hoping for a beginner-friendly start.

I enjoy it when if I plan my combat well, I get rewarded with a win. With the primarily chance-based combat model of BG3, best-laid plans too frequently meet catastrophic failure. I felt really limited in what I could do with each character per turn, especially i.t.o. crowd control, and there was nothing to be done to mitigate the effects of chance. I ended up doing my best to avoid combat because I just found it so tedious and unrewarding.

Out of combat, everything was also random, and I ended up only taking actions at which my characters had the best chances of succeeding, so I couldn't do the things I actually wanted to do. You don't get to see how high a number you have to roll before you commit to an option, so that was also frustrating. Failing just one of the many random rolls throughout the game often meant ending up in yet another impossible fight or walking into an insta-death trap, meaning I was spending as much time reloading the game as playing.

The high risk low reward setup just had me so on edge the whole time that I didn't want to move further in the game. Uninstall. Not for me.

comment:
I really wanted to like this game, but after 2 hours I wasn't feeling engaged in the slightest. The main drawback for me was the combat and movement; I've played dnd and other table top games before, and yeah sometimes the dice just hate your guts that day, but *every encounter* I had felt like I was missing 80% shots 80% of the time, while the enemies rarely missed. even with low hit chance. 

Moreover, I quickly realized that stat checks aren't pass fail, but rather a random d20+/-skill, which wouldn't be much of a problem except for the fact that your base stat does little to nothing to influence the roll. My roided out tank fails a 5str check because he rolled a 1 and his 15str only gives +3 on rolls. Dumb. Hilarious when you're with your friends and they can roast your luck, but just unfun and frustrating in a game where you can just reload and reroll until you get the outcome you want, which brings me to my biggest complaint...

There are no stakes whatsoever. Unless playing on high difficulty, there is nothing stopping you from saving before an encounter or interaction and then just re-loading until you get the desired outcome, which you will eventually find yourself doing. Even if you want to forbid yourself, you're likely to come across a check that will block you out of entire questlines should you fail, and when you too roll a nat1 on such a roll....well.... yeah

I'm sure plenty of people like this kind of thing, in fact most people seem to. It's just not for me. If you find enjoyment in the randomness, then good for you. I like my games a bit more deterministic

comment:
You wanna know what kept me playing for 57 hours despite my negative review? Sunk cost fallacy. I can't recommend this game, even on discount, and I bought it during sale. Writing this feels as tiring as playing the game itself. If you enjoy this game, good for you, but this is just not my cup of tea.

Firstly, the audiovisuals of this game is very striking, music is nice, sound deisgn is cool and the world is visually impressive. Cyberpunk 2077's gameplay, however, feels very dated, it has the makings of a movement shooter but it is an first person RPG, first and foremost. There are a few interesting gameplay designs such as netrunner builds, and gun hipfire accuracy and ADS recoil being tied to stamina is a creative solution to not making guns too op. 

One key reason I found this game unenjoyable is believability and immersion, because its story, setting and gameplay conflict with each other. That and there is no nuance or creativity applied to the gameplay. A game can have variety, it can have impressive visuals, It can have amazing music and sound design, but if it cannot be fun, why would you want to experience the other things? The combat and stealth lack nuance or creativity and is unengaging, you do it once, you've done it all. The game is also buggy despite the fixes made, and the story felt unengaging because the protagonist is boring and lame.

She'll judge people for killing well being a cold blooded murderer herself its very strange and one of the most infuriating aspects of the writing in this game. It's something that really should've been explored with the game TRYING to explore gang violence in an interesting way. She feels unrealistic and very stupid, with no real depth, an absolute dumpster fire of a character thats also the main protagnist so you have to deal with her stupid ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the entire time you're playing.

The gameplay is really boring and easy even on its hardest difficulty, but its flashy enough and its cool guns makes it mindlessly fun even though its still bad. Theirs a lot of ways you CAN approach fights but its rarely neccessary and you can get away with just run and gunning which is significantly less interactive and repetetive. Character customization is neat on a astetic level. The whole game infact is pretty cool visually, a lot of the ideas and potential for narrative themes kept me playing but a lot of it doesn't go anywhere or isnt explored in an interesting way. (my hours are bloated quite a bit from leaving the game on a few times at night)

It's a waste of time, don't play this game.

comment:
This game looks great, it has amazing artistic direction, the mechanics are fun, as are the companions. Despite this, I have endeavoured to play this game in multiplayer with a close friend who got me this game.

This was a mistake. 

The multiplayer for this game may be the worst implemented multiplayer, SHOCKINGLY bad, I have ever seen in a video game to date - and this is coming from someone who tried Halo Infinite Co-Op when it came out. It has a plethora of game breaking bugs (not allowing you to do Long rests when two player characters have companions, not auto-saving at all, blocking main quest progression due to the aformentioned issue with companions). Not to mention there are bugs that bug out an entire co--op playthrough from seeing main story cutscenes. Accidentally trigger the bug? You will need to restart your co-op campaign. 

This game absolutely should not have shipped with multiplayer, and should not be a multiplayer tagged title, nevertheless it is, and given that fact alone I highly discredit it for all of its accolades, as this is what Larian considers among their core features of the game. 

And they will never fix it either; as many people have, even since the BETA for this game, expressed myriad of issues that I cannot even begin to list here. Shockingly bad for supposedly a 7/7 GOTY award winner and colloquially known as "one of the greatest games of all time". Yep, and so is Battletoads I guess too. Total slop.

comment:
I tried. I really, genuinely tried. But after restarting Act 1 multiple times, I have to face reality: I cannot subject myself to 80+ hours of this.

First off, the combat. The game hands you this massive smorgasbord of cool spells and tactical abilities, but only lets you touch one per turn. It’s like paying for an all-you-can-eat buffet, but the waiter forces you to eat a single fry, wait 10 minutes while eight goblins chew their food, and only then allows you to take another bite. The combat doesn't explain itself, your attacks miss constantly, and then you sit there watching paint dry until your next turn. No wonder this campaign takes a billion hours.

Then there’s the roleplaying. In a game celebrated for its writing and characters, why is my protagonist a mute mime? Everyone else gets Oscar-worthy voice acting and theatrical monologues (altough like somsone else already said: it's the extremely cringy theater kids at school trying way to hard), while my character just stands there giving intense, silent eyebrow expressions like a confused background extra.

Clearly people love this game, but if you don't already enjoy tabletop dice-math and aggressive turn-waiting, it feels like doing administrative paperwork in fantasy armor. Hard pass.

comment:
I started playing Witcher 3 some days ago, just before they announced the remastered version. Since my PC is quite old, I downloaded the classic version, which used to run fine. However, after the release of the remastered version, the classic one now fails to launch. I tried both checking the files and reinstalling the whole game; neither fixed the problem. 

Despite having played the game to almost the end of the main campaign, the impossibility of playing it from now on doesn't cause me any frustration – one chore less to do; it is the impossibility of a refund that weights more. It took years in between the purchase and the first time I tested it. 

Now on to what I think of The Witcher 3 as a game. The writing is OK for the most part (anyone used to reading the classics may think it is mediocre at best); the written content, on the other hand, could be less boring, considering it was based on books (books, however, that couldn't reach success on their own merit, and are now widely known thanks to the games, and indeed, when I tried reading one of them, “The Last Wish” I think was its title, it tasted like uninspired cheap porn); the graphics are well done, which is meaningless given that some of the best games ever made have very simple graphics; the background music and ambient sound effects are quite good; as for the game-play, which is by far the most important component of a video-game, it is easily the worst part of the Witcher 3 experience, both combat and walking or riding a horse controls are atrocious; also CD Project Red brutally “ubisofted” the game by making it unnecessarily open-world with lots of question marks marking repetitive tasks, a complete disrespect to the player’s time.

Whenever Geralt hits a physical roadblock, there is a sorceress who just happens to have the exact spell to fix the problem. The only way to lift a curse from character #234 is giving them witcher potions that could kill them? No problem, Yen has the exact spell for helping them survive. Need to swim deeper and can’t hold breath? Yen just has the spell to cover you there too. Bridge is broken? Can’t cross it? How lucky Philippa came along then, she just happens to have the fix-broken-bridge spell. Is the White Frost too frosty to stand and you forgot to pack your sweater? Yen has just what you need, a warm sanctuary spell to keep the frostbite away. The Wild Hunt is very wild indeed, and hunts in packs, wouldn’t it be great to get invisible when there are so many of them around? Guess what? Yen just happens to... Because why bother writing clever quests to solve these obstacles if you can make your mages conjure the solution out of thin air? This way you make room to fill up the game with higher priority content, like sending Geralt after some old man’s goat

Having played the series in order, I was expecting Witcher 3 to be an improvement over the second game; it is clearly a downgrade instead. In Witcher 2, the story starts with Geralt in jail, falsely accused of regicide. In what is arguably one of the most dramatic cut-scenes in the history of video-games, he fails to protect the king and watches powerlessly as the true assassin escapes. He suffered torture and would probably be hanged if not for Roche, who gives him a chance to prove his innocence by capturing the true culprit. The main objective is very clear, Geralt is caught in the middle of a geopolitical struggle and, as a player, you immediately want to see how the story will unfold. As for Witcher 3, well... Geralt starts in search of a woman, and when he finally finds her, or rather is found by her, he is then given the heroic task of – guess what? – finding another woman. And that is the whole plot. A much more fitting title for this game could be “Finding Ciri”. 

Do not think, however, that finding Ciri is going to be easy. The Novigrad section plays like this: find Triss, she may know about Ciri → find Corinne, she may know about Ciri → find Dandelion, he apparently was with Ciri → find the crime bosses, they may know about Dandelion → find Junior, he may know about Dandelion → find Dudu, he knows about Dandelion → find Priscilla, she may know how to find Dudu. Then the infamous butcher of Blaviken and slayer of monsters, Geralt, is required to use his quite specific set of talents to help the professional bard Priscilla to write a play in order to attract Dudu from wherever this undoubtedly very important character is hiding. It was at this moment that my tedium gauge reached stratospheric levels and I unconsciously started button mashing the controller through the cut-scene. I stopped playing the game then, but forced myself to keep pushing some days later, and made it to the Isles of Mist.

I should thank CD Project Red for completely breaking the classic version or I would probably torture myself even more.

EDIT: With respect to the problem of launching the classic version, a user in the comments provided a link that solved the problem. So I went on and finished the game. To my surprise, the achievement for completing the main campaign was obtained by only about 22% of players. So, despite all the universal praise this game received, 78% of its digital renters never even bothered to actually finish it.

comment:
A Gentle Dystopia

Ah yes, the promised land is finally here. After a botched release and years of updates improving, expanding, and stabilizing the game along with the release of the massive Phantom Liberty expansion. All is forgiven, Polish devs. But is it? As much as there is about Cyberpunk 2077 that I like and as much as I respect the support CD Projekt Red continued to put into it. We need to talk about the massive elephant in the room that never actually left. Borrowed time.

Majora's Mask is probably one of the most famous examples of making time itself part of the gameplay. Even though its three day loop, that doomsday clock is always ticking. The player constantly understands that time has value. For more modern examples, look at games like The Blood of Dawnwalker or Kingdom Come Deliverance II. Neither necessarily hangs one giant doomsday clock over the player in the same way. Instead, time becomes part of the player's agency. Dawnwalker gives you a limited amount of time before the endgame, with quests and major actions advancing that clock. Deliverance II takes a more situational approach, where certain quests and events will move forward without you if you wait too long. Personally, I think Deliverance II takes this idea a little too literally. Persona 5 is another great example. You have a limited calendar and have to decide how to spend it. Do you improve a relationship? Work on yourself? Explore the palace? Prepare for the next major confrontation? All of these systems are asking the player some variation of the same question. What are you going to do with the time you have? And Cyberpunk presents one of the strongest possible versions of that question. When you're dying, what do you do with your time?

Apparently nothing. Get up samurai, we're going drag racing. Get up samurai, we're clearing every gig and side mission on the entire map. Get up samurai, we're going bowling. This is the massive elephant that I don't think gets criticized nearly enough. The story presents V with a very simple and horrifying problem. You are dying. Your life is disintegrating in front of you. The writing becomes emotional. Relationships start forming. People begin attaching themselves to V. Johnny is slowly taking over. Every lead toward a possible cure should feel increasingly desperate. Your entire story is supposedly happening on borrowed time. And then Cyberpunk almost immediately throws that idea out the window. The clock doesn't actually exist. Take as long as you want. Do every gig. Help every fixer. Buy every car. Make every friend. Finish every companion storyline. Explore every corner of Night City. Eventually, whenever you finally feel like it, go choose your ending.

That's not meaningful agency. That's a story telling you that your time is valuable while the game design simultaneously tells you that your time is infinite. And that creates a massive disconnect. Your relationships with people begin to lose weight. Desperately taking gigs because you need money to upgrade your cyberware stops meaning anything because... why not just do everything? Eventually you'll be swimming in money anyway. The writing constantly asks for an emotional response from the people around V. Meanwhile, V suppresses the biggest problem in their life, another identity is literally eating away at their mind, their body, and eventually their entire existence. That should hang over everything. Every relationship. Every choice. Every job. Every conversation with Johnny. Instead, the uncertainty loses its weight. The confrontations with Johnny lose some of their urgency because, at the end of the day, who cares? Johnny, you and me are going bowling, again.

Once again, modders enter the scene. Modders add an actual doomsday clock, progressing V's deterioration according to the in-game passage of time. Other mods add life sim elements like eating, drinking, sleeping and generally maintaining yourself. The most baffling thing about all of this is that the foundations for these systems are already sitting inside the game. There are food vendors everywhere. Vending machines everywhere. You have a bed. You have showers. You can buy multiple apartments and living spaces. These places are presented like somewhere V can return to, decompress, sleep, shower, eat, and temporarily escape Night City. But for what? The game has all these little pieces suggesting that V is supposed to be living in Night City while simultaneously dying inside it, yet almost none of them carry any real mechanical consequence. And that becomes even stranger when you consider how heavily the writing emphasizes borrowed time. Every new person V grows attached to is potentially someone they're going to lose. Every relationship V builds is happening under the shadow of an approaching death. Every lead toward a cure should matter because another day wasted is another day gone. But without any meaningful passage of time, that shadow never really moves. And that's why, even after all the updates, all the fixes, Phantom Liberty, and everything CD Projekt Red poured into this game, part of Cyberpunk 2077 still feels half cooked to this day.

One of the biggest contradictions is still sitting there at the heart of V's story. Untouched. Unfixed. They wrote about a person discovering that their life suddenly has an expiration date, but never implemented the one element that could have made that premise truly meaningful. Your life is supposed to be on borrowed time. The grim story of a dystopian hell where one person is desperately trying to find some meaning in the trash heap around them loses much of its weight when the game refuses to make time matter. For all the work CD Projekt Red has done rebuilding Cyberpunk 2077, this contradiction has been sitting there since the beginning.

The elephant never left the room.

comment:
Decent, shallow game based around D&D 5th ed. 

There's a lot you can see (like Astarion getting obliterated with the POWER OF THE SUN, highly recommended), and many of the non-obvious solutions to a problem were planned for by the devs beforehand. Quests are decently written, and can be solved in multiple ways, with multiple outcomes (sometimes).
Larian Studios clearly cared about making this game, which is VERY rare nowadays and worth giving a shoutout to.
One other  good thing I will mention is that it tries to have multiple endings, and it kinda does (like 3-4 endings for a regular character, 4 for Shadow the Darkurge and like 2-3 per companion). Decent. 
I'm saying "kinda" because you're going to play it once, anyway, so effectively it has one ending.


Now the schizorant:

The game offers no moral quandries (ooh do I save the orphans or do I LE KILL THEM! MWAHAHA...?), leaves you with nothing to think about after finishing it, and its replay value is next to non-existent, seeing how you can do most of the things in one playthrough and it's too exhausting to finish this entire ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game again and wade through soymillenial nu-DND writing to like, see a different scene or two.

The gameplay itself is alright. Meh.
Really, you finish it and you feel mildly amused for like 20 seconds or so and then you never think about BG3 again in your life, which is how I believe most of the brainfried world we're living in right now feels most of the time - spaced out, not very passionate about anything because that's cringe, and absolutely holding no moral opinion at all, of any sort, even the wrong one.

The entire game feels like second-monitor interactive slop, made so you can click on something while you watch your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Joe Rogan podcast or Hasan Piker stream highlights or whatever on your main screen. It saddens me to say so, because again, the devs cared and it shows.

I don't hate BG3. I hate that I'm so indifferent about a modern AAA D&D game, which seemed like a pipe dream for a nerd (like me) ages ago. Sadly, I feel like it's insanely overhyped for what it is, most of the other PC D&D games mog it in every metric but graphics.


Should you play it if you got it for free? Yes. 

Should you play it with your friends who don't play PC games? Not really, it's too confusing for a non-epicgamer who's  glued to his computer 24/7, and too shallow for the nerds.

Should you pay a full price to play it alone? No. 
I mean it's fun, but not for the price tag it sports. maybe pick it up on a sale.


Play the OG DND RPGs from the 90's-early 2000's, and no it's not just the boomer in me they're actually better, and more "mature" (well, as mature as a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ skinnerbox PC game can be). 

Not to mention the obvious which is making an entire game be based on Californian sensibilities and demographics is nonsensical. 
The world does not begin and end at the borders of the Los Angeles metropolitan area; the "representation" they're going for is insanely exclusive but - gotta get that Blackrockbux! ♥♥♥♥ off.

Also, fun fact: includes literal zoophilia. Gotta move that Overton window some more, I guess. Thanks, Belgium.

6.5/10, I kinda liked it for one playthrough.
Good for people who never played a role-playing game in their life, but I really  wouldn't recommend it otherwise.

comment:
I probably won't be the first one to note how the game has tersely described itself in the last text message during Swedenborg-Riviera quest:

[spoiler]
[quote]U followed all the clues - like the GOOD DOG
u are. So? Do you feel ENLIGHTENED??? xD
YOU HAVE BEEN PWNED BY SW33TE11l3[/quote]
[/spoiler]

PWNED - exactly how I felt after finishing the game. It also just so happened that I got this quest after the main story line, so it was the very last thing I did in the game, how fitting.

I waited through the horrors of the initial rushed launch in 2020, I waited through the following years of patching, until the Phantom Liberty DLC, then some more years of patching and only then I finally got the game in 2026 ([i]with 65% discount, mind you[/i]), expecting it to for sure be done by now and ready to play.

But it is not, it is still not. Even after 6 years since the release it still feels rushed and rather abruptly done - like on that meme of drawing a horse. I don't mean bugs or crashes - there is almost none of those, from technical point it is quite stable and polished ([i]nha![/i]). I mean the actual game, the story - it is all "artificial", dumbed down, with a plastic taste and just empty - a ([i]very beautiful[/i]) husk that does not have a life inside. What it does have and a lot of is generic conversations with meaningless options in dialogues, pointless grinding, insufferable female V ([i]male V is probably the same[/i]), vastly annoying characters ([i]with a few exceptions[/i]), SJW vibes and loads of "[i]choom[/i]", "[i]sitch[/i]", "[i]deets[/i]", "[i]prolly[/i]", "[i]delta[/i]", "[i]preem[/i]", "[i]nova[/i]", "[i]saka[/i]" and other cringe crap.

That is not the game that we were promised and waited for.

I regret paying money for this, even with 65% discount. If I knew what it was going to be like, I would probably not bother playing even a pirated game. Ah yes, and plus 2 months of NVIDIA GeForce NOW subscription, because my wooden PC would never be able to run it with at least 10 FPS. By the way, even NVIDIA's Ultimate tier can barely handle 60 FPS at maximum graphics level in 4K, and that is already with upscaling, so don't expect miracles there. It does run on Steam Deck with a tolerable performance and lowest possible settings, but this is not a way to experience a game with such beautiful graphics, so NVIDIA GFN was my only option.

To summarize, as someone said in a [url=https://youtube.com/watch?v=P99qJGrPNLs&lc=UgzZCUExNYh2kEQgE2B4AaABAg]comment[/url] under the original teaser trailer "Bullets" a couple of weeks ago ([i]so that is in June 2026[/i]):
[quote]cant wait for this game to release[/quote]
Yeah, me too. So sad that it still has not.

comment:
This game is overrated due to the branding of Baldurs Gate" and its close match to D&D mechanics.

Combat is over 50% of this entire game and it feels bland (dialog is the another 40% and movement is the remaining 10%). 1 Action per turn, no cover system, missing 9/10 times when hit chance is 70%, too many gimicks to try to gain a single extra action one turn that just seem like moving tokens around from one panel to another in some cases, you don't even get this option for every class and not until you're a good clip into the game. As a Wizard you get a ton of spells and cantrips but most are pointless to use, you just gravitate to using the same 1 or 2 all the time. I found myself heavily relying on Magic Missile just to ensure that I was actually landing some hits since you miss like your blind most of the time even at point blank range. Cantrips are a last ditch effort when you have no more spell slots but are very weak and never seem to improve in damage as the game progresses. As a Barbarian you just have the option to hack and slash and you whiff a lot so combat really has minimal choice required. As a barbarian it's walk up to something and keep swinging one (miss). action (critical miss). per (miss). turn (15 dmg). at (miss). a (critical miss). time (critical miss).

Yes, they have a "Karmic Dice" feature to help with your attack rolls but this spills over to checks outside of combat too and swings both ways. The result is you make too many rolls you should fail (20% chance of success) and fail too many rolls you should make (75% chance of success). Fortunately this feature can be disabled.

Several mechanics were stapled on and feel hollow and pointless:
Camp supplies - Types of supplies you use don't matter for effect. Not like you gain extra bonus if using different types of supplies (there's like 20 different items that are "supplies" but there is no point). As long as you have 40 supply vlaue you can recover in full. Not even finished with act 1 and I've got 1200 supplies and I've been full resting after every battle. What's the point of even having them in the game as a requirement to rest? Who is running out of these things?

Alchemy - Everything is so finite you get very few materials to craft anything. And seems like pretty much everything you can craft are things you can find and buy elsewhere. No limited unique super power craftables looks like. A huge missed opportunity here to have an alchemy skill that allows you to identify rare components to use for unique things. I just don't see the point - you collect a bunch of random bibs and bobs and eventually after a lot of gathering you can craft a basic heal potion.... OoooOOOoo not like they're 15 gold at any trader infinitely.

Relationships - Everyone seems super sex depraved. You can bone anyone in camp with a few dialog selections seems like. You have this whole "party member approves/disapproves" to build some liking between characters but it just seems the only end goal is to bone like we're playing Leisure Suit Larry.

Leveling - Leveling is a joke. While you have a TON of options at initial character creation, you don't really get much choice at each level (the few level ups that there are. 30 hours in and just about level 5). You don't get stat points to add in. It just sort of automatically raises various stats and you get maybe 1 or 2 choices on your level up. You get a new spell slot so you can pick which one from a static selection that you saw last level up. Or some small perk choice. There's really not a lot you can pick and you don't really know what you're getting as a choice on the level up ahead of time. It's not like you're getting stat points and a perk that you can count on each time to develop your character. It's like maybe you get to chose another cantrip or spell. Maybe you can swap a spell out..etc. Just very bland, no choice of progression. If you want to multi-class it's a bit tedious and puts you at a serious disadvantage because you'll be getting level 1 stuff for that other class rather then whatever the higher level stuff you would be getting for your class...etc.  

There's a lot more issues with this game that I won't even go into detail here (loot, camera, save scumming, critical success/failure, mind-worm skill tree...etc) that I think people overlook with rose tinted goggles of the Baldurs Gate series or being a D&D fan. While the graphics are good, the game is pretty well programmed. Story seems decent - though a little ostentatious with some of the side stories of characters. But... the combat is pretty lame. Yes, maybe it's very close to D&D and when you're dealing with pen and paper that may be fine but in a computer game it feels pretty limited and dull. Compared to other titles that are tactical combat RPG style such as a Divinity 2 or Wasteland 3, this combat feels like a massive step backwards for the genre. I don't care that I can stack crates and jump on them mid-battle when I can't even take cover behind one. I would say people should try either of those 2 games over BG3 if they haven't played them yet.

If you're huge fan of D&D or Baldurs Gate for the sake of the name "Baldurs Gate". You'll probably love this game. But if you're coming from playing something like Divinity 2 hoping for something even better - this isn't it. Definitely do your research and watch videos specifically showing the combat in this game and if it's something you're going to enjoy for over 100 hours. Because that is the vast majority of what you'll be doing in this game.

Update: Played another 16 hours hoping it might improve. It doesn't. There's just so many things that are more of an annoyance than fun. This game is WAY over rated by fan boys. Controls are not intuitive, too much BS for the sake of BS with all the little systems to try to jazz up the sad combat/action system. Pathfinding is god awful. "Jump over the lava to this platform", "oh you mean run through the lava 75% of the way and jump the last 2 pixels of distance, draining 99% of all your HP?".

You just feel like a weakling peasant through this whole thing. 40 hours in, still using what amounts to fallen sticks with doo-doo on them as weapons rather than anything decent. Glad my super awesome armor is just base protection and gives a +1 to some random saving throw I have yet to come across. Meanwhile a bee sting is enough to lay me out. Yup, ready to take on the world baby!

So many times you end up doing things you didn't want to do due to janky controls. You want to throw a potion? Well you can't just right click on it in your hot bar you have to pull up your inventory, right click to throw then close the windows down carefully to not click and throw it where you don't want. Left click on a poison potion in your hotbar thinking "this surely will give me a UI to throw it right?" no no... we DRINK the damn thing. That makes perfect sense. I'm sure there's a million cases in the game that you're going to be GLAD you have the freedom to drink poison right from the hotbar with 1 click rather than throw it. People think it's amazing that you can dive head first into lava and cast buff spells and heals on the enemy and other crap you would really NEVER want to do. It's not freedom, it's frustration and lazy programming expecting people to have to handle this stuff. And this idea of trying to sneak and steal is pathetic. What's the point of stealth and sneak at all? So many things are red and you're not allowed to take them technically because it's stealing but you can. But even if you're hidden and no one sees you take it, magically everyone in the place KNOWS you took it and the entire town is willing to go to war with your over a stolen heal potion. Like W.T.F?

Out of all turn based action RPG's like this I've played this is definitely the worst one. Don't fall into the hype of getting this. I think this is too highly rated by people that like that you can see pee pee's and tah tah's.

You are CONSTANTLY being called on your phone by some random NPCs you've never met who act like they know you and call you to tell you they have a job for you. It happens ALL THE TIME even in the middle of other quests and conversations with characters so you get double dialogue at the same time (YOU CAN"T REJECT THE PHONE CALLS, your character answers automatically, even though the game says there's a reject button) and it interrupts your dialogue during missions and breaks all the immersion and flow of mission and conversations. You won't run into any interesting situations, you can't just walk around and enter some clubs or something, there's a ton of buildings and clubs etc everywhere and you can't enter anywhere, they're just facades. NPCs just spawn and despawn randomly if you turn around even next to you and sometimes even right in front of your eyes. The only good thing about this game honestly are the voice acting and dialogues (especially in main missions) but even these very quickly get boring because it feels like 90% of the game is listening to dialogues and only 10% is actual gameplay. When you enter a vehicle, the game often just stars playing some random radio station and it continues to play after you leave the vehicle. You have to open a radio menu and scroll through a whole list of radio stations to the "No station" option and select it to disable the music. EVERY TIME.
