I did it and the guy still killed himself because apparently you have to pick a specific dialogue option later (neither dialogue option suggests what's gonna happen and the one that prevents him from killing himself is clearly the wrong one if you did the optional quest but I guess the devs didn't talk to each other so yea, let's ♥♥♥♥ up the players playthrough). Sometimes your character just randomly climbs something in from of them even if you don't press the jump/climb button. I've had it happen when doing a mission stealthily and my character would just expose themself by climbing a cover I was hinding behind. One time I was covering behind a fence during a shootout and my character just climbed it and jumped down behind it, several stories down and I just died. I seriously can keep going on with this crap for hours and I literally just started the game. On top of that, the game still crashes occasionally (after several years?) and whenever you launch the game you have to watch an insanely long unskippable intro of logos you don't care about and other crap and people have to make mods to let you skip it. What a game! I put off buying this game for years and I finally bought it and I honestly regret it, not worth it at all.

this game is GARBAGE
You load into the game expecting to play a masterfully crafting strategy game, I am yet to encounter any strategy. I have encountered a whole lot of READING, but no strategy. Fortunately every single good build in bald relies on these mechanics to break the fight in some way so you are never in any danger at all unless you are unskilled (you roll badly). The story is great but you enter the latter half of the game and it is littered with all these pointless meandering fights which suck the life out of you because they are neither challenging nor interesting. comment:
Masterpiece of the game! Enjoyed over 400 hours on PS5/PC and got me hooked to ER lore but also to Dark Souls series and Bloodborne. But thumb down because of awful technical quality of PC port (played on 5800X3D, RTX 5800, 32 GB RAM, Samsung PCIE4 NVME). After 30+ million sold copies, somebody would think FS would hire proper developers and make this masterpiece perfect on PC, but even 4+ years after release, PC port have:

- framerate still locked to 60 fps max, full screen mode unusable
- no FOV options
- no widescreen support
- no any upscaling tech - dlss/fsr/xss
- abysmal RTX mode which even devs suggest to turn off for better performance
- improper input pooling causing stutters
- huge pop-ins even when plenty of vram available (LOD, geometry, textures)
- badly implemented shader compilation "on-the-fly" causing massive stutters after every vga driver update (why not then compile them on game or area load?)
- very irritating flickering shadows in certain situations
- no option to disable awful chromatic aberration filter
- no option to disable vignette filter
- no option to disable too aggressive sharpening filter
- no option to disable camera reset if no lock target
- camera distance not dynamic in boss battles
- missing PS gamepad icons - why not autodetect which type of controller is connected?

Yes, mods help with most of these issues, but than you loose multiplayer.

A gorgeous game with honestly a poor combat system. I can understand why the combat system works for tabletop rpgs. I can understand why players of dnd enjoy this game. comment:
5/10

Elden Ring has mountains of potential but it is simply held back by some very clearly rushed and lazy development choices. this game suffers from a similar fate to dark souls 1, in that the second half of the game is awful. The difference here is, not only was the first half of ds1 good, but the seconds half (while not great) didn't take terribly long. Elden Ring is a half-baked game.  Ill stop ranting and ill just go beat by beat. To start off, this game is only half open world. The first half is open. The second half 100% is not. This sucks even more because the open world is very very good in this game. Seriously the open world is some of the best I have seen. if you don't like souls but like rpg's you will like Elden Ring. Anyways the bosses and their awful balancing is where this game falls short. To start off we have Margitt as the very first boss. Margitt isn't great and he foreshadows certain awful trends you see later in the game.  He has very delayed attacks, which in a vacuum is fine, but as someone who knows how much this mechanic gets spammed later on, it simply seems like a way to unfairly increase difficulty. Margitt also has very long combos that make it unclear when they end, which is another trend we see later on. Finally, Margitt has a small dagger that he uses if you get to close after he attacks. The problem here is, it is unclear when this dagger will come out, so you can punish what you think is an opening, and then take damage to no fault of your own. 4/10 boss. next is Godrick. Godrick is better but still not great. I don't havve a ton to complain about with him, he is a  fairly solid fight 7/10. The next boss you will probably fight is Renalla. Renalla is a gimmick fight packaged with the souls classic: boss that constantly runs away from you and spams op projectiles. That pretty much is the entire fight. First phase is a gimmick waste of time. Second is just chasing her around trying not to get hit by her annoying projectiles and summons. 2/10 boss, chasing a boss isn't fun. The next boss you will most likely fight is Loretta, and boy is this a nice change of pace. Loretta is a fantastic fight and really shows you fromsoft still has the ability to make really solid fun and fair experiences. My only minor complaint is her second phase projectiles can be a bit much at times, but that isn't really a big deal. 8.5/10 has that Fromsoft touch. Next up we have Draconic Tree Sentinel, or DTS. DTS brings us back to the awful bosses. DTS features spammy AOE projectiles, and attacks that have a delayed massive shockwave that will hit you even if you dodge the initial swing. Not much to say here, this boss abuses delayed attacks slightly less than the others but thee big problem is the awful AEO shockwaves produced by many of his attacks. these waves come out slightly later after DTS's weapon hits the ground which feels weirdly unnatural even though that is more reallisiticaly how it works. Point is it feels bad and to make it even worse it does a ♥♥♥♥ ton of damage. (I forgot to mention this earlier but it is worth noting how inflated these bosses AP and HP is). Dts gets a 3/10 not the worse but Fromsoft can do way way better. Next up is, technically a miniboss, but it is just the first phase of a later boss so ill just talk about it there. Anyways next is Morgott (Margitt is weaker kind of fake shade of Morgott). Morgott is one of the biggest offenders of the stupid long combo. morgott spends so much time just comboing it is awful. Not to mention he is way way faster than you to a point where it is unfair. This fight basically consists of Morgott aura-farming doing crazy flips and combos while you wait for the single attack you can get a hit off of. this boss really demonstrates how so many Elden Ring fights are just two sets of attacks: all the attacks it's impossible to get a hit on, and the about one or two you can get a hit on. this system just leads to a lot of waiting and waiting for getting the corrects attacks. Anyways Morgott still has all the usual, delayed attacks, too much HP, too much AP, way to damn fast, etc... just with more combos to really waste your time, 5/10 better than Margitt because he looks a bit cooler and instead of waiting while he does nothing, you wait while he flips around comboing the air. Our next  boss is really where the quality goes from bad to borderline unprofessional garbage. The bosses from here on out are so bad it is crazy to think this same company made Sekiro and DS3. These bosses are all some of the absolute worst in souls (I would seriously rather fight bed of chaos than most of these). Started off we have a contender for worse souls boss,  the First Giant. Fire Giant features and even more inflated Hp pool, with tons of one-shots, awful terrain, annoying projectiles, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ camera, and to top it all off he constantly runs away form you making you get on and off your horse to try and keep up with him. 
This fight is a slog, it is awful. One of the most boring terrible fights ever. I could go over all of the bad stuff about the second phase but I do not want to talk about this awful fight any longer. 0/10 remove from the game. Next on the list we have the God Skin Duo. This boss is just Ornstein and Smough, but awful. instead of having opposite attack styles and kind of attacking one at a time. They attack in fairly similar ways and they don't let up meaning most of this fight is spent running them around the terrain trying to separate them so you even have a chance. 1/10 really undercooked gank fight. Now this next boss, this next boss is actually very very good. I'd even say the best boss in the game by far. Next up we have Maliketh. Now ill admit his first phase is kind of mid, but once Maliketh comes out it is such a fun fight. first of all, all of his attacks are telegraphed in a way that is predictable and makes sense. Second, you can respond to all of his melee attacks with a counter attack (especially by strafing which I really like). Third and finally of all, his health is fairly low. The only thing here is his massive AP, but I think that is fine because he is ALSO pretty flimsy so he is more of a speedy glass cannon type. 9.5/10 FromSoftware you dog. Next is a mini boss. Sir Gideon Ofnir. Ill keep it short and sweeet. He just spams verry OP projectiels and runs away from you. 0/10 bad unless you get good RNG and he doesn't spam his really OP spells. Our next boss would be Godfrey and Hourah Loux and ill, be rating these two seperatley even though they are the same fight. For Godfrey I basically no comments, an overall really reallly good fight, 8/10. For Hourah Loux, he is way too fast and has too many grab attacks making it really hard to even take a breath in the fight. 2/10 feels like the speed of a Sekiro boss. Now for the final boss and this one is also two bosses. Radagon, and Elden Beast. radagon is an extremely unremarkable mid filler fight. Nothing super interesting about him, he is just a basic souls boss, 6/10. Now for Elden beast, Elden Beast sucks. Elden Beast commits so many dark souls sins. he runs from you all the time, he spams projectiles most of the fight, his health bar is massive, the camera can be a little weird, his arena is huge giving him ample room to run away from you, and finally, he is just an ugly looking boss. For a final boss he is very underwhelming 3/10. 

I hope you enjoyed my rant about this game, If you are wondering why I have so many hours, it is because the bosses in this game take ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ages to kill!

comment:
This is perhaps the hardest review I have ever had to write, because I literally have to recommend against playing what I think is a great game, but I cannot, because it is marred by a thick buggy web that prevents my enjoyment of it.

So first off, the game does have some great characters, excellent musical score, an interesting world / plot, and an overwhelming amount of choices you can make so that no 2 playthroughs are alike. The writing can be a bit weak / contrived at times, but this is a D&D high fantasy game, it comes with the territory.

The game is split into 3 acts, and Act 1 is absolutely brilliant. It's a slow burn that really gives you time to warm up to the gameplay and learn how the combat works, but it doesn't hold you hand so much that it hampers that feeling of natural exploration and discovery. My how I loved act I.

Then comes Act II.... and well, the game starts to break down. Plots resolve incorrectly, progression doesn't work randomly for some quests, enemy AI kept breaking. The nonsense just kept piling up, but I was having a good enough time I could ignore most of it.

Then Act III, which is larger than Act 1 and 2 combined. It's a disaster, SO MANY quest bugs. SO MANY issues with the enemy AI. Things that worked ok in Act 1 and 2 are just broken here. My characters would glitch through doors randomly, when I issued commands in combat, the character would start to take the action, nothing would happen, then I lose my action. Jumping is just all out broken, my characters would freeze in mid air then would make the death falling noise and I would take damage. Enemies would freeze in combat and do nothing for a full 10+ seconds, EVERY. SINGLE, ROUND, making it a nightmare of a slog to get through a single combat. I would often focus down enemies simply because their AI was bugging out and I just couldn't standing watching them sit their and drool while doing nothing again.

I can put up with A LOT for a good game, but no matter how good BG3 is otherwise, it's just to much to bear. The game seems to be getting worse with each patch, which is mind boggling. This game needs to be rebuilt from the ground up in a working engine, because this is just not a good experience as is. I honestly don't think most of the people reviewing this game well made it through Act 3, because there is no way you can ignore this many issues.

Maybe the game works better on consoles, that could be worth looking into as it's a real shame to miss out on such a good narrative experience, especially since this is perhaps the most epic D&D based game ever released. I really wish the studio that made it had let it cook longer, but oh well, not much we can do now.

comment:
This is hardly the greatest form of activism, but we are all called to do what we can where we are. Elden Ring, along with just about everything else FromSoftware has created, is a solid entry in the canon. There is no denying this. This review has nothing to do with the base game. Yes, I think you know what this is actually about. The ugly little elephant which consistently plagues the gaming industry as well as the many aspects of modern life, I'm afraid. Consolidation of power, income inequality, the end of individual ownership. You see these phenomena play out in all walks of life. And yes, it's infected even the most beloved studios of our day. Perhaps this is inevitable, but this is no reason to give in to mediocrity and extortion.

The implications of "horse armor" need no introduction. Once implemented, they tend to signal a decline in the equitable partnership between player and developer. Bethesda, Ubisoft, EA, Activision, to name the obvious ones. Oh microtransactions. Oh gated content. Oh Pre-order bonuses. "They are totally optional. They are purely cosmetic." "Content" of this kind is completely overwhelming in the space today, so commonplace that few even seem to notice or remember a time before their coercive ubiquity, but those of us who do remember, we are still out here, and we still care. I know whoever decides to read this cares too. And you can do something about it.

As a very simple and free form of activism, I implore you not to buy the new Elden Ring "DLC," or any DLC like this. As others have said, this very well could have been a free update. I hope it goes without saying that no one who loves FromSoft would begrudge giving them money for genuine add-on content to their games. However, we all know this is not coming from the hardworking developers. No, this is yet another push from shareholders to extract what little money you have to spare. It really isn't about $5. It's about the intrinsic and ever diminishing supply of one's own time. It is long overdue that we all reckon deeply with this fact. You're getting older. You don't have as much freedom to do the things you want to do anymore, and as more of life gets behind you, the equation will never pencil out in your favor again. So for all that is good in the Universe, please stop wasting your life.

The writing is good, the environments are nice, and the soundtrack is great. However, I've ran into so many gameplay issues and bugs in the game that I've completely lost interest in playing. The main issues:

- Useless autosave system. A major portion of my playtime is just redoing hours of lost progress because I forgot to quicksave enough. Why couldn't they at least make it so that it autosaves after major conversations/events or after leveling up, for example?! The most annoying part is having to redo all of the inventory management. It has to be the worst autosave system I've ever seen in a game.

- Amount of bugs. I've encountered a high amount of bugs during my playthroughs. I've had to redo progress way too many times due to annoying things like enemies teleporting to where they shouldn't be, getting stuck out of bounds, visual bugs, aural bugs, or various other annoying issues.

- Other issues include enemy vision going through terrain or solid objects when sneaking, being forced to stop sneaking and/or enter combat when you are in the vision cone of a non-hostile NPC that is not involved in combat in any way, and accidentally interacting with something while trying to just move your character. What a great idea to make every single interaction use the left mouse button! Trying to move to a specific spot for a sneak attack? Nope, you pickpocket your ally and get spotted. Trying to read a book on a shelf? Nope, you steal an item and the whole town wants to kill you.

- Misleading conversation options with irreversible outcomes. I've noticed that there are a lot of conversation options that seem completely neutral/non-hostile, but unexpectedly lead to the other party becoming hostile towards you. Even if you never attack them and only help them fight the other enemies, they will remain permanently hostile towards you, and there is no way to talk to them or pacify them. If you manage to knock them out with non-lethal attacks, the narrator says that they died, even though they didn't, and they remain hostile, which means you can't help them. It's just so lame that the only options are to take the very obvious "good" path, or to fight them to the death, nothing in between.

- Co-op conversations. It's very disappointing that only one player can participate in a conversation. NPCs can interject, but players can't? Not even when it's a non-verbal conversation, like a skill check. A lot of the time I end up just feeling like an NPC during conversations because I can't interact in them in any way, even though my character is standing right there next to the player leading the conversation. To utilize your characters properly, you have to already know what options the conversation will have beforehand.

My tips for any new player are to hammer the quicksave button all the time, avoid stealth builds, and choose only the most obvious conversation options. For co-op, turn on the "eavesdrop" option in the settings, so you don't miss important moments, and try to keep your characters balanced enough to be able to succeed in most skill checks by themselves, since you can't pass the check to another player.

comment:
This is one of those games that makes one realize that less is more. There are so many quests, so many encounters so many characters, an utterly overwhelming amount of content that is easily missable and yet very little of it is actually all that interesting or complete. The story's pacing starts slow before speeding up and slowing down immediately right after. It's combat falls under the same pitfalls as typical Dnd 5e combat, ie. it only becomes more prolonged the higher level you are.

chapters 1 and 2 are fine, good even, I was having fun right up until chapter 3, where a lot of the game really starts to show it's faults. One that is obvious almost immediately is that some companions just straight up lack a lot of meaningful content or development, Wyll and Laezel being where it is most obvious, at least compared to Gale, Shadowheart, or Astarion. This can be noticed as early as chapter one, but it is painfully obvious by the time you reach Baldur's Gate, some characters pretty much have their arc mostly complete and you have to wade through a couple more encounters to actually finish them. They feel like padding more so than organic parts to the it stories. There's also some weird thing with how the game handles events or how characters react that sometimes gives you the impression you unintentionally sequence broke a questline? it's very jarring, it's made me replay entire sections only to be frustrated by the same thing happening.

Lastly, the combat, the main thing that the DnD system cares to have detailed mechanics on, it's as bad as it is in the tabletop. High level encounters are prolonged slogfests where very little meaningfully happens for most of the combat until one side starts losing pawns. One example being the Yurgir fight (it's avoidable, yes, but it is a good example of what's to come) where you take forever to actually get through it, because Yurgir's minions have so much hp, you just spend a good chunk of the time letting your big spells take care of things and hope they get caught long enough in something like Hunger of Hadad to never become an actual problem. So many fights are like this and after a while it just starts being a repetitive rather than interesting set of encounters. The early game doesn't suffer from this as much because hp numbers are normal, but by the time you're around level 7~ you start encountering enemies with 100s of hit points and it just makes battles last forever. 

You may disagree, but there's a reason why people who like this game joke about endlessly replaying chapter 1 and 2, chapter 3 is not interesting enough to want to play through and it makes me feel like this game has been a huge waste of time

comment:
Not Recommended — Legitimate Players Get Punished While Cheaters Remain

It's hard to recommend a competitive game when you can get punished despite never cheating.

I received a 20-hour cooldown after VAC flagged my gameplay as irregular. When the cooldown expired, I gave the game another chance, only to have my very first match disrupted and receive a 7-day cooldown. I have never used cheats, and I even tried closing background applications to rule out potential software conflicts.

Meanwhile, encountering suspected cheaters in actual matches remains frustrating. It feels backwards when legitimate players end up afraid to play because of repeated anti-cheat detections they cannot explain.

I'm not claiming that every VACNET detection is wrong, but legitimate players deserve transparency, a reliable way to appeal potential false positives, and confidence that they won't risk escalating penalties without understanding why.

After receiving repeated cooldowns despite not cheating, I no longer feel comfortable playing CS2. I don't want to risk a permanent VAC ban over something I haven't done.

Until Valve addresses these concerns and provides a clearer process for affected players, I cannot recommend CS2 to anyone who values their account and competitive experience.

comment:
My biggest issue with Baldur's Gate 3 is that the gameplay is simply weak. Substantially inferior to Larian's previous games.

The writing, voice acting, and "world building" (lore, interactions, etc) are excellent, but the actual combat and progression systems feel like a significant step backward from Divinity: Original Sin 2. The root of the problem is its commitment to Dungeons and Dragons. What works at a tabletop doesn't automatically work in a video game.

DnD's rules are designed to support a group of players and a human Dungeon Master who can improvise, interpret edge cases, and ignore bad rules when they get in the way of fun. In Baldur's Gate 3, those same rules become rigid restrictions. Combat is slower, more random (to the point of being frustrating), and far less expressive, constantly held back by arbitrary action limits and dice-roll dependency. I wanted to experience the whole thing. The characters are really nice and I really wanted to know them better, but honestly... The gameplay is unbearable. Seriously, this is the first time in my life that I felt BORED playing as a barbarian.

comment:
The ruleset or whatever it is called in D&D completely runied the experience for me as a wizard during our 4-player co-op playthrough.

It is genuinely not fun to waste all your spell points and/or actions on misses, and deal single digit damage in three turns, just to die to a single strike from one sneaky enemy. During our playthrough the general impression was that the meta is damage, no matter the fact that the game has a wide variety of interesting spells. It's just not worth it to try to stun an enemy for 1 turn and miss, instead of trying to actually damage it. Waste of potential.

The game was also full of technical problems. Bard trying to give us buffs for dialogues, the game confirming it at first, and then not adding the bonus to the final throw value - these sorts of bugs ruined tense moments. 
Constant desyncs and crashes during several phases of the game also ruined the experience. We finished only because of 1 member like the game out of four. Shame.

To be fair, the game looks good and most of the characters have an interesting story. Music also stands out.

It really says a lot about the gaming industry that this could became a GoT. If you are not a fan of the ruleset, I would say you should play Divinity Original Sin 2 instead of this. It was developed by the same studio and it is much more enjoyable.

comment:
TLDR: This isn't a good game, it's got nothing to offer other than some pretty graphics.

I decided to give this game a chance (despite the fact that i'm not a fan of RPG games) because I like open world games and this game's city looked cool. And so I started playing, trying to focus on the positives – the beauty of the city, just driving around, doing missions as an excuse to spend some time immersed in it. I did succeed in that – at times the game hit me with some stunning views of the city's architecture. From that aspect I won't deny that some mad talent and hard work must've gone into its creation. The city has no depth to it though, it's just a pretty postcard – whenever I tried to explore it I found that there's nothing there. Can't really have no fun interactions with the environment or the NPCs.

Beyond that though, this game definitively confirmed to me, together with my previous excruciating attempts at playing The Witcher 3, that the developers at CD Project Red have no idea how to make an entertaining videogame.

This game's story is bad. It's generic, it's pompous, event though it has no right to be, since it's a dookie. It's filled with exposition dumping from a bunch of talking heads with stiff animations that explain to you why you should care and why it's essential for you to shoot 30 more guys for the story to progress. The story tries to touch on all your typical dystopian topics like corrupted corporations and governments, the violence, the meaning of life, but it fails to say anything meaningful or impactful.
 
The main character is arrogant and unlikeable. Their immature desire to hit the "big leagues" coupled with the overdone voice acting and terms like "delta", "nova", "choom" etc. really didn't evoke any emotion other than embarassment. I wanna emphasize just how much they dropped the ball with the story and the delivery of the voice lines, because I didn't feel this way about Cyberpunk Edgerunners, which used those same made-up slang terms, but didn't feel nowhere near as cringe, and it also succeeded at delivering a better story and showcasing the beauty of Night City much better.

The gameplay is there and it's just okay – and that is not okay, you know what I mean? There is nothing special, no scratch that – even remotely engaging about the gameplay. It's your typical "choose your own approach" game (similar to the Far Cry or Hitman games). Shooting is generic, driving is generic, stealth is generic. It's all serviceable, it's there, but it leaves you not being able to shake off the feeling that you're playing something you've already played dozens of times before. And let me be clear, I don't mind generic, it's just there's no fun gameplay loop here.

I could sit here a bunch more nitpicking about various things that rubbed me the wrong way about this game, like all the times I was tasked with finding a circuit breaker to restore power to progress a mission, or how a manual save system really doesn't fit an open world game like Cyberpunk and losing minutes of progress from accidentally dying while messing in the open world isn't fun. But I think it's time for a conclusion.

For all the hype that was created around this game before its release, even after all the patches it's nothing special. It didn't innovate, it didn't push games to a new level in any way. From where I'm standing, this game isn't worth the money that's being asked for it. And I bought it during a sale, so that's saying something.

comment:
Recommended? No.

Cyberpunk 2077 might be the first game I've played where I genuinely enjoy the characters, world, story and combat while simultaneously wanting to launch the entire installation into the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sun.

The vanilla character customization is embarrassingly shallow for a game whose entire setting revolves around modifying the human body. Night City is full of people with cybernetic limbs, mechanical jaws, artificial skin, exposed hardware and insane body modifications. Meanwhile V gets some lines on his face and apparently we're supposed to go, “Yep, I'm a cyborg now.”

So naturally, I went to mods.

That was a mistake.

Want cybernetic arms? Great. Download the arms.

Except you also need a framework.

And another framework.

And a cyberware core.

And an equipment system.

And an Atelier system.

Then you launch the game and discover the store exists BUT THE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ARMS AREN'T IN IT because apparently you downloaded the framework for the arms, the store for the arms, the system for equipping the arms, and everything else required to contemplate the philosophical concept of an arm — except the actual ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ arm.

Quit game. Nexus. Download. Vortex. Deploy. Launch game.

Now there are six stores.

Four are empty.

WHY ARE THEY THERE?

Install more mods to populate them.

Quit game. Nexus. Download. Vortex. Deploy. Launch game.

Want gauges? Same ♥♥♥♥.

Want facial cyberware? Same ♥♥♥♥.

Want clothes that don't look like V dressed himself by blindly sprinting through a futuristic Goodwill? Welcome back to Nexus.

And God help you if you install a giant mod collection hoping somebody else has already assembled all this into a coherent package. I tried that. I ended up with 300+ mods, stores containing nothing, stores containing nothing but shoes, mountains of Fem V cosmetics I couldn't use, dependencies for mods I didn't want, and absolutely no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ idea which piece of this Jenga tower was responsible for what.

I eventually deleted the collection and discovered I'd spent more time modding Cyberpunk than playing Cyberpunk.

The frustrating part is that underneath all this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, I actually like the game. I care about these characters. Panam is fantastic. Night City is incredible. When the combat and cyberware fantasy clicks, it's awesome.

That's precisely why this pisses me off so much.

A game called CYBERPUNK should not require an undergraduate degree in ArchiveXL, TweakXL, RED4ext, redscript, Codeware, Equipment-EX, CET, Virtual Atelier and whatever other technological incantation I've forgotten just so my character can LOOK LIKE A ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ CYBORG.

The modding community has produced some genuinely incredible work, and individual mod authors clearly put enormous effort into it. But the user experience of the Cyberpunk modding ecosystem is atrocious. Dependencies stacked on dependencies, content separated across downloads, storefronts separated from merchandise, inconsistent installation methods, and documentation that frequently assumes you already understand the ecosystem.

After hours of troubleshooting, installing, uninstalling, launching, quitting, relaunching and wondering why another ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ store is empty, I have reached enlightenment:

Maybe the real cyberpsychosis was the mods we installed along the way.

10/10 Panam.

9/10 Night City.

2/10 character customization.

0/10 second job as an unpaid Night City systems administrator.

comment:
This remaster is a disaster. Whoever greenlit its release instead of delaying it seriously needs to be fired. 

I own The Witcher 3 on Steam, PS5, GOG, and Xbox Series X, and I've now tried the remaster across multiple platforms.

On PS5 and Series X, it's essentially unplayable for me. There's constant stuttering while riding Roach and during nearly every combat encounter I've experienced so far. It's a miserable experience, and I won't be playing either console version again until CDPR releases a patch addressing the performance issues. Then there's PC.

Before the remaster, I could comfortably average 90–100 FPS on Ultra settings. After the update, I'm lucky if I can reliably maintain 45–50 FPS. That's an enormous performance hit. Also, the dialogue audio is far too quiet compared to the rest of the mix and I'm constantly having to adjust the volume just to hear characters speaking. 

I've also encountered more bugs in roughly two hours with the remaster than I remember encountering throughout my previous Witcher 3 playthroughs.

This update should have been delayed. There's no good reason it needed to release in this state. I understand that it's a free update, and I appreciate that, but being free doesn't excuse releasing a buggy, poorly optimized remaster with the expectation that the problems can simply be fixed later.

I loved the original Witcher 3, which makes this even more disappointing. But based on my experience across PC, PS5, and Series X, I cannot recommend the remastered version in its current state. Until CDPR addresses the severe performance problems, stuttering, and visual bugs, I'd stay away.

comment:
101 hours. Cyberpunk finally defeated me.

I got a lot out of this game, and when Cyberpunk is good, it can be really fun. The combat is great, building out your character and cyberware is addictive, and a lot of the gigs and side missions were easily my favorite parts of the game. They were quick, gave you an objective, let you approach it your way, and then got the hell out of your way.

Unfortunately, once I started focusing on the main story, I hit a wall.

The pacing is absolutely exhausting. Walk with somebody. Listen to them talk. Get in a car. Listen to them talk. Follow somebody. Listen to them talk. Sit down. Listen to them talk. Repeat.

Some of these sequences feel like they go on for 20–30 minutes, and because the game is committed to first person, so much of the storytelling is literally just standing there staring at another character while they dump dialogue on you. There aren't interesting camera angles or cinematic cuts to keep scenes visually engaging. You're just trapped in V's head waiting for people to finish talking.

The braindance sequences were especially miserable for me, and I hated how often the game takes control and momentum away from you for scripted rides, conversations, slow walks, scanning, following characters, and other sequences where you're technically "playing" but barely doing anything.

That's what makes it frustrating, because underneath all of that is a game I actually enjoyed. I loved sneaking into buildings, hacking cameras, throwing knives, using suppressed pistols, upgrading cyberware, experimenting with quickhacks, buying ridiculous cars, and figuring out different ways to clear an objective. When Cyberpunk lets me play Cyberpunk, I like Cyberpunk.

But eventually I realized I was spending too much of my time waiting to get back to the parts I enjoyed.

I even tried Phantom Liberty, unlocked the Relic tree, entered Dogtown, and almost immediately found myself thinking, oh God, more walking and talking.

I wanted to finish the main story. I really did. After 101 hours, I figured I had to. But gaming shouldn't feel like homework, and eventually I realized I was forcing myself to finish something I wasn't enjoying anymore.

So I'm calling it.

Great world. Great combat. Great character-building. Some genuinely fun side content. Terrible pacing, overly long dialogue sequences, too many moments where control is taken away from the player, and storytelling that I found incredibly stale.

After 101 hours, Cyberpunk didn't beat V.

It beat me.

4/10 — Not Recommended.

comment:
Cyberpunk 2077 feels like a game that should have been incredible, but instead left me completely cold. This is exactly the kind of game I should love: a massive open world RPG in a cyberpunk setting, something that could’ve been GTA in a Blade Runner world, but it just doesn’t come together.

Even after getting past the intro and into the open world, nothing really grabbed me. The action feels slow and clunky, lacking any real sense of energy or excitement, and combat never becomes fun enough to carry the experience. Movement and gunplay both feel off, making moment-to-moment gameplay more of a chore than something engaging. And the driving flat out sucks.

The presentation didn’t help much either. While the world is detailed, the character designs and overall aesthetic lean into a kind of generic, lowest-common-denominator modern style that lacks the distinct identity you’d expect from a cyberpunk setting. Every character, for the most part, was ugly and suffering from the worst tropes of the woke gaming era. This game WILL feel aged in just a few more years. More importantly, it just doesn’t feel like true cyberpunk - the soul, grit, and atmosphere that define the best works in the genre are missing here.

The story also failed to hook me early on, which is a major issue for a game this dependent on narrative and immersion. Without that pull, there’s not much left to keep you invested - especially, not for 60+ hours.

In the end, it’s a game full of ideas that sound amazing but don’t translate into an enjoyable experience. I wanted to like it, but after just over an hour, I was bored and ready to move on.

On paper, it is everything I want. In execution, it is duller than a plastic butter knife left on a burner.

Take this with a grain of salt because I'm fairly certain this isn't my genre. But this game has too many random gotcha moments, like being teleported to a high difficulty area with fast travel locked off if you open the wrong chest near the beginning of the game (which is not telegraphed, it's just an ordinary chest). Or random objects that disobey the global reset rule on resting (elevators). Or bosses that have claustrophobic arenas where you spend more time fighting the camera than the boss (mad pumpkin head).

As I say, for fans of the genre, this game may be excellent. It's very pretty, the art direction is superb, and the combat controls did *NOT* feel clunky (bar the continued insistence on making sprint/roll the same input), so those are all high points. I've heard the reviews. My friends have all had resounding compliments for this game. I was so, so eager and excited to play. One of my favorite games of all time is Gears Tactics, so I figured another turn based game would be fun.
For backstory, I have never played DnD so I went into this game completely blind.
I simply cannot have fun playing this game. I cannot enjoy a game where I have to google my every problem. 
I have no idea what 1D4 means. Does the game explain it? No. 
I have no idea how combat works. Does the game explain it? No.
I have no idea how spells or cantrips work. Does the game explain it? No. 
I have no idea how statuses, races, or camps work. Does the game explain it? Guess.
Any random action can have a negative consequence. I don't like when I see a door, I have to consider if opening it will kill me. I don't like being punished for exploring.
If you like rolling dice and RNG, then maybe you'll like this game. 
If I don't enjoy the first hour, or the three that follow, I can't see myself ever enjoying it. This game is made for some people, but I guess I simply am not one of them.

comment:
I will likely change my review once the developers release a bunch of fixes, but as of now the remaster is a buggy mess. I barely even started playing and already got a random infinite loading screen while doing the first quest + 2 freezes that forced me to restart the game (while closing the stash in the first inn and another time while closing the glossary).

Performance with regular ray tracing (not even talking about path tracing) is also very poor. It looks good but not even nearly good enough to justify such stark dip in FPS count and latency. This is in part because ray reconstruction is basically mandatory here, but it's simultaneously a demanding feature. However, without it the RT looks so bad, you might as well turn in off entirely and be done with it. Also, changing the basic RT settings to performance barely provides performance gains (a mere few FPS) but makes the game look noticeable worse, so that's not really an option either.

Speaking plainly, it's just bad. No use sugarcoating it. With mid-range GPUs I'd definitely recommend reverting to the previous version for now, perhaps even regardless of the GPU used. Or just wait until they fix all of this and improve performance, which might take a while.

comment:
While playing any of the Infinity/Aurora engine games, did you ever caught yourself thinking: 

- Damn, wish this game had platforming! 
- Maybe you would like to spend hours opening barrels and crates to find no loot? 
- How about spending a LOT of time in inventory management, due to small and generic icons, and a LOT of crappy loot?
- Do you want a really clunky UI, that not only doesn't improve on the genre games that preceded this one, but it also makes some things worse?
- You think that highlighting interactable items is too easy, and you want to pixel hunt for items?


If you answer yes to any of the questions, maybe this game is for you...

On a more serious note, this is one of those times that I wish I could leave a neutral review, but Steam doesn't have the option. THE GAME ISN'T BAD, but it doesn't feel like a Baldur's Gate game. Heck, sometimes it doesn't even feel like a Forgotten Realms game. The are a lot of generic places, places that doesn't feel like their lore accurate counterparts, etc...IWD for example got a lot of the ambiance right, and more than 20 years later, BG3 failed to stand on it's predecessors shoulders.


There are also other problems, like some minor bugs, but I find baffling that more than 2 and a half years after release, Larian still manages to introduce new, major bugs with new patches, like with the most current one. Other downsides if I'm being nitpicky: No LVL 20 (the cap is at 12), a party of only four characters, lack of nuance with party relationships, very low variety of armor/weapons, mechanics info (like crit range or calculating base dmg+elemental dmg from weapons is missing), some staple items, like the Bag of Holding and the Holy Avenger are completely absent and the loading screen drives me nuts, loading to 100% and then staying at 100% for a long time, to actually load (the game is on a nvme SSD, so I don't think this is a me problem).

As a last complaint, after seeing the longevity that NWN1 and 2 got by having amazing toolkits, you'd think Larian would give us something comparable, maybe even better after two decades, but, no...There's nothing.


On a brighter side, the game looks good, most of the voice acting is decent to really good (and there's a LOT of voiced lines), The music is good when it is present, some of the small tidbits and sidequests are very well written and the game is long (that can be a plus or a minus...) and very replayable. 

With all that said, I'd say I've played 3/4 of the game, and it keeps growing on me. I might change the review to positive after I end my first run.

comment:
The negative review is for this: Do not buy it at full price, especially not if you have a mid-range PC like mine AND especially if you are a completionist like me. I tried to experience all the content the game had to offer in a single playthrough, which led to me "optimizing" it (meaning completing all side jobs, fixer gigs and NCPD scanners). Here is my extensive review:

Six years after its original release, I thought the game would be in a pretty great state, but it is still pretty disappointing. I think most people who praise it, they do so because they compare it to the dumpster fire it was on release. But the game still feels unpolished, even unfinished, and it's still riddled with bugs. Not game-breaking ones, but they are still there. I had to install numerous mods in order to get to a decent playable state (fix for junky melee combat, pedestrian behaviour, quality of life elements for HUD and menus, like filters etc, de-scaled skill checks which were impossible after leveling up)

Gameplay wise, the RPG elements are minimal, the dialogue options are mostly different flavours of the same choice, the combat is repetitive and the enemy AI is extremely stupid, even in Very Hard difficulty. The side content (gigs and NCPD scanner jobs) are all duplicate brain-dead quests (read flavour text, go to location, sneak/shoot, loot chest, read flavour text). And no, the city is not immersive at all for me. All the places feel the same.

Its only redeeming quality, the story and characters, are overshadowed and diluted by the immense amount of mediocre side content that continuously distracts you (text messages, calls, etc) and forces you to engage with it ("wait for a whole day until the next mission objective", "find something else to do until [character] contacts you"). 

As always, I think the level design would have benefited if was a more linear and condensed experience, allowing the player to progress through the map gradually and learning to organically traverse through the levels, instead of blindly following quest markers.

I'm considering playing it again and focusing only on the main mission, just to experience the story in a more condensed way, but I am dreading the thought of having to go through all the tedious character progress and repetitive combat.

EDIT: I played the game again, and engaged only with the main quest. It was a far more enjoyable experience for 2 reasons: 1) I was already accustomed with the in-game universe (slang, concepts, characters) and I realized this was part of why I felt lost all the time during my first playthrough, and 2) I was not distracted by the side content and I was able to focus on the story and characters).

Bottom line: Cyberpunk 2077 is a good game but its held down by the open world elements that feel they were forced and rushed by the devs, because apparently these are the minimal expectations for a AAA release.

comment:
Lengthy review because this is one of the very few games of it's genre that has never shown itself to be anything other than mediocre at best and downright awful at worst.

To preface, open world RPGs are my favourite genre. I absolutely adore medieval fantasy and the exploration that comes along with these games. I've played and finished more games in this genre than I can count. I've even seen this game compared to astounding games like RDR2, which is one of my favourite video games ever. Witcher 3 has never, in my approximately 5 times trying to play it, NEVER held my interest for more than a few hours at a time. There is just absolutely nothing to get you through and even on the rare occasion where I have made it a good 10 hours into the game, it never particularly even gets any better. It is just slog after slog after slog. I may force myself to sit through it one day but for now it's impossible.

Story aside, the combat of this game is categorically the most game ruining thing about it. The combat alone is the biggest reason I have decided to put this game aside so many times, remaster "reworked combat" included. It is so shallow and beyond god awful that it's not even like "so bad it's good" it just is the worst thing that CDPR have ever designed. If this game had the same combat that Blood of Dawnwalker, a AA witcher inspired game itself has? It would be probably manageable to actually sit through the snoozefest of a story. But when the main thing you're doing in this game is either story or combat and both of them are terrible? It's the least sustainable thing possible and I wholeheartedly think you are a masochist if you put yourself through it.

Graphics, sound, actual exploration? All fantastic. Please for the love of god for the next game just make everything else as interesting and fun as those 3 things.

It should be telling that half of the positive reviews on the page say absolutely nothing of the game, and more the actions of CDPR making the remaster and DLCs free for anyone who purchased before the fact. I'm aware that they did a really good thing in doing that, however I can't in good faith recommend a terrible game based on that fact alone.

comment:
I woke up after 50 hours jumping like a frog on some platforms like a turn-based Mario.

There are no tactics. There's a mnemonization of spells, items, and stats. Instead of thinking about which hill to place your shooter on, you wonder how the Magic Brooch of Ass you're wearing affects your rolls against the Sudden ♥♥♥♥ Spell.

They advertise that you can fight with the environment. Okay, you set something on fire, the enemy burns. It took a staggering 5% of their HP. So, back to the Sudden ♥♥♥♥ Spell stats. The only effective way to play the environment is to push them into a cliff, but the developers designed a loot loss to prevent anyone from playing like that. But if they stuck to "realism," the loot from a burned fireball victim would be unusable too.

The characters are crap. Protagonists and antagonists. Most attack both melee and ranged at the same time, making tactics pointless. They're jumping around like monkeys (a turn-based Mario), making it impossible to create any sort of structured gameplay. Battles are chaotic in the worst sense of the word.

The monkeys jump around like in a zoo, but at the same time, there are strict rules for blocking characters. You can't send your tank to the front because your team is blocking it. And it's set up the way it is because scripted dialogue set you up at the beginning of the battle. So, good luck with a tank at the back. This happens many times; you'd have to trigger conversations with the tank to keep it in the front. But why would you choose someone else as your main character if a tank with low charisma is supposed to talk?

Therefore, to do ANYTHING in this game, you need to have online help open because nothing is intuitive. There are difficult games, very difficult games, but intuitive. Where losing is fun. Here, you have great sessions with Gemini and discussions on how to prevent Gale from dying in the first turn. In BG3, losing is frustrating because you have no control over your initial setup, every enemy has a ranged attack, and everyone can jump like a monkey. It ends with you being surrounded and pelting your team with everything they can: arrows, spells, bottles of various substances.

That's what the Viet Cong did to every commando unit they spotted in the jungle in Vietnam. But those commandos were hiding, and my team of clowns has to engage in open battle. Often after swaggering dialogues.

As for the lesser sins, the inventory menu is clunky. Like something from 2000.
The camping system is tedious. Halfway through a dungeon, you have to return to camp because your spells and special moves have run out. Furthermore, camping is clearly at odds with the main plot, which counts down to a specific event in single days. Your camping days are unrelated to this; the dialogues constantly state you have a few days left until the event, but you've already camped a dozen times.

If you grit your teeth and endure what I've described, the game is beautiful. Maybe you're into D&D stats, then this is the game for you. But I had to tell the truth about the gameplay because it was touted as a game with good tactical combat, which it isn't.

comment: The positive reviews and glazing for this game are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. CD Projekt Red lied to customers, admitted they did so, apologized for it, then charged for the content they cut with the Phantom Liberty DLC. How are people defending the Phantom Liberty DLC? They are charging you for the content that was promised pre-release for the actual game. The night life district was shown in original trailers and press. They didn't finish any of it, locked it off behind gates and unfinished areas in the initial release, and then sold it back to you later for $30. This game is everything wrong with modern video games. A cinematic, open-world piece of ♥♥♥♥ with bugs out the ass and a story that would've been better suited for a short movie. The Johnny Silverhand storyline is decent, don't get me wrong, but you are essentially watching his story. You are a part of his conundrum and journey from being a rebellious rockstar to a titan taking down Arasaka and Militech. I ran across the city on foot even several times looking for something unique, and there's nothing. I got so much more enjoyment doing the same thing in Grand Theft Auto IV. You have no influence on the world around you. The RPG elements are meaningless and there are no branching storylines to speak of. I even tested multiple storylines by saving and retrying dialogue to see what the different outcomes would be, but it's meaningless. It's about as bad as Fallout 4. People are high on copium wishing this game was what they were hoping for before release in 2018. They got duped and feel stupid for it, so they've convinced themselves it's good when it's not. You're better off watching a movie like "Network," "Soylent Green," or "They Live" if you want some kind of Cyberpunkian story. Do not play this game, I'm warning you.

comment:
I've waited years to finally write this review. Years passed, my old GTX 1080 finally retired, and I thought, "Maybe this time it'll be a better experience." So I reinstalled the game. Again.

At one point, I even thought I owed this game a fair chance, so I bought it multiple times on different platforms. Maybe the problem was me. Maybe another platform would finally reveal the masterpiece everyone kept talking about. It didn't.

The Witcher 3 might be the purest definition of "overrated." The combat is clunky, the gameplay is often painfully boring, and too much of the experience feels like a tedious checklist wearing an RPG costume. Yet somehow, it's still treated like gaming royalty.

At this point, I suspect the surprisingly decent female character models have contributed more to this game's reputation than the actual gameplay.

I couldn't justify spending hours writing a serious review for a remaster that doesn't deserve that much effort, so I decided to use AI to put my thoughts into words instead. The developers had years to work on the remaster. I gave it a few seconds. Honestly, that felt proportionate.

And somehow, CD Projekt managed to add NEW bugs to a game that's been around for more than a decade. Most developers try to remove bugs over time. Here, apparently, they're being collected.

Then there's path tracing. It barely changes the way the game looks while absolutely murdering performance. Nothing says "next-gen" quite like sacrificing a ridiculous amount of GPU performance so you can squint at the screen and wonder what actually changed.

It's 2026. More than a decade later, and after years of patches, updates and a "next-gen" overhaul, this is where we are. Maybe it just needs another 10 years of patches. After all, we're not in any hurry.

Almost forgot: thanks for the free launcher, ads, and telemetry.

A truly impressive legacy.

comment:
239.4 hours on record
Last played: December 2, 2024

I don't hate Grand Theft Auto V. I had fun with it, but after 239.4 hours, I eventually realized how repetitive the experience had become. GTA V was once something I could easily spend hours playing, but over time, the appeal faded & the game started feeling less like entertainment and more like an endless checklist.

GTA Online has an enormous amount of content, but that doesn't necessarily make all of it meaningful. You earn money, buy something, use it to earn more money, unlock another item, complete another activity, then repeat the same process. There is always another vehicle, property, business, outfit, weapon, cosmetic, event, achievement, or collectible waiting for you.

Eventually, I started asking myself: what am I actually working toward?

The biggest problem is the pursuit of exclusive & rare content. GTA Online has accumulated years of limited-time items, event rewards, promotional content, rare vehicles, clothing, liveries, tattoos, collectibles & other items. Some can still be obtained through specific requirements or returning events, while others have been removed or are no longer normally obtainable.

That creates a strange situation where someone can spend hundreds of hours trying to build the "perfect" collection, only to discover that something they wanted was tied to an event from years ago.

If the item is no longer obtainable, there is no amount of grinding that can get it back.

That's what makes the completionist mentality particularly frustrating. You're not simply trying to finish a game. You're trying to keep up with an ecosystem that has been evolving for years, while some of its history is permanently locked behind time-limited availability.

And even the items that remain obtainable can require an enormous investment of time.

For example, GTA Online's money-making activities often involve cooldowns, preparation missions, travel, matchmaking, setup, completion, & repetition. Even one of the game's major solo money-making activities has a cooldown between finales. Multiply that type of waiting & repetition across the countless things a player might want to purchase, unlock, or collect, and the hours add up very quickly.

My 239.4 hours alone equal roughly 9.98 full days of continuous time.

That's almost ten entire 24-hour days of my life spent inside Los Santos.

And that's only the recorded gameplay time.

It doesn't include time spent researching how to obtain items, watching guides, waiting for events, comparing prices, sitting through loading screens, or deciding what to do next.

That's where the opportunity cost becomes impossible for me to ignore.

I'm not saying video games need to be productive. They're entertainment, and entertainment has value. But once a game stops being entertaining & you're continuing only because you've already invested so much time, it becomes worth asking whether that time is better spent elsewhere.

GTA Online can make that especially difficult because there is always something else to obtain.

You can never quite be finished.

Another update arrives.

Another vehicle is released.

Another business becomes available.

Another event begins.

Another exclusive item appears.

Another achievement becomes something to chase.

Then the cycle starts again.

One sequence of the game eventually replaces another.

And eventually, Grand Theft Auto VI will replace this generation's attention with a new world, new characters, new gameplay systems, new content & potentially another online ecosystem to explore. Rockstar currently lists GTA VI for November 19, 2026.

That's not a criticism of GTA VI. It's simply the natural progression of the franchise.

My concern is how much time people can spend trying to completely exhaust an older game before moving on.

You could spend hundreds of hours collecting vehicles, grinding money, unlocking cosmetics & pursuing exclusives, only for the next Grand Theft Auto to arrive & give everyone another massive world full of things to collect.

The sequence never really ends.

That's why I'm no longer interested in chasing every GTA V exclusive simply because I don't have it.

If an item is available, great.

If I miss it, I'm not going to let a virtual item dictate how I spend my time.

Some people genuinely enjoy collecting everything, and that's perfectly fine. But for me, the collection itself eventually became more burdensome than rewarding.

I also don't think GTA V deserves to be treated as a bad game because of this criticism. It has had an enormous impact on gaming, GTA V's single-player campaign remains memorable, & GTA Online has maintained an extraordinary amount of content for years.

My criticism is much simpler:

There is such a thing as having too much of a good thing.

After 239.4 hours, the repetition became difficult to overlook.

The game went from:

"What should I do today?"

to:

"What else do I still need to unlock?"

That distinction matters.

At some point, you're no longer playing because you genuinely want to. You're playing because there's another box left unchecked.

And I don't want a game to become a second job.

My last session was December 2, 2024, and I'm comfortable leaving it there.

I don't regret every hour I spent in GTA V. I had fun, experienced the world, played with other people & made memories. But I also recognize that my time has value, and I don't want to spend hundreds more hours chasing increasingly obscure items simply because the game provides an endless list of things to obtain.

Grand Theft Auto V was fun, but it became repetitive.

GTA Online has more content than most players could reasonably exhaust, yet that abundance can also become the problem.

With GTA VI arriving, I'm choosing not to spend more of my time trying to complete an ecosystem that was never designed to truly end.

I do not recommend it anymore.

comment: I *really* wanted to like this game. The Witcher 3 holds a very special place in my heart, and I waited ten years for the studio's next big thing. I pre-ordered the game and upgraded my GPU just to run it. But, after 80+ hours on the original build, and giving an honest chance to the new update, I have to admit that this game is just kind of bad. The gameplay is uninspired and boring, the characters unlikable and uninteresting, and the world building simply cringy. As a graphics nerd (literally a researcher in the field), the rendering tech on display is really exciting, but significantly marred by overall low image quality and stability, as well as awful art direction. Exceptional materials and rendering quality is paired with clunky character design, poor AI and animation systems, and a bland, sterile game world; it reminds me of those "hyper-realistic" Minecraft texture packs that tweenage me thought were So Cool (tm). The utter lack of charm, grace, and storytelling prowess on display here, qualities abundant in TW3, makes me wonder how heavily the Witcher games actually leaned on their source material; I haven't read the novels, so this is baseless speculation on my part. I won't be finishing Cyberpunk, and unless you're one of the lobotomites who fawns over open-world Ubisoft games, I'd recommend you play something else as well.

comment:
[b]“I got The Urge… The Urge… to DANCE!!!”[/b]
[i]-Creature hit by “Otto’s Irresistible Dance”[/i]
[hr][/hr]

I would describe [b]Baldur’s Gate 3[/b] as “bootleg D&D”.

It’s a “popcorn” game, which is to say it’s fun and good but ultimately artistically insignificant, just barely a step above other popular generic fantasy games, and I’m giving it a thumbs down ONLY because I don’t think it deserves the 720.000 “overwhelmingly positive” score.
(However, I’ll change it into a thumbs up if the score ever dips below it)

[h1]X-Factor[/h1]
Locales are good looking and have variety in them, physical and voice acting are on point, music does the job but sprinkles in some banger tracks, and the changes to the original D&D rules are mostly great and well implemented.
Also, it’s offline D&D, so if you ever missed a session or want to see how a build works you can always fire up this game and just do it.

Despite being a series of rigamarole fetch quests, most setpieces are very cool.

Importantly for replayability, even more than multiple classes with multiple abilities granting no end to how you can build your character, is the modding scene, adding just about everything to freshen the game up for a second and third go-around.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
It’s D&D fifth edition.
If you don’t know what that is: You choose how good a character is at something by slotting a certain number of points in six scores that define who you’re playing as.
On top of this you choose a “class” or what kind of things you’d want your character to be centered around, each class providing different mechanics to achieve this, both inside and outside combat, along with different equipment to give you that extra edge to succeed.
There’s a lot of nuance but that’s pretty much it.

[h1]Story[/h1]
You find yourself aboard an alien ship and infected with a brain parasite that threatens to turn you into a monster, so partner up with an unlikely cast of characters in your quest to seek a cure for this shared burden.

A good hook that gives an excuse to be joined by anyone, no matter how good or evil they are, as you need eachother’s expertise to find a solution to this problem.

The story progresses mostly through dialogue, simply walk up to someone to talk and be either given quests or advance them.

The game also features LOTS of side stories and especially questlines for the ones that either want to explore more of this world or to satisfy their inner completionist.

[h1]Downsides[/h1]
An interesting and focused story that could’ve been told in a couple of hours was instead overfilled with generic writing and other filler content stretching it to about a 100 hours where the game keeps bumping into weird pacing, losing momentum, reiterating over already-made points, and sending you off onto yet another wild goose chase when it doesn’t want you to get to the point, again, all of this isn’t necessarily a bad thing depending of the level of writing required for your enjoyment.

In D&D players can say and do anything they want whenever they want and the DM reacts to it.
In BG3 you’re stunted in your roleplay choices, because of course you can’t have a simple system that accounts for every possibility, but even then, I don’t exactly like how most dialogue choices are: Yes, Yes, Snarky Remark, *attack*.
Also, unfortunately outside a few quips almost no companions interact with eachother, only with the situation at hand which makes them feel more like reactionary robots than the alive characters that should’ve been.

From a purely aesthetic aspect I don’t think anyone will argue about how bad the camera system, the overcrowded UI, the million magical effects overlapping, and other constant immersion breaking aspects of it are, although there are community-made mods that thankfully partially fix some of those issues.

It’s very generic.
That itself isn’t a bad thing but if you want anything more than what the term “fantasy game” conjures in your head, this is not it.
A lot of characters are set up to be interesting in the themes they could explore, but then the writing team ♥♥♥♥♥ the bed and makes them say the same generic trite lines over and over again.
[hr][/hr]

It tries to replicate the tabletop RPG feel but fails to capture its spark.
What is the true TTRPGs experience?
True D&D is a social exercise where you hang out with friends and say dumb stuff and you all laugh at the dumb stuff you say with the plot/campaign only there to give a pretext/context and game rules as a safety net to avoid a guy just going "and then I punch him and he dies and we win".
This game is singleplayer at heart while all TTRPGs are to be played with friends.
It has a hard focus on story but without having good writing to justify it, nor trying to capture the insanity and/or silliness that is player agency.

An even better description for it would be “Singleplayer MMO from the 2000s” but with better graphics that’s only related to TTRPGs due to its D&D playrules.
If that’s sounds like your cup of tea, I’d suggest it, even at full price as there’s a lot of content for those who have the right appetite for it.

Game just does not feel finished. There are still tons of bugs and I will list a couple of the most common/memorable at the end of my review. 

My three general complaints are: 
1. You level up way to fast to the point where it feels punishing to play the hacker playstyle. Every mission you can kill everybody no matter what by only clicking a few buttons. I do think this is a general game issue because the game feels very easy even on the highest difficulty. The only real challenge is when I tell myself "I will only use [x] weapon for this mission." Some enemies have "resistances" to certain forms of combat, but attaching that to the ram system negates it due to the many ways to regen ram or overcharge mode, which allows you to sacrifice hp to hack increasing your ram pool near infinitely. 
2. I don't know if this is just me, but the main story fails to entertain me. This is okay because the side missions are honestly more fun than the busywork the main missions provide. Too much dialogue, too much following frustratingly slow NPCs, and too many tasks and decisions that feel unimportant. 
3. Lastly I know its hard to make games look good while flying; but having flying cars around, millions of dollars in the bank, and being unable to buy one feels kinda bad for a futuristic game. 

All that being said: The world has amazing atmosphere. Driving around, especially in the rain or at night, feels just amazing. The music, the views, and just something I cant explain gives me a amazing feeling of being small... of peace. I do wish there were driving sounds though. 

Here is a list of bugs I have experienced so far. 
1. Picking up items or opening a chest frequently causes things to go flying.
2. NPCs t-posing while driving their cars.
3. Story NPCs get hit by cars during cutscenes causing their dead bodies to drag on the floor while talking to me until they start a different animation and get revived.
4. Enemies glitching into walls and floors.
5. Enemies seeing you through walls and floors.
6. Once a enemy I killed glitched so hard his body was shot into the sky while his head was stuck on a railing causing his entire model to be a massive tapestry spanning over a block and crashing my FPS till it unloaded.
7. Cyberpsycho missions, while being some of the most fun, are also insanely buggy with their triggers. Three times I have had to fast travel, skip 48 hours in time, and then go back just to have things spawn or trigger.
8. Constant floating items, occasional floating NPCs, and briefly floating cars before they crash down. 

The bugs are the main reason I just cannot recommend this game. They break immersion more than anything else.

comment:
Before I start, I would like to say that this it not a negative review. I have very complicated feelings towards this game. Feelings that could not be measured by a simple like or dislike. 

Let's start with the positives. I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ LOVE the art direction of this game. Each region feels distinct and full of detail, conveying a beautifully tragic war-torn world so well, albeit one that feels as though it can be saved and its not all hopeless, and yet despair lurks around every corner.

I loved a lot of the NPCs, they feel considerably more fleshed out than some of the previous Souls games, not to say they didn't have any, but a lot of them made me really question the choices I was making along the way, in particular Varre, who I found intriguingly creepy as hell. It has some of my favorite character designs as well! Blaaid, Alexander, Godrick, Mohg, Malenia, I could go on! The voice acting is top notch as well, some of the best I've heard in a game. 

The music was pretty nice too, unfortunately I'm usually too distracted by my mission or fighting a tough boss to really appreciate it for what it is. 


What made me leave a "negative" review, however, was the difficulty. Not that it was HARD, this genre is known for its relatively high difficulty. It was brutally hard, moreso than every other Souls game I have played, (1 and 3, 3 I have the most experience with) but it's not even that!

The difficulty of this game is....is just....all OVER the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ place!!!

Like...ok. You start out in Limgrave. You have barely any health to speak of, so you need to start leveling Vigor. My advice to you all, get that ♥♥♥♥ to 40 IMMEDIATELY. And then towards the mid-late game, get it to 60. I have gripes with this, more on that later. Liurnia, a bit more difficult, but not a huge step up.
Every region after that has a rather large jump in difficulty. ESPECIALLY Caelid. ♥♥♥♥ Caelid! But wait!! It gets even WORSE!!

When you get to the late game areas, (Leyndell, Mountaintops of the Giants, Crumbling Farum Azula) the game just throws as much ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at you as it possibly can, and doesn't ever hold back. JESUS. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. CHRIST. I have NEVER seen such a horrific difficulty spike in any game up until this point! 

The Fire Giant was the first boss to really question my sanity. It is INSANELY tanky, and while largely telegraphable, it will destroy you in 3-4 hits. With 60 VIGOR. 

60 Vigor is practically MANADATORY at this stage of the game. Everyone and everyONE will ♥♥♥♥ you up in 3-4 hits. I say 60 because it's the second softcap. After that you get barely anything from Vigor. Which ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ SUCKS BECAUSE YOU DON'T EVER GET ENOUGH HP TO WORK WITH!!!

As are summons. The PC version is the definitive version because the online is free. You NEED co-op to beat most of these bosses. Especially towards the end. Spirit Ashes can work too, but here's the thing I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hate about this. NOT. EVERY. BOSS. WILL LET YOU. SUMMON. SPIRITS!!!! WHY?!!! This is a HORRIBLE design choice!! They're not even as good as a player can be! Just let me USE them for Christ's sake!!


But THEN....Maliketh.

Maliketh, and the boss you fight at phase 1, the Beast Clergyman, might just be the worst boss I've ever dealt with. And right before, in my mind it was the Fire Giant. 

Imagine a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ as tanky as the Fire Giant. Now make him INSANELY mobile, have multiple AOE projectiles, and make much of his attacks go through the pillars that LOOK like they're safe, but oftentimes won't protect you from ♥♥♥♥. I mean this to BOTH bosses by the way.

Maliketh, is even worse. Now give him a sword that can DRAIN YOUR HEALTH OVER TIME, AND! Reduce your Max HP, Make him even MORE mobile, and make him tanky too. 

I am stuck on this boss right now. You need two summons. Not one, TWO. One is not enough. And many times for some godforsaken reason I hardly get anyone online to help! 


There's another aspect of Elden Ring I really don't like, unrelated to difficulty.

It is, by far, the most walkthroughiest game, I have ever played. You NEED a walkthrough for most of this game. After a while I just gave up playing it blind. There's no shame in using one either, especially for games like this. Dark Souls 3 could be like this too, but I used it more for building my character rather than much of the game itself!

NPCs have the most obtuse questlines in the world. They practically DEMAND a guide. How are you supposed to know what to do next, what items to get to progress a questline, without using a guide?! It's ridiculous!!

Pages upon pages, videos upon videos, all just to be able to play this game without losing my mind. And I'm still losing my mind. 


Dark Souls 3 could be like this at times, I remember Irithyll being absolute HELL in regards to difficulty. But in regards to difficulty CURVE, that is the big ass difficulty spike of the game, but a lot of lategame areas tend to generally be more fair relative to the area. The final boss of the game was notably easier than Irithyll's own. And, ♥♥♥♥, Margit the Fell is harder than most Dark Souls 3 bosses, and is the FIRST major story boss! That tells you everything about this game. 

Speaking of which, I have yet to beat the final bosses, (yes there are TWO of them in a row, and if you die at the second one, you have to start from the first one all over again, ♥♥♥♥ THAT.) But I CAN tell you that both of them have twice as much health as the final boss of Dark Souls 3. BOTH. OF. THEM.


It all combines into the most unaccessible, harder than hardcore, not for the faint of heart or the short of temper Souls game, I have ever played. For their first attempt at an open world Souls game, I'd say FromSoft did a pretty good job, but its also meandered with questionable design choices that ultimately lessen what I would've otherwise called the best Souls game! It shows a lot of promise!!....but holy ♥♥♥♥, are the lows some of the lowest I've seen in a game. 

I wouldn't give it a flat out thumbs down because I DO like a lot of this game. I ultimately did have fun most of the way through, and if a video game is fun, that's great! I would give it a more, thumbs sideways, I guess???

I say "not recommended" not in the sense that the game sucks, it doesn't, I know I sound like I think it sucks, but its moreso certain aspects that really get under my skin, enough to make me not recommend it for most people. I would just start out playing either Dark Souls Remastered, or Dark Souls 3, if you want to get into these games. Elden Ring is for the most hardcore ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on the planet, clearly. 

And from what I heard the DLC gets even worse due to certain mechanics, and DLC of Souls games generally being even more brutal than the main game, but that is standard at this point. The late game is brutal enough for me, and honestly I'd say it's too much. I'm not ever getting the DLC.

Also also, WHO CHARGES MONEY FOR CHARACTER CLASSES, ARE WE REAL, PEOPLE?!! CHRIIIIIST!!!


If FromSoft makes another open world in this style, I would like to see FromSoft do a much better job with the difficulty curve, making it a lot smoother and fairer in regards to where you are, and make the NPC questlines easier to follow without a guide. Quest design in a 9th gen game this obtuse is beyond stupid. That is not to say show markers pointing every step of the way, just make it so we don't need a guide. There's a lot FromSoft can do in regards to making a game like this so much more accessible without really "dumbing down" the difficulty. 

At the end of the day, I DID like this game. Unfortunately, I wanted to like it even more. But once I realized how massively flawed this game can be, I don't really think I can. It's far from the masterpiece everyone makes it out to be. But it's still a good game! I just feel like it can be so much better than what it actually is.
