comment:
One of the most disappointing big-budget games I've ever played. The main missions are 90% dialogue and 10% gameplay. Almost every mission consists of traveling to a location, talking to a character, then traveling somewhere else to talk some more. That wouldn't necessarily be a problem if the story stayed engaging after Act 1, but it quickly loses its momentum.

Almost the entire plot revolves around figuring out how to safely remove the biochip that's slowly killing V, yet there's never any real sense of urgency. The story falls into the same repetitive structure for dozens of hours with V doing mercenary favors for a handful of characters, who then promise to give him a lead on removing the chip. You simply follow these breadcrumb trails from one character to the next, with every mission padded by lengthy conversations that have no real meaning. The game constantly pauses to let you choose how to respond, but outside of the ending, very few dialogue choices have any impact and most conversations play out the exact same. For a game that prides itself on player choice, the RPG mechanics are incredibly shallow.

I've played dialogue-heavy games like visual novels and JRPGs, so Cyberpunk simply having a lot of dialogue isn't the issue. The presentation and writing are just so boring and bland that it's difficult to sit through. Every conversation is just you looking at the other character speak in first person, making them all feel the same and drawn out. There are no traditional cutscenes, no cinematic camera angles, and very little physical character animation when talking. The dialogue itself also starts to feel repetitive because almost every character talks the same way. Everyone constantly throws around the same handful of phrases like "preem," "delta," "zero," "choom," and "gonk." The game leans so heavily on its slang that many characters end up sounding interchangeable. A few stand out, but most of the cast feels surprisingly one-dimensional. 

For a game that's so heavily driven by dialogue, the English voice acting is also a letdown. Male V constantly delivers lines in that stereotypical gruff AAA protagonist voice - "gotta find a way to jack in," "maybe there's another way through"... Once you notice it, it becomes hard to ignore. I found Gavin Drea's performance terribly flat, especially considering how much dialogue V has throughout the game. Keanu Reeves doesn't fare much better. His performance often sounds overly restrained, like he's trying to channel John Wick in every scene by speaking in an exaggerated rasp. It's unfortunate that the two voices heard in nearly every conversation are among the weakest performances in the game.

Now, during the 10% of the main missions where you're actually playing a game instead of talking or driving between checkpoints, Cyberpunk is genuinely fun. The gunplay and stealth mechanics are solid, and there's a good variety of weapons and playstyles to experiment with. The stealth gameplay reminded me a lot of the PAYDAY series, with mechanics like marking cameras, distracting enemies, and silently taking guards out one by one. I just wish the game rewarded stealth more often, since carefully clearing an entire area usually takes twice as long as simply shooting everyone for the same outcome. Outside of combat, though, you're mostly walking, waiting for elevators, or searching for power boxes to open doors so you can continue walking.

If you want more gameplay, you're expected to spend time doing side gigs. They're enjoyable at first, but after a handful you've essentially seen everything they have to offer. The same goes for the cyberpsychosis encounters, which amount to fighting dozens of bullet sponge enemies with a large health pool and very little mechanical variety. None of the side content ever becomes particularly challenging or memorable.

Cyberpunk 2077 is an extremely disappointing and repetitive game that loses its appeal shortly after the first act. Its amazing premise and story is buried beneath dozens of hours of repetitive dialogue, terrible voice performances, and excessive padding. comment:
The game became boring for me during Act 3 (the biggest one)—including the stories, the vast majority of the quests, and the combat. Ultimately, there weren't enough good points to save the overall experience.
1) Character development is too diluted in political correctness. You can still choose to go down the evil path, but it brings no real sense of fulfillment. Most of the time, you just suffer penalties, and your choices don't truly impact the world around you. Nothing quite changes; the main story just runs its course. Character arcs are full of improbable, epic secrets, yet they still feel dull and flat. I felt no personal involvement.
2) Combat, on Tactician difficulty, is way harder at the beginning of Act 1—I would even say almost too hard, with archers insta-killing you from miles away. Then you start to mitigate things, and the end of Act 1 and most of Act 2 become enjoyable. Finally, it becomes way too easy in Act 3, with only a few hiccups here and there. It mostly becomes tedious (like enemies maiming your Mage Hand, "stun immunity" that doesn't actually work, or counterspell avalanches). Your powerhouse team breaks everything, and you just have to rest... often.
3) Quests are globally well-written but have no impact on the world. In the end, you just do them for the sake of it, like chores.
It's not the first time I've felt this way about a game that is obviously well-made. Maybe it's just me, and I can't feel the intensity anymore... or is it just gone, erased by today's lack of creativity?

comment:
Rockstar's most refined skinner box. GTA Online has interesting aspects but is ultimately dragged down by greed and spaghetti code. Recent events may come to mind, but the reality is that the writing has been on the wall. Shark cards were always around, servers were peer-to-peer, shareholders had their meetings. It was only a question of "How" Rockstar will try to screw over players, not "If" or even "When". 

As a skinner box, GTA Online acts somewhat like an idle game: Spend time to build up your resources, and use those to get more resources. Higher rank means more weapons and health, higher stats give small but useful benefits, more money lets you buy more content to play as well as more methods to make money. It contrasts from traditional idle games by... being GTA, so to speak.

Of course, the fundamental flaw here is that Rockstar doesn't respect your time. No, it might be better to say that GTA Online is designed to waste as much of your time as possible while you try to make progress. The various businesses players can purchase will take several hours to fill up to capacity, but can easily have all product turned to dust with raids or by encouraging the entire lobby to sabotage sell missions. 

The heists are the best and worst part of Online. The most interesting content by far, self-sabotaged by legacy code, greed, and plain old bad game design. Enemies randomly firing off their entire magazine in one short burst, limited healing that can only be refilled in free roam, challenges that can't be retried from checkpoint, damage reducing payout and said reductions carrying over between checkpoint restarts, and full restarts only being possible by exiting the heist entirely and going back to free roam. 

Not to mention the jury-rigged stealth mechanics that never get fully explained AND have variable rules every time they appear. Some stealth encounters require you to stay pacifist (and don't tell you), and others have guards with a 0 second delay before they alert everyone. Even in the new Kortz Center Heist, the stun gun is silent for the entire heist until you exit the building, where it's so loud that even using a melee takedown will alert guards halfway across the map. 

The two most recent heists, Cayo Perico and the Kortz Center, have severe tonal dissonance. Even ignoring the numbers, they fail to live up to the fantasy of looting of a large island or museum. You can put in the time and effort to do every prep mission, clear every guard and avoid every camera, but in the end each person can only carry a handful of loot. It silently begs the question: Is it really a heist if you leave so much behind?

Rockstar is never going to fix that dissonance, nor do they care to. With the recent patch that came with the Kortz Center Heist, it's clear that Rockstar does not want players to experience GTA Online in any way they please. They want sessions to be weekly, they want players to wait on timers before playing, and they do not want people to experience everything too fast without putting real cash in. 

Considering this is the Legacy version's review, it's worth noting how horribly unstable the netcode is. Infinite loading screens make it nearly impossible to play for half an hour without needing to restart after entering/exiting an interior, moving to a new session, or entering/exiting any mission. Even years ago it wasn't great, but trying to play this recently felt like all the exaggerations you could make about bad netcode coming true.

Even before this patch, I wouldn't recommend getting into GTA Online. It asks for a lot of time and effort from you without giving nearly as much in return. If you really have to play it, find a way to bypass the grind (not with shark cards) and only do whatever catches your eye.

If you're crazy about idle games that hate you but love your wallet, maybe play it. Otherwise, find another game. 

Oh, right. GTA V Story Mode. It's... okay, I guess. The story and characters are nothing to write home about, neither great nor bad enough to say much about. The ending is arbitrarily split into 3 decisions with 2 bad options that no one wants to pick. Felt like there weren't that many missions, maybe partially because the Story Mode DLCs got retooled into some of the Online ones. The gameplay is fine, someone else might find it more appealing but I don't have much to say about it.

GTA V Story Mode is probably worth the price, on sale, but seeing how they've made GTA Online so hostile to its playerbase, Rockstar does not deserve the money.

I am truly convinced this game allows for multiple ways to interact with quests, or skip them, is because one way or another, a part of the quest will certainly break.

Before you even consider dropping 60,- (or whatever your currency is) for this meal filled with broken glass shards, these issues are not exclusive to me, but for countless of consumers who bought this between 2023 and the present. Extremely negative impressions of this game.

First, I completely disagree with this whole skins thing. It's gambling addiction. The game pushes you to spend more and more money. On top of that, you can really feel how many cheaters are in the game.

The interesting part is that I have a top-tier PC and a 480 Hz monitor, which really does give an advantage in the game. I'm from a region where my ping was around 100, and now I play with an average ping of 20. Because of that, I do pretty well in Competitive and in regular matches. I'm just an ordinary working guy who plays in the evenings and on weekends, and sometimes I play well.

But after a year of playing, almost 600 hours, I got hit with a low Trust Factor. I don't act toxic in chat and I don't insult anyone. So the only conclusion I can draw is that it's because of how I play. Yes, a couple of times I had over 40 kills, and quite often over 30. But that's no reason to give me a low Trust Factor.

Now, when I play with friends, we get matched against blatant cheaters and it's impossible to play. There is no clear way to get back to normal matchmaking, and playing with a low Trust Factor is simply impossible. I don't want to ruin the game for my friends. It's just a terrible feeling.

I really don't recommend it.

comment:
Baldur's Gate 3, while decent, is extremely overhyped and underwhelming.
Having played both Baldur's Gate 1 and 2 to death, and loving every moment of it, I was severely disappointed in how they handled its nominal successor.

Where BG1 and BG2 gave a long, intricate, story-rich adventures that felt like they spanned a full country's worth of areas, BG3 offers three and a half areas (the Underdark area of part 1) with a small bit of story, and a few sidequests here and there. 

It also comes with its fair share of annoyances, such as:
-Not being able to pause, ever, citing "you don't need to!" as their reason (it's usually true, but absolutely not 100% so).
-When engaged in conversation with a person or an object, it's *always* the character initiating the conversation (on purpose or by accident) that does the skill check, regardless of how (un)realistic it would be for them to do so (here they could have learned a ton from the creators of the Pathfinder games)
-Time only being counted through long rests makes the game less immersive
-Inventory handling is a mess
-Being able to teleport items to your camp is unimmersive
-Being able to teleport to and from your camp at will (outside combat) is unimmersive
-Movement in combat is buggier than it should be
-Several instances of mechanics or effects are mentioned and never explained, leaving it as an exercise to the reader to attempt to work out what they do (i.e. google it, and hope to avoid spoilers in the process - they show up in the dumbest places)
-Only four party members at a time leaves less room for party dynamics and "on-the-fly" story
-Almost all party members are highly good-aligned, leaving you with almost no choices if you want an evil-aligned campaign with members that have a story

In sum:
BG3 is far smaller, shorter and less engaging than the originals, and only does one thing better than them: Graphics and voice acting, which seems to be where they put 70% of their time and effort, despite this being a *roleplaying game*. If you like RPGs, play all the other good ones before you bother with this one (on sale).

I feel like I cannot recommend this game based solely on how many hours it takes to finish. Act 3 became a slog for me, and I really had to push myself to get through it.

Note to Larian: guys, you really need to start finishing your games.

- Every map is on a cliff (literally), just like in DoS2. I would prefer some open maps and, overall, a world/map design closer to BG1/BG2.
- Every map gives me sensory overload—Act 2, for example. I really like detailed textures, but everything eventually blends into a kind of visual mush that’s hard to navigate.
- Act 3 feels unfinished, and even nearly three years after release, it’s still riddled with bugs. Companion quests end abruptly, and the overall ending left a bad taste.
- Somehow, I can’t recall much of the writing. It’s not bad, it’s not great, but it’s nowhere near BG1/BG2.
- Ultimately, this doesn’t feel like BG3, but more like DoS3. [spoiler]Balduran is a mind flayer... how dare you?!! Also, his betrayal at the end was… strange/funny. What in the nine hells happened with Viconia? Jaheira is way too animated, and Minsc isn’t such an “idiot.” And much more—the sense of adventure just isn’t there. I feel like this game really missed the spirit of the original series.[/spoiler]

comment:
Definitely very overrated game. Dialogs are cheesy and characters are cringe. They have zero development and you don't care about them. They're trying to look and sound cool by swearing and acting "badass". It's just comical. Reminds me of those cheap action blockbuster movies from 90's where characters are badass, swearing, smoking and killing everyone. It's just dumb.

Another thing I didn't like is amount of talking. There is so much talking... If I wanted to watch and listen, I would watch a movie and if I want to play the game, it means I want to be in action and play the game, not to watch those cringy cutscenes & listening to those dumb dialogs all the time. I'd say amount of talking is 50/50 in this game. Basically, half of the time you will be watching & listening to those cringy dialogs rather than playing.

Another problem with it is the world. It's so empty, shallow and soulless. You can hit "talk" button on any NPC, but NPC just says a completely generic line like "Watch it, chico" or "Get lost" and walks away and the entire simulation shatters. They don't have schedules, they don't have routines, and they don't have lives. They are just mindless, moving cardboard cutouts designed entirely to fill up the background of your monitor so the city looks packed in trailers.

You are walking through an environment that looks 100% real, but behaves like an old 2004 video game. You can look at a street vendor cooking food, but you can't buy it. You can see a pool table or an arcade cabinet, but you can't interact with it. It is essentially a giant, gorgeous theme park where you are allowed to look at the pretty lights, but you can't touch anything.

In short, this game is overrated crap.

comment:
Baldur’s Gate 3 - Overwhelmingly Tedious and Boring

I genuinely tried. Seven hours in, multiple sessions. Somewhere around the middle I had a tiny moment of “okay, maybe I’m starting to see it”- that lasted about five minutes.
This is one of the most boring games I have ever played.

BG3 feels like taking every slow, fiddly, overcomplicated part of tabletop RPGs and turning it into a video game - then making every single action take three business days. An Indian drama...

The introduction is atrocious. You are dumped into a wall of classes, races, abilities, resources, dice rolls, actions, bonus actions, movement, spell slots, concentration, inventory, companions and unexplained mechanics with barely any useful explanation. Character creation somehow manages to be both absurdly detailed in places and bizarrely restrictive in others. I spent more time fighting the character creator than creating a character. I eventually made a Wood Half-Elf Ranger because “stealth sniper -> get spotted -> RAAAAAGH” is basically my natural playstyle, but the game certainly didn't make understanding my choices easy.

Then there is the actual gameplay.

Combat is an RNG simulator where my greatest enemy is apparently the number 1.
Miss. Miss. Miss. Critical Miss. Miss. Miss.

Congratulations, you have successfully spent several minutes positioning your character so that a dice roll can tell you to go f*** yourself.

And the damage progression? Incredible.
Hour 1: 1–9 damage
Hour 7: 4-11 damage
Absolutely revolutionary.

The combat is painfully slow. Every movement point matters, every action takes ages, enemies take their turns one by one, animations drag on... Pathfinding is janky and a single misclick can send your character climbing some invisible wall or walking somewhere you absolutely did not intend. I have played games with clunky controls before, but BG3 somehow makes most games' control schemes look like divine intervention.

Exploration isn't any better. You click on a ladder: “You can't go there.”
Click again: suddenly you can. Click beside a doorway: your character attempts to scale the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Himalayas. Try to scout around a corner: congratulations, you've been teleported into combat.
I repeatedly felt like I was fighting the interface rather than the enemies.


The world itself has not grabbed me either. I explored the Grove, picked up a pile of vaguely described errands that they call quests, fought some goblins, got annihilated by an owlbear, got blown up by a statue, stumbled into fights I wasn't prepared for. Spent half my time rummaging through containers for mediocre garbage. The game constantly tries to give the impression that there is supposed to be something fascinating around the next corner, only for the reward to be another conversation, box of junk or fight.

The loot is particularly underwhelming. Forget about finding cool gear and becoming noticeably stronger. 
You get another item with slightly different numbers, same ugly piece of armor, pile of useless arrows and another 20 minute inventory-management session.

And yes, I understand that the game is about player choice and role-playing rather than conventional power progression. That doesn't make the gameplay engaging.

The story, after seven hours, is essentially: YOU HAVE A PARASITE. FIX THE PARASITE.

FIX THE PARASITE.
FIX THE PARASITE.

I KNOW. I HAVE BEEN TOLD. PLEASE STOP BEING A BROKEN RECORD.

The characters haven't done anything for me either. The voice acting is generally good but great performances cannot make characters interesting if I don't care about what they're saying.
Shadowheart is probably the closest I've gotten to actually liking a companion. Still not enough.
Astarion is entertaining to listen to but insufferable.
Lae'zel is an aggressive noseless ♥♥♥♥♥, any line coming out of her makes me physically cringe and want to put my hands on somebody (the writer or smth...).
Gale is a parasitic f*** who has 3 moves, then becomes utterly useless until you go rest.
And the whole party has so far felt more like a collection of personalities I am managing than people I actually want to travel with.

The romance system also feels hilariously prominent for a game that otherwise tries to take itself so seriously.
Apparently everyone is horny enough to jump you after approximately three conversations. Fantastic.
I'm sure this has nothing to do with the soulless gooners that actually LARP sh** like this.

The music is underwhelming at best. It's competent but repetitive and generic compared with games whose soundtracks actually stick in my head.
I ended up wanting to turn it off, replace it with actual good OSTs, like The Witcher's or Lies of P's...

And then there's the technical side.

The graphics look MEDIOCRE for a 2023 game, yet the performance is absurd.
My PC gets hotter running this heap of trash than Cyberpunk 2077 on max settings with Ray Tracing.
It's artificially big and visually inconsistent. Manages to make my hardware work overtime while I stare at two people standing in a room talking about a spermatozoid...

The funniest part is that I can understand why people like the freedom. BG3 clearly allows variying approaches to situations. That's the only place I can really see effort put in.
But for me, that is not enough. I need the actual GAMEPLAY to be fun.
Not "options to potentially make gameplay exist are vast"... Empty theatre room.


This feels less like an adventure and more like administrative work with dice. Pick up item. Miss item. Open door. Miss door. Walk somewhere. Accidentally climb something. Sort inventory. Equip slightly better trousers. Start combat. Miss. Miss. Critical Miss. Watch six enemies spend an eternity deciding whether to move three meters. Finally get a turn. Use an ability. Miss. Get one-shot. Rest. Repeat.

I have games sitting in my library that give me more entertainment in six hours than BG3 has given me in seven. The Darkness II's entire amazing campaign is shorter than the amount of time I have spent trying to convince myself this game is going to click.

Maybe it gets better.
Maybe Act 2 is secretly the second coming of gaming
Maybe Act 3 gets you a horned girlfriend IRL

I genuinely do not care enough to find out.

Clearly I'm not the target audience. But after seven hours of giving it a completely fair chance, I don't see a masterpiece hiding underneath the geriatric systems. “Overwhelmingly Positive” is absolute insanity.

Pretentous CRPG buried under a mountain of slow combat, RNG, inventory management, awkward controls, weak progression, tedious traversal and endless dialogue.

I didn't ragequit because the game is difficult - it's just tedious.
I rage-quit because I was bored out of my mind, realizing I'm wasting my precious and finite time doing the paperwork/homework equivalent of a "video game".

And when a game makes me look at my backlog and think, “I could be playing literally anything else right now,” that's the end of the road.

I'd rather chew the 40 euro I gave for this game, that might be more fun too.

3.5/10

comment:
The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered: A Technical Mess
I was really looking forward to playing The Witcher, but unfortunately, the current technical state has made the experience extremely frustrating.

The game suffers from serious performance and visual problems. I'm experiencing a lot of lag, along with constant visual glitches that make the game feel poorly optimized.

The lighting is especially problematic. Puddles on the ground can appear completely black, textures constantly flicker, and Geralt's skin tone changes depending on the lighting. At one point, I removed his armor and ended up with a white body and a black face. Geralt's hair can also become almost neon white under certain lighting conditions.

There are visual bugs everywhere: clipping issues, black pixelated spots appearing across the landscape, flickering ground textures, broken lighting, and objects that are either far too bright or strangely dark. Frame generation seems to make things even worse, introducing additional shimmering and flickering.

Overall, the lighting system simply doesn't look right, and the combination of performance issues, texture problems, flickering, and rendering bugs makes the game feel unfinished.

The Witcher 3 is an incredible game, which makes the state of this remastered release even more disappointing. Right now, it feels like a pathetically unoptimized mess rather than a polished remaster.

I sincerely hope the developers address these issues, because in its current state, the technical problems seriously hurt the experience.

comment:
This game is half of what it could be. The combat is good but plain as most encounters are simply a point and click adventure even on very hard with boss enemies being nothing more than bullet sponges often without unique moves, the story is uncompelling and a bit boring as it lacks depth and especially flow, most of the game can be boiled down to: have hope of fixing the problem, the hope fails. This is then repeated thought the game, on the same problem as absolutely nothing changes about the story. 

Graphically the game is very technically good, and clearly a large amount of effort has been put in here and it leads to some very mixed results with some scenes such as narrow alleys filled with rubbish and homeless really emphasising the cyberpunk aesthetic, where as other scenes such as underneath overpasses really fall down feeling empty, like its just come out of a map editor, there's no litter blowing in the wind, no water dripping from above, no weeds growing out of the ground no dirt from peoples shoes, no discarded cigarettes, just completely soleless, npc's are part of the problem too with foot paths that are 4 meters wide only having 1 meter used as a npc walk area with an incredibly dense crowd, its like watching a line of ants cross a desert. homeless NPCs that are in the non squaller areas just look silly as they sit in perfectly clean clothes with no possessions, no sleeping bag, no cardboard box to sit on and no begging sign, a 5 year old could do a better job of creating a cyberpunk homeless person.

While the game started out with a bad launch it dose seem to have tided its self up in the bugs and crashes department on first sight, but as you play you will start notice the jank and bugs that have been left in the game, even after all these years of patches, police can for example, crash into cars, which will cause other police to shoot  at them (not intended) but when they get out of the car to engage the other police they will stop because the other police are friendly, then get back in their car and crash and the same thing will happen over and over again. not to mention one boss which got stuck on a bin bag or the final boss which just stopped moving half way through the fight. Then there are the crashes, crashes in an unmodded game should be incredibly rare, in cyberpunk 2077 their not, I have more crashes in my time playing this game without mods than in my heavily modded Fallout 4 that I have spent more time playing.

The voice acting is atrocious with the exception of Keanu Reeves parts which are generally well done if not quite annoying. The rest of it just so painful to listen to especially the main character.

The game is not unplayable but when you take the amazing ttrpg that the games based on and you take the masterclass in video game and rpg design and execution that is the Witcher 3, well it's like combining green and orange and expecting to get some wonderful new joyful colour and instead you get 'prison wall grey'. If you want to play cyberpunk, play the TTRPG instead and if you want to play an actually good RPG on steam, play the Witcher 3. Bethesda could have done a better job of this game and that's saying something.

comment:
If you've never played a Dark Souls, Demon's Souls, or even Bloodborne, starting here is okay. I recommend this game to anyone who has never played a FromSoftware game before. But if you've already played their previous games AND you're hoping to encounter something new, sadly, this is not the case.

The game literally recycles animations, items, attacks, enemies, and mechanics from its past games. Same animations, same attacks, same items, all with subtle reworks to item images and slightly different animations, but underneath, it's the same. I played the previous FromSoftware games and liked them, but I can't ignore that this feels like the same game.

In fact, this game could be called Dark Souls 4, and I'd be okay with it, because that's what it is: Dark Souls with mods.

Btw, I know Demon's Souls came first, but the same lineage is there: Demon's Souls, Bloodborne, Dark Souls, and now Elden Ring. The only game that really escaped this pattern is Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, which actually changed things.

If you look at FromSoftware's games over time, you can see a pattern. They take what they already did, adjust it, and try to perfect the formula, but they don't create enough new things. Look at Armored Core and Frame Gride, for example. It's the same idea, trying to perfect the formula, and then they continue with Armored Core and Another Century's Episode.

I don't care if they reuse elements from past games, but do you know who does this too? Activision with Call of Duty.

And look, Elden Ring is fun, but there are a lot of things that feel like Bandai Namco the publisher, not the developer put its hands on parts of the game. I remember playing Code Vein, the typical Souls like that tries to be unique but ends up feeling like, "Hey, look, I'm Dark Souls too." It was disappointing, with its vague story and some parts like The Depths: Tower of Trials, where the enemy damage made no sense.

Elden Ring also starts with static images instead of the kind of cinematics that gave context at the beginning of Dark Souls, Sekiro, or Bloodborne. I remember thinking, "Wow, wait a second." There are things in Elden Ring that feel like they were just written into the script because yes.

The Fire Giant is a good example. You're close to the end of the game, there is no cinematic and barely any context, and when you reach him, the fight doesn't feel special. Remember Dark Souls III and Yhorm the Giant? If you did Siegward of Catarina's quest, he appeared there, and suddenly the fight had more context and feeling. It felt like you had to finish something.

In Elden Ring, the Fire Giant feels like a boss placed there just to fill an empty, soulless scenario.

The game also has too many bosses. You enter a cave, explore for a while, suddenly a health bar appears, "epic" music starts, and you fight another boss. Then you do it again. Because it happens so often, bosses stop feeling special.

Even the main bosses were a disappointing experience for me. There is so much recycling. Look at Margit, the Fell Omen. I saw that guy like three times, or maybe it was Morgott, the Omen King, because they all look the same. Down in Leyndell, Royal Capital, there is also an illusion that is basically a copy of Margit or Morgott. Even Godrick the Grafted didn't feel that unique to me.

Radahn was also disappointing. Only in the DLC do you really see his power. I understand that the version we fight in the base game is weakened, but still, we're fighting this legendary warrior while he's riding a skinny, scrawny horse.

Malenia, however, actually felt special. She was fun. And the final Marika/Radagon encounter was cool because it felt like the game was telling me, "I'm the Elden Ring." Not me saying it the boss itself felt like it was saying that.

Godfrey was also disappointing. I expected a real version of the Elden Lord, something like when you fight Gwyn or even the Soul of Cinder. Not because I wanted a harder fight, but because of the feeling you get when you fight them for the first time. Godfrey didn't give me that feeling. He felt weak.

And then there is co-op. I bought this game expecting to play with friends, but if you want to play with friends, forget it or at least, that's how it felt to me. You get invaded constantly, and it becomes annoying when you're just trying to explore.

In past games, invasions had a purpose. You could farm items for the covenant you joined and get special rewards, like Darkmoon Blade from the Blade of the Darkmoon. In Elden Ring, that doesn't exist in the same way. Invading other players often feels like PvP for no reason.

And you already have THREE different arenas for PvP. Some people prefer invading because they enjoy it, and that's fine, but from my experience, getting invaded while trying to explore with friends made no sense.

So don't expect to easily play through the whole game with friends. I ended up playing almost the entire game alone, even though I bought it expecting to play with them, and eventually they just left the game because of things like this.

I'm also worried about the direction FromSoftware is taking. This "new DLC" attitude of "it's just $5" makes me worry that in the future the company could become like Activision, Bethesda, or Ubisoft. I really hope that never happens.

And then you see the new FromSoftware game coming to Nintendo Switch another Souls game, or basically Bloodborne with jumps. Do you see the pattern? The direction they're taking? Maybe I'm wrong. I hope I am.

So, who is Elden Ring for?

If you've never played a FromSoftware game: play it. It's fun, huge, challenging, and has an incredible amount of content.

If you've already played their previous games and you want more of the same formula, you'll probably like it.

But if you've played them all and you're hoping to find something genuinely new, think about it before buying. Maybe you won't care that it's the same formula. Maybe you'll love it anyway. But maybe, like me, you'll regret the purchase.

When I watched the trailers and gameplay, I had this feeling in the back of my head saying, "Hey, this is the same game as the past FromSoftware games." And literally, it was.

I wasn't wrong.

comment:
After having played and 100%ed Dark Souls Remastered, instead of going to play Dark Souls 2, I chose to buy Elden Ring at full price while waiting for a discount that never came during this Summer Sale. Regardless, I bought it, played it, and 100%ed it.

At first, the game was amazing. Big map, lots of weapons, and so many things to explore. I wanted to put in as many hours as possible. Up until the end of the early game, I was having a great time. But eventually, the game started feeling very repetitive, and it only became good again at the very end, when I was already bored and underwhelmed.

One of my biggest issues is how often content gets reused. The same bosses appear multiple times under different names, many enemies feel copied from previous Dark Souls games, and the dungeons quickly start blending together. As time went on, it became more and more evident to me that the developers created a huge map without always knowing how to fill it in a meaningful way. At times, I genuinely felt like I was fighting the same boss for the fourth time in a different location.

That isn't to say the world doesn't have great areas. Limgrave is amazing, Caelid is memorable, and several of the endgame locations are excellent. But areas like the Mountaintops of the Giants, Altus Plateau, and much of the underground felt tedious to explore. Also, because the world is so diverse, it doesn't give you one specific vibe. One moment you are in a dark cave and the next in a flower field, it doesn't feel like the world is corrupted and dying, unlike Dark Souls.

The same applies to the bosses. Some are absolutely fantastic. Malenia, Godrick, and the Elden Beast are obvious highlights. The problem is that they're surrounded by so many repeated encounters that they lose some of their impact. The standout bosses are great, but they're buried beneath a mountain of recycled content.

To be fair, the world is packed with locations and things to discover. The map rarely feels empty. My issue is that much of that content follows the same formula: enter a dungeon, loot a corpse, get ambushed by a group of enemies, fight a familiar boss, and move on. After dozens of hours, it became very tedious.

Another problem I had was the difficulty balance. Groups of small enemies were more dangerous than the actual bosses most of the time. Most bosses that were supposed to be major challenges got destroyed within seconds by my max-level Mimic Tear and Bloodhound's Fang. What's funny is that I wasn't even trying to make an overpowered build. A friend simply told me Bloodhound's Fang was a great beginner weapon, and I liked the concept of the Mimic Tear. Apparently that was enough to beat Malenia, supposedly the hardest boss in the game, on my first try, as well as a lot of other bosses. The only challenges I had were Starscourge Radahn, Valiant Gargoyles, Elden Beast and Dragonlord Placidusax.

I never wanted to avoid using the Mimic Tear because it's part of the game. The developers put it there. But that's exactly why I think Spirit Ashes hurt the balance. It feels like they were added to make sure bad players could finish the game without quitting, but in the process they ruined many boss encounters.

Also, fall damage was my true nemesis. I probably died to it at least ten times more than I died to actual enemies, and I'm not exaggerating. It's not funny, it's just annoying.

Beyond gameplay, I think Elden Ring exposes some of FromSoftware's outdated design philosophies. Back in 2011, when the PS3 era was at its peak, those design choices felt innovative because the games achieved so much within relatively small worlds. The map of Dark Souls 1 remains my favorite map in any video game. Not because it's massive or packed with content, but because it's so cleverly interconnected and thoughtfully designed.

The storytelling is another area where I think Dark Souls 1 handled things better, the characters too. I still miss Siegmeyer and Solaire... And you would always come across them because there was only one or two ways to go. Here the NPCs (if you manage to locate them), feel passive-aggressive towards you, and they are not even memorable (bar Alexander). 

DS1's lore complemented the atmosphere and world design, while in Elden Ring it often feels like important story details are hidden inside item descriptions simply for the sake of being hidden. The story itself is actually very interesting, but I had to Google large parts of it to understand what was happening.

Personally, I think the game would have benefited from clearer storytelling: more cutscenes, more meaningful dialogue, more explanations, and NPCs who play a larger role throughout the adventure. I wish they wouldn't just spawn outside the boss gate to help you, but actually followed you or something, or made an actual epic entrance. It feels so outdated and 2010-coded. The storytelling actually got even worse for me with all the similarities between names... Godfrey, Godrick, Godwyn and other examples, some of which are fought more than once under different aliases or forms. This is not lore or worldbuilding, it just makes the player discombobulated, like reading a Dostoyevsky novel.

Furthermore, all questlines and even major bosses feel intentionally hidden to the point where a guide becomes absolutely necessary. To me, that doesn't feel rewarding but pretentious. And yes, I absolutely hate Ubisoft games and dislike Bethesda's too, but this is the other far end of the spectrum, which is almost as bad...

That's what frustrates me most about Elden Ring. Beneath all of my criticisms, it is a game I kinda enjoyed. The gameplay is excellent, many locations are memorable, and several bosses are very well designed too. The story is also surprisingly good once you actually understand it.

But despite all of that, I don't understand why so many people call it the greatest game ever made. It's a good game, but I don't think it deserves that level of praise. If the world had been smaller and more tightly designed, if the storytelling had been more direct, and if the enemy variety had been more original, I honestly think the game would have been far better than what we got.

And yeah I didn't even mention the poor performance, locked 60fps with no DLSS, bad camera, and subpar hitboxes.

comment:
Act 1 Druid and Goblin camps are bad areas, If i had not played the areas after I would have deleted the game in the first 4 hours. High miss chances so the fight drags on for no reason. Gameplay rules are poorly telegraphed and explained compared to other CRPGs that I played. Inventory is poorly designed and for some reason trade inventory with merchants has better sorting with tabs,  some special and quest related items are not highlighted as special or items of interest (Frost staff parts, parts needed for forging of special items, quest item in act 2 that removes debuffs related to the area).The game does not inform you that some quests are time sensitive or have time triggers.

The Underdark and Mountain Pass are much better gameplay-wise and the difficulty of the encounters is better paced. Some encounters give you a 'Surprised' debuff even when you ambush the enemy.

Act 2 Gameplay and Story are much better. The area feels like the Asylum from Divinity 2.

Act 3 The game is still good, has some quests that seem like they were cut short or not fully implemented into the game, higher amounts of diversity, has more characters from the previous games.

Sarevok and Viconia are badly implemented; there is no reason why they are even in the game, badly character assassinated. Sarevok feels like he got mind-wiped by the man in black, Viconia could have been replaced by another new character and it would have made no difference. It would have been better if these two characters had only items related to them implemented.

Jaheira had an okay implementation, some parts of the voice acting sounded phoned in. For example, in the first two games she shouts a battle cry “For the Fallen!” and in Baldur's Gate 3 she says it deadpan without emotion as if the voice actor wasn't coached on how to voice it.

With Minsc, they focused on the comedic part of his character. I found his character to be the best implemented. The only problem was his class; he lost his berserk ability and his stats were heavily based on Dex compared to the games before where he was a more STR-based character.

Ending:

The final sections leading to the end boss drag on eternally. There are too many enemies; it feels like they are coming endlessly. If you have a weaker PC like mine, it would be best to take a book and read it while waiting for turns to pass. It got so bad that I forced myself to google a workaround for this part. (There is a shortcut or alternatively you can become invisible and run through it while avoiding the enemies). The choices before the fight feel poorly implemented, forcing you into a binary decision where you must change a character if you choose option A or kill another if you choose option B.

In the end boss fight I had the impression that I would be able to call in the allies that you collect beforehand, but was sadly disappointed (You can only call them in the preceding section).

You can cheese the boss fight by running directly to the portal and ignoring the enemies by teleporting or becoming invisible. After you start fighting the boss on normal difficulty you can kill him in 3 turns. I only got 2 characters through the portal.

In conclusion, the game was in and of itself enjoyable but was not near the Hype that everybody was showering over it.

I would rate it 6/10.

comment:
After decades of playing role-playing games, BG3 simply doesn't appeal to me. Larian's approach is more akin to a scavenger hunt than role-playing. Many encounters seem to be built around "you should have known" rather than organic progression, and the game penalizes you for not exploring every square inch of every map. Yes, it's well-made and packed with content, but the experience strongly favors min-maxing, guides, and meta-gaming. You'll love it if you like investigating builds and making the most of every interaction. This isn't the kind of classic role-playing game you want if you want to play your character without constantly checking every wiki page and barrel.

REVISION: After putting in more time, I’m changing this to a "Positive" rating, though with heavy caveats.

While I still find Larian’s "scavenger hunt" style of exploration and "meta-knowledge" encounters frustrating, I can't deny the sheer level of detail and craft here. If you are willing to play the game the way it wants to be played, it is a brilliant experience.

I'm still grappling with the idea that it's a universally acclaimed "masterpiece." The game is a brutal, complex CRPG that frequently punishes you for not consulting a guide or, say, a random barrel. However, it is a high-quality product that rewards a specific playstyle. It's a strong game nonetheless.

REVISION 2: After waiting a while and coming back to it, the same feeling remains: a strong start, but a disappointing follow‑through. Act 1 sets expectations the rest of the game never really meets. The pacing drops, the content quality becomes inconsistent, and many quests start feeling like chores compared to the early high‑stakes encounters. It’s worth a try if you’re curious, but overall I’m still not as happy with it as most people seem to be.

The remaster, while it does make the game look much more impressive than before SOMETIMES, is actually not worth your time. Why only sometimes? Because the remaster also introduces a metric crapton of visual glitches that weren't there before. Flickering textures, overbright lighting, you name it, it's got it.

The new graphic settings menu is also extremely buggy on controller. Some settings not "letting go" of your cursor, randomly popping out of the menu and back into the main menu, ...

Some settings also don't do what they say they do. For instance, changing the preset on DLSS to any other setting does absolutely nothing. Turning DLSS off altogether literally turns EVERYTHING into extremely blocky textures.  DLSS is supposed to decrease your image quality in favor of AI upscaling and some more FPS. Here, you absolutely need to keep it turned on just to keep your game looking like it at least belongs in the 21st century. That is NOT what DLSS is supposed to do.

Aside from that, the game runs smoothly on 1440p and all max settings for me (with DLSS turned on for reasons stated above), but for some reason, I have absolutely MASSIVE input delay (2 to 3 seconds) despite my frame latency being relatively low (< 50 ms at all times). No matter what settings I change, the input delay stays the same. This isn't a frame latency issue, it's a game issue, and it makes the game completely unplayable. So yeah, I couldn't even tell you what updates they made to the actual game mechanics because the absolute fundamentals of the game are already so hopelessly broken to begin with.

tl;dr, as it is now, the remastered version of this game is a massive waste of your money. If you don't already have it, definitely do not buy it until they get their act together and fix this broken mess of a game.

comment:
Nach nun etwa 59 Stunden und dem Gefühl, dass ich nahezu jegliches Interesse daran verloren habe, das Spiel weiterzuspielen, möchte ich meine Eindrücke teilen.


[h1]Mein erster Durchlauf – Balanced[/h1]

Ich bin auf [b]Balanced[/b] gestartet, also mit einem ausgeglichenen Verhältnis zwischen Kampf und Exploration.

Das Spiel führt einen relativ tunnelförmig von Encounter zu Encounter und treibt dabei gleichzeitig die Story voran. Zwar gibt es Abzweigungen und alternative Wege, allerdings vermittelt einem das Spiel sehr schnell, wenn man sich in ein Gebiet begibt, das offenbar „zu schwer“ ist.

Ich bin beispielsweise dazu übergegangen, solche Gebiete zunächst schleichend zu erkunden – nur um erneut vermittelt zu bekommen, dass ich dort offenbar noch nichts zu suchen habe.

Was mich dabei besonders gestört hat: [b]Viele grundlegende Mechaniken werden kaum oder gar nicht erklärt.[/b]

Nach etwa drei Stunden starb meine Gruppe in einem Kampf, den ich im Nachhinein nicht einmal hätte führen müssen. Daraufhin wurde ich wieder an den Strand am Anfang des Spiels gesetzt. Es wurde in all der Zeit einfach nicht gespeichert... >_<


[list]
[*]Wie das Camp funktioniert, musste ich selbst herausfinden.
[*]Dass man regelmäßig Short Rests und Long Rests nutzen sollte, musste ich selbst herausfinden.
[*]Dass man praktisch nach jedem relevanten Schritt speichern sollte, musste ich ebenfalls selbst lernen.
[/list]


Ich habe mich anschließend bei Freunden erkundigt, wie man eigentlich sinnvoll progressen soll, ohne ständig auf Heilung oder Exploits angewiesen zu sein. Wirklich hilfreiche Antworten bekam ich dabei kaum.

Kurz vor Akt 2 kam dann nach einem extrem anstrengenden Kampf gegen die Phase Matriarch Spider der Punkt, an dem ich meinen ersten Charakter endgültig aufgegeben habe. Ich hatte schlicht keine Perspektive mehr für meinen gewählten Schleich-Charakter. Kaum passendes Gear, kaum passende Items und Händler, die für diese Spielweise kaum etwas anbieten.


[h1]Zweiter Durchlauf – Explorer[/h1]

Also neuer Versuch: Zwerg-Barbar auf [b]Explorer[/b].

Und plötzlich ist das komplette Gegenteil der Fall.

Die Kämpfe sind inzwischen so einfach, dass ich teilweise das Gefühl habe, sie auch mit einem einzelnen Charakter gewinnen zu können. Sicherlich helfen mir die inzwischen bekannten Mechaniken, aber auch das Verhalten und die Fähigkeiten der Gegner spielen dabei eine große Rolle.

Mittlerweile bin ich fast durch Akt 2 und habe unter anderem die Githyanki Creche nahezu vollständig ausgelöscht.

Dabei tritt allerdings ein weiterer Punkt auf, der mich mittlerweile massiv nervt:

Mechaniken wie [b]Entwaffnen[/b], die einem Schlichtweg nicht erläutert werden und denen man einfach ausgeliefert ist. Man müsste das Spiel und alle Mechaniken, jeden Schritt kennen, also das Spiel studieren um darauf reagieren zu können. Bedeutet, jeder weitere Kampf, wird ähnlich ablaufen und entweder ich Informiere mich, nutze buggy Interactions oder lade Kämpfe zich dutzende male neu um sie zu überwinden. 

Meine Charaktere werden gefühlt in jedem Kampf ständig entwaffnet. Gleichzeitig kann ich meine Waffen teilweise nicht einmal unmittelbar wieder ausrüsten, geschweige denn aufheben... 

Das Problem ist weniger, dass es diese Mechanik gibt, sondern dass das Spiel einem praktisch nicht erklärt, [b]wie man damit umgehen oder sich davor schützen soll.[/b]

Im Internet findet man dann Hinweise, dass mehr Stärke die Wahrscheinlichkeit reduzieren soll. Drei meiner Charaktere haben bereits 18 Stärke – und soweit ich zu diesem Zeitpunkt weiß, liegt das Maximum bei 20. Viel mehr kann ich also ohnehin nicht dagegen unternehmen.

Und wieder stehe ich vor dem gleichen Problem: Ich muss auf eine Mechanik reagieren, von der mir das Spiel praktisch nichts erklärt.

Und die Belohnungen sind einfach nicht existent. Etwas zu überwinden das extrems schwierig war, droppt in der Regel nichts was auch dementsprechend "WoW" oder "Geil" auslösen würde.  Solche Items sind hinter weirden Interaktionen versteckt. 


[h1]Das eigentliche Problem[/h1]

Und genau hier liegt für mich das grundlegende Problem mit BG3:

[b]Ich verstehe nicht, wo der Spaß entstehen soll, wenn man das Spiel nicht vorher ausgiebig recherchiert.[/b]

Jede Entscheidung fühlt sich potentiell wie ein Fehler an. Man speichert ständig, lädt Kämpfe neu, weil man zu viele Ressourcen verbraucht hat, verliert möglicherweise wichtige Items und erfährt teilweise erst Stunden später, dass man etwas hätte anders machen müssen.

Informiert man sich vorher im Internet, stellt man wiederum fest, dass man bereits vor 10 Stunden Entscheidungen getroffen oder Items verpasst hat, die man jetzt gerne gehabt hätte.

Also lädt man einen alten Spielstand.

Das erzeugt bei mir keinen Entdeckerdrang, sondern eher das Gefühl, das Spiel ständig gegen sich selbst absichern zu müssen.

Natürlich gibt es unglaublich viele Möglichkeiten und Entscheidungen. Aber wenn die Konsequenz daraus ist, dass ich nach jeder größeren Entscheidung überlegen muss, ob ich gerade möglicherweise einen wichtigen Inhalt für die nächsten 10 Stunden zerstört habe, dann nimmt mir das einen großen Teil des Spielspaßes.

Auch die Charaktere tragen für mich bisher nur begrenzt dazu bei. Man kann natürlich seine Begleiter meucheln und auf viele Dinge völlig anders reagieren – aber das bringt mir wenig, wenn ich anschließend nichts davon habe außer Nachteile. 

[b]Karlach ist für mich bisher die einzige Figur, die ich wirklich sympathisch finde.[/b]

Und nur wegen ihrer Geschichte möchte ich mir die restlichen ~100 Stunden ehrlich gesagt nicht antun.


[h1]Fazit[/h1]

BG3 bietet offensichtlich enorme Freiheit, unzählige Möglichkeiten und sehr viel Content.

Für mich fühlt sich diese Freiheit allerdings nicht wie Freiheit an, sondern wie eine Ansammlung potentieller Fehlentscheidungen, deren Konsequenzen ich ohne vorherige Recherche kaum einschätzen kann.

Nach rund 59 Stunden habe ich deshalb schlicht das Interesse verloren, weiterzuspielen.

[b]Für mich persönlich mehr Frust als Spielspaß.[/b]

Maybe in einer Gruppe anders...

comment:
[h1]Probably the biggest letdown of a game.[/h1]

I have to preface this and say that this is my first soulslike experience. Elden ring videos and players promise hard gameplay, great story, and cinematic experience. In reality? It's [b]unmeasurable disappointment[/b] on several fronts.

My first issue is that this game was supposed to be made for controllers. You'd think with controllers your movement would be optimized with omnidirectional movement, variable speed, etc. No. No it is not. Too simple of concepts for these simple devs. In order to sprint in this game you have to hold the same button you dodge with (B as I'm on Xbox controller). So if you were to do something as simple as dodge while running, you have to hold the direction and quickly release and tap your dodge button again. This is already awkard of a movement and you'd think it'd be fixed in early builds of the game. Nada. On top of this awkward movement, your dodge actually only starts once the dodge button is released. This wonderfully stupid idea of a mechanic makes reactive playstyles (what'd you'd expect to play as a game centered around boss fights) useless. The amount of time it takes for you to actually do what you inputed is elongated by dumb design. This leads to another problem later on. [i]I'm just gonna forego the horrible auto-lock and let other players tell you about that dumpster fire.[/i]

My second issue is FPS being locked. 60hz is stone age. People have to spend $60 to get this game (crazy ik). When you can get a 60+fps monitor for $80. Let's think here, are your customers going to say "God I hope this cinematic game is locked at 60fps". Seriously unless you're a foot in the grave you can see the slop that is 60 fps. Did you buy a actual monitor? Something beyond 60fps? Yikes you're going to see some stuttering if your hz isn't divisible by 60 f*cking fps or has freesync. Now in the defense of this game, I understand that the game is based around the 60fps for engine reasons and for console players. Yet, WHY is it 60 fps when ported to PC. I'm writing this review 4 years later and there is still no support for higher framerates. Dollar per frame game.

My third issue, difficulty. This game isn't "hard", it's tedious. I started playing this game in hopes of dodging bosses last second, paying attention to a flurry of attacks as they came out, and getting bested because I lacked the mechanical skill to beat a boss. Reality? This game has THE MOST BORING BOSS FIGHTS. Let me explain. Every boss has movepools.  Which when learned make the boss easier, but Elden Ring makes it BORING. However, the fun should lie in going against new bosses right? Maybe getting lucky and beating them first try? Well unless it's one of the billion copy print dungeons with bosses that might as well be 2D for the lack of depth to them, you're going to die (probably in those dungeons too). You'll be hit with a move you can't properly dodge because well you've never seen it before.Or even worse, you have yet the timing is slightly different, with extensions of range or attack(s). Some people may not have a problem with this whole "see a new move, die and come back pattern". And to those people I say, "Keep flipping those burgers." The allure in bossfighting games is making yourself a betterplayer. One able to become better in any situation as you progress. Not dying 2-3, 4 times before you get the boss to a next phase where you'll have to repeat the same steps. This loop? It's not skillful dodges, parrying, or anything cool like that. It's just dying, learning, and coming back. That is profoundly boring. If all your bosses can just simply be put into a youtube video devolving strategies to counter every situation, you didn't make a skillfull game, you made a knowledge gap. [u]Seriously the bosses might as well be a quizlet looking at each boss's attacks like flashcards and memorizing.[/u]

And you'd know I'd take it all back if the story was redeeming. Stories can carry bad gameplay after all. But truth be told you won't really even learn the story in this game. You have to go OUT of your way to find what this game is about. Other RPGs I've played such as Fallout 4, Cyberpunk 2077, Pokémon, all find ways to sprinkle in story if you just go a little bit off the game's main course. This game? You pretty much need a guide to get a inkling of it at all. You will have many questions when the game starts and as it progresses, you'll just have more and more. It's hard to find motivation to do quests with characters you know nothing about. This game doesn't motivate you to do anything, you pop in the world, you look around a bit, and you're confused. I understand that it is a game for adults, so make the story a bit complex. However at the start of the game, you as a protagonist get the sole goal of becoming the Elden Lord from a good cutscene. Now it may just be me, but [u]why does it sound like we're setting up a tv show?[/u] Could it be that it just said a bunch of characters nobody knows, gave the tiniest amount of backstory that you don't really understand, and had a vague direction? Maybe...maybe. But surely this is a good story. It will tell you a bit more as you start the game... Yeah no, this game has bad storytelling. Not necessarily a bad story I hear if you have thousands of hours to waste reading every item, replaying for minute things you missed because the game [b] Doesn't Have Story Direction [/b]. My advice F-Soft, narrow the guage just a little bit more so people can know why they should give a crap. Then the whole discover the lore thing works. 

But hey, if all that sounds appealing to you, go ahead and pay your $60 for 60fps. Have fun wasting your time memorizing an interactive textbook everyone else has already read, memorized, condensed, and posted the results of online.

Edit 1: I've since beat Elden Ring and it was unfulfilling. I have yet to play the DLC (got a gamekey bundle for cheap). At this point in time everything still stands. Play modded if you can. But unless you're an achievement hunter like me, better steer clear, there's some enjoyable moments in this game, but the bad camera control, crappy controls, and 60fps still make this game hard to enjoy. It's sad that unpaid modders make the fixes that paid devs couldn't. That said, if you have a fit girl you know, go there. Don't buy.

comment:
C-bug 1997

since when people have started to give high ratings, highly positive reviews to the broken games? since when and how they became so blind and ignorant?

despite all the false marketing they did back then of this game for being the video game version of the original Cyberpunk rpg boardgame which is released in 1988, i've delayed to play this game for 5 to 6 years, thinking they would eventually fix it...
but what is the end result? the game is still broken and full of bugs.
graphic shaders are burning in the middle of the night city, down on the road. in-game npc characters, enemies and sometimes other half-main characters starts to act weird and even get stuck somewhere.
i've lost the count how many times i had to quick save and reload those saves in order to get the game's command scripts work. because otherwise once the game decides to break itself, it won't simply let you interact with the things or the characters that you need for completing the missions. as if it's a quick save/reload simulator.

𝐍𝐈𝐆𝐇𝐓 𝐂𝐈𝐓𝐘 𝐌𝐀𝐏 - O̶P̶E̶N̶ ̶W̶O̶R̶L̶D̶
this is not even a massive game with extremely large map. the map is very small and the locations which you can have access to is very limited. this alone quickly eliminates any excuses for this game being broken and bug infested even after the 6 years.
apart from the Badlands and some other specific story-related locations, the every part of the city feels all the same as if all the structures and the roads are being copy pasted to everywhere only with slightly applied changes through the indistinguishable editing.

comment:
i'm conflicted on whether i just barely recommend this game or just barely advise against it. i might change my overall rating, but for now, i can't recommend it, particularly when i've had so many people tout it as the greatest game ever made.

i'll start with the things i enjoy; 

a great story with meaningful decision making.

excellent voice acting and casting. 

a wide variety of playstyles.

beautiful graphics. 

proper atmos support that scales with a home theater very well, plus a generally decent audio mix (for a video game).

and now the things i don't like; 

poor balance with difficulty scaling where enemies just get insane amounts of health while you start dying in a couple hits and don't get enough resources like ammo or upgrade materials to keep up. elden ring is a prime example of how all games should balance difficulty. make it as hard as you want, but do not use difficulty sliders. know your audience and balance accordingly. breath of the wild and tears of the kingdom are great examples of the opposite end of the difficulty spectrum, making the game very approachable to beginners and children while still being challenging. difficulty sliders are simultaneously one of the laziest forms of game design and a nightmare to program. no one wants them; just properly balance your game. this has been long proven with time, going back to some of the earliest games like mario bros, which single-digit children could beat, or a grown adult could rage at. that is perfect game balance. a difficulty slider requires devs to finely tune like 5 versions of their game instead of 1, and almost no one puts in the time to do this because it sucks and costs a ton of money. i will never comprehend how so many video games still get this wrong today.

the combat is fairly uninteresting as well. while i enjoy the talent trees, item varieties, upgrade materials and general out-of-combat RPG elements, the combat itself is pretty shallow. not that bad, just boring and not much room for skill growth. 

poor optimization as you get into higher framerates 100fps+. changing even the heaviest settings barely changes your framerate. the difference between medium-high 4k and ultra 4k + ray tracing is like 30fps average. though if you are just aiming for 60fps this game is optimized surprisingly well given the scale of the world and how good most things look.

third party CDPR launcher every time you start the game, paired with nags to log into your CDPR account for a single-player game. blegh. 

way too much unskippable crap every time you launch the game. like two minutes between game launching and gameplay, and only about 5 of those seconds are spent actually loading into the world.

the UI and general UX when using a controller is bad. so many elements just force you to use the joystick cursor, such as the horrid menus that won't properly scroll through your items, settings etc with the d-pad. the joystick mouse SUCKS. just build proper controller support. this isn't a competitive shooter where MKB matters enough to warrant neglecting controllers this much. 

the quest tracking is frustrating and inconsistent. sometimes i'll be on a main quest, then someone will call me and start another main quest, and that will override my current quest tracking. if you're not paying attention to the quest marker moving, it can have you trek like 15 minutes across the map for a completely different quest. other times the exact same scenario will happen and it WON'T override my quest tracking even though i'm only doing main quests in both scenarios. i haven't been able to figure it out but the inconsistency drives me nuts. it shouldn't be touching my quest tracker at all until i complete my current quest chain or otherwise clear my currently tracked quest. 

while i love the decision making style of storytelling, the logic behind some of it borders on nonsensical. SPOILERS, but i played blind and i wanted to get a good johnny ending, and as i am about to invade Arasaka tower, he warns me that he doesn't want me helping Corpos, which makes sense. the other option is to kill yourself, of which he also disapproves, so naturally i went with invading Arasaka tower so i could kill Adam Smasher which i figured would matter more to him, and also because killing yourself is a pretty lame ending, but nah he just brutalizes you for selling out to the Corpos, never mentions a word about you killing Adam Smasher and basically says you're dead to him. i spent the entire story trying to veer things towards a good ending with Johnny but one vague decision killed that entire plotline and gave me the bad ending. i wouldn't have minded it much if it was obvious which one he preferred, but he literally objected to both and told me earlier in the game to promise that i'd kill Adam Smasher. it was such a lame way to end my favorite aspect of the story.

and speaking of the ending, i can't tell you how much i despise rollback endings. there is nothing more insulting than beating a game then just reverting to your save from two hours ago and wiping all your loot from the final zone. Zelda games do that as well and it never stops pissing me off, but at least they have the decency to only roll you back from the final boss instead of a giant quest involving tons of loot. just implement new game+ so you can have a persistent world, and if players make mistakes on a playthrough and miss items or endings they can just run it back with NG+. rollback endings are just a lazy way to avoid having to implement a changing world, which admittedly is a ton of work, but again let's look to Elden Ring for an example of how tremendously well this works if you spend the time to flesh it out.

honestly i could say more, good and bad, but i will conclude by saying that this game certainly has a lot to enjoy, i just don't care for much of this games design philosophy.

comment:
For a game that has as much positive press and reviews as this one has, the experience just fell completely flat for my taste...

Sure the game is a technical marvel (after all of its patches) with an expansive map and a bunch of activities to do, but the story was just flat out ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and did not entice me to "Become a Night City Legend" or even stay to explore the city, build up my character, etc... I was unable to be immersed by the game at all, and while some of the supporting characters were somewhat likeable, most of them are just annoying. 

Additionally, the mid/bad voice acting, the clunky mechanics for combat, driving, movement, etc just were not at all what I was expecting based on reviews of this game from others and clips online. Around the halfway point of my playthrough I just decided to take out any non-mandatory tech/cyberware upgrades I had done to myself, although I kept the skill tree upgrades. I was so upset by how disappointed I was at this game, that I didn't even want to try and build up my character to be a cybernetic slayer after a certain point, and just played as a near baseline human V.

I really did come in with an open mind, and wanted to like the game. I also had a bias that I thought I would really love it since I love open world games. But other than looking pretty visually and having a huge map, the campaign and storyline were just so intolerable for me, that for the main game I just picked the quickest ending (which has a very fitting name by the way) and also for Phantom Liberty I technically got to the quickest ending possible just out of spite (if you know, you know)

Overall, the game was breathtakingly BAD for something with this much hype behind it. Genuinely, my favorite mission and the only satisfying one to me was meeting Hanako at Embers...

comment:
Overall it's recommended, but it isn't recommended because these developers need to learn a lesson, that they refuse to learn. It truly has the worst camera you can imagine in gaming. Fromsoftware just thinks it's the best thing ever, and it's never going to change. It's angle is such that you cannot accurately judge how far your weapon is going to hit, or how far the enemy is away from you. It's not high enough to see forward past your character, and it isn't zoomed out enough to keep track of what is going on. It also isn't reliable for actually locking on to the enemy. Sometimes they'll be in view, but you cannot lock onto the enemy, because some invisible hitbox is making them untrackable. You'll hit the camera lock key, and then the camera faces whichever direction your character is facing, which could very well be the opposite direction from the enemy. Add to this the enemy becoming aware of your presence, and you'll be getting attacked with no knowledge of the attack incoming.

The circling of enemies is a place where the camera should be zoomed back, so the camera isn't as disorienting, especially when the enemies are mobile and jumping around. I honestly feel like what makes this game difficult at all, is because of the camera.

In addition to this, multiple enemies are extraordinarily difficult to take on, because the camera locks on to one, and all your weapon strikes go in that direction. You have to keep changing the lock on to deal with enemies as they come at you, but naturally with such a close camera, you really can't keep track of what's going on. The difficulty should be in facing multiple opponents, but the camera plays the biggest opponent of all.

Then there are hitboxes that lock you in place. So many objects, and obstacles to make sure you can't move freely. Some terrain is easy to go over, and some just stops you in place. However you can always move freely when a large drop is nearby. It's like they designed this stuff to be artificially difficult. You get trapped in these hitboxes, and combined with the awful camera, you have no escape available. It feels awful and terribly designed. Maybe you wouldn't fall off cliffs as often during combat if the camera zoomed out more, but they refuse to do this.

Enemies have tracking attacks that you cannot get away from. You must dodge at the exact perfect moment, or you have zero chance. Enemies chain together attacks where if you dodge one, you get hit by the second strike before you can dodge again. They also have defenses, so if you ever attack the guy, before he attacks you and opens themselves up, they can counter your attack, and return with a follow up strike that you cannot dodge out of. This is a pain when opening up the enemy requires dealing with numerous tracking strikes. You'll have to get dodging down to a tenth of a second accuracy.

Then there are the ambushes that are set up to make sure if you are new at all, you will die a lot. Given the death mechanic of dropping all your money/experience, you'll have to put yourself back in the ambush to get your money back. I feel like a better designer wouldn't need to add cheap ambushes and what are essentially jump scares to add difficulty.

Keyboard and Mouse controls are absolutely awful, and this is yet another developer who doesn't care about accessibility for left handed people. Menu controls are hardbound to wasd. You cannot change it to a left handed orientation. This is also yet another Japanese developer that does not allow you to bind all keys on the keyboard. For some reason the Japanese HATE the keys: , . / ; ' [ ] \ - =  as they simply don't allow them to register. Capcom is the same way.
Left handed people are screwed by developers like this. Autohotkey is not an adequate solution, because keys can be locked in a pressed position, and you have to hit the key again to get it to unpress. Only left handed people get discriminated against in this world, and nothing is done about it. No one cares.

The content, world design, and weapons are the best part of this game. Learning the opponents when it isn't a cheap situation is also fun. The game would be perfect with a better camera.

Fantastic art direction and graphics. Some areas are insanely cool and pretty.
But a large part of the game is the same area with slight variations (Limgrave, Limgrave + water, and Limgrave but yellow).

Great character and monster design. Cool bosses.
But many systems in the game make it insanely easy to volontarily or accidentally completely cheese these bosses. Also ♥♥♥♥ Malenia heal on hit.

Great theorical variety of weapons and builds.
But a lot of weapons are copy pasted, and the overall weapon balance is HORRIBLE. How are BHB and Flails part of the same game. For builds, everything is better on strength, except for casters.

Completlely one of its kind PvP systems. The closest is maybe For Honor, and even then it's quite different and has no invasions.
But again, HORRIBLE balance. They tried to do some things about it, like for example in the 1.10 big rebalance patch where they tried a completely new direction, but at the end of the day the game still has many flaws.

Overall Elden Ring has very very solid fundamentals, but fumbles in the easiest sections like number balance. It's like if someone painted the Mona Lisa but added a dog turd in the corner of the piece. So close to perfection.

The best part of the game is how good the PvP community is. I met tons of awesome people there. Such a shame that the game will never be balanced.

comment:
130 gigabyte game that runs terribly on high-end devices.

The scope of the game is as impressive as it is ambitious; however, the combat system and the way in which the game feels to navigate makes for a grating, miserable experience, no matter how good or bad the decisions are that you make.
Even on the regular difficulty, enemies will constantly use the terrain and their vast understanding of the niche inner workings of combat to put the player(s) in lose-lose situations.
Story moments being locked by default for player characters who are unconscious was another glaring downside.
Why in the world would the level 17 dragon in the grand-scale final battle be less of a problem than the infinite magic missiles being sent out 
God forbid you want to pick any of the non-damaging spells that require any sort of creativity to use; the game punishes you heavily for not min-maxing your build to deal as much damage as possible, no exceptions. It does not help that the enemy always seems to know your next move and will make your time as miserable as possible within what they are capable of doing, having access to an infinite number of spell slots and class actions at their disposal. 

The most damning aspect was that the payoff for it all -- for 280+ hours of gameplay and half a dozen false starts with different groups of friends to get a game together -- is that the ending feels empty. The entire party can just fail checks and miss pretty significant context for the story as a whole.
It feels as if the multiplayer aspect of the game was tacked on at the very end; This Game Was Not Built For Muiltple People To Play It At Once.


It's probably a good game and fun experience if you have no friends.

BG3 was hard to get into and sometimes felt like a chore to complete. But I did complete it.

I enjoyed the customization, though not a fan of displaying sexual organs and body types. Those aspects did not contribute to the experience in a positive way and broke the fantasy setting for me. I have no idea why there is a trend in games and movies to use modern vernacular in fantasy settings, especially in a role-playing game. Use of modern expletives were jarring and broke immersion each time. Unlike other games in the series, this felt like a modern milieu with a D&D skin.

The story was ok and the character progression felt interesting.  Mechanics seemed balanced and there was plenty to explore. I can tell a lot of work went into it. Also, I liked the return of Minsc and enjoyed his character.
