comment:
It had a rough beginning, no doubt about it. However, since then, this game has become an absolute masterpiece. There is no game on this Earth that has ever made me feel what this game has. It is a masterclass example of what exceptional story writing should be. There are no happy endings in Night City, and no game has ever made me, as the main character, feel so powerless. 

When Phantom Liberty was released, I was expecting a simple DLC that added a few extra hours of gameplay, but man was I wrong and I couldn't be happier about that. This DLC alone is better than 99% of the full-fledged games I have played throughout my entire life.

Aside from the story and the writing, the characters are exceptional by themselves, especially Johnny, the other main story characters, the romance options, and honestly, all the character of Phantom Liberty. No matter what you do in this game, whether it be focusing on the main story, doing side quests or gigs, or simply exploring, you will find gems hidden away at every corner of this map.

The combat is phenomenal. It is highly responsive, bloody, and gritty. There are dozens upon dozens of builds you can do, focusing on melee, snipers, blades, netrunning, drugs, spray and pray, stealth, and on and on. There are various types of weapons such as the basic ballistic firearms, but also power firearms that pack a greater punch and can be increased via certain builds, smart weapons whose ammunition locks onto targets and can be more effective with a netrunning build, explosives, burning, poison, blades, dildos (yes, I'm serious, you can beat people to death with dildos), hammers, etc. You can also forgo weapons altogether and focus purely on netrunning hacks which permit you to do various things such as spread viruses, knock enemies out, force them to commit suicide, and so on and so forth.

You could replay this game a dozen times and have a different build each time. How many games offer that much freedom?

Vehicles in this game are also quite beautiful and fun to use. Some of them are a little too slippery on the road for my liking, but those are the minority. There are at least 40 cars from my count that you can either buy or find throughout the world and use, a good chunk of them being original/unique vehicles such as Johnny's Porsche 911 that you can find through a quest.

And lastly, the music? I have to say, without a doubt, the Official Soundtrack of Cyberpunk 2077 is the BEST soundtrack of any game out there, hands down. Samurai? Phantom Liberty (the song)? And atmospheric music like Killing Moon? Absolutely out of this world. Its very rare that I listen to music in videos games outside of said video games, but I see myself coming back to the OST very often.

There is nothing more I can say. Get this game, it is a masterpiece, the greatest game of the last three decades, and I have no doubt it'll remain on that pedestal for me for many years to come.

10/10, without a doubt in my mind. Masterpiece.

comment:
Great game. Not quite on the level of Witcher 3 (the world and characters are just less diverse and interesting) but still well above par compared to most games. I’d highly recommend getting Phantom Liberty as it’s possibly better than the main story. What this game does best is the big missions/heists that feel very cinematic and action-packed. And of course the sheer detail of the environments is insane. Can’t say many of the characters have a great deal of depth, with the exception of Johnny and Reed who are genuinely well written and multi-faceted.

There’s a fairly solid progression system and ability to approach things different ways - unlike most games, many boss battles including the final boss can be beaten in stealth. I did however find that once I’d found the groove of my playstyle and a few key strong weapons it didn’t change up much after that. In an ideal world there’d be some more unique weapons/perks that allow for some goofy or niche playstyles late game, but I can’t complain too much as there is a fair degree of customisation and progression.

At points I did wish they did lean more into the cyberpunk world gameplay-wise e.g. having a drone companion, or a flying car, or something. At points it did feel like GTA with a futurist late-capitalist skin on it.

However overall, I can highly recommend! Looking forward to Projekt Red’s next game.

comment:
Cyberpunk 2077 is still in 2026 a gorgeous game. Night City looks absolutely stunning and on a modern PC you can crank the graphics settings all the way up and still enjoy an incredibly smooth experience. Your GPU may sound like it's preparing for takeoff, but hey, that's a small price to pay for pretty neon lights.

There are plenty of side quests to keep you busy, and some of them are genuinely great. That said, I still found myself wishing there were more. Apparently, I have developed an unhealthy appetite for wandering around Night City doing increasingly ridiculous jobs for complete strangers.

The biggest problem, however, is the main story. It's simply too short. If you focus mostly on the main quests, the game ends before it really feels like you've gotten your money's worth. You spend all this time building your character, exploring Night City and becoming murder machine, only for the main story to basically end too soon.

Thankfully, Cyberpunk 2077 has some solid replay value. You can approach the game with completely different builds, whether you want to be a stealthy hacker, a heavily armed psychopath, a katana-wielding lunatic, or some other combination of questionable life choices. Changing your stats and playstyle can make another playthrough feel surpprisingly different.

Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 is a fantastic-looking and incredibly smooth game with a huge amount of potential content, but I can't help feeling that the main story should have been significantly longer.

8/10 – Would happily return to Night City, preferably after committing several more crimes and spending another 40 hours of doing anything but meeting Hanako at the Embers.

comment:
Elden Ring is probably one of the best games I've played when it comes to challenging gameplay. I have around 80 hours, completed all achievements and played multiple runs, mostly with Bleed/Arcane builds.

I'm a huge fan of difficult games, and Soulslikes are basically made for me. Getting destroyed by a boss, learning what you did wrong and finally beating it feels ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ amazing.

The bosses are easily one of my favorite parts. My personal favorite is Malenia, mainly because she looks amazing and her fight is insanely difficult.

Pre-nerf Radahn, however, was a different story. That mf absolutely destroyed me. Beating him before the nerf is probably my favorite achievement in the game.

This is also why Elden Ring reminds me of Geometry Dash. I've got around 650 hours in GD, and both games have the same basic loop: fail → learn → improve → repeat. In GD, you learn every click and transition, while in Elden Ring you learn every boss attack and when to dodge or attack.

The difference is that Elden Ring gives you more freedom with builds, weapons and strategies, but that feeling of finally beating something that seemed impossible is the same.

If you want to understand the GD comparison better, check out my Geometry Dash review. There's also a really good YouTube video at the end of it that I think is perfect for getting into GD.

The game can be annoying as hell sometimes, but honestly... it's Elden Ring. It's supposed to piss you off. And I actually love that.

I haven't played the DLC yet, but it's definitely on my list.

8/10 –1 controller.

comment:
It started innocently enough—a couple of canceled plans, a few unread text messages, and a growing preference for spending my evenings locked in my room. To anyone on the outside, it just looked like I was going through a phase or slowly falling off the grid.

The real culprit was Elden Ring...

If playing it on a controller is hard, mastering it on a keyboard was pure masochism. Once I stepped into that world, I was hooked. I lost count of the hours spent frantically remapping keys, missing dodges because my fingers slipped off WASD, and throwing myself at brutal bosses for whole nights. Friends called to hang out, but I always had a quick excuse ready. My girlfriend wanted to talk about where we were going, but I brushed her off, too consumed by managing my quick-slots and camera angles to notice how far away I was pushing the real world. Slowly, the invitations stopped, the texts dried up, and my room became completely silent except for the endless, aggressive clicking of my mechanical keyboard.

By the time I finally defeated the final boss—fingers aching, wrists stiff—and watched the end credits roll, the high of victory vanished instantly. I looked around the dead silence of my empty, dark room, hit by a sudden, crushing wave of loneliness. I had conquered the Lands Between on the hardest control scheme possible, but I had completely ruined my life in the process.

Or so I thought.

As I sat there in the quiet, staring at my own reflection in the dark screen, a sudden realization washed over me. I hadn't actually lost a great life. The relationship I had been ignoring was already dead long before the game; we were only staying together out of comfortable habit. The social circle I missed was full of surface-level friends I never really felt connected to, and my daily routine before this had been a soul-crushing, exhausting cycle I hated.

Elden Ring hadn't destroyed my life; it had actually burned away all the noise, obligation, and dead weight I was too afraid to let go of myself. It didn't leave me broken—it gave me a completely clean slate.

I stood up, stretched my tired fingers, walked over to the window, and pushed it open, letting the cold morning air fill the room. I shut down the PC, picked up my phone, and smiled. I was completely alone, but for the very first time in years, I was free to build something real from scratch.

comment:
The original fromsoftware rollslop wasn't released in the US. The Chinese version of Demon's Souls had full English translation and English voice acting and would run on a PS2 in the US.

Elden Ring is the best of Fromsoftware's games in this style. I played it close to release, and came back to it several years later to complete the achievements. It is absolutely a 10/10 game. Whether starting a fresh save or replying in new game+, it is an enjoyable experience. It excels at both gameplay and storytelling. I believe a real testament to this game is the robust amount of online fan content for this game: guides, tutorials, mechanic breakdowns, lore discussion and speculation, mockery. So many people enjoyed this game so much that, after they finished the game, they still wanted to live in this world.

Without explanation, Fromsoftware released a version of Demon's Souls which an American could enjoy while also not making it easy to obtain. That same spirit persisted to Elden Ring where I could enjoy the game once when I first played it, and again years later when I came back to it on a whim.

Hell, when this game came out, it was just a public Beta. Also, the fact that 2.0 and Phantom Liberty are not available on PS4, despite the original release being on PS4, PROVES that that was just the Beta and not a complete version of the game, as the REAL game can't be played on that hardware.

Not to mention the dozens of other lies in their marketing campaigns which are still ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to this day. 

So, to all the corporat ♥♥♥♥♥ in the head offices: I wish you nothing but suffering and I will never, ever, forgive you for your lies and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ practices. Ok. That said, many artists and technical workers put their blood, sweat, and tears into the game, and what exists now, PARTICULARLY with Phantom Liberty, is an excellent piece of art and a fantastic Action-Adventure game. It's a great Cyberpunk (the genre) experience that is incredibly relevant today.

So, to all of the artists and workers: Thank you, and fantastic work! May you find happiness and satisfaction in this dystopian hellscape that we all live in. 

I've put a ton of time into the game, mostly because I love the cyberpunk genre, and also because the game is very replayable. For example, each of the endings reveal different aspects of the story and universe, making it worthwhile to try them all. There's also several different character playstyles that you can try, and the difficulty levels are well designed. Overall, I think it's a very fun game (at this point in time), and thus I do recommend it.

However, some additional criticism: 
My biggest gripes, aside from the corporats, is that the gunplay is poorly designed. I'm not sure if that's because firearm access is too restricted in Poland for the devs to have experience with real firearms, but they did NOT do a good job. Guns are serviceable from a gameplay standpoint, but the design is pretty mediocre to ♥♥♥♥. Case in point: SMGs are MUCH stronger in the game than Assault Rifles, which is just ridiculous. SMGs fire pistol rounds, which are tremendously weaker than rifle rounds. Also, many rifles that should be classified as Precision Rifles and use those perks, are instead made Assault Rifles and use perks that don't help them at all, effectively making them garbage on higher difficulties (which are more fun and immersive, despite being a little more bullet spongey).

I also HATE the design of the gear system and the RNG stores. An Edgerunner SHOULD be extremely particular and deliberate in choosing their gear. Weapon Modification should have been a MUCH larger focus (not just in terms of stats, but looks as well), and gear acquisition should have been based on player choice, not ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gacha-style RNG disposable loot where a weapon is useless in 20 minutes and you're on to the next piece of ♥♥♥♥ gun that sucks and you're just praying for what you actually want, but it never comes, and you can't find it, because RNJesus hates you. So then you default to iconics, which are fine, but again, the player should be crafting/modifying guns into THEIR OWN Iconic weapons. That's what a real edgerunner would do. 

Lastly, the Modding scene is pretty good. So that's nice. 

Final Score: 8/10. But ♥♥♥♥ the corpos.

comment:
This game has been on my wishlist for a long time and honestly one of my biggest regrets is not buying this one earlier. I waited to do this review until after I finished my first campaign and started a second one just to taste the full extend of the game and its replayability and this game is just amazing.

When I first started playing this game I was immediately hooked, everything is just so well done: the graphics, the story, the characters, the environment and even the combat system (as someone who usually doesn't like combat games in general). I completed my first campaign in 80 hours and it was just amazing, a little bit overwhelming at the beginning when you realize the level of freedom you can have but for me this is really something I love in this game.

This game is a masterpiece and I have never seen something quite like it, the amount of content it has is just unreal and even after 100+ hours I haven't explored all the content it can have. This game is also great about the difficulty levels since you can adapt it depending on the kind of campaign you want to make, which I appreciate a lot. 

Going in I knew it was going to be a good game but I wasn't convinced about how I was going to enjoy personally but as you can see in this review I have been enjoying it very much. I can't think of a single negative comment regarding this game, is totally worth the full price even several years later.

comment:
I have hundreds of hours between PS4, PS5, and PC on Witcher 3 - It's one of my favorite games of all time, and in spite of all the bugs and quirks, it still is.  The remaster was not my first rodeo on the path, as I've done multiple playthroughs on Death March, and I still love it.  I'm sorry to hear many users are struggling with performance issues.  Fortunately, my game is stable and the new lighting and aesthetic looks truly phenomenal to me personally, minus taking the Aerondight into a dark cave, put your sunglasses on guys wtf.  

These are some of the problems I've experienced in the remaster, and they've royally triggered my Cyberpunk 1.0 release crisis PTSD big time.

1. Strong punches not landing in fist fights like they used to.  You close the gap and punch air all too often.
2. Switches, broken animations just trying to activate switches.  Geralt's switch animation just struggles to work, and takes an absurd number of tries to finally work.
3. The yellow quest arrows in the minimap are constantly bugging out.  There's one correct yellow arrow to the correct quest objective, but also 5+ other random yellow arrows that appear at random, not always but often.
4. Many caves have invisible walls and character collision problems.
5. Lots of model issues, like heads still making different facial expressions even after they're decapitated and laying on the ground.  I've seen a few body models with the heads appearing in the chest area after they're killed, looks funny but still buggy.
6. I completed the Master Armorer quest and upon turn-in, it unequipped my swords, then raised their item level and level requirement well above my current level at the time.
7. Many new quest dialogue options that should start as yellow are all grey.
8. Several quests literally can't be turned in, the NPC just doesn't acknowledge the attempt to interact and finish.  Used to encounter this a lot after the original release years ago, might be an old issue.
9. Accessibility options are hit and miss, most notably is auto apply blade oils, like wtf this never works even after trying the work around with unequipping/re-equipping my swords, toggling the option on and off.  Resorted to an add-on that fixes the issue, like what the hell man did you guys even test this at all?

I started my remaster with a fresh NG+ and have generally enjoyed the play-through but this remaster feels sloppy as hell and is honestly a reminder of how crappy a hyped up CDPR release can be.  It makes me honestly not even care about the expansion next year because great another layer of buggy crap piled on a game they fail to QA proper and it's just a joke at this point.  Hey it's free... I would gladly have paid a few dollars for a proper (re)release, no question.  Maybe you can pay me for the QA instead.

I still recommend the game and still love Geralt and the world you've built around him.  Top notch swords!  But also shame on you CDPR for putting your game out in this state.

comment: I played GTAV for the first time upon its original release on my PS3, wondering how on Earth that old console was able to process a game like this. And now, as I am writing this review in autumn 2026, GTAVI is coming out next month. Considering that GTAV has sold around 220 million copies by this point, along with all of its re-releases, it has obviously proven itself to be an enormous success in virtually every regard, whether we're talking about critics' reviews or fans' opinions. GTA games have always been a cultural phenomenon and a major force in pushing the boundaries of gameplay, immersion and, especially, vast open worlds. And I think most people would agree that GTAV became the series' highest point in all of these areas. I should note, however, that before GTAIV I personally wasn't a fan of the series for some reason. But GTAIV changed that completely. Its new engine and more realistic approach to almost everything, combined with a serious story and a huge leap in terms of immersion, finally sold me on the series. So, when GTAV was about to be released, I decided to buy a PS3 Super Slim primarily to experience it at launch, as I had previously been a PC gamer. It's crazy to think that this was 13 years ago. So I guess now is the perfect moment to draw some conclusions about GTAV and decide how we will remember this game. Personally, I would say that in many ways this game still holds up remarkably well, despite its dated movement and shooting mechanics, which feel rather clunky by today's standards. But when talking about GTAV, we cannot ignore the elephant in the room: GTA Online. And this is where two completely opposite opinions about GTAV can coexist. There is GTAV's single-player mode: a crime comedy set in a huge and immersive open world that also serves as one of the best portrayals of Los Angeles in a video game, as well as an amazing time capsule of the early 2010s. And then there is GTA Online, a rather controversial multiplayer mode, which was arguably one of the main reasons Rockstar ended up taking 13 years to release GTAVI. Back in 2013, when GTA Online first launched, I genuinely enjoyed it. It felt revolutionary for its time in terms of multiplayer and what could be achieved in an open-world game. But I think many people will agree with me that its monetization eventually ruined a large part of the experience. Not to mention how much Rockstar changed the tone of the game itself through all those updates. A good example would be the heists. The original heists were quite innovative and worked surprisingly well for their time, both in terms of gameplay and immersion. But then Rockstar added the Doomsday Heist, which turned GTA into some kind of absurd spy-drama parody of itself. And, of course, much of the later content was also tied to increasingly aggressive grinding and monetization. To put it simply, today's GTA Online is a bizarre and incredibly grindy experience, filled with flying futuristic cars, flying bikes, Batmobile-like vehicles, and an enormous amount of content locked behind some of the most monotonous grinding imaginable. So, as entertaining and enjoyable as the single-player experience is, the online mode has become almost the complete opposite for me: bloated, bizarre and, ultimately, rather boring. So, this is my final take on GTAV after all these years. And because of me actually playing to get 100% achievement completition, I think it's indeed valid. If you agree with me, feel free to rate this review positively.

comment:
For years, I was vary of FromSoftware's games. Still am, to a degree. My first experience was Sekiro and I found it abysmal.
I'm so glad that I still gave a try to what followed right after (Elden RIng and AC6), because this... is easily one of the most epic experiences I've played through.

[h3]Story - 7.5/10[/h3]
Elden Ring is a legend of a big, ancient world, at its most dire moment of history. With myths of old a plenty, and legendary warriors and beasts and gods to face. Your character is essentially just a nameless chosen one; you don't really get to write the whole story, but you experience the aftermath of one long, long history. And you get to decide how it ends.
From videogame's standpoint, ER's story is built largely the same way as other souls games. You have a vague, major, endgame objective. You have a rough direction of where you're supposed to go next. But since it's an open world, you are more than free (and kind of encouraged to) walk off this path from time to time, and explore.
Exploring not only grants you additional side content - there are several branches of side quests which unlock extra ending options for the main story. Not to mention - explain the lore, giving you some much needed context for everything that happened before, and what's happening now.
Is the main story good? - It's okay. The lore is the strongest point. And the only reason I'm rating it this high is because, for once, FromSoftware bothered with making it more or less comprehensive and at least somewhat directly narrated. Yes, you'll still get a very, very solid chunk of lore and story information from nitpicking, searching for deeper meaning, and reading every description, of every item, and trying to interpret some story behind every little decoration. But even without it, you'll at least understand the main story, core characters, and the motivation of most characters, including your own.

[h3]Gameplay - 8/10[/h3]
Out of all soulslikes... I'd say I only loved Nioh 2 more than that in terms of gameplay. The combat feels impactful, animations having weight, commitment. It's still a tad limited in terms of movesets, especially due to all weapons having only one equippable special attack. But you can dual wield; you can switch between one handed grip and two-handed, unlocking extra moves; you can use some defensive option in your off-hand, or a ranged weapon, or even magic one. Plus you have extra slots for other weapons, if you really want to diversify your gameplay.
The result is still a bit slow and limited, but miles ahead of the Souls series, or Sekiro, with only one weapon and one skill slot for the entire game.
As for other aspects...
Progression is pretty standard for souls games. You level up attributes for flat stat bonuses, you don't have any skill tree, and you gather new weapons, armor and special skills that you can equip on weapons.
Open world, the newest addition to FS games, and the most controversial for many... I'm okay with it. I definitely enjoyed the exploration and the sheer scale. The best part of it is that if you feel stuck on some boss/dungeon - you can always just walk in some other direction.
The only drawbacks for me were, as mentioned, some limitations to the combat in terms of moveset. Also - restrictions to weapons with fixed, unique skills, unable to be buffed by any other element OR change the attribute it scales with. And one more thing - frequent reusing of the same enemies over the course of the game. Not enough to feel completely repetitive, but noticeable.

[h3]Graphics - 9/10[/h3]
By now, it doesn't look as impressive, but it still holds really, really well. At release, it looked incredible. There's not much to add here - characters, enemies, gear, locations, backgrounds - all of it looks amazing. The best part, in my  opinion - this is one of those games that you start, see some landmark far, far away in the background and think to yourself: "I wonder if we'll be able to actually get there? Like, normally, on foot, not through some cutscene that teleports us there." And in most cases in this game, the answer is "yes." The map is enormous, and yet you get to explore almost every inch.

[h3]Sound - 9/10[/h3]
Voice acting and soundtrack were always quite iconic to the souls games, so it's no wonder that Elden Ring also carried it on well.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
9/10. In terms of combat, Nioh 2 remains to be my leader amongst soulslikes so far. But if we're talking overall? - Elden Ring holds the crown proudly.

comment:
Overall, one of my favorite games of all time. 

Source Material: I love the Witcher books and comics, and this game is a very good adaptation that respects the source material. There will be some "uhm-acktually" redditors that will tell you how this game does things differently than the books, but no one likes those people. Compared to the TV show, this is an AMAZING adaptation. There are plenty of references to the source material that attempt to expand on what has been planted. For example, all the different Witcher schools, the progression of the Nilfgard v North Realms war, the development of Ciri as a person. So many interpretations that I feel did the source material great justice.

Story: The main plot is okay, but that is because the real emotion and depth of this game lies in the side missions/quests and exploration. So many of the side quests are extremely interesting, emotional, and fun. Something you learn from this game, that is brought up a lot in the books, is that there is rarely one correct answer. Or in other words, most situations are not black and white. The moral-dilemmas this game puts you through are things I wish I could mimic in my own writing.

Combat: Probably the most contraversial topic for this game. I personally like the combat. Yes, like all RPGs, if you min/max and grind all the side content, you will be over-powered regardless of what difficulty setting you are on. I recommend you try to implement, swords, signs, potions, and bombs equally into your combat style. This is what makes you feel like a true Witcher. Of course if you make a 100% Sign build with maxed out armor and skills, then of course you're gunna mow people down with Signs. Read the beastiary for additional hidden tips for fighting monsters and try them out! 

Finally, I highly encourage you to treat this game like a savory steak that you take at your own pace. Don't just sweep through every region going to all the points of interest. This makes it more of a chore than a game. Take your time and do what interests you.

comment:
[h2]Grand Theft Auto V Steam Review[/h2]
[b]Rating:[/b] 🟢 [b]Recommended[/b]
[hr][/hr]
[h3]The Ultimate Nostalgia Trip, But Make It 60 FPS[/h3]
If you had told me back in 2013, huddled over a humming, overheating PlayStation 3 with the original dualshock clacking away, that I would one day be cruising down the Vinewood Hills at a buttery-smooth 60 frames per second on Steam, I probably would have cried.

Back on the PS3, GTA V was a technical marvel. We all stared in awe at the sun setting over Los Santos, forgiving the occasional texture pop-in, the 30 FPS drops during massive explosions, and the agonizingly long loading screens where you could easily go make a sandwich while Trevor was loading in. It was a masterpiece of its generation.

Fast forward to playing it on Steam, and it feels like meeting an old friend who just got a massive glow-up.

[h3]What’s Better on Steam?[/h3]
[list]
[] [b]Performance & Fidelity:[/b] Going from the console versions of the past to a modern PC setup is night and day. The draw distances, the crisp 1080p/4K resolution, and the fluid frame rates breathe entirely new life into a world I thought I knew by heart.
[] [b]Mods & Customization:[/b] While the vanilla game is fantastic, the PC modding community is the real MVP. Whether it's graphical overhauls, quality-of-life tweaks, or just messing around, it adds endless replay value.
[*] [b]Seamless Convenience:[/b] Having it right in your Steam library alongside your achievements, screenshots, and friends list makes jumping back into Los Santos effortless.
[/list]

[h3]The Verdict[/h3]
Coming back to this game after years away feels weirdly comforting. Sure, the radio ads are permanently burned into my brain, and I can still navigate the map blindfolded, but the charm hasn't faded one bit. Michael, Franklin, and Trevor are just as chaotic and entertaining as they were a decade ago.

If you’re on the fence about double-dipping or jumping over from the old console days, do it. It’s a nostalgic masterpiece that still holds its own, and experiencing it without the hardware limitations of 2013 is the ultimate way to play.

[i]Ah ♥♥♥♥, here we go again.[/i] 🎮🔥

comment:
470 hours, every achievement, Honour Mode included, and I'm still not convinced I've seen everything.

Baldur's Gate 3 is the most reactive game I've ever played. Almost every problem has four solutions, and whatever weird fifth idea you try, the game usually saw it coming. Talk your way out, sneak past, shove them off a ledge, or skip the fight entirely. Your choices stick, and people remember them.

The writing and voice acting carry it. Astarion, Karlach, Shadowheart and Lae'zel are some of the best companions in any RPG, and Dark Urge is worth playing at least once because it's the strongest version of the story. My Durge run was a Lolth-sworn drow necromancer (Death Cleric / Necromancy Wizard / Spores Druid) with a small undead army in tow, and the game rolled with all of it.

Combat is 5e done right. Height, surfaces and positioning all matter, and multiclassing goes deep enough that I was still theorycrafting builds hundreds of hours in. The Patch 8 subclasses only made that worse, in the best way.

Honour Mode is the final exam. One save, no reloads, and bosses with legendary actions that punish lazy play. It forces you to actually learn the systems instead of save-scumming past them, and every dialogue roll gets tense when you can't undo it. Those golden dice were earned.

It's not perfect. Act 3 is massive but can still chug in the Lower City, inventory management is a chore, and a few companion arcs and quest threads wrap up more abruptly than the rest of the game deserves. None of that comes close to outweighing what Larian pulled off.

This is the new bar for RPGs. See you in hour 471.

 Had I known earlier this year about the upcoming remaster I would have waited until embarking on this 3rd playthrough, but here we are. I think the fact that it's a new game plus might be affecting the scaling but I guess I can't change that now. I still love CD Project Red and obvs still recommending the game as it is a bobby dazzler, but can not play the remastered update until this issue is fixed. comment:
[List]
[H1]Foreword[/h1]
[*]Loved Baldur's Gate 1 & 2 (Shadows of Amn & Throne of Bhaal), including Siege of Dragonspear - they are in my list of all-time best and favorite CRPGs.

[*]Never touched tabletop Dungeons & Dragons, but I considered myself an avid RPG-er (western ones). Advanced D&D 2nd edition and 3.5 D&D are some of my favorite systems.

[*]Played in 2-players co-op.

[*]Played on Balanced difficulty as to avoid excessive metagaming that will break roleplay.

[*]Explored every place and did every content (hence the hours) - as long as it didn't contradict roleplay.

[*]No achievements because of some cosmetic mods used and the absolute necessity of using the Item and Spell Bug Fixes mod. The game is almost unplayable without this imo. Imagine building your character with care and with roleplaying in mind to later finding out too late that half the skills, feats, and equipment your character is using don't work as intended.

[*]Held back from playing the game since its launch so that it could be enjoyed post bug-fixes, dlcs, and polish - biding literally 3 years of time thinking it the 'messiah' of CRPGs from the word of mouth and hype surrounding it.

[*]Played with keyboard and mouse.

[H1]The Good[/h1]
[*]The game is very aesthetically pleasing. The best looking CRPG to date. HDR support.

[*]No loading screen, unless you're changing regions.

[*]Co-op up to 4 players.

[*]Character models are excellent (not including custom-created player characters). The dialogue camera captures this beautifully.

[*]Fully voiced but there are odd fews which are not - probably due to time constraints.

[*]Very accessible and beginner friendly to anyone wanting to dip their toes into D&D or just fantasy CRPGs in general.

[*]Throwback to events from BG 1 & 2 with old characters returning. Jaheira and Minsc are brilliant in this and easily are the most interesting characters/ [spoiler]companions[/spoiler] in the game.

[*]Overall great OST, but somehow not as memorable as the classic ones for me.

[*]Massive amount of content you can sink hundreds of hours into. It is not one of those RPGs that end abruptly.

[*]Non-linear path on which you tackle the main quest and side quests, embark on an adventure of your own making.

[*]All the combat animations, spells, and visual effects are flashy and smooth, not janky.

[*]Pet [spoiler]owlbear[/spoiler].

[*]A conclusive ending.

[H1]The Bad[/h1]
[*]Bugs. Not worth all the wait. Just to list a few: Web (level 2 spell) useless, failed saving throw against it will instead free you. Shatter spell no AOE indication. Combat log showing wrong calculation of spell DC, shove DC, damage modifiers, attack rolls. Tooltips not accurate, Evasive Footwork not lasting one turn, Shield Master feat practically useless. There are many others that I can't possibly list the majority of them but the mod I mentioned in the foreword mitigated this problem to a bearable degree.

[*]Ability and skill checks don't detect who you bring into your party. Want to succeed an Arcana check even though you have a wizard just by your side? Tough luck.

[*]The stealth and surprise system made me want to tear my hairs out. Many unexplained intricacies/ bugs that will make a simple stealth attack fail. For example: successfully killing an enemy with stealth attack will result in the remaining enemies not being surprised.

[*]Master volume is too low. I needed to turn to my headphone external controller to crank up the volume.

[*]As per standard of today's game industry, no beautiful faces to choose from for your human female PC. Resolved this by using mods.

[*]Memory leak - constant micro-stutters - if your game session is on the longer side. Also two instances of buggy dialogue scenes that lock you up and require a restart of the game, only happened when the game's running long.

[*]Initial romance routes are too strict. Not choosing the correct 'thirsty' option in that particular time will make you unable to romance that companion for the rest of the game.

[*]Further into the game, there will be feats that are not listed in the enemies' abilities. E.g. darkvision not listed, [spoiler]Cazador cannot be disarmed despite not having Permanently Armed feat[/spoiler].

[*]The voice acting doesn't cover all the info that is given to the player - you need to consult the journal/ trust the journal more than what's being said to get the full picture. E.g. [spoiler]Investigator Valeria pledging the City Watch help for the final battle was never mentioned in dialogue[/spoiler].

[*]Some subclasses are clear dev's favorites. Assassin is lackluster compared to Gloom Stalker and playing Hunter subclass felt like you have a grenade launcher in your hand - its AOE capabilities far exceed a Fighter's.

[*]Many villain expositions. The villains bored me.

[*]Thematically, no subject deeply explored nor a hard question asked. The game is massive and coupled with high production value, but it is generic fantasy. It will not cause any restless night or contemplation.

[*]Camera controls using mouse and keyboard are janky. Oftimes, the environment will mess your camera up and rotating using Q and E has input delay if pressed successively.

[*]The ratio between combat and dialogue skews heavily towards the latter. Felt like the devs are allergic to trash mobs and encounters - even though BG 1 & 2 had those aplenty. It could last up to 30 minutes - felt like an hour - before the next combat encounter.

[*]Balanced difficulty is not it. It rests more on the easier side and even becoming too easy oftimes. The bosses we faced usually can only act one turn before dying, and the final one didn't even have a single turn.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
[*]There are plenty of CRPG goodness here, especially for those not looking to bog themselves in the genre's usual complexities. But if you perhaps are looking for a CRPG that has a well thought-out system, way less bugs in its core mechanics, stays truer to the classics, and most importantly, ask deeply the questions regarding gods, faith, destiny, soul, philosophy, and morality, play Pillars of Eternity 1 instead.

[h1]7.2/10[/h1]
[/list]

comment:
I think The Witcher 3 is the best game ever made. I have been playing it since 2015, and completed it on multiple consoles as well as PC. I have appreciated every patch and improvement to what I perceive as an already perfect game from CD Projekt Red. I was actually in the middle of finishing another playthrough when the Remastered upgrade was announced. I waited until its release, and then finally unlocked all of the achievements in the game. It took some work, but there's no game out there that I enjoy playing more than The Witcher 3.

This isn't a traditional review. I mean, how could it be? The the game has been out since 2015! What I can tell you is that the story is unlike any other. I'm a big fan of the books, but some of the stories in this game are just unforgettable. Take all of the time you can to truly appreciate the secondary missions and contracts. They are my favorite part of the game.

The expansions are incredible. Hearts of Stone has some of the best characters in gaming, and I'd even say all of fiction. I've played through it multiple times, and it's likely my favorite expansion of any game.

I've been invested in The Witcher since the very first game. The Witcher 3 has everything that I could dream of in a video game. An incredible story, visuals that have only become better over time, a developer that truly cares about their work and have invested A LOT into it, and one of the greatest soundtracks in gaming.

If you haven't played this game yet, please play it. The Witcher 3 has had an incredibly positive impact on my life, and I can only hope that it has the same positive impact on you too.

comment:
I haven't played games like this since Icewind Dale, and when BG2 first came out.
First, this is as amazing as everybody says. It's really taking the genre to new levels and it well done.
Modding support is great, and the multi-player is a great option if you have other friends playing.

I forgot how brutal these games are though. You can die in an instant because the enemy has a bomb they throw taking your whole party out on the first turn. Has happened more than once sadly. comment:
There are not many games out there that can make you spend hours upon hours playing without noticing the passing of time. Elden Ring is one of those games. It builds on the legacy of its predecessors, making necessary QoL changes, keeping the good features and trashing the bad ones, while also introducing its own, like the Flask of Wondrous Physick. The abundance of Sites of Grace and your mount, Torrent, make it easy to navigate the vast landscapes of the Lands Between. The world itself is beautifully crafted, made up of various biomes, castles, dungeons, and secret areas.

If you've never played a Souls-like, in my opinion, this is the perfect game to introduce you to the genre. The game has an abundance of bosses, some of which are, yes, copies of regular mobs, but it honestly didn't bother me throughout my playthrough. Learning from firsthand experience is essential to overcoming the challenges, and dying is just part of the process.

To be honest, I got lost in the story and didn't enjoy it as much as I enjoyed killing bosses. Some of the quests are also nearly impossible to progress without a guide, but that is to be expected from a FromSoftware game.

comment:
Okay, I have over 400 hours in Baldur's Gate 3 as of the time of this review... I STILL haven't finished the game. You may have questions about that.  Questions such as, "Why?" and "What exactly have you been doing for 400 hours?"

Well I'll tell you... I HAVE BEEN RESTARTING THE GAME OVER AND OVER AGAIN BECAUSE I KEEP FINDING OUT THAT I'VE MISSED WHOLE ASS PARTY MEMBERS AND SWATHS OF OTHER CONTENT BECAUSE I JUST HAPPENED NOT TO LOOK UNDER EVERY SINGLE ROCK AND EXPLORE EVERY SINGLE CAVE IN THE GAME.

...

But seriously, this game has so much content (and so many variations of choice and consequences built in) that it's literally impossible to see everything or experience all of the branching paths and areas in a single playthrough. Even now, on the dozen or so subsequent playthroughs I've started, I'm constantly finding new things and new options that I just waltzed passed previously, blissfully unaware.

One one hand, this is amazing game design and Larian needs to be commended for making one of the most sprawling RPGs ever created. On the other hand, it will consume your life... I only just made it to the final act and the amount of quests, NPCs, and other things to explore is staggering and a little intimidating.

I'll finish it one day... hopefully. 

TLDR though: 10/10 game, S-Tier, etc. More than worth the price tag and practically in a league of its own.
If you haven't played this game already, put it on your list for sure. It's a gem.

comment:
If you have never played this game, now is certainly the time

As far as story, its one of the best for any game I have played, the cutscenes and dialogue are so rich and wonderful compared to what you get out of most AAA games today, not to say that you should go get every line of dialogue, but you will probably wont get bored of it, some of the quests are called Witcher Contracts, where Geralt is hired to kill a monster, it usually starts with Geralt questioning whoever posted the bounty, then investigating the scene of the monsters attack or lair to determine what kind of monster it is, and then the game will give you an update in the codex explaining what oils, potions, bombs, and signs can be useful to help aid you, and then you get a boss battle with the monster, these are some of the best quests in the game for their immersion, each one feels like a proper detective mystery with their twists and turns

As far as tone and writing its really great, the Witcher loves to be in a morally gray mess, where Geralt is forced to choose between two bad options, this makes for really engaging decision making as a player, as you really want to find the right way out, but it keeps it hard to find

As for gameplay, now it is better than its ever been, I play on death march and love it, its punishing at times, but its not masochistic, this is still a game from 2015, its not at all bug free, but its solid, I have played this game thru the main story 3 times and am going for a 4th before Songs of the Past, I only beat Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine last year, when I finally got the game on PC, gameplay does not get stale after this many hours, it didnt even need any gameplay updates for me to want to play it over again for the next DLC either

I love this game and I think you should play it, now that you get the existing DLC for free, to me its a no brainer, tons of extra content, and they arent even gouging you, its a great deal at full price, its an amazing deal on sale, narratively you will be sucked in and the gameplay is good enough to keep you around

comment:
I originally played The Witcher 3 shortly after release on my Xbox One but that was before the DLC and on a standard 1080p television. I bought the game on steam on sale with the DLC included for free! Few companies are as dedicated to making their product the best they can as CD Projekt Red. The free Remaster update looks stellar on my computer's 4k monitor and it runs smoother than it ever did on my old Xbox One. It's like experiencing this amazing RPG for the first time all over again. 

If you like fantasy games and RPGs then this is the game for you! The world of the Witcher is full of interesting stories and lore; CD Projekt Red brings that world to life here! While I tend to play RPGs where the character is a blank slate, Geralt is a unique established character who can be played in several different ways and feels fitting to the story, I've really grown to love Geralt and RPing as him. 

I expect great things from the upcoming DLC & Witcher 4.

comment:
Awesome game. Still not perfect of course, but runs well on my PC(mid-high end) without any bugs. This whole playthrough's been on a Dualshock 4 controller with gyro aiming. Graphics turned up to max, including path tracing.

At the time of this review, I still haven't finished the story because I've been taking it slow. Contrary to the fast-paced world of Cyberpunk, I'd say Night City and the Badlands are best experienced without rushing it. I've been taking the train, walking, not using the minimap or the on-screen quest marker for immersion's sake. This helped me familiarize myself with the world and appreciate the beautiful, near photo realistic world that the people at CD Projekt put together. It is a truly a beautiful game like no other.

The gameplay is varied, if you let it be. You can of course just be a jack of all trades, but then you're missing out on some the role playing aspect of the game. There's a plethora of guns, blades and some other high tech weapons. Cars are all original. There seems to be a lot of original music in the game which helps with immersion. When it comes to music, the radio stations are all great, with DJs voiced by people like Mike Pondsmith and Sasha Grey. 

All in all, it is realistic, immersive depiction of a cyberpunk future. If you can afford it, I'd say this game is worth the full price. Great game. (Might come back later to add and edit this review.)

comment:
After more than 350 hours in Baldur’s Gate 3, I can confidently say: this game is phenomenal.

What makes it so special is the freedom it gives you. You can talk your way through trouble, sneak past it, fight it head-on, or try something ridiculous and discover that the game actually allows it. Exploring different approaches is part of the fun, and the world’s reactions make your decisions feel meaningful.

The writing and performances deserve enormous praise. Characters have personality, conflicting motivations, and enough depth to make conversations worth paying attention to. Even smaller encounters can turn into memorable stories. There is so much care in the dialogue, environments, and little details that exploration feels rewarding beyond simply finding better equipment.

The combat is another highlight. Positioning, terrain, preparation, and the interaction between abilities give battles plenty of tactical depth. A clever plan can completely change an encounter, while a terrible plan can lead to something hilariously memorable. Experimenting with classes and builds adds another layer of enjoyment—and another reason to start a new character.

The replayability is incredible. Different choices, party compositions, and approaches give you reasons to revisit the adventure. This is a huge game, but its appeal goes beyond its size: it gives you room to make the experience your own.

It does ask for some patience. There are systems to learn, plenty of dialogue, and decisions that can keep you staring at the screen while you consider the possibilities. For me, that is a big part of the appeal. It is a game worth taking your time with.

More than 350 hours is probably the strongest recommendation I can give. Baldur’s Gate 3 combines tactical combat, fantastic storytelling, and an extraordinary amount of player freedom into something truly special.

Highly recommended. Just be careful with “one more quest.” That is rarely where the evening ends.

comment:
The game's resurrection from its first release through Phantom Liberty is well documented. A bug filled failure, victim of greed and crunches. But instead of walking away with their tail firmly between their legs, CDPR took the complaints and criticisms to heart, and began a long-term renovation. By patch 1.61, the game actually was playable and you didn't wait for the inevitable crash. With patch 2.0, they rewrote everything from skill trees to fundamental game play. Phantom Liberty may be the only DLC released for the game, but it's one of the best, period. 

The game is based on Mike Pondsmith's TTRPG, and the influence of that game is all over the DNA of 2077. CDPR made changes to fit a video game better, but the fundamental story of living in a world under corporate oppression, the wealthy beyond the law's reach, and survival meaning sometimes giving up on your dreams, remains. The graphics, five years later, are still a benchmark. The story and the characters will draw you in, and your choices often make more of a difference than you think. 

If you can't tell, I love this game. 1300+ hours (and counting), I still find new things every playthrough.

comment:
Elden Ring is a masterclass in open-world pacing and spatial direction, effectively translating linear Souls-like level design into a sprawling horizontal sandbox without a single traditional quest marker.

The Good:

Horizontal progression: If a boss or area walls you in, the open world lets you walk away, explore elsewhere, and return later overpowered, completely bypassing artificial difficulty spikes.

Environmental cues: Natural landmarks, architecture, and lighting do the heavy lifting of navigation, reducing reliance on conventional map UI.

Systemic flexibility: Spirit ashes, mounted combat, and flexible build paths provide structural options for players of varying skill levels.   
Scribd

The Bad:

Late-game balancing: Endgame scaling sharpens aggressively, narrowing viable playstyles and heavily punishing off-meta builds.

Obtuse quest design: Key triggers and NPC questlines rely on obscure progression paths that practically require external guides.

Verdict:
A landmark achievement in systemic world design, though it inherits and occasionally magnifies FromSoftware's historical friction points.

comment: "I want to live." The Baldur's Gate 3 experience is a masterclass in modern storytelling. The characters and companions have multiple dimensions and uncertain futures, shaped by the player. The world and story oozes with emotional complexity, with some parts of the story truly making the player contemplate their morality and human ethics. The freedom presented in how the player approaches the story and characters is also represented in the excellent combat and character customization, which stay mostly consistent to the end. The paradoxical nature of the companions and story authentically capture the human experience in its rawest form. The desire to love, despite the pain. The urge to act whole, despite being broken. The longing to keep going. "I want to live." If you take away one thing from my review, just play the game man.

comment:
Great game, enjoyed playing it. Even though I've never played games of such genre before, I got used to the core mechanics quite quickly.

The world is immersive and beautiful (although I had some FPS drops in the lower/upper city when many NPCs were wandering around). The music is great. The first look of the Mountain Pass while listening to its soundtrack got me stunned.

Good voice acting and characters are lively, although sometimes they get pretty annoying with their likes and dislikes, but I get it. Some scenes at the end of characters' questlines were emotional, which is cool.

The endgame bossfight was kind of a letdown and very frustrating but I guess that's my problem (skill issue, so to speak).

I guess I will replay it someday. I believe there is more to see, and I wonder how the game will end up if I make different decisions during my playthrough.

🎮 The Witcher 3 Next-Gen: Ultra Path Tracing Guide for Mid-Range Specs (RTX 5060 Ti 16GB / i5-12400)
If you want to experience The Witcher 3 Remastered with full Path Tracing on mid-range hardware without the game turning into a slideshow, this setup balances maximum visual fidelity, smooth performance, and image sharpness.
By leveraging the massive 16GB VRAM pool on this specific GPU and using Reshade to counter upscaling blur, you can get a locked, beautiful 60 FPS experience on a 4K TV.
🖥️ Hardware Setup
• GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti 16GB (Note: The 16GB VRAM is mandatory here. The 8GB version will completely collapse under these path-tracing settings).
• CPU: Intel Core i5-12400
• Display: 4K TV (60Hz / HDR) running at an actual 1440p pixel ratio
⚙️ In-Game Settings
• Graphics Preset: Ultra
• Ray Tracing: ON (Path Tracing Enabled)
• DLSS: Performance Mode
• DLSS Frame Generation: ON
• NVIDIA Reflex: ON + Boost (Highly recommended to mitigate Frame Gen latency)
🎨 Visual Enhancement (The Secret Sauce)
• Reshade: Enabled (Using sharpening filters like CAS or LumaSharpen).
• Why? This completely counteracts the softness introduced by DLSS Performance mode, giving you the crispness of a native resolution without the massive performance hit.
📊 Performance & Metric Results
• Frame Rate: Locked 60 FPS (matching the TV's refresh rate).
• GPU Usage: ~75% Utilization. Because Frame Generation easily pushes the game to the TV's 60Hz limit, the GPU doesn't need to max out at 100%. This keeps the card running cooler and quieter.
• CPU Usage: ~45% to 50% Utilization. The i5-12400 has plenty of breathing room, completely eliminating any processor bottlenecks.
• Input Latency / Feel: Played with an Xbox Controller. While Frame Generation introduces a slight input delay, playing on a controller naturally smooths out camera movements, making the latency completely unnoticeable during actual gameplay.
(If you turn Frame Gen OFF, native performance sits around 45 FPS in most places and dips to 35 FPS in dense, shadowy areas or Novigrad. Using Frame Generation is heavily recommended to smooth out those drops).

comment:
If you are looking for an open world RPG that respects your time while giving you endless reasons to play, this game is a must. The campaign story is incredible, ofcourse, but what truly sets it apart is the massive amount of content packed into the world. You never run out of engaging things to do.

What makes the experience so enjoyable for long sessions is the pacing. You are never forced to grind or get stuck doing tedious filler tasks just to move the main story forward. Every side quest feels like its own actual story with meaningful choices, unique monster contracts, and fascinating lore.

The cutscenes also deserve a special mention. They are cinematic and captivatin, pulling you straight into Geralt's journey. Best of all, the developers hit the sweet spot where it is just the right amount of dialogue and cinematic moments to keep you hooked without ever feeling like the game is taking control away from you for too long.

The upgraded visuals, smooth performance tweaks, and expanded content make exploring the world feel brand new again. Combined with the massive expansion stories like Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine, the sheer volume of high quality content makes this one of the greatest games made this century.

10 out of 10. Worth every single hour so far.

comment:
You! Nerd! You already know you want this game, buy it already!!

For the non-nerds and more hesitant. This game has the ability to rob you of many hours. You will get caught in that familiar trap of "Oh, one more quest and then I'm done" and by the time you've bought that new item you're in Act 2 wondering how the sun is rising.

In all seriousness, this is one of the most immersive D&D settings. For a video game there is a huge level of freedom. The game does its best to warn you of any mechanics you're misusing. There are a plethora of ways to play and you might end up spending more time in Character Creator. That is a large part of the fun too, this is an RPG after all. Your choices will matter, you might not see it right away but talk to a friend who also played and you'll discover how different you approached the battles.

Thank you for reading and I hope you pick this up

comment:
Review:

Baldur,s Gate 3 redefines systemic reactivity in computer role playing games, translating tabletop freedom into a digital space where player choice consistently reshapes narrative and mechanical outcomes.

Strengths:

Improvisational sandbox: The physics engine, surface interactions, and verticality allow creative problem solving that treats spells and environment as interactive tools rather than scripted events.

Reactive narrative branches: Companion arcs and main storylines adapt dynamically to player decisions, maintaining narrative coherence across vastly different playthrough paths.

Cinematic dialogue direction: Full performance capture elevates companion writing, grounding moral dilemmas and interpersonal conflict in genuine emotional stakes.

Weaknesses:

Third act pacing: Act 3 suffers from structural fatigue, dense urban navigation, and a noticeable drop in narrative focus compared to the tight pacing of Act 1.

Encounter balance: Combat scaling flattens in the mid game, where optimized builds easily break action economy limits and trivialize major encounters.

Verdict:
A monumental achievement in systemic role playing design that sets a new benchmark for player agency, tempered by pacing issues in its final act.

comment:
[h1] Absolutely life changing. [/h1]

I've played this game before, but I've been gifted it here on Steam recently. (576h played prior)
Needless to say, this game is top tier. As a fan of Roleplay, RPG, fantasy, vampires, demons and all things whimsical alike, I love this game wholeheartedly. I've heard MANY good reviews about Baldur's Gate III before and I've always wanted to try it myself, just to see what is what. But from watching snippets of gameplay on social media, I feared I might find it excruciatingly difficult to grasp. 

Luckily, the Community is incredibly welcoming, and even though I made many mistakes during my first blind run ever, the amount of tutorials and instructions from fellow helpful gamers are more than enough to fully understand the more difficult bits of the game; especially if you've never dabbled in Dungeons & Dragons before! 

The game's replayability value is insane. Despite having many saves and hours within the game itself (with them being significantly less on my account because of the gift), I keep finding new things that I have not encountered before. I also keep making new characters... Each run is unique in its own way and that's what I love about Baldur's Gate III so much. Not to mention all of the precious characters. 

10/10, 5 stars and even a Michelin star if I may. Yes, the game is expensive, but absolutely worth the price. What a great job, Larian Studios!

comment:
Grand Theft Auto V is one of the best selling games of all time for a reason. You can easily see just how much care went into making this game. Everything in it just clicks.

The world is massive and beautiful, with one major city, a bunch of smaller towns, camps, highways, beaches, dense forests, farms, lakes, rivers, the desert, mysterious mountains, parks and much much more. It's not just one city like in GTA 4. So if you're not a fan of Los Santos, you can find plenty of areas that will suit you. 

Character and vehicle customization make a return at a grand scale with the options to change your haircut, facial hair, add tattoos, even piercing. Clothing tattoos range from cheap street wear to expensive suits and tuxedos. 
Vehicle customization is so much fun by itself - you can add spoilers, bumpers, change entire bodyworsk, add custom paint jobs, change wheel colors. I've easily spent hours just customizing vehicles. Add to that hundreds of hours driving them around.

The combat is also really good, but I would argue not as fun as in GTA IV. You have waaaay more weapons, which can also be customized, but the ragdoll physics are not as impressive anymore.
The story and characters are memorable, but not as impactful, as the tone is lighter and I would describe it as an action-comedy flick. 

Missions are more chaotic and really want to make you replay them over and over again. With the exception of the missions where you have to do yoga or slowly walk around the port doing mundane tasks.

The radio is once again amazing - nothing will top West Coast Classics, Radio Los Santos, Non-Stop-Pop FM, FlyLo FM and Radio Mirror Park.

I still think the forth game has the best story, San Andreas offers the player the most freedom, Vice City has the best vibe, but V, while not perfect, combines all of this aspects together really well. And, well obviously, looks the best.
Give it a shot for the singleplayer alone, don't bother with online.

The amount of content you get for your money is absolutely mind blowing with very well over 150 hours required if you want to properly experience just one playthrough, and that's not accounting for the unbelievable replayability. Even the smallest, seemingly insignificant side quests have story relevance and multiple ways to go about completing them, everything is made with such painstaking attention to detail and a dynamic world in mind. The writing is utterly phenomenal, the characters believable, the voice actors just amazing and all this with people new to the world of D&D taken into consideration. Everything important is explained and shown to you in the world, with smaller tidbits of lore scattered in books around the environment, painting a complete picture of Faerun. And if that wasn't enough, the combat ties a perfect little bow on the whole thing, it's fun, it's challenging but fair, and rewards you thoroughly for using the environment and making smart choices, giving a true tactical sandbox experience. Overall, I have nothing but love for this game and I genuinely can not think of any way to improve it except to make that sequel. Thank you, Larian Studios, for the unforgettable experience!

comment:
Of course I 1000% recommend this to everyone. It was my 5th playthrough, but my 1st time on PC, and I never get bored. You venture into the world of The Witcher, hunting monsters and experiencing brilliant stories—even in the side quests. Now that the remastered version is out, it is more awesome than ever before. There are some minor glitches, but they aren't that important. Gameplay-wise, if you compare it to Souls games or current-gen games, you might not like it. Combat is just swinging a sword and using some basic magic, and that's about it. But I never get bored or tired of this clunky gameplay; instead, I feel so satisfied that I don't even notice time passing. The slow-mo executions and finishers are absolute gems.
Long story short, if you are looking for a Souls-like game and are a combat-focused person, this game is not for you. But if you like venturing into a vast open world, love hunting monsters, and want to immerse yourself in attractive stories and atmospheric sounds—like the wind blowing through the trees, rain, and eerie, chill environmental audio—this will be your game.
And come on, CDPR is the best studio because they always look out for their fans. Support them at all costs! Personally, I've bought this exact same game on every single gaming consoles.

comment:
Recommended | 70 hours

Geralt of Rivia has two swords, one facial expression, and somehow more emotional range than most RPG protagonists with a full dialogue wheel.

Who is it for? Everyone. If you've never played an RPG, this is a good place to start. If you've played fifty, you'll still find something here.

Story and quests. This is where the game earns its reputation. The main story is strong, but the side quests are the real show. A contract to kill some random monster turns into a family tragedy, a village feud, and a moral dilemma where every option feels slightly wrong. Other games give you "collect 10 wolf pelts." The Witcher gives you "collect 10 wolf pelts, discover the wolves were a cursed family, reconsider your life choices."

Worldbuilding. Velen, Novigrad and Skellige feel lived in. Peasants complain, soldiers are bastards, and everyone has a reason to be miserable. It's bleak in a way that's oddly charming.

Graphics and sound. With the next-gen update it still looks great. The soundtrack is excellent, especially in Skellige, where the music does half the storytelling.

Gameplay and combat. Exploration and questing are excellent. Combat is the weak link. It's mostly roll, hit twice, roll again, cast Quen, repeat until the drowner dies or you do. Progression is underwhelming too. Most level-ups give you small percentage boosts that you won't notice, and gear is level-locked enough that you'll carry a legendary sword around for ten hours before you're allowed to use it.

Performance. Ran smoothly for me, no notable issues.

Value. Worth full price, and the DLCs are worth buying too. Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine aren't filler; they're some of the best content in the game. Whatever you think of CD Projekt Red's other launches, they got this one right.

Pros

Outstanding side quests
Strong main story
Rich, believable world
DLCs are excellent value

Cons

Repetitive combat
Flat, unrewarding progression
Gwent will consume more of your time than the actual war

Bottom line: Come for the monster hunting, stay for the side quest about a baron's family that ruins your evening. Ten silver out of ten.

comment:
Many can recall the- to be blunt, frankly abysmal release of this particular game. But, like No Man's Sky, it aged like a fine wine because they got stuck in and fixed it. Horray! Sadly, it's the case that a lot of bigger studios are still releasing things with the day-one players having to pay to bug test something after it's public rather than the other way around BEFORE release.

The tirade aside, after picking it up after some time AFTER that, it's not only good fun, but... Personally compelling. I played, at the time, a Body/Cool build that, at its peak, made it so no problem could not be solved with a five-knuckle-shuffle. I was the Juggernaut, ♥♥♥♥♥.
I believe they changed it so Cool is now stealth centric, but at the time it had skills for chaining kills in combat... I digress.

Story wise, I really liked ingraining myself in everything. Beginning as a random nomad and ending up an untouchable legend... But, the more intriguing thing to me was how it handles the idea of individuality.
Spoilers beyond this point.


Night City is advertised to us as a place where you can be or do anything- and the gameplay can match that with how many different ways you can tackle any given problem, I was just taking the direct solution. Individuality is in surplus, and it manages to instead remain a commodity to the player after the first act... Once you are threatened with losing your very Self. The looming idea you're slowly being overwritten by someone who died, and, depending on your choices, is about to be born again through you. Can run from it, make peace and accept it, or try to get Him out. Both you and 'Silverhand have to come to grips with your shared existence, whether the parties like or not. I appreciated that we were able to become friends or, at the very least, find mutual respect. I think His special Sun ending is one of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥' coolest endings in a game. You and him against the world. Worlds, physical and digital.

comment:
Honestly, I wish I could forget everything about this game and play it again for the first time.

The Witcher 3 is one of those games that stays in your mind even after you finish it. You start playing because you want to kill some monsters and do a few quests, and before you realize it, you're getting attached to the characters, making decisions you actually think about, and spending hours exploring places you didn't even need to visit.

The best part is that even some random side quests feel more interesting than the main story of other games. You never really know what you're getting into. Sometimes you accept a simple contract, and somehow it turns into a story that makes you sit there thinking about it long after it's over.

And the world itself? Absolutely incredible. The music, the atmosphere, the villages, the forests, the people you meet, and even the little details make everything feel alive. You can spend an entire evening just riding around on Roach, exploring question marks on the map, and completely forgetting what you were supposed to be doing.

Geralt is also such a great main character. He's not some perfect hero who always does the right thing. He's just a man trying to get through a complicated world, and sometimes there isn't even a good choice to make. That's what makes the story feel so real.

And don't even get me started on the DLCs. Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine are worth experiencing on their own. Blood and Wine especially feels like a whole new adventure rather than just extra content.

If you've never played this game, do yourself a favor and give it a chance. Don't rush through it, don't just follow the main quests, and take your time with the side stories. That's when you'll understand why people still talk about this game years later.

And if you've already played it and uninstalled it, maybe it's time to come back. There are always quests you missed, choices you want to make differently, and moments you want to experience again.

For me, The Witcher 3 isn't just a game I finished and moved on from. It's one of those experiences that makes other games feel a little less special afterward.

Now excuse me, I need to go check on Ciri. 🐺⚔️

comment:
[h2]Honestly I went in fully expecting to hate this game from all the cult-like hype.[/h2]

I've played DnD here and enjoy turn based games so this sounded like coming home. What makes DnD memorable is the random bits of actions you can do to trip up the dungeon master. I genuinely think Baldur's Gate 3 is the first video game that captures that table top spirit with the amount of stuff you can do.

[b]The turn-based combat is crazy good[/b] where it's not just enemies taking turns trading stat checks, combat is treated like an actual playground where highground matters, lighting matters and environmental hazards matter. All coupled in with movement economy to manage around, surprisingly complex yet surprisingly simple.

The tabletop freedom extends way past combat where spells isn't nerfed for video game balance, speak with dead for example is quite paramount in opening separate narratives rather than useless voiceline fluff. Game lets fail going forwards as in a bad roll doesn't mean game over but forces you to adapt to the gamble you took as you would in actual DnD if the promised nat 20 was not so promised at all in a dire situation.

I initially played this on console a couple of years back but it's quite intoxicating playing it on PC, there's just nothing quite like it. Especially now that there's a huge workshop scene to extend the game further. However I will say it did take multiple sessions to get into it at the beginning. It's crazy slow if you don't know what you're doing, however [i]once the snowball gets rolling it REALLY gets rolling.[/i]

This is a solid recommend from me 10/10 🎲🎲

Honestly, the base game is just the tip of the iceberg. There’s already a ridiculous amount of content, freedom, different choices, builds, characters, and ways to play the game. If you’ve never played it before, I’d say now is the perfect time to start.

comment:
This is unique game to me, it has access to great mobility. And the story is wonderful. Sometingh of Lord of The rings, lands, doomed by the same fault. We have in Ghostbusters, the one with the paining.

In the game's world, Marika and Radagon are described as "two halves" of a single divine being. However, they do not function like an ordinary person with two names; they possessed separate consciousnesses and distinct personalities, and for a long time, they could even physically exist in two different places:

• Queen Marika – the vessel for the Elden Ring, a goddess elevated by a cosmic deity (the Greater Will). Over time, she began to doubt the established world order and rebelled against her creators.

• Radagon – a red-haired, powerful warrior and champion. Unlike Marika, he was blindly loyal to the Golden Order and the Greater Will.

1. Marriage to Rennala: Radagon goes to war and subsequently marries Queen Rennala, with whom he has children (Ranni, Radahn, Rykard). At the same time, Marika rules from the capital and has children with Godfrey (e.g., Godwyn).

2. Radagon’s Return: After Marika exiles Godfrey, she suddenly summons Radagon back. Radagon abandons Rennala, returns to the capital, and... becomes Marika’s second husband and the new Elden Lord. People in the game world were shocked that a "mere champion" had received such an honor—for they were unaware of his true identity.

3. Divine Incest: The union of Marika and Radagon produces twins—Malenia and Miquella. Born of one and the same god, both have been afflicted by powerful curses since birth (Miquella’s eternal childhood and Malenia’s scarlet rot).

• Marika seeks to destroy the system: She takes up the hammer and shatters the Elden Ring, aiming to free the world from the influence of the Greater Will.

• Radagon seeks to save the system: He seizes control of the same body, grasps the same hammer, and attempts to repair the fractured Ring.

George R.R. Martin—this world is beautiful.

Mohg, Lord of Blood, serves the Formless Mother, for her power manifests through blood. When the Formless Mother’s body is wounded or pierced, "Bloodflame" spurts forth—a burning blood that Mohg wields in combat.

As the son of Queen Marika and Lord Godfrey, Mohg (along with his twin, Morgott) was born an Omen—a being covered in horns, deemed cursed by the ruling Golden Order. Consequently, both brothers were taken from their mother, bound in holy shackles, and cast into the sewers beneath the capital—the Subterranean Shunning-Grounds—to be forgotten forever.

The Formless Mother communicates with the world through blood, and the blood of the Omen serves as an exceptionally potent and appealing conduit for her. The goddess sensed the suffering, the pain, and the powerful blood—amassed in the darkness—of the imprisoned demigod.

The Finger-Eater is responsible for rot, while the Frenzied Flame represents chaos.

All Fingers in the Lands Between were born of a being named Metyr, the Mother of Fingers. Metyr was the first star-born entity sent to the world by the Greater Will, serving as a colossal antenna for receiving divine signals. It was she who gave birth to the Two Fingers, so that they might convey instructions to mortals.

Metyr descended upon the Lands Between in prehistoric times—long before the rise of the Erdtree and the birth of Queen Marika. This was the absolute first epoch in the world's history, often referred to as the pre-Elden era.

It came into being the moment Queen Marika attained godhood and ushered in the Era of the Erdtree. Crucially, the Two Fingers were present at the birth of the Erdtree, even though their Mother (Metyr) was already "damaged" and severed from the god by then.

Before the tree became golden, there existed the ancient Crucible of Life—a primal, wild form of matter teeming with life (hence the horns of the Omens or the traits found in ancient beings). In this era, the world was ruled by Dragon Lords (such as Placidusax).

The Crucible was the primal, pure form of the Erdtree. Before the tree grew vast and golden, it existed as a gigantic, wild, and chaotic crucible of energy in which all life in the world was fused and united as one. There was no division into races or species of humans and animals; everything pulsed within a single source of biological evolution.

Because all forms of life were united within the Crucible, beings that drew power from it manifested the traits of various animals simultaneously. It manifested as the sudden growth of:
• Asymmetrical horns
• Scales on the body
• Reptilian tails
• Bird feathers

Let me write more, when I 100% do this title.
