comment:
The moment I stepped foot into Night City, it somehow managed to steal my attention for 6 months straight.

The beautiful, yet depressing dystopian world as well as the memorable characters and great story engaged me enough to not only play through the entire game twice in a row, but also actively made want to play the DLC and chase after all the endings when most other games make me lose my interest after the credits. (Cough, Horizon Zero Dawn)

Some moments in the game genuinely left me speechless due to how eerily close we are to making the exaggerated setting of this game's world into a reality. Social Media algorithms irresponsibly dictating our perception of the world? Vulnerable teenagers who delete their facebook selfies out of shame receive targeted advertisements for beauty products? Mass surveillance laws are disguised as ineffective child protection measures? Ex-Disney stars monetize your grief with AI deepfakes of your dead relatives?

I believe that this game is not just a phenomenal immersive experience, but also an important reminder for us to reflect on the relationship we have with the technology we rely on.

comment:
quests only progressing when you rest at grace is the most stupid sht ever imo. Like in what NORMAL gameplay loop am I going to an off-path rot pool, kill the monster there, find nothing else there, then randomly decide "yeah I'll just go back the for the fun of it even though there was nothing else there", to find the continuation of millicent's questline, then teleporting back to the nearest grace and walking back to that same rot pool 4 times just to continue her questline that happens in that exact same spot and ends in that exact same spot, that otherwise has NO OTHER ORGANIC REASON for me to be anywhere near the rot pool. Teleporting and walking back to the same spot 4 times to get the next dialogue option for events that could have happened in 30 seconds is the most unintuitive and inorganic "exploration"/progression I've ever seen. 

It would make sense if that rot pool was on a path that was 'on the way' to another point of interest, but its not. its literally a tucked away corner of a nothing burger area, that forces you to climb UP a fking ladder 100 times to finish a quest that takes place ALL IN THE SAME SPOT. 

Every NPC questline is genuinely a vaguepost sim that punishes you for exploring every nook and cranny of an area 'too early'. PUNISHED, FOR, EXPLORING?????? It's like the exact opposite of the design philosophy that is otherwise implemented EVERYWHERE ELSE IN THE GAME.

Still, the games a classic but if you don't already own or even if you do I'd suggest waiting about a month or so for them to fix the bugs they've created installing this remaster modlist. Even story and progress gets bugged, made every choice for the best ending which leads up to Witcher 4 but game just decided to give me one of the worst endings and to mock me further T-poses Ciri removing her hair and cloak and levitating it 30 feet away from her in a cutscene. Games a mess at the moment, give it some time before you buy and jump in it.

comment:
Elden Ring is honestly one of the most incredible games I’ve ever played. The world is absolutely beautiful, and I loved how much freedom you have to explore and discover things on your own. Every area feels mysterious and unique, and there were so many moments where I just stopped to look around because everything looked so amazing.

The combat can be really challenging, especially in the beginning, but finally defeating a boss after struggling with it for ages feels so satisfying. I also really enjoyed experimenting with different weapons, builds, and spells.

What I love most is that the game doesn’t constantly tell you what to do. You can just explore, get lost, find something completely unexpected, and somehow end up having an amazing experience.

It can definitely be frustrating at times, but for me, that made the victories feel even more rewarding. Elden Ring is a beautiful, challenging, and unforgettable experience that I would absolutely recommend.

comment:
Very cool game with a lot of really beautiful locations, fun exploration, and challenging combat (this is my first Dark Souls game but I'm told this is to be expected). There are lots of truly-interesting lore concepts that are tied together with a hair-thin thread; I think it's best absorbed as abstract fragments of story rather than trying to piece together a cohesive larger narrative.

I recommend playing with some kind of walkthrough/guide if you care about any particular questlines, items, or endings. The *fun* difficulty comes from the fights. The *less fun* difficulty comes from obscure and hard-to-follow questlines--NPCs will disappear to locations you have no way of knowing and expect you to stumble into them three times in the correct order or whoopsie, you've locked yourself out of a quest you didn't know existed. Sometimes you're expected to rest and come back and talk to the same NPC multiple times to get new dialogue, but nothing indicates that you're supposed to do this. Several times I returned to a location to find that someone I'd completely forgotten about had died offscreen in a way that was theoretically supposed to mean something to me. Overall I really enjoy playing and the questlines are fun to complete, it can just get frustrating trying to follow a particular story and not having any way of knowing what to do next.

comment:
One of my favourite games, and one of those that set new standards for their genre. It might even be one of the best games up there.

The story is amazing, and the game is really complex (in the best way) and engaging. It constantly keeps you experimenting and thinking, and there's almost always more than one way to approach a situation.

The characters are exceptionally well written, with only a few exceptions. The voice acting is amazing, with outstanding performances across the whole cast.

Visually, the game is gorgeous. The art style is amazing and every place feels polished and fitting for the setting. Larian did again an amazing job.

The music ranges from good to very good. My problem is that I played Divinity: Original Sin 2, Larian's previous big game, and Baldur's Gate 3's music is heavily inspired by its soundtrack, which was better overall. I must admit I was a bit disappointed.

Another important thing to add: Larian delivered a fully finished game for the current standard price. Unlike most games nowadays, where studios rush releases and finish the content later (often releasing it as DLCs and charging for it!), Larian gives the the complete experience from the start.

Two small caveats: the game can be a bit overwhelming if you're new to the D&D rules, and a better tutorial on how they work would have helped me. I also would have liked more of a middle path between a "good" and an "evil" run. It feels like you're pushed a bit toward one extreme.

Story: 10/10
Music: 7/10
Characters: 10/10
Voice Acting: 10/10
Graphics and artstyle: 10/10

If turn-based games are your thing and you don't mind investing a bit of time into learning the rules, this game is a must.

comment: A one-of-a-kind game that really captures the chaos of dnd while having a lot of story and character endings. It has a great and simple story. The characters are memorable, each with their own issues and struggles that make them feel human and not just characters in a game. The voice actors did an amazing job, and the music is amazing as well. The game is very replayable not just because of the endings, but because of the dozens of classes and the freedom of combat you get. You can collect 50 barrels of gunpowder and prepare a nuclear explosion right behind the boss, you can use gnomes as weapons, and you can eradicate anything and anyone that crosses your path because why not. The relatively small world this game allows you to explore does not feel small because there is so much going on everywhere you go. You dont get bored of this game because every time you start a new save file you find something new. And on top of all this it is moddable. In my opinion the character customization is a bit lacking. There are a select few face presets and barely any body types. Other than that, its an amazing game.

comment:
Saints Row 3 meets Deus Ex: Human Revolution... with more bewbs and trash (literally) everywhere...

Get it on sale if you are looking for more games to play and enjoy 1st person stuff, it has some good moments. can be a time sink.

Unfortunately the ending was somewhat spoiled for me before I started playing, so that does factor into my experience. Also, I don't have the fanciest tech to play games on, so i do play on lower graphics/quality settings.
Started playing because Keanu Reeves, Continued playing because Panam Palmer. I eventually lost interest in playing the story... Partly because the MC is bland and poorly written compared to the side characters, and partly because for a game with like 10 (supposedly) different endings, the fate of the mc is incredibly underwhelming and basically the exact same thing just with different colors regardless of which ending you work towards. DLC had a chance to address this, but attempts to do so by disregarding anything meaningful about the base games story, choices and side characters that made the game interesting.

The story and writing aren't terrible by any means, just... unsatisfying? The main character honestly felt so irrelevant despite so much of the story revolving around the chip in their head... If I could choose to play as any character, I would have picked  anyone other than V. All the other characters in the story felt more realistic and fully written. Honestly I'm having more fun after making a new character and running around pretending the main story doesn't exist after unlocking stuff.

gameplay is nothing special compared to other games that were released prior to cyberpunk. Most 1st person shooters have smoother mechanics. clambering and vaulting and dodging and whatnot exist in other games and are better implemented in many of them. 

Leveling system was... different. I played most of the game without investing points, then when stuff got tough I put points in and got some cyberware implants and suddenly there wasn't a challenge anymore... (though i didn't play on the hardest difficulty, I didn't enjoy the gameplay enough to make everything more bullet sponge-y)

It is a big open world, and it isn't entirely empty by any means, so there is stuff to do to kill time.

boxing side quest was kind of fun, would have been cool if there were more fights scattered around or something more to that bit.

ALSO a note to any devs that ever make video games: (though doubtful any of them will ever read this...)
-Locked first person in an open world single player game is the worst decision you can make if you aren't fully diving into shooters or horror. Maybe a racing game... but a hybrid like cyberpunk? Open world, stealth, shooting, melee, driving, climbing... Has nobody noticed or stopped to wonder why the modding community has been working so hard on third person mods since BEFORE the game was launched?? It's not just for this game either... Even more frustrating with how bad the 1st person controls are for everything non-story. 

I have played a lot of games on multiple consoles over the last 15 years and I can't think of one 1st person single player story focused game that wasn't horror or a shooter that I or anyone I know played and didn't wish it were 3rd person. (or at least had the option to switch between) (I want to say the Kingdom Come games, but again, they would be so much more fun with optional 3rd person)

comment:
Elden Ring is the rare open-world game that actually earns its size. The map is huge, but almost every corner has something worth finding - a dungeon, a boss, a weapon, or just a view - and the game never holds your hand toward any of it.

Combat is the usual FromSoftware loop of learning attack patterns and not getting greedy, but the open world and spirit ashes make it more flexible than previous Souls games. You can brute-force a fight, come back later, or summon help. The bosses are the highlight: memorable, hard, and usually fair once you stop panic-rolling.

Build variety is excellent. Strength, magic, faith, and hybrid setups all work, and the weapon types keep things interesting past the first 20 hours. Performance is solid on a decent PC, though the occasional stutter still shows up.

It is long, sometimes opaque, and the late-game difficulty spike is real. If you like figuring things out yourself and don’t mind dying a lot, it’s one of the best games of its kind. About 130 hours in and I’m still finding new stuff.

comment:
I would say the main story is the least interesting and most tedious part of this game. Everything else is mostly great. The controls takes a long time getting used too, even when remastered, and they still feel a bit clunky. The bugs in this new remastered version is out of control. There are so many bugs, nothing gamebreaking, but it still gets tiring after encountering a bug every 5-10 minutes.

The side missions are way more interesting than main story. I felt myself getting more invested into side quests than main story. I feel like the main story line is littered with "filler" quests, especially towards the end of the game. Everytime you think you will proceed to a major story event, 1,2,3 filler quests pops up out of nowhere. There is so many potions, decoctions and tools to play with. Only problem is that most of them feel completely useless. You pick ur 1-2 potions and 1-2 decoctions that suits ur build and then never touch anything else in the game. I played on highest difficulty and still had no reason to ever switch.

I give this 8/10. The "new" graphics are insane and definitely the peak aspect of the game.

comment:
Much can be said about art and gaming, or you can just mention this masterpiece and talk about something else. Dark Souls is surely one of my favorite games of all time due to its influences, atmosphere, and highly philosophical themes, which take direct inspiration from several sources, including Berserk.

Nihilism, purpose, and meaning have always been connected. The entire genre is built around struggling and overcoming, no matter what.

As a complete fan of the Souls series, I struggled to start Elden Ring. The promise of hundreds of hours was intimidating compared to years ago. But once I started, that was it, I could not put it down. To everyone who is still thinking about playing it but feels intimidated, just do it.

I have been gaming all my life. I've been to Lordran, Drangleic, Lothric, and Yharnam. But the Lands Between, that place is special, even among the best.

Overall, I went into it with the highest expectations, and the game still completely blew me away.

If I could only take a single game to an island...

Nothing feels better than spending 20 minutes warming up your aim just to get one-tapped by a guy who apparently has a PhD in headshots.

The gunplay is great, the maps are iconic, and the smoke grenades are actually pretty cool. Unfortunately, my teammates seem to have been selected by a random number generator.

You can have an amazing game where you drop 30 kills and feel like the next s1mple.

Then the next game happens.

You bottom-frag, miss every shot, forget how to use grenades, and somehow walk into the enemy AWPer three rounds in a row.

The best part is the teamwork. Nothing brings people together like four strangers screaming at each other because someone didn’t buy a smoke.

And let’s not forget the economy system. One round you’re rich. The next round you’re buying a P250 and praying.

CS2 is stressful, addictive, occasionally infuriating, and somehow I keep coming back.

comment:
One of my all time favorites, no doubt. 

The greatest achievement of this game is the feeling that you're truly living out the story and steering it beyond superficial pathways. There are so many branching pathways and different stories to be discovered within this game that it genuinely makes each play through a new experience (given that you don't do the same things over and over). 

It's also got excellent mods that are easy to download. 

Apart from the player impact on the narrative, the game also populates it's world and narrative with genuinely compelling characters everywhere you look. It's a real joy just to talk with everyone, learn their stories, joke with them, ♥♥♥♥ with them, trick them, lie to them. The possibilities are endless. 

The companions are great. Though not all of them are very interesting to me. Wyll is... boring. And I know this is unpopular but I DESPISE Astarion and don't feel an ounce of sympathy for him. Total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ bastard who does not deserve the love he receives. He's an interesting character, don't get me wrong. But he's like... the Draco Malfoy of this game. A snotty prick who receives far too much love for what a piece of ♥♥♥♥ he is. 

But regardless. The story and the characters are the main attraction here. The gameplay is also very fun and full of interesting variety. I was initially reticent to play a turn based combat game like this (I don't play many of those), but I loved it. I've played DND with my friends before so this was very easy to love for that reason. 

The world is interesting, but I'm no where near as interesting the mythos or legends of the world than I am the personal narratives and personalities that inhabit it. 

What else can be said? It's a masterpiece in choose your own adventure storytelling beyond anything that's ever been made. You get to feel like you're in control of a great fantasy epic. What's not to love?

Baldur's Gate 3 is more than just a brilliant tactical RPG it’s one of the most emotionally rewarding stories about free will and reclaiming agency ever written in gaming.

    Astarion’s Romance: Romancing Astarion is an absolute masterpiece of character writing. Watching his arc evolve from defensive snark to vulnerability, trust, and genuine affection made every moment worth it.
    Shadowheart’s Personal Journey: Saving Shadowheart, guiding her away from Shar, and helping her locate and rescue her parents is one of the most poignant, satisfying companion arcs in RPG history.
    Unmatched Player Choice: The central theme of agency runs through every decision. Watching your companions break free from their abusers, gods, and past trauma because of your bond with them is incredible.

comment:
Title: Never Fade Away...

A lot of time has passed since launch, and only now can I truly say it: this game is a masterpiece. The work CD Projekt Red put into turning this around is fantastic.

The plot tackles real, massive issues reflecting our own world. This isn't just a brief main quest that feels like a small add-on to a massive map—it’s a deeply human story filled with heroes, villains, and losers. It asks what it really takes for a "nobody" to become a legend, and more importantly, what price you pay for that success. This is pure, authentic Cyberpunk. To be honest, I wasn't sure CDPR could pull it off, but the voice acting and performances are fabulous. They brought Night City to life so convincingly that you instantly buy into its ruthless rules and struggles.

Gameplay at launch was okay, but weak. Today? It’s phenomenal. The world is packed with hidden details, easter eggs, and its own urban legends. As for bugs, I rarely ran into anything major—just the occasional floating car or clipping geometry. For where the game stands today, it plays great. It just needs a few tiny polish tweaks, but nothing that ruins the experience.

The map is huge, and the DLC filled in every empty space seamlessly. There are countless small stories to uncover and interesting places to explore. The level design and world-building deserve serious praise.

Summary:
Without spoiling anything: trust me, you won't regret playing this. It’s far from a typical video game story—it’s something much deeper. Accept the rules of Night City, jump in, and experience it. The writing and acting ensure this world never feels like a hollow cardboard set; the city is cruel, and you will feel every bit of it.

Score: 9/10 (Play it, and you’ll understand why).

comment:
TL;DR

An incredible genre defining souls-like experience for returning veterans and new players to the genre like myself. The soundtrack transports you to another world and the beautifully crafted open environments keep the feelings of discovery and wonder riding high past the story's conclusion. All the same can be said about the DLC, sometimes feeling like an entirely new game with its new systems and ideas. This is easily in my top 5, probably even top 3 games of all time. If you haven't played a souls-like game before and are looking for where to start, start here. You won't regret it. It's time to get gud. 

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I finally understand what the hype was all about. I didn't play the game until many years after its release. It was my first souls-like game and while it took me time to learn the mechanics, it was extremely rewarding in every aspect. The build crafting, open world, different endings, combat, soundtrack; the list goes on and on. It might have the best soundtrack I have ever heard in a videogame. It was so good I had to replay it again with a different build after my first playthrough. I heard some complain of lack of story, but this one critique that repeatedly kept me invested. It reminded me of the saying, “show, don't tell” because the game lets you piece many story beats together through your own imagination and experiences with the world. I say this but if you really care enough, there’s plenty of story lines here through character interactions, quests, and bosses. Somehow after completing this game almost a year ago I STILL find videos online of quests, bosses, or weapons I never knew existed in the world. That sense of wonder and fantasy is what makes you want to come back and play even after replaying the game numerous times. Upon writing this, I might just go back and replay the game again. It’s just that good.

comment:
One the best RPG's ever.
I have dumped over 100 hours into this game just in this last playthrough and I regret nothing.

The immersion of the world of Cyberpunk 2077 is the best and greatest aspect of this game. The word of a futuristic dystopia, but not a gray and desolate one - instead a colourful one full of distractions which are there to cover the real rot within. The world works so well that sometimes you just drive around to take the city in.

The second best part is the characters - each of them feel as if they belong in their world and their place, some good, some bad, most both at various times. Many of them memorable and unique. The interactions with those characters are what draws your character into the world and make the stakes feel personal.

And for the third part I will add the wide variety of approaches in this game: You can play stealth, netunning, melee with berserk or grab your biggest gun and go full FPS - all of those options are available and all have their benefits and drawbacks and it is up to you to choose which of those to take.

Whatever had gone down with this game in the past, at this point the game stands as an example of what an RPG should be - a game when you play a role in a world that is foreign to you but is native and understable to its inhabitants - and becomes native to you through those characters and enviroments.

Thanks for the great game, CDPR!

comment:
Fantastic game, 9.5/10. Thanks to it's basis on a long-running pen and paper RPG there is a huge amount of backstory and lore to make the world feel real and interesting. Combine that with well written, realistic and fallable characters and excellent voice acting (maybe Johnny aside, depending on your opinion of Keanu's acting) and it's hard not to get sucked into this game. I've just completed it after 2 months and nearly 140 hours and I still don't feel ready to leave the world yet.

The only negative thing I can say is that the Romantic Hangouts aren't great. I understand why they added them, but I would honestly have preferred not to have them in the game. Sure, it sucks when the questline ends and you no longer get to interact with the character you've built a relationship with, but having them turn into a flat robot that only gives stock responses somehow makes it even worse. [spoiler]It's especially bad if you choose The Star ending after romancing Panam, they actually recycled lines from this ending in the Romantic Hangouts with her. This broke the immersion a bit for me when V and Panam spend their last evening together on the clifftop overlooking the camp.[/spoiler]

That said, definitely worth playing and for me it trumps The Witcher 3 in character design. Some moments will really hit you in the feels.

I will almost certainly play through this again as female V at some point.

comment:
Really enjoying it so far!

I'm still only on Act 1, but I'm having a great time with Baldur's Gate 3 so far. The combat is really fun and engaging, although it feels a little easy at times. I'm hoping the difficulty ramps up as I progress further into the game.

The dialogue is enjoyable, and I like how much freedom you have with your choices, although sometimes there's a lot of dialogue to get through.

I'm playing as a Sorcerer at the moment and having a blast with it. One of my favourite parts so far is being an absolute menace and making some rather questionable decisions when dealing with people. It's great having the freedom to be evil instead of always playing the hero.

I've still got a long way to go, so it's too early to judge the whole game, but so far I'm really enjoying it and looking forward to seeing what the rest of the adventure has in store.

Recommended!

comment: Easily my favorite game of all time as far as story and world building go. It's pretty hard in certain areas but it doesn't seem unfair. (In the base game at least.) You always have the ability to go train and come back stronger. It's the only game I've ever beaten and felt like I had achieved something.  I'm now a 5 time Elden Lord between PC and console, and now that the fall is here again, and there's a chill in the air, I'm going back in. Don't be afraid to look up tips for when you're stuck, or to search for videos that uncover things about the history of the world that you've missed. There are exploits that can make the game easier but still challenging that have purposefully been left in to make the game more accessible for us casuals. Just play it. Even heavy spoilers couldn't take away from the sense of wonder I felt, and still do, at the scale of this world's history and the depth of the characters.

comment:
Counter-Strike 2: A Song of Smoke and Betrayal
Hear ye, hear ye, Lords and Ladies of the Competitive Realm!

Counter-Strike 2 is a battlefield worthy of legends. A game of steel nerves, cunning strategies, and glorious headshots. Here, friendships are forged in fire, rivalries are born in blood, and every round is a tale worthy of the bards. The thrill of clutching a 1v5 is sweeter than victory at the Iron Throne, and the sound of an AWP firing is music to the ears of even the coldest lord of Westeros.

The skins? Oh, what a splendid treasury! From crimson blades worthy of House Lannister to dragon-lore rifles fit for the Targaryens, one may adorn their arsenal in magnificent fashion. For in this realm, it is not merely how you slay your foes, but how gloriously you do so.

The competition is fierce, the stakes are high, and when both teams are evenly matched, the battles are glorious. Every smoke is a scheme, every flash a deception, and every defuse a race against the Stranger himself.

BUT LO, A DARKNESS GATHERS BEYOND THE WALL.

For this realm is plagued by a most vile affliction: the poison of cheaters.

Wallhackers, who see through stone as if blessed by the Three-Eyed Raven. Aimbotters, whose arrows never miss, whose bullets find skulls with the certainty of a prophecy. Suspicious lords who turn corners with knowledge no mortal ought to possess. They roam the servers like White Walkers, corrupting the living and extinguishing the joy of honest warriors.

And what of the honourable player who trains for countless hours, perfects their aim, studies the maps, and fights with all the skill they possess? They are left wondering whether they were bested by a better warrior or struck down by some foul sorcery beyond the laws of the realm.

'Tis a cruel fate, to enter the arena seeking glory, only to discover that the enemy has brought a dragon to a knife fight.

Still, when the stars align, the teams are fair, and the cheaters are banished beyond the Wall, Counter-Strike 2 remains a magnificent contest of skill, teamwork, and nerve.

My verdict, therefore, is this:

A glorious game with the heart of a champion, the soul of a warrior, and the potential to rule the Seven Kingdoms of competitive shooters.

Yet its throne is besmirched by treachery, and its kingdom weakened by those who forsake honour for hollow victories.

Valve, the realm cries out for justice! Sharpen thy anti-cheat, strengthen the Watch, and cast these foul sorcerers into the frozen wastes!

For a kingdom cannot thrive when its honest warriors grow weary of fighting shadows.

Would I recommend it? Aye.

But I would sooner trust a Lannister with my gold than trust every death replay in this cursed realm.

comment:
Ball dur’s gay 3: Being the overseer of a bunch of hormonal young adults is one of my favorite games. It is also the absolute manifestation of the saying “more than the sum of its parts.”

There isn’t a single way in which this game isn’t a mess. It’s a narrative mess, it’s a design mess, and its performance is selectively a mess. (I genuinely don’t know what in the Seven Hells my boy Gor Gor is cooking up in Wyrm’s Rock, but that place ran like a crippled snail.)

But I loved most of it.

I loved playing it and somehow interacting with an even more screwed-up version of D&D 5e’s mechanics, defying everything that is holy in game design, complete with its messy proficiency system and terrible class balance.

I loved the characters, even with the blatant favoritism.

I loved making my build and absolutely obliterating the game, even though most of the items sucked big tarrasque scrotum. It was genuinely funny watching late-game bosses fail to even take a turn before being sent straight to Hell. (I played on the game’s second-hardest difficulty, Tactician.)

The story also has some notable moments of excellence, which I won’t mention here.

Buy it. Play it. It gets a recommendation from me.

Don’t expect a rating.

The world is massive, the storytelling is incredible, and the side quests often feel as meaningful as the main story. The attention to detail and the depth of the characters are truly impressive.

That said, it wasn't completely my type of game. Some parts felt slower than I usually prefer, and I couldn't connect with it as much as I have with other games. Even so, I can fully appreciate the quality and effort that went into creating it.

While it may not be one of my personal favorites, I would still highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys RPGs, rich storytelling, and immersive open worlds. It's a game every gamer should experience at least once.

comment: If the amount of time I've spent in this game isn't enough to show how much I love it - Well, I'll begin with the story.  From the main storyline to the companions, you can tell Larian really poured their hearts into it.  There's so many ways to experience this game from the strong, good aligned path to a much darker, more gruesome one.  And if you opt to play Dark Urge Origin, it delves even deeper into some pretty crazy stuff.  But I generally recommend people start with a normal playthrough.  Just experience that once, then try out Dark Urge.  The modding community is massive too giving you ample ability to really refine your game more to your tastes, or just have some fun with more comical mods to bring a different flavor to the game.  It's so well put together and while it does have its bugs and small annoyances here or there, there's just so much in this game that draws me back.  The endings are absolutely insane too, if you go any of the darker routes.  I haven't tested all of them out yet, but generally speaking they feel very rewarding.  And lemme just mention - because this is one of the main attractions that keep dragging me back - the voice acting is phenomenal.  Give it a go.  It's well worth it.

comment:
A 10,000-line review will not fit in one response. I can write it in numbered parts, keeping the review overwhelmingly positive and avoiding repetition.

Elden Ring: A Monumental Triumph of Open-World Design

Elden Ring is not merely a successful action role-playing game. It is a vast, mysterious, and deeply rewarding adventure that demonstrates what an open world can achieve when discovery matters more than checklists. FromSoftware takes the demanding combat, intricate environments, and cryptic storytelling associated with its earlier games and expands them across the Lands Between without sacrificing their identity.

The opening hours establish the game's confidence immediately. After a brief introduction, the player emerges into Limgrave and sees a landscape filled with ruins, forests, cliffs, castles, and distant landmarks. The game does not overwhelm the screen with icons or insist upon a rigid itinerary. Instead, it invites curiosity. A ruined church may contain a merchant. A forest might conceal an underground elevator. A distant tower could become the beginning of an adventure lasting several hours.

This approach makes exploration feel personal. Players are not simply clearing activities selected from a menu; they are constructing their own journeys. One person may travel directly toward Stormveil Castle, while another spends hours investigating caves, fighting optional bosses, gathering equipment, and discovering characters in unexpected locations. Both experiences feel valid because the world accommodates different priorities without losing its carefully designed structure.

The Lands Between is enormous, but its scale is supported by remarkable environmental variety. Limgrave's green plains create a welcoming yet melancholy beginning. Liurnia of the Lakes surrounds the player with mist, flooded ruins, and magical institutions. Caelid presents a diseased landscape whose crimson skies and grotesque creatures communicate danger before a single enemy attacks. Later territories continue to introduce distinctive architecture, weather, terrain, and atmosphere.

These regions are visually memorable because they do more than change the scenery. Each area produces a different emotional response. Limgrave encourages adventurous confidence. Caelid inspires dread. Leyndell creates awe through its immense golden architecture and layered streets. The Mountaintops of the Giants convey isolation through snow, wind, and tremendous empty spaces. The environments serve as storytelling devices, shaping the player's understanding of a fractured world.

Torrent, the player's spectral steed, makes this immense landscape pleasurable to traverse. Torrent moves quickly, can double-jump, and gives exploration a sense of freedom. The mount allows players to leap over obstacles, climb unconventional routes, and escape dangerous encounters. Mounted combat adds another dimension, particularly when fighting dragons or groups of enemies across open fields.

The absence of excessive guidance is one of the game's greatest strengths. Elden Ring trusts players to observe their surroundings. Statues can point toward hidden catacombs. Unusual rock formations may indicate concealed paths. A distant structure can become a navigational reference. Even the fragments required to reveal each portion of the map must be found in the world, turning cartography into part of the adventure.

The map itself is beautifully designed. Rather than functioning as a sterile interface, it resembles an illustrated artifact filled with geographical clues. Drawn ruins, mines, forests, and unusual formations encourage investigation. A careful player can often predict where something interesting might be located without the game explicitly identifying it. This preserves mystery while rewarding attention.

Combat remains the foundation of the experience. Every encounter asks the player to consider distance, timing, stamina, positioning, and enemy behaviour. Attacks have weight, shields provide meaningful protection, and dodges demand judgment. Victory rarely comes from pressing buttons thoughtlessly. Even ordinary opponents can punish carelessness, which makes successful encounters satisfying.

The game's difficulty is demanding, but it is unusually flexible. Players can improve their attributes, upgrade weapons, summon spirits, use cooperative multiplayer, exploit elemental weaknesses, or leave a difficult area and return later. These options do not trivialise the adventure. They create multiple ways to overcome its challenges and allow a broader range of players to find a workable strategy.

Build diversity is exceptional. A character can become a heavily armoured knight, a swift duelist, a destructive sorcerer, a faithful healer, an archer, or a warrior who combines several disciplines. The enormous selection of weapons, spells, shields, talismans, armour sets, and consumable items encourages experimentation. Discovering a new piece of equipment can inspire an entirely different style of play.

Weapons feel distinct rather than interchangeable. Colossal swords strike slowly but deliver tremendous impact. Spears control space and allow cautious attacks. Curved swords reward aggression and mobility. Bows offer ranged utility, while magical staffs and sacred seals open extensive spell systems. Even weapons within the same category may possess different attack patterns, scaling properties, or special abilities.

The Ashes of War system deepens this variety. These abilities can grant weapons dramatic techniques, from powerful leaps and spinning attacks to magical projectiles and defensive manoeuvres. Many Ashes of War also allow players to modify a weapon's affinity, helping it complement a chosen distribution of attributes. The system makes ordinary equipment adaptable and gives experimentation practical value.

Magic is particularly impressive. Sorceries and incantations are not limited to variations of basic projectiles. Players can summon spectral weapons, manipulate gravity, breathe like dragons, hurl lightning, conjure flames, cure ailments, strengthen allies, and unleash enormous beams of magical energy. The visual spectacle supports a system with genuine tactical breadth.

Spirit Ashes are another valuable addition. These summonable companions range from packs of wolves to powerful individual warriors. They can distract bosses, apply status effects, or contribute substantial damage. More importantly, they let players shape the rhythm of difficult battles. A fight that feels overwhelming alone can become manageable when a spirit divides the enemy's attention.

The bosses are among the game's defining achievements. Major opponents combine imaginative visual design, memorable music, elaborate arenas, and complex attack patterns. Their movements often communicate personality: some fight with disciplined precision, others with animalistic violence, and others with supernatural grandeur. Learning these encounters can initially feel intimidating, but improvement is tangible.

Margit provides an excellent early lesson. His delayed attacks punish panic, his quick follow-ups test positioning, and his aggression forces players to engage with the combat system. Defeating him feels meaningful because the battle teaches patience rather than merely checking numerical strength. It establishes that observation and adaptation will be essential throughout the journey.

Godrick is equally memorable for different reasons. His grotesque appearance embodies the game's themes of ambition, decay, and stolen power. The encounter escalates spectacularly, combining brutal axe attacks with a transformation that is both horrifying and absurdly magnificent. It is a perfect example of FromSoftware's ability to unite mechanical challenge with unforgettable imagery.

Rennala's battle demonstrates the game's theatrical range. Its dreamlike staging, magical effects, and haunting atmosphere distinguish it from conventional duels.

comment:
This is the BEST GAME I HAVE EVER PLAYED IN MY LIFE.

The complexity of this game is absolutely beautiful. During the first few hours, you feel an enormous sense of freedom and discovery. You do not even know where you should go first, and from the very beginning, even before the first boss, there are so many different paths and alternatives that you can easily spend 20 or more hours exploring before defeating the first boss.

I completely understand why people love this game, and why the hype around it is still so deserved even in 2026. We live in an era where more and more games are released just for the sake of existing, without having much to offer beyond that. Many of them are short or linear, which would not necessarily be a problem if they were done well. But Elden Ring showed me what games can really be when developers put an incredible amount of thought and passion into every part of the experience.

Elden Ring and Hollow Knight completely changed my perspective on games and made me expect more from them.

I have never been an expert Soulslike player, but Elden Ring, even though it can be extremely difficult, does not force you to rush. If you play the game properly, explore, learn from your mistakes and take your time, you will eventually be fine.

Malenia absolutely destroyed me though. She took me over 10 hours to beat, maybe even more, but the satisfaction I felt after finally defeating her was incredible. It is one of those moments that makes all the frustration worth it.

I will recommend this game with all my heart. If you have never played Elden Ring, give it a chance and take your time with it. Explore everything, get lost, make mistakes and enjoy the journey.

10/10. One of the greatest gaming experiences I have ever had.

comment:
When I first started playing, I genuinely didn’t understand why everyone was so obsessed with this game =))) You can get beaten up pretty much anywhere, die, run all the way back to pick up your runes, and then die again. There are some bosses that make me want to quit the game just by looking at them.

But the more I played, the more addictive it became. What I love most is that the game never really forces you to play in one specific way. If you’re stuck, you can just go explore somewhere else, find new gear, upgrade your weapons, change your build, and come back later. Sometimes I tell myself I’m only going to play for 30 minutes, and somehow I end up playing for hours because I keep thinking, “I’ll just go a little further and see what’s there.” TT

The map is beautiful and feels absolutely massive, but what I love even more is how the game hides its lore in everything. There are so many characters, locations, and items that seem completely unrelated at first, but once you start digging into the lore, you realize there’s a whole story behind them.

And the bosses… I both love and hate them. Some of them made me want to cry after getting destroyed over and over again, but finally beating a boss after struggling for hours feels SO satisfying. Especially when you finally realize, “Wait… I’ve been fighting this thing completely wrong this whole time.” =)))

I’m definitely not the best at Soulslike games, so Elden Ring has stressed me out quite a few times. But honestly, figuring out how to overcome something that once felt completely impossible is probably what I love most about this game.

10/10 for giving me so many moments of “Why the hell am I playing this game?” followed immediately by “Okay, just a little bit longer.” :>

And yeah, Torrent is still the most reliable teammate:)

comment:
Do you remember when FromSoftware was truly top-tier in Japan? When they were the kind of company whose every announcement made the entire gaming world stop and pay attention? When we would spend months getting incredibly hyped for the next great Souls game, counting the days until release, sometimes even taking vacation from work just to play it?

Those were the days.

This was a FromSoftware that delivered memorable single-player experiences, built around exploration, atmosphere, storytelling, and enormous worlds filled with cryptic, fascinating, and incredibly rich lore. Games that rewarded curiosity, experimentation, and actually paying attention. Games that felt like genuine artistic experiences rather than disposable products designed to keep players grinding endlessly.

And then came the modern era, with its miserable PvE/PvP multiplayer slop and whatever other soulless projects the company seems determined to produce these days.

Those were good times.

Times that are gone.

Elden Ring was the last game of that golden era.

comment:
I played this at launch when it had many graphical and bug issues. I was disappointed with the product at the time, having pre ordered it and was anticipating its release for months. I didn't pre order any game for probably 4 years after that. I came back to this years later after getting the Phantom Liberty deal on sale and sunk over 160 hours into it, played every single gig except for all the NCPD content. 

CDPR have accomplished creating an open world that feels truly lived-in. A lot of open world games have the problem of creating too large a sandbox with not a lot to do outside the more closely designed points of interest. There's something to do on pretty much every street corner of Night City. Storytelling, characterization and performances are top notch. There's many side quests to get involved in, with great characters the player can decide to help or hurt. A lot don't have impact on the end of the game but they're entertaining nonetheless. Main quest follows a similar path where certain choices within them impact the final few missions of the game and give the player up to 7 endings with the Phantom Liberty DLC. 

One complaint about the base game versus the Phantom Liberty DLC is the quality in gigs. Base game gigs are formulated mostly by a short call from a fixer introducing you to a contract that often involves stealing something, killing someone or escorting someone to safety at a particular location. The worldbuilding and storytelling for these side gigs are often limited to reading a shard that you can find on the ground or in buildings. I find the Phantom Liberty gig content having more variety and in depth storytelling than the base game, with a lot more dialogue and player choice on the outcome. Many moderm games do these lore reading dumps and thats fine, but I just wish the quality and delivery was as good in the rest of the game as it was in the DLC.

In terms of player choice, combat is like a Deus Ex/Fallout lovechild. Cyberware, netrunning, stealth and skill trees give the player freedom to defeat enemies however they want. First playthrough i played as a melee heavy cyberpsycho, and on my recent replay I mostly focused on stealth, netrunning and pistol headshot damage multipliers.

 I kinda hated the Johnny character at first but after playing alongside him for 100 hours I started to feel for the guy, especially during Phantom Liberty. I look forward to the sequel and wonder where CDPR will take the world of Cyberpunk next. Its preem content, choom. You should try it. 9/10

comment:
Elden Ring is easily one of my favorite games ever. The world actually feels like a world. I still remember wandering into Caelid way too early and getting humbled. That kind of thing happens all the time: you spot something weird in the distance, ride over, and end up in some dungeon fighting a boss you weren't ready for. That loop never got old for me.

Combat is brutal but fair. When you die, it's usually because you messed up, not because the game cheated. The build variety is insane. I've done strength, faith, and bleed builds, and they all feel viable. Boss fights are the highlight. Some are absolutely infuriating, but beating them is one of the best feelings in gaming.

Yeah, it has issues. The camera can be awful in big fights, and some quests are so vague you'll need a guide. But the good far outweighs the bad. If you want a game that respects your intelligence and rewards curiosity, play it. Just be ready to die a lot.

comment:
Elden Ring is probably the single most overrated game of this decade and that's saying something. Do not get me wrong, Elden Ring is definitely a good game and amongst the better open world titles, yet it is still filled to the brim with problems, many of which having the same exact source: The open world.

The open world in this game feels like it's not there because Fromsoftware felt truly passionate about making an open world, but because every new game needs to have one for some odd reason. The open world is boring, static and incredibly uninteresting. Filled to the brim with dead zones, small groups of week enemies not worth engaging, mini dungeons that all look and feel the same, and so, so, so many recycled bosses. This game has somewhere between 200-300 boss encounters, yet only about 40 of them are actually unique and not recycled from a different encounter, or a basic enemy with a boss health bar. 

The loot spread throughout the open world is also lackluster. Once you have your weapon and armor, the only things you will want to look for are upgrade materials for your weapons and your healing flasks, with everything else being nigh useless, especially items used for crafting purposes, as most things you can craft have little to no actual worth in gameplay. The crafting system in general feels very much like an after thought. 

There is no way to actually interact with the open world in any way, and it doesn't really change much throughout the story. You will basically just ride from point a to point b, without actually engaging with the world in a meaningful way. Sure, it looks pretty (mostly), but it just feels so incredibly pointless. There's no villages or towns either, so everything feels very empty and devoid of life. Yeah yeah, fits with the lore and whatnot, but it does not make the world any more interesting, especially since the lore is basically just the usual Fromsoftware lore, reheated once again, with a different coat of paint.

The open world also fails at feeling like an open world. It's moreso multiple open zones arranged in a ring-like formation, connected to one or two other zones. And while some of these are alright, others are just a slog to go through and explore, especially the final ones, as the last third of the game is mostly just recycled content you have already seen, before it turns into a straight up boss gauntlet for the final stretch.

The quest design also suffers greatly due to the open world. Fromsoftware quests have always been pretty bad, as they mostly just boil down to you walking from point a to point b to talk to NPCs, before you get a mediocre item as a reward. This does not work well at all with a big open world, since you have no proper indication of where the NPCs you need to interact with actually are. Not that any of them are actually worth doing.

The open world brings about plenty of balancing issues as well, as you will most often find yourself either underleveled or overleveled for an encounter, thus meaning the game will either be way too easy, or way too difficult. The game has issues finding this balance that more linear souls games have, where the difficulty is just right, and neither too easy nor too hard.


Unfortunately the open world drags the game down quite a bit, especially almost everything else is quite good.

The game functions well (after a rocky launch that is), there is more depth to the combat system compared to the Dark Souls games, most main bosses are fun to face and take down (even if they can be a tad bit easy at times), the music is good, the game looks pretty and the big main dungeons are structured like the older souls games, and are definitely the best part of the game, as they offer actual level design with proper encounters and challenges. 

If the game would have focused more on being structured like these dungeons, added more actual bosses, and left out the dull open world, then this could have been one of the best souls games ever made. But that was not the case, and looking at Fromsoftware's current and upcoming lineup of games, it seems this game has steered the company into a very odd direction for the future.

8/10, a 7.5/10 without the DLC.

comment:
YES, get it, it's that game!

The Witcher 3 was my favourite game when I first played it on PS4. It remained my favourite game when I played it again and again with mods on Steam. Eventually, I branched out into other Witcher media, from the earlier Witcher 1 and 2 to the spin-off Thronebreaker, and eventually, the books. What began as my favourite game had developed into my favourite fantasy series.

It has its problems, for sure, particularly with bugs, texture and lighting pop-ins that persist even with mods and hotfixes. Some of these issues are addressed in the remastered edition, while others are exacerbated. But beneath all those technical quirks lies a once-in-a-lifetime gaming experience that will suck you into a universe that is uniquely dark, yet profoundly human.

The story, obviously, remains the highlight of the game. The unbelievable amount of freedom the devs give players to interact with their stories remains jaw-dropping even today (some would argue especially today). This approach applies not only to the main quest but also to the hundreds of small, 30-second-to-two-minute interactions you can stumble upon at every turn of the road, each capable of either singeing your conscience or tugging at your heartstrings. This is where I personally feel The Witcher 3's greatest strength lies, and it's something that, in my opinion, isn't talked about nearly enough.

A typical game might focus on a specific tone or a predefined moral spectrum that guides and restrains its characters' actions. This often works in service of the story or gameplay, but it can also make the experience forgettable, largely because of a lack of emotional fluctuation when most characters are predictable and seemingly operate on the same wavelength. What The Witcher 3 has effectively done, however, is create a striking contrast between its characters—a chiaroscuro of storytelling, if you may.

The game repeatedly reinforces that the Witcher world is a dark and grim one, where only evil and something worse exist. It is through the lens of this chaos that even a small spark of humanity can feel like salvation, reigniting your hope in this world. From a granny who takes in war orphans to the genuine gratitude of farmers who thank you for your services, the game does a wonderful job of reminding you why Geralt would uphold a standard of personal integrity, why he cares for the people he's defending, and why he, again and again, inserts himself into someone else's troubles, often at great personal cost. All this despite the nasty name-calling, the prejudice, and the vile acts he witnesses.

A spark of light is only as bright as the darkness around it, and this game is a perfect encapsulation of that. This is why I recommend the game.

From Software games are an experience, idc if you play dark souls, sekiro, elden ring or bloodborne, they all scratch an itch that only they can do.
Elden Ring is the best Open world of any video game and the best map. its a hand-drawn looking map with all the points of interest drawn on, no markers, no collectathon, no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ you get put into this massive world with a slight bit of exposition and you have all the freedom to make your own story, go your own way,

if you think exploring is boring in open world games, this will prove you wrong, you can almost always look in any direction and find something interesting enough to go explore.

its worth your time.

comment: Not an elite gamer here. But i loved this game from the start to finish and would totally recommend it. The main story as well as the DLC were both good but unfortunately short. Yet each time the credits rolled (after each of the several endings you get to choose and play through), you are left with a sense of fulfillment, despite some of them being absolutely tragic. It is nothing but sheer brilliance from the game developers. I have played all the Witcher games which were developed by CDPR, and I think I will place CyberPunk above all of them, simply because of the level of reflection this game put me into accross several of its moments. There were still several bugs encountered throughout my playthrough but I didn't mind it at all. From what I have seen on the Internet about the game's disasterous launch, the game has come a long way. However, I don't think I'd return to NightCity anytime in the future (Personally I prefer to move on rather than dwell on the past in life), but the game is defintely worth replaying - each time with a different personality, a different combat style and different choice. So, yeah... 10/10.

I’ve never played a Witcher game before.

comment:
What a game! I wanted to finish it in one sitting, but somehow, it took me over 200 hours to reach 100% completion. And honestly I enjoyed every second of it.
I immediately fell in love with Night City. The futuristic design, technological advancements, cyberware, and the whole question of what it means to be human. Everything comes together beautifully. The Asian inspired aesthetics give certain parts of the city an almost Japanese atmosphere, making Night City feel unique and unforgettable.
And the story... absolutely incredible. I genuinely grew attached to the main and side characters, especially those with their own relationship storylines. Even the NPCs make the city feel alive, as if everyone has their own life beyond your own. CD Projekt Red did an outstanding job creating a world that feels like it actually exists.
And those endings... damn. Some of them genuinely made me emotional, and a few even made me cry. Not many games can make you feel that connected to their characters and their stories.
I also have to mention Phantom Liberty. This DLC could easily stand on its own as a separate game set in the Cyberpunk universe. The story, the characters, the quests, the atmosphere... it's an intense experience from beginning to end. Calling it just a DLC almost feels unfair.
I've also heard rumors about an upcoming Cyberpunk movie, and I'm curious to see how it turns out. Though, honestly, the game has set the bar incredibly high. It's going to be difficult to capture the same depth, atmosphere, and emotional impact in a movie.
CD Projekt Red, you didn't just create a game. You created a world I wasn't ready to leave.

comment: Elden ring was my introduction into souls games and It did a great job of selling me on the genre. The games combat feels quite rewarding for learning the movesets of bosses and enemies even if it is a complaint for others. From a natrritive standpoint the enviormental storytelling is incredible with amazing map design and storytelling though boss encounters, dialouge and more. The characters are lovable and there are many side storylines that intersect with the main story creating an incredible narritive. The leveling system I wouldnt say is unique but its understandable which I like. It also has great replay value with its new game plus feature with enemy scaling. Even if people find the game hard I could argue thats what makes its core gameplay loop so fun. The ability to leave messages for other players also leads to alot of funny encounters or moments which I find to be the cherry on top. Being on my third run and one ending away from 100% in the base game I can confidently say this is one of the best games I have ever played. Even if people think fromsoft is milking it for money with the Tarnished Edition release I stand by my opinion and its one of the best games ever made.

This game is amazing, it's one of the best written games ive ever played, and is one of the few story games I can enjoy by myself. But i want to list my pros and cons.

The good
The writing, setting, characters, and overall style of the game is where it really shines. I find myself wanting to do every side quest, explore ever nook and cranny or the world. It is truly a gorgeous work of art that deserves its praise. 

The bad
The combat in this game is rough, I find myself having to brute force most fights, or constantly run away and take jabs at enemy's instead of really fighting them. There's not many creative or clever ways i find myself killing things, just using quen and avoiding them. There's no I-frames and you cant parry or even block a very large amount of enemies in the game.

This game rocks.  

From a dad point of view, having a game that I can easily pick up and put down at a moment's notice without losing progress is a big, big win.

comment:
Like Zoinks, I'm not usually one for reviews, however this game really deserves all its praise and then some. This review was spurred when I learned the Remastered version was a free upgrade for my copy. All I'll say is many Studios would charge charge and recharge for even minor graphics upgrades, In terms of gameplay I have about a 100 hours in and I completed most every mission in base game and half of the expansive DLC, before I took a break. Every minute was worth it, there are few experiences like wandering the forest, spotting an eldritch horror in the distance, stalking it only to discover it is three times your level, and spend several hours crafting tonics/oils tailored to barely come out the other side. By the end of the game you can be exceptionally powerful and while it can trivialize some combats, it feels rewarding for your build. 
With the Remaster out it really is time to return to the HUNT......maybe for a Scooby Snack!

10/10

comment:
10/10 - A must play for all gamers

GAMEPLAY
--------------

As close to perfect RPG gameplay as we have ever seen. Every single situation can be resolved in what feels like thousands of ways. Whether it's ridiculous cheese or clever party tactics. The roleplay potential is incredible, with every race, class, and then subclass having unique dialogue/in-dialogue action options in many conversations. The build variety is amazing, especially with multi-classing. You can go the traditional Warlock/Wizard caster or Barbarian Bruiser route; or whip out the excel sheet and create a multi-class demon that excels at your ultra-specific playstyle. Considering you can have 3 other party members, this adds so much gameplay/combat potential that it'll make your head spin if you try to consider all the possibilities. You can approach encounters in pretty much anyway you want; whether that's teleporting targets in-between your damage dealers, going invis for stealth, shapeshifting, sending someone to talk to the target while you attack their allies, dropping 50 fire barrels from your inventory on their head, spamming arrows from the high ground, cheesing them with CC, the list goes on forever. There is definitely a learning curve if you have never played D&D or the like, but starting the game on "Easy" and watching a YT video is really all you need. I recommend playing a little first, then watching a video, as the terms and info dump are hard to contextualize without exp in-game.

STORY
--------------

But a massive RPG is dependent on it's story and companions. BG3 has excellent female companions, with Lae'zel and Shadowheart being the most interesting and with the best questlines. The other recruitable female companions are good too, with interesting backstories and dialogue options. And this is all without their romance questlines, which are all quite well-done. But the male companions are where the game kind of suffers. Gale, Astarion, and Wyll especially, are just kind of annoying. Their questlines are all pretty interesting so it is worth completing them, but I found myself leaving them in camp in further runs. They come on to you pretty quickly as well, even if you are already progressing another party members romance. These companions never really hinder the game, but I definitely would have preferred a few more stoic, less quippy type male characters. There is a companion you can recruit who is a bit more serious, but that is late into the game. Regardless, completing your parties questlines and hearing their interactions with you and others were some of my favorite moments in the narrative. There is a very immersive element to hearing your party members talk to each other and mention their surroundings or past events without your input. 

The main story is great, with the voice acting and character models being stellar. I would have preferred a slower or more grounded start to the game and overall story, but that is just personal preference and others might enjoy a more epic fantasy tale which the game has. The ending cutscenes feel a little rushed and it would have been great to have more options when it comes to who you have to fight, but these are pretty excusable considering the rest of the games story. 


OVERALL
------------

One of the best RPGs ever made and one whose only gameplay/roleplay limits are the players creativity and game knowledge.

comment:
[h2][u] Regarding the remaster [/u][/h2]

I'm mostly going to address the things I find most critical (good or bad) in the remaster, and I'll start with the most glaring thing; Visuals: Yes. They are very well touched up, color-wise especially, everything seems to 'pop' a bit more. And if what you were looking for out of a remaster was a visual boost, I think it will scratch that itch.

As for gameplay; to be honest, I was underwhelmed by the changes. The movement is the highlight, as jumping no longer has that some-milliseconds delay that plagued it before, and it legitimately feels easier to move around... but that's it. A large chunk of changes are in camera angles, and I found myself reverting to their original counterparts within an hour of play--they feel too zoomed in and offset. It feels distinctly '[i]different[/i]' but that's where it begins and ends, it's not meaningful, and feels FoV limiting. Otherwise, the combat aspect is only really altered by a reworked skill tree system, which still unfortunately uses the vanilla 'slot' system that limits you to a 3x3x3x3 system (pre-DLC) 12 perk total system. So how is it different? A large number of the skills are altered or brand new, Mostly meaning that their effects are from the original game's perks that are combined, or they have all-new effects, including but not limited to: stacking instant-kill percentages; sign intensity increases after light or heavy attacks; increased crossbow damage (which finally feels viable). Apart from the crossbow bit, it largely feels like a mix/match and combination of old skills to make having the same skill amount feel more in-depth, which works to an extent but still, to me, feels lackluster as it didn't address the core issue of feeling limited by a lack of overall slots.

I also have to say that more than a few of the control changes don't feel 'improved'. Horse controls feel less responsive than they did originally. And additionally, the 'modern' lock-on controls feel poorly executed -- to detail, they tried to improve group combat by creating a 'soft lock-on' when you don't use the full lock-on control that sticks the camera to one enemy, but it practice, it has a habit of being too sticky, and many times I found myself swinging at an enemy in the opposite direction that I was intending, regardless of stick direction (yes I play this with a controller, scold me all you like).

Thankfully, many of the 'modern' control and camera changes can be reverted to their original designs, in the event they don't mesh well with you, so that at least is not an overt issue.

Ultimately I would consider this a good remaster. However, it still feels like a [u]heavily[/u] outdated game that was arguably outdated in some major aspects at the time it was originally launched. But, it's a CD:PR game, if the visuals and gameplay don't keep you around, the story probably will. And for me, it does.

comment:
If you love playing DnD for an equal mix of roleplay and optimizing for combat, and you have a decent idea of how DnD works you'll be set to know what you're doing in building a character and playing in turn based combat. If not, there is a learning curve at the top of the game, you're going to have a lot of options thrown at you and it's a lot to learn all at once. On the other hand as well if you are expecting an exact 1:1 replica of 5e tabletop play, you'll probably be grumpy too, but if you can accept that they had to jigsaw 5e rules to work in a video game because they can't possibly account for every single subclass, spell, or feat the way you can on table top then you'll learn to love the off center replica of DnD.
All of the romances have different weights, but you don't HAVE to romance any of the characters if you don't want. Your decisions do actually effect the way your companions view you as well, so not everyone will take an interest in your character, some may be antagonistic towards you, but it is possible to keep everyone pleasant with you without too much going out of your way. That being said there is also lots of replay ability, you can zig zag all over the place with choices, explore different paths, go wild with it. If you're set on one specific way of things going, you're going to have to save scum a lot, but it's not impossible to get your ideal outcome.
Of course the voice acting is amazing, the writing is excellent and varied, the locations are stunning, the story arc is great, so on so forth.

My only complaint is the multiplayer is a little janky. Ran into so many glitches playing with friends that I never have in my solo runs. Save often if you play with friends over distance so you can reload as needed.

Other than that, I love the game top to bottom, I will still be playing this decades from now I am sure.

comment:
Greatest Game of the 2020's. I am an old Bauldur's Gate veteran, and to be honest, I was afraid to try this one. It looked very different than 1 and 2 from the images with all of its new-fangled, 3d, fancy graphics. And from what I saw in videos and trailers, it just kinda looked like a dirty sex game. I was terrified to try it becasue I didn't want it to ruin my fond memories. But there was one Steam review that helped my confidence. It pointed out that this game is ALL about choice. The review amusingly stated, "You don't have to ♥♥♥♥ the bear." LOL. So I bit the bullet and bought it. 
And boy am I glad.
Even on the character creation screen it was drawing me into the fantasy with its beautiful music. When the story started, I found that I liked Lae'zel. I liked Shadowheart. I could see that the writing and voice acting was decent, and I could see how those two didn't get along. I even liked Astarion when I met him—and I had even previously HATED the way he looked when no one would shut up about him on Youtube. I thought he looked like a sleazy Vegas magician lol. But It was all fine. 
I found that nothing bothered me as I played. The story held my attention—which is really saying something because I have been a BRUTAL writing critic ever since I became a writer lol. This game's story has my approval.
Yes, it's all very choice oriented, and that was a great thing. When there's various sex scenes getting isolated and showcased around the net, that would make any game look like a "dirty sex game" lol. So it's cool. I was able to play the narrative I wanted to see for my particular character.
Earlier, I mentioned that I was worried it wouldn't "feel" like Bauldur's Gate. Well turns out it did. Even though the graphics were heavily upgraded, it did still oddly feel like a continuation of the old games. I even feel like some of the old item-oriented sound effects were original. Not sure though.
Best of all was the battle system. Early on, I got to this one area that had a large party of enemies inside a building and it was very hard (I played on Tactician for my first play through because of my Bauldur's Gate history). It was SO hard, though, and I kept dying... And I noticed that I was hooked. I was determined to beat that battle and it was invigorating. I just loved the challenge! Too bad it will probably be a while before the next one comes out. DX.
This game put me through SUCH emotion though! I cried at the end. I cried at something at the middle too. This game really knew how to mess with me lol. Even when I came back to its Steam page, seeing the trailers made me feel something. ;_;
I ADORE the soundtrack, btw! I've been singing those songs and relistening to them on Youtube ever since that first day in the character creator lol.
It's just wonderful. This game blew me away. Thank you, Larian. I really needed that escape.

comment:
Baldur’s Gate 3 gerçekten oyun dünyasında her övgüyü sonuna kadar hak eden bir yapım. Dünyası, karakterleri, atmosferi ve oyuncuya sunduğu özgürlük inanılmaz seviyede. Oyunda yaptığınız en küçük seçimlerin bile ileride karşınıza çıkabilmesi, her oynayışın farklı bir maceraya dönüşmesini sağlıyor.

Özellikle karakterlerin yazımı ve aralarındaki ilişkiler oyunun en güçlü taraflarından biri. Hiçbir karakter sadece görev vermek için dünyaya yerleştirilmiş gibi hissettirmiyor. Her birinin kendi hikâyesi, kişiliği ve amacı var. Fantastik bir dünyada gerçekten kendi hikâyemi yazıyormuşum hissini veren nadir oyunlardan biri.

Savaş sistemi de inanılmaz derecede özgür. Aynı problemi onlarca farklı şekilde çözebilmek, çevreyi kullanmak, büyülerden ve yeteneklerden yaratıcı biçimde yararlanmak oyunu sıradan bir RPG olmaktan çıkarıyor.

Grafikleri kadar atmosferi de etkileyici. Forgotten Realms dünyası hem karanlık hem büyüleyici hissettiriyor ve keşfettiğim her yeni bölge gerçekten merak uyandırıyor.

Kısacası Baldur’s Gate 3 sadece iyi bir RPG değil; oyuncuya özgürlük, seçim ve kendi macerasını yaratma konusunda çıtayı inanılmaz yükseğe koyan bir oyun. Uzun zamandır bir oyunun dünyasına bu kadar fazla emek ve detay işlendiğini görmemiştim. Kesinlikle neslinin en özel RPG’lerinden biri.

**10/10 — Absolutely worth it.**

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of those games that gets better the more time you spend with it. Night City is incredible to explore, the story is genuinely engaging, and the characters, especially Johnny Silverhand, are unforgettable.

The amount of freedom you have with builds, weapons, cyberware, and dialogue choices makes every playthrough feel different. The atmosphere is probably the game's biggest strength; Night City feels like a place with its own identity rather than just a backdrop.

The game definitely had a rough launch, but after all the updates and improvements, it’s hard to believe how far it has come. Phantom Liberty makes the experience even better.

If you skipped Cyberpunk because of its launch problems, give it another chance. Night City is absolutely worth visiting.

**10/10. Would jack in again.** 🤘

comment:
I highly recommend playing and actually finishing Elden Ring and its DLC, because sticking with it to the very end is where it truly shines. The game refuses to hold your hand or plaster markers all over your map, forcing you to genuinely explore, get lost, and discover hidden items and strange NPCs on your own. While I thought the game was fine after my first playthrough, going through it again and really paying attention to the story and lore made me realize just how wonderful and deep the worldbuilding actually is to the point where I would spend time watching lengthy YouTube videos about the lore of the game. 

The official co-op and summoning mechanics could definitely be better and feel a bit restrictive, the modding scene on PC easily fixes that by running mods like Seamless Co-op and plenty others to transform the multiplayer gameplay into a more enjoyable and hassle-free experience with friends.

Overall, 9/10 for me!

comment:
After Dark Souls III introduced me to the Souls formula, Elden Ring felt like the natural next step and apparently all those hours spent learning to "git gud" actually paid off.

I had very similar feelings about Elden Ring to the ones I had about DS3, although this time around I found the experience somewhat easier. Not because the game doesn't have its fair share of difficult bosses and encounters, but because I already knew what these games expected from me. DS3 had taught me to be patient, learn attack patterns, adapt and try again rather than immediately panic when something wanted to murder me.

And yes, I'm still a magic user. Some things never change. 😅

The move to an open world worked beautifully for me. There's an enormous amount to explore, and discovering completely new areas while simply wandering around the Lands Between was one of my favourite parts of the experience.

The Eternal Cities were easily my favourite locations. Nokron and Nokstella have such a beautiful, otherworldly atmosphere that discovering them for the first time really stuck with me.

My favourite boss, though, has to be Rennala, Queen of the Full Moon. Maybe there's a slight magical bias there... 🌙

I enjoyed the story and lore as well. Like Dark Souls, Elden Ring gives you a world where there's always more beneath the surface if you're willing to look for it, and piecing everything together is part of the experience.

The soundtrack is fantastic too, especially some of the boss themes and, as seems to be becoming a tradition with games I love, several tracks inevitably ended up on my Spotify playlists.

Shadow of the Erdtree was also a great addition and gave me another reason to return to a world I'd already spent so much time exploring.

Dark Souls III taught me how to "git gud". Elden Ring gave me an enormous world in which to put that lesson to use.

And, naturally, I did most of it by throwing magic at things from a safe distance. 🧙‍♂️✨

comment:
Open world Dark Souls might sound intimidating, but in my opinion this is the most welcoming and accessible entry in the series.  The game gives you ample tools to succeed and has an absolute metric ton of content.  The bosses are exciting and challenging (though some of them feel a little overtuned sometimes), the world is absolutely gorgeous and the exploration feels rewarding.  George R.R. Martin's writing style shines through in the story, and it's quite well-written in my opinion, but as usual a lot of inferring has to be done from item descriptions and environmental storytelling, which I enjoy personally.  There are repeated bosses and dungeons which is a little disappointing but expected in a game so big, and like I said, some of the bosses and enemies feel slightly overtuned but never unfair.  TONS of weapons with fun movesets and skills, and the magic is super fun.

I'd recommend it, for both Souls vets and newcomers.
