comment:
10/10
Very simple - it is THE GREATEST RPG OF ALL TIME.
1) Strory - complex, with twists and turns, engaging and immersive.
2) Characters - feel real, unique and interesting.
3) Side quests - amazing content, both the witcher contracts that help remind you what is your real job and the secondary quests which from time to time will break your heart and have you make an impossible choice.
4) Gameplay - the fighting is smooth, the world exploring on Roach(horse) is a delight.
5) DLC's - WOW! cant even decide which one between HOS and BAW i love more, both are easily the best added content ive seen in a video game.
6) GWENT - last but not least, a card game that i spent on probably 1/4 of my in game time, and the only problem is i ran out of gwent content. MORE! MORE!


Not only it holds up in 2026 - it is updated for free by the devs from time to time, that shows a true love from the devs to the project, which is an absolute delite in our cash-grab days.
played it as a youngster in school, and playing it as an adult with the same joy!!!
THANK YOU CDPR!

comment:
Cyberpunk 2077 is a great game, and the story is amazing. Personally, I really liked playing as male V.
It is sad because this game had so much potential, but CD Projekt Red did not develop many parts of the world enough. For example, driving could be better, there could have been flying cars, more stores you can actually enter, and more NPCs with different voices and animations.
When you leave the main storyline and just explore the city, the game can still feel empty. It has improved compared to before, but I expected much more. The physics, cars, NPCs, and animations can still be very buggy and sometimes do not feel smooth. It is disappointing that even after almost six years, some of these problems are still there.
I think Cyberpunk 2077 could have been one of the greatest games of all time if it had received another five or six years of development, but CD Projekt Red made the choice to release it when they did.
The game is still worth playing and finishing, especially for the main story. The Dogtown/Phantom Liberty storyline is also very good. But if you like exploring the open world and paying attention to small details, you will notice many of the game's weaknesses.
I finished the game, experienced all the endings, and completed all the achievements. My favorite ending is “(Don't Fear) The Reaper.” I really enjoyed the idea of V and Johnny deciding to attack Arasaka Tower alone instead of risking the lives of their friends.
Even with all its problems, I recommend Cyberpunk 2077

comment:
Why are you even reading this review, at this point everyone in the world know that this is a great game with an amazing story, there is literally nothing i can say in this review that hasn't been said in a million other reviews and videos, so instead i will give you my thoughts on the book series this is based on that i read 10 years ago and only barely remember (Minor Spoilers ahead)

The first few books are good but not great, they are a collection of adventures that Geralt goes on that introduce you to the world and characters with a loose connecting narrative, but once Ciri becomes a major part of the story the books become an ongoing narrative instead of a collection of adventures, its at this point that the books really get good and its also around here that Yennefer really comes into her own in the story and stops being so abrasive and you come to really know and like her, the books stay great to the end, even if they get a bit weird in the final book with the archeologist in the modern time discovering relics of Geralt's time and with Ciri dimension hopping

All in all i really enjoyed the books and really recommend them, my only major complaint is that EVERYONE wants to have sex with pre-teen Ciri in these books including her own father and it gets a bit hard to keep reading scenes where Ciri almost gets SA'd and barely manages to escape just for the same Scenario to happen again and again across the books, i get its medieval Europe but it still felt like a bit much

If you read this far then i commend you and recommend that you toss a coin to your witcher (The devs/author) and buy this game and read the books

P.S. only season 1 of the Netflix live action witcher was any good and it still deviated allot from the books and added allot of its own stuff

comment:
[h1] "A happy ending? For folks like us? Wrong city, wrong people." [/h1]

Cyberpunk 2077 is a story rich RPG featuring a beautiful open world, with the best character writing I've seen. The game covers themes such as freedom, identity, greed, and social inequality. It's an unforgettable experience worth playing. Jackie Welles & Johnny Silverhand are [b] GOATED [/b] support characters!

Story: You play as V, a lone merc in Night City, a futuristic violent dystopia dictated by greedy capitalist mega-corporations. You take on the most dangerous jobs trying to stay alive and make a name for yourself. There are 3 life paths to choose from: Nomad, Streetkid, and Corpo. They don't make much of a difference gameplay-wise, aside from unique dialogue options and shaping V's perspective on the world. After your biggest high stakes job goes FUBAR, the story truly begins as you race against time for your life! 

Gameplay: This game feels like a mixture of GTA and Borderlands because of the interactivity, stores, looting, class building, and the leeway to play however you like. Unfortunately, some elements are not well polished, but its not that bad because they can be fixed with mods. Majority of the cars handle terribly! I got around the map 90% of the time using motorcycles because they're really fast and consistently handle well. Another thing I did not enjoy too much was the early game. Enemies scale heavily to your level at all times, so the beginning is kind of rough because your guns aren't strong and targets feel tanky. Shotguns, revolvers, and snipers became my go to weapons. You'll be fine if your aim and positioning is really good. Mid to late game is when you can really start going crazy. 

Environment: Along with the story, this is another great aspect because of its visual storytelling. It shows you how bad things are, instead of telling you. The city is plagued with advertisements, some even reaching the sky! Gangs rule certain city districts, crime thrives more often in some places, and you can really see the poverty and flourishment of areas. What I truly did love were the small mentions of the 2076 Edgerunners crew. You can find iconic items left behind by a few members which is very cool, it makes the city's history feel more connected on a deeper level.

Side Quests: There are many to do and they give you really good rewards, but they aren't special because they follow a repetitive format. The only good quests are the character story missions, these deepen your bond with key characters, allowing you to learn their history and help them out with personal troubles. 

TL;DR Cyberpunk 2077 is one of the best story rich RPG games you can ever play. It has some issues gameplay wise, but they're relatively minor and won't hurt your overall experience. Never stop fighting, my chooms!

comment:
I have a great love for Elden Ring with some caveats.

Having already played through the original Demon's Souls, Dark Souls 1 and 3 multiple times, I believe I have a good enough amount of experience to speak on Elden Ring with some good context.

Elden Ring is simultaneously amazing and yet a little tedious. 

The parts I love are why I have loved all the Souls games before it: great exploration and world building, atmosphere, and a wonderful sense of progression as you slowly build your character. Gameplay is top notch and is as varied as it has ever been in terms of weapons and potential builds.

On the other hand, the shift to an open world has introduced some unfortunate open world tropes, such as a lot of emptiness and open space between all the cool and interesting things to do. The dungeons are all hand crafted with the typical souls level of quality, yet the vast amounts of space between them leaves me wishing it was just more of the densely packed and intertwining level design the souls games are known for.

I haven't quite finished my first playthrough, and even though I'm having a great time, I already don't believe I'll want to play through it again immediately like I did my other Souls games, for the open world reasons I listed above. 

It's a weird feeling because, for me, Dark Souls 3 was the peak of the Souls formula. The level design was top notch, the world was slightly more linear, but the intertwining design of the levels made it so when you unlocked a shortcut to a previous area it immediately felt so gratifying. Some of that magic is lost in a massive open map. There's lots to do, yes, but it's so much more spread out that you get those magic moments much less often.

While I love this game, and I do highly recommend it, enter into it knowing the drawbacks of any open world game. 

Thankfully, this is not the open world formula you may be familiar with in Ubisoft games, where the map is just littered with side quests that pad the run time but leave you feeling empty inside for pursuing. In Elden Ring, there are virtually no markers. You need to go find them for yourself. Exploration is almost always rewarded with some cool item or spell or weapon. But the amount of time spent wandering between these cool moments can sometimes feel quite long, especially if you like to explore every nook and cranny like I tend do to. 

If you go straight for the main quest markers, your time with Elden Ring will likely feel quite different. But for me, I like to take my time and uncover everything. I think my natural tendencies may be why I haven't enjoyed it as much as DS1, or 3. As there is simply so much to explore and so much nothingness between the true points of interest.

If you're a fan of the genre, though, this is a must play. Enjoy it in the way you enjoy playing these games, and be ready for an incredible journey.

PS I have also experienced much of the game on a Steam Deck. While not the ideal way to play, it's well enough if you can tolerate 40fps. Only very occasionally did it dip from this, so it's a decent way to experience the game if you're not able to use your computer or tv for any particular reason.

comment:
Elden Ring is a masterpiece of a game. It is quite fun and for a player who has never played a Dark Souls type game, learnt it pretty quickly. Every enemy challenges you, one slip up, all over. The bosses feel impossible, but after learning attack patterns can be felled; which gives a stellar dopamine rush. Even if you think you're not capable because it is too hard, too harsh or simply unguided, it is, but you can do it. The price is definitely worth it, and it is rather well optimised but don't boot it up with your school chromebook. The graphics are spectacular and feel like real life. The voices and sound quality sound realistic and with headphones you are practically transported to The Lands Between and feel like you're walking around.
The story is great and very deep, and for a first time player walking around can make you feel lost, or you're just going in circles, but this is all intended. The optional tutorial shows you immediatly how un-hand-held it is. This lets you spend 100 hours not progressing, or 20 beating the game. It is up to you.
Overall, BUY ELDEN RING, it is truly one of the games of all time. It is a canon life experience for every human born in the 21st century.
5 STARS: 10/10: 100/100

comment:
Recommended, but there's a lot of wasted potential.

First off, Cyberpunk 2077 is a genuinely enjoyable game. The atmosphere, visuals, combat, and overall design of Night City are impressive. However, the longer I play, the more I notice just how many opportunities were missed.

On the technical side, I've experienced some rendering issues that may or may not be related to my PC. I've lowered my graphics settings considerably, but the problems persist. I've also encountered a handful of bugs that required me to save, completely close the game, and restart it. Annoying, but nothing that has ruined the experience.

My biggest complaint, however, is Night City itself.

For a city that looks so alive, it feels surprisingly dead.

There's an incredible amount of detail throughout the world, but very little of it actually responds to your existence. You can spend hours completing side activities, fighting gangs, and building your street cred, but it rarely feels like any of it carries meaningful weight in the world around you.

Take the gangs, for example. If I spend my time hunting down members of a particular gang, eventually they should recognize me as an enemy and attack me on sight. On the other hand, if I've consistently avoided conflict with another gang, maybe their members should acknowledge that. Even something as simple as different dialogue, attitudes, or reactions based on your history with a faction would make the world feel significantly more immersive.

Street cred could have been so much more than a number. Imagine having separate reputations with different gangs, where your actions determine whether you're respected, feared, tolerated, or hated. That alone would give side activities a much greater sense of purpose.

Cyberware customization is another missed opportunity. For a game centered around a society obsessed with body modification, installing cyberware has surprisingly little impact on your physical appearance. Being able to customize the color, style, or design of your implants would have added another layer of immersion and personal expression.

But all of that ties into my biggest issue with the game:

You never really feel like you're part of Night City.

At times, it almost feels like The Truman Show, except nobody is actually watching you. Nobody seems to care who you are, what you've accomplished, or what you've done to the people around them. You can be an absolute menace to a particular gang, and the next group you encounter acts like they've never heard of you.

The city is beautiful, flashy, detailed, and full of people, yet somehow manages to feel strangely lifeless. It's almost like exploring an incredibly elaborate movie set rather than living in a functioning world.

And that's what frustrates me the most. The foundation for something truly incredible is already there.

Despite all of this, I still recommend Cyberpunk 2077. I've had a lot of fun with it, and there's plenty the developers got right. I just can't shake the feeling that Night City could have been so much more.

It's a great game set in an incredible world that doesn't always seem to realize you exist.

comment:
Grand Theft Auto V is not just a video game; it is a monumental cultural phenomenon and a sprawling, technicolor mirror held up to the face of modern capitalism. From the moment you step into the sun-drenched, smog-choked streets of Los Santos, Rockstar Games delivers a masterclass in open-world design, storytelling, and social commentary. It captures the chaotic essence of the American Dream, chews it up, and spits it back out in a glorious explosion of high-speed chases, bullet-riddled bank heists, and dark, unfiltered humor.
At the beating heart of this epic narrative is the franchise’s most ambitious storytelling mechanic: the three-protagonist system. By weaving together the lives of three distinct criminals, the game offers a multi-layered perspective of a deeply flawed world. There is Michael, a retired bank robber trapped in a toxic, wealthy suburban nightmare, suffocated by the boredom of his own success. Then there is Franklin, a young, ambitious street hustler trying to escape the cycle of the ghetto by climbing the ladder of organized crime. And finally, Trevor, a volatile, unhinged, and borderline psychotic meth-dealer who embodies the absolute, chaotic id of the GTA franchise itself. The ability to seamlessly switch between these characters creates a dynamic, cinematic rhythm where a tranquil day at a luxury mansion can instantly dissolve into a chaotic desert shootout.
The true star of the show, however, is the map of San Andreas itself. The attention to detail is staggering. Los Santos feels alive, reacting dynamically to the player's presence. Pedestrians yell on their cell phones, traffic clogs the freeways at rush hour, and the neon lights of Vinewood reflect beautifully off the hoods of stolen supercars. Whether you are planning a meticulously detailed, multi-stage heist, diving into the ocean depths, hijacking a military fighter jet, or simply driving down Del Perro Beach while listening to a satirical talk-radio station, the level of player freedom remains completely unmatched.
Ultimately, Grand Theft Auto V stands as a timeless masterpiece because it doesn’t just let you play in a world; it forces you to experience its madness. It is a brilliant, cynical, and wildly entertaining critique of celebrity culture, government corruption, and consumerism. Decades from now, when historians look back at how video games evolved into the definitive art form of the 21st century, GTA V will undoubtedly stand tall as the pinnacle of interactive entertainment.

comment:
Great game with many flaws, especially if you played their previous games. For one don't come expecting the "best game ever made" with it's outdated quest system and "rpg" mechanics outside of making your own little themed build. It's open world is static, largely empty with lot's of sprinting around on torrent.

comment:
The Witcher 3 is one of those games that makes it really easy to lose hundreds of hours.

The world is absolutely incredible. There are so many places to explore, characters to meet and stories to discover that even random side quests can turn into something memorable.

And that's probably my favorite thing about the game: the side quests. They don't just feel like filler between the main missions. A lot of them have their own stories, characters and choices, and some of them are honestly better than the main quest.

The characters are also a huge part of the experience. Geralt, Ciri, Yennefer, Triss and the rest of the cast make the world feel alive, and I actually cared about what happened to them.

The combat isn't perfect and can feel a little repetitive after a while, but there's enough variety with signs, potions, weapons and builds to keep things interesting.

The game is huge, and that can sometimes be a little overwhelming, but there's always something worth doing or discovering.

Even years later, The Witcher 3 still feels like one of the best open-world RPGs around.

🟢 MUST PLAY — Incredible world, great characters and some of the best side quests in gaming. A massive RPG that's absolutely worth getting lost in.

Masterpiece ahead,
in short praise the Erdtree!

and then sadness...
Be wary of scarlet rot,
in short suffering required ahead

therefore praise the message!
Could this be a boss?
try rolling,
and then bloodstain?

try jumping

and then defeat...

This game is beautiful, daunting, disturbing, frustrating, and at times impossible, but I love it all the same. It's just forgiving enough to keep trying, again, and again, and again... and again. The story doesn't even make sense sometimes, unless you really dig, and FromSoftware puts a lot of trust in the player to figure things out. It's so rewarding when you do figure it out, though.

Ultimately, Elden Ring has mastered atmosphere and immersion. I keep coming back to discover something new, prove that I can do it, or just admire the beautiful world. 

Note: My first play-through was on PS5, but then I restarted on the PC through Steam.

comment:
For me, Cyberpunk 2077 is an interesting and enjoyable game because of its futuristic setting, exciting missions, and engaging storyline. What I like most about the game is how it presents a world where advanced technology plays a big role in people's lives. The city is full of bright lights, tall buildings, cybernetic enhancements, and different characters that make the game more realistic and immersive.

I also like that the game gives players the freedom to explore the city, customize their characters, and choose different ways to complete missions. The story makes the game more interesting because the decisions you make can affect certain events and relationships throughout the game.

However, I think the game can sometimes feel overwhelming because of its large open world and numerous missions. Some activities can also become repetitive after playing for a long time. Despite these weaknesses, I still think the game offers a memorable experience.

Overall, I would recommend Cyberpunk 2077 to players who enjoy open-world games, action, and science fiction. For me, its graphics, storyline, and freedom of exploration make it a worthwhile game to experience.

comment:
Finished the base game about 2 weeks ago:))

Elden Ring is definitely one of the most immersive and best gaming experiences I’ve ever had. Literally a massive achievement in every part of game design. Even despite having so much difficulty and frustration through the bosses, dungeons, etc., I still don’t think I can ever get an experience like this from any other developer. It’s packed from start to finish with content in a world that’s so dense and rich.

There’s just something special about simply existing in this world and then slowly understanding the history, conflicts and circumstances that brought everything to where it is in The Lands Between. After finishing the game, I decided to watch a bunch of lore videos. It really hit harder thinking about the grand moments when I understood the actual weight behind them, realizing that the journey through this broken world has ultimately meant. 

Elden Ring’s story is completely outstanding in its own regard. In the fantasy open world, it depicted the cycles in terms of generational and familial tragedy, the cycle of violence and the hope of a brighter future. It's clear that the vision of the story is so well directed, well driven and how almost every mechanic ties into this game. I really love that the game never tells you that there’s not a single correct way to fix everything because either; you’re given this world that’s already been shaped by countless of failures, ideals and conflicts, and then you’re left to decide what kind of future should come from it, even if it means embracing something completely unknown. 

Overall, this game has been frustrating to the max lmao. But it’s overwhelmingly beautiful, mysterious and genuinely breathtaking. An insanely, well crafted game that’s impressive in its technicalities and somehow just those things make Elden Ring truly the experience instead of it just being a game. 

10/10

Top 10 Favorite Bosses!
1. Maliketh, The Black Blade 
2. Malenia, Blade Of Miquella, Goddess Of Rot 
3. Godfrey/Horah Loux, First Elden Lord
4. Starscourge Radahn 
5. Mohg, Lord Of Blood 
6. Dragonlord Placidusax 
7. Radagon/Elden Beast 
8. Rykard, Lord Of Blasphemy 
9. Morgott, The Omen King 
10. Lichdragon Fortissax 

Favorite Weapons:
(mainly did a Dex build. Switched around with Intj/Dex, faith/dex, arcane/dex, pure dex builds because I’m curious on how other builds work lol. Glad there’s enough larval tears)

- Nagakiba: PROBABLY MY FAVORITE?? extremely versatile and the reach is so good. I always see myself coming back to it. Slapping unsheathe, spinning slash, double slash, sword dance ash of war with either cold or keen (to apply any incantation to it) is the way)

- Moonveil Katana: mostly my main weapon for intj/dex. It’s just fun to use along with sorcery spells 

- Cross-Naginata: slap the repeating thrust ash of war. It’s so good. 

- Uchigatana: carried me at times from the start. Sometimes pair it with Nagakiba. 

- Morgott’s Cursed Sword: honestly carried me in tough ass bosses and in some places, especially in navigating through Castle SOL. 

- Eleonora's Poleblade: mainly used it for an arcane/dex build. Made me feel like Darth Maul lmao. 

And then dipping my toes into the Shadow Of The Erdtree DLC a bit…

- Milady: yeah honestly, I see myself using this weapon more often. Especially slapping the Wing Stance on it or pairing it with a shield for guard counters or maybe using deflecting hardtear. Cold or keen. I’m straight up aura farming on them bosses with the wing stance! (just to be obliterated).

- Rakshaka’s Great Katana: SO GOOD. LIKE REALLY GOOD.

- Leontiel's Greatsword: It’s so fun. Worth buying the new tarnished dlc pack for $5 (plus torrent skins!!)

comment:
An example of what you would wish for in a game. From an RPG perspective, an amazing storyline, loads of customisations from visuals to builds and memorable companions.  A game where choices matter!

A game that is not loaded with millions of microtransactions that prey on your fear of missing out or impulsiveness. A one-time purchase that was followed by many updates and improvements at no cost, and earned the well-deserved awards of Labour of Love and Game of the Year.

My advice is to take your time with this gem. This is not a game you should speed through or expect to finish in a few hours. Take your time and check out every nook and cranny, there is so much to explore. It took me approx. 120 to 150 hours on my first campaign due to leaving no stone unturned. Even after that, there is replayability, as different decision/moral paths taken will provide different story outcomes.

If it is your first time playing this kind of game, it might feel overwhelming at first. If that is the case, lower the difficulty, enjoy the story, as that is where the gold is. Save plenty and take the Honour mode difficulty on a repeat run, later!

With amazing mod support and the amount of mods made by the modding community, the game only gets better. Also don't forget the co-op multiplayer option, just don't expect the human-controlled custom "companions" to follow your ideal campaign script. Expect them to be more like sabotage buddies.

All in all, a game that I would recommend to any friend! 10/10, perfect experience! Well done, Larian, on this gem!

comment:
Witcher 3 is still one of the best games ever made. Simple as that.

I first played it on my PS4, my last ever console, and I'm glad a game like this is on PC. Otherwise I never would have got to experience such a masterpiece. With the remaster out I had to buy it again, and it feels like a whole new game. Sunsets over the hills, fog rolling through the swamps, rain hitting the mud in Velen. Textures are sharper, faces look way better in cutscenes, and the lighting alone makes it hold up next to stuff coming out today.

The world is where it really flexes. Velen is grim and miserable in the best way, with burned villages, hanged men and swamps full of things that want to eat you. Novigrad is a huge packed city that feels lived in, and Skellige has the cliffs, storms and Viking vibe. You'll stop riding just to look at the view.

Even the side quests are better written than the main story of most games. Your choices come back to bite you later, some quests have no good answer, and the love saga hit me harder than I expected. The characters stay with you long after you finish.

The fights feel better too with the reworked animations. Swings look smoother, hits have more weight, and mixing signs, bombs and potions mid-fight feels natural. Monster hunts are still the best part: you read the bestiary, pick the right oil, and it pays off. The remaster also adds some quality of life stuff that makes it smoother to play.

Got all this for 20 euros, which feels like a steal. Hundreds of hours for the price of a pizza night.

If you haven't played it, buy it. If you have, the remaster is a great excuse to go back.

comment:
[b]Baldur's Gate 3 is my new favorite game of all time.[/b]

I picked it up during early access and it hooked me right from the start. After about four hours I shelved it, since the full launch was only four months away and I really wanted to play it from beginning to end. Now I have over 500 hours in the game, I've played through it more times than I can count, and I've 100% completed it. That's something I haven't done with any other game in my Steam library.

[b]The Characters & Story[/b]
The narrator is amazing. Her voice work and the writing behind her lines are so well done.

The story is decent, but what really makes the game for me is the cast. Every character you meet along the way is fantastic, and they make you genuinely want to help them. My favorite is Karlach. She is such a sweet, kind-hearted character, and her questline is really good. The best questline in the game, though, belongs to Shadowheart. Her story can go in multiple directions, and you get to influence who she really becomes in the end. The romance system is decent too, though some romances are far better than others.

[b]Combat & Builds[/b]
The builds are incredibly customizable. Honor Mode kicked my butt and I had to restart more times than I'd like to admit, but my Gloom Stalker/Assassin build finally got me through it. The most fun build I've played is a Monk/Rogue. You get so many attacks, and the movement is amazing. Between the build variety and the mod support, the game stays fresh even on a sixth or seventh run.

[b]Player Freedom[/b]
You can play it however you want. If you want to be the good guy and save everyone, you can. If you want to be the bad guy and take everyone out, you can do that too. The replayability is crazy.

[b]My One Criticism[/b]
Act 1 is top tier, above and beyond anything else, but Acts 2 and 3 just don't feel as fleshed out. Act 1 gives you so many places to explore, from the open world at the start, down into the Underdark, all the way to the Grymforge. The later acts don't quite match that. Don't get me wrong, they're still better than most games being made today, and I would rather play them than most AAA releases. The drop is just noticeable.

I can't say enough good things about this game. The characters, the storytelling, and the performances from every voice actor are outstanding. If you haven't played it yet, do yourself a favor and pick it up.

[b]Final Score: 10/10[/b]

comment:
Baldur's gate 3 is one of two games that I have managed to replay. Why? 

It comes down to the roleplaying potential, but more than that, just generally good character writing and surprisingly fun gameplay.

Whether you're a min/max kind of player, casual, or heavily invested in RP, this game really has it all. This, and Expedition 33, were my first turn-based games ever and after them both, I honestly have not been as interested in other playing style. I really was not expecting that at all.

In a land far, far away (Germany) a young girl (30) saw a white-haired, red-eyed dude on her Instagram feed, she heard him talk. She was enamored.

After 280 hours, she finished the game. She cried, she laughed, she now has a gaming setup with a self-built PC. She tried other games in numerous genres and sits at her silent, creamy, colourful keyboard most evenings.

10/10

comment:
I went into Baldur’s Gate 3 with absolutely no D&D experience, so I really didn’t know what to expect. It ended up being a great introduction to that world and style of gameplay, and I never felt like I needed to already know D&D to enjoy it.

The characters were probably my favorite part. I actually cared about them and wanted to see how their stories played out. There are so many different choices, relationships, and storylines that I ended up doing multiple playthroughs just to experience different romances and see how making different decisions changed things.

I even did an evil playthrough, which is usually really hard for me because I always end up feeling bad and making the “good” choice in games. 😂 The fact that Baldur’s Gate 3 actually got me to commit to an evil character says a lot about how much freedom the game gives you to play a completely different story.

After more than 230 hours, I still feel like there are things I could have done differently or storylines I could have missed. Definitely recommend it, even if you’ve never played D&D before.

comment:
So where do I start? 

Its my THIRD TIME giving this game a chance, first two times it did not click for me, because at launch the bugs was horrendous so refunded it within 2 hours, then the year after that I found the combat was too complex for me/complex system in micro managing everything in such horrendous UI AS WELL as the clutter, now that its on sale I thought maybe '3rd times the charm' and its been about 18 hours or so. I have always been a huge fan of the Dragon Age series (except Veilguard), Middle-Earth Shadow of Mordor/War. My first problem is honestly the combat, ITS dreadful for those who are not familiar with DND + Turn-based, I had to lookup guides on YT AND LEARN ABOUT DND EVEN WATCHED ENTIRE TABLE TOP EPISODE GAMES LOL, because the game does not do enough to explain. comment:
Right out the gate the graphics in this blew me away. Everything is just so gorgeous especially with HDR. People always like to claim that we've hit the limits of graphical fidelity every few years and at times I've thought we've been pretty close. I still think there's plenty of gains to be made in the coming years but I do think its mostly going to come down to very minor details and more fluid and detailed animations.

Now as far as gameplay, the big question was if they managed to make it better and less of a slog than it was before. I've always felt the gameplay was the weakest link in the formula and the game stood almost entirely on great story writing, world building and music and you just played through the gameplay to get to the good parts. I don't think that they've completely solved it in this remaster. Even with the new skill tree it just feels like there's something a bit lacking. I think because of how big the game is, the pacing of level ups and skill points comes pretty slowly and none of them really stand out to me as big game changers. Some of them are surely more powerful than others but I just never found myself super excited for that next level up, it just felt like here's 10% more power or something like that. 

The combat itself I think feels better but I did not go back to play the original before hand so I'm just going off my memory of what it felt like before. It certainly hasn't blown me away though so I think if your hoping for a completely different experience combat wise you might be a little disappointed. Its hard to explain exactly what's wrong with it but it just never feels like a banger. Perhaps some of the changes with the new dlc will help even more but I suspect the combat is always just going to be a bit on the average side. It is a testament to how good the rest of the game is though that I don't care that the gameplay itself isn't all that exciting.

comment:
50+ hours in, and I’m still having a great time.

If you like RPGs with gameplay and choices that actually matter, I highly recommend this game. I originally came for the world and gameplay, but what really kept me playing was how much freedom the game gives you to approach situations in different ways.

As someone who enjoys the kind of RPG experience you get from Fallout, I really love the feeling of being able to make my own decisions and live with the consequences. Some choices don't just give you a different line of dialogue — they can genuinely come back to punish you later. And honestly, I love that. Not every decision needs to have a perfect outcome.

The combat, character progression, exploration, quests, and build variety all work together to make me feel like I'm actually playing my own character rather than simply following a predetermined story.

After 50+ hours, I still find myself wanting to explore, try different choices, and see what happens.

If you enjoy RPGs where your choices have weight and consequences, this is definitely worth playing.

comment:
This -to me- is the greatest game ever made. Don't let the hour counter fool you - I have played Cyberpunk 2077 since half a year after the original release and have since then played over 1500 hours on Xbox. The story is great and very well told - Night City itself feels like a real, vibrant place with fascinating stories and discoveries at every turn. 

This alone would have been enough to lock me in for a descent amount of time, but the combat is the thing that kept me coming back year after year because there is nothing even close to the combat in Cyberpunk. The different cyberware augmentations and the massive skill tree allow dozens of different playstyles. You have a wide selection of standard and iconic weapons. The latter can be improved throughout the game in the crafting menu and also the cyberware can be upgraded. 

The driving is ridiculously fun, arcadey and allows for descent vehicular combat. The exterior of cars you own can also be customized. Additionally, you have a fast travel system, a subway, and self driving taxis  to be able to switch the means of traversal from time to time.

When the gameplay and the design of night city clicks, it is the best video game experience out there and one, that I will keep sinking hours into.

comment:
I've played this on PS4, played on gog and now here too cause I'm retarded. The game is amazing: base, HoS and B&W (best DLC in ANY game that's I've played). 

The combat is debatable... it's nothing extraordinary, but not terrible... mediocre might be an accurate way of describing it. 

The story is immersive and well crafted. It's one of few games where your choices have noticeable consequences. A lot of times, it's trolley problems where someone gets screwed and you have to choose. 

The music is pretty well done. It's been 11 years since my first playthrough and I still hum the song that Priscilla sings. Unfortunately, this remastered update bugs out an unholy amount, especially from Skellige and the music cuts off time to time. 

Exploration is memorable, but will get repetitive eventually, due to the size of the world. The remastered, however, absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ butchers it. Sure the game is old, but my goodness... you can tell the team that worked on this remaster is either autistic or simply terrible at their jobs. Once you hit the bog area, there are sooooooooooooo many ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ "invisible assets". You have to literally jump to get past invisible matter because my guess is some assets have bigger hitboxes than they should. It's annoying, but tolerable until you hit... you guessed it Skellige. There were so many of these that it ruined immersion and if I was 10 years younger, my controller would've met the fate of my old computer mice, 360 and PS4 controllers. 

Now, to address the elephant in the room... "the big patch". The remastered patch makes the game look very nice for most part. However, like I said, there are so many immersion breaking moments due to poor coding, programming or management. There's so many annoying bugs aside from that. Some include Gwent cards disappearing (Eredin, I'm looking at you), visual glitches where people (especially in Novigrad) are either T-posing or walking around without faces or dialogue choices going completely invisible (Epilogue). Also, there are a handful of places where the lighting is ass and A LOT of moments where lighting changes mid-scene, further breaking immersion. It is extremely evident that it was either a) rushed b) the devs are just incompetent (og devs killed it with Blood of Dawnwalker) or c) half-assed because they just needed some clout before their new DLC. My guess is all of the above. Still not sure why the tutorial sections runs at like 40 fps on my rig.

This game was originally a 9/10 -> 9.5/10 with the B&W DLC, but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ this remastered patch was a kick to the ♥♥♥♥ and has single handedly lowered it to 8/10. Would I recommend the game? Sure, but unlucky because your experience will be objectively worse than the people that played it 6 years ago, ironically. I was originally excited for new DLC, but now I am genuinely worried after the terrible experience which was solely due to awful devs. Why would you replace the mofos that were able to make Blood of Dawnwalker for DEI tards???? Don't even get me started on the initial ugly ass Ciri of W4 and the following gaslighting after they made her less ugly lmfao

comment:
what is left to say about this game that hast been said already, the absolute mastery of the craft that fromsoft shows time and time again is flooring, they are one of the few developers that you can trust to always deliver something special and ER is the best example of this.

I remember my first playthrough all those years ago now, the map just kept zooming out and out and the world felt never ending. Its to the point where last week while i was on my 20 something run of the game or more i STILL discovered a path down to an area id never seen before. I remember the first time i found all the hidden cities, the first time i entered caelid by accident, the first time that i discovered that a random cave in a random beach leads down to an interconnected network of underground tunnels full of bugs, viscera and magic that leads you to one of the endings of the game. I can only hope that the next big thing that fromsoft works on doesn't get scope creeped by this and they're able to deliver something just as special even if its different.

Or maybe it's like the once a year family gathering, where you see your cousins or family friends that are pretty much like your siblings. You could runaway with them and drink mango juice on a balcony in Italy, or eat your favorite food on a table outside while your family is off to the side. Or you can run in the fields and play games only they knew how to play. Or maybe it's like having that one dream you can't seem to forget. The one where you had a life, you had friends, people you loved, and situations that didn't happen in everyday life. It was a dream that made you feel alive, like you can fly in the sky and touch the clouds. It's the feeling you get when a calm song plays in the car and you're in the passenger seat after having fun all day. comment:
Where do I even start with Baldur's Gate 3?

I've been playing D&D since I was around 11, so there was absolutely no way I was going to miss this game. I hadn't played the previous Baldur's Gate games, though, so BG3 was actually my introduction to the series. I got it as soon as it became available, and almost 1,000 hours later... apparently I'm still not done with it.

Achievements aren't really the focus for me here. I'm currently at 46/54, but BG3 is one of those games where I'd much rather start another character, try another choice and see where the story takes me than worry about completing a checklist.

The amount of freedom and variation is probably what I love most. Even after so many playthroughs, different interactions, consequences and unexpected outcomes can still appear. You make one seemingly insignificant choice differently and suddenly you're seeing something you've never seen before. It makes every run feel like its own D&D campaign rather than simply replaying the same story.

The modding possibilities make that experience even better. I love that the game can be modded so easily, although I've mostly kept mine to quality-of-life and graphical improvements. For me, it's about polishing and improving the experience without changing what makes the original game so good.

All three acts have something I love, although Act 2 is definitely my favourite. The atmosphere, the story and everything surrounding the Shadow-Cursed Lands just work incredibly well for me.

I love the companions too, although Gale, Astarion and Shadowheart have a special place among them. Gale takes first place when it comes to romance, though. ❤️

As for my own characters, Wizard is easily my favourite class and Drow my favourite race. Character creation gives you plenty to play around with, and combined with all the classes, subclasses, races, backgrounds, dialogue options and different ways of approaching situations, the replayability is enormous.

The story itself is great, but what really makes it special to me is how much it feels like *your* story. My most memorable Tav will probably always be my very first one, whom I played essentially as myself.

That adventure ended in Act 2 because I made a... let's call it a "wrong" decision.

The soundtrack deserves a mention as well. There are some beautiful tracks in there, and naturally, a few of them have found their way onto my Spotify playlists.

My main disappointment is knowing that development was, in some ways, rushed towards the end and that a number of things had to be cut. There are places where you can wonder what BG3 might have looked like if everything originally envisioned had made it into the finished game.

But even with that disappointment, what we got is still far more than excellent.

After 979.5 hours, countless characters, different decisions, romances, successes, catastrophes and apparently the occasional accidental premature ending, I'm still finding reasons to return to Baldur's Gate 3.

And I'm definitely not finished yet.

comment:
One of the best RPGs ever made. CDPR has this somewhat ungodly capacity to bring to life worlds and stories in a way very few could. The characters, the universe they're in, the amount of little side quests you can take part in that help expand your understandking and knowledge of the world, are truly something incredible. It recently got a face lift with new graphical improvements and some extra love, preparing it for the upcoming expansion.

Hundreds of hours of content for you to entertain yourself. The game isn't free of problems or errors though. With the many updates it has received over the years, you would think it's as polished as it can get, but there are still thousands of small bugs or problems that by themselves aren't much to complain about, but they stack.

I'm talking about little details such as missing textures, wrong level of detail rendering, missing/buggy props in the world, weird AI issues and broken-ish quest paths. Nothing too serious or repetitive as to take you out of the immersion, but they're there and at least in my case, annoyed me a tiny bit both in the Next Gen version and now in the Remaster.

Combat and some other gameplay systems are very dated and it shows. Combat itself is a weird console-in-mind simplistic hack and slash mash with little build variety, you can roll/dodge away from enemies and it has a lock on feature but it doesn't really have much depth and it is a bit buggy at times. Other gameplay systems such as gear durability, lack of gear scaling, weight limitations, and such are very clearly a product of its time, but thankfully you can toggle some accesibility settings (that they introduced over the years) to QoL your way out of them, but a few still remain.

Another small problem is that the story constantly references events from the past (or the books) that you might not understand or know at first, but it doesn't affect the main story of this game, You will end up going down a few rabbit holes to learn more about the universe tho, you have been warned.

The previous two titles are even older and even more dated, but I'd still recommend giving them a go (or at least watch some playthroughs) if you want to learn more.

comment:
Cyberpunk 2077 is, in my opinion, the best story-driven RPG I've played in years. What makes it so special is that every part of the game feels carefully crafted. The main story is emotional, gripping, and filled with unforgettable moments, but what truly surprised me was the quality of the side content. Unlike many open-world games where side quests feel like repetitive filler, Cyberpunk's side missions are so well-written and unique that they often feel like they could be part of the main storyline. Many of them introduce memorable characters, unexpected twists, and meaningful choices that make every mission worth playing.

The attention to detail is simply incredible. Night City is one of the most immersive worlds I've ever explored. Every district has its own identity, architecture, atmosphere, and people. The city constantly feels alive, with crowds walking the streets, traffic moving through highways, advertisements covering every building, and countless small details that make the world believable. Even the Badlands outside the city have their own unique atmosphere, making the contrast between the urban chaos and the empty desert feel natural and immersive.

Visually, Cyberpunk 2077 is absolutely stunning. The lighting, weather effects, reflections, animations, and overall art direction make almost every location look like it belongs in a sci-fi movie. Whether you're driving through the neon-lit streets at night or watching the sunrise over the Badlands, the game is full of breathtaking moments.

The RPG systems are another reason why I love this game. The skill tree gives you the freedom to create completely different builds depending on how you want to play. You can become a deadly Netrunner who hacks enemies from a distance, a stealth assassin using throwing knives and silenced weapons, a cyber-enhanced samurai with katanas, or a heavily armored tank charging into combat with shotguns and LMGs. Cyberware implants, perks, iconic weapons, and countless equipment combinations make character progression incredibly satisfying.

Replayability is another area where Cyberpunk truly shines. Every new playthrough can feel completely different thanks to the different lifepaths, dialogue options, character builds, romances, endings, and even your character's gender. The choices you make throughout the game often change conversations, relationships, and the way certain missions unfold, giving you plenty of reasons to experience the story multiple times.

What really sets Cyberpunk 2077 apart is how all of these systems come together. The outstanding writing, unforgettable characters, meaningful side quests, incredible attention to detail, gorgeous visuals, deep progression systems, and the living, breathing world create an experience that feels unique from beginning to end. Very few games manage to combine storytelling, gameplay, exploration, and role-playing this well, which is exactly why I consider Cyberpunk 2077 the best RPG I've played in a very long time.

comment: Despite not being perfect, it is my favorite game of all time. Even though character creation uses "Type A" and "Type B" instead of male and female, the game is sensational: the story is incredible, and the gameplay is extremely satisfying—ranging from overpowered builds to ones that are just pure fun. The soundtrack is amazing in every corner of the game, the graphics are excellent, and the environments are like works of art—reminiscent of Kentaro Miura’s panels. On the downside, accessibility and UI customization are terrible, which is unfortunately all too common in most games today. The only thing I’d really like to see is more quality-of-life improvements, though those are things you only really start to miss after sinking many hours into the game. And YES, the Tarnished Pack should have been a free update; that is the one thing you should be ashamed of doing, and that we should be ashamed of buying.

comment:
This is what happens when a very determined guy with a dream gets told "No" at one point in his life.
And responds with: "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ watch me."

Larian went a long way, and grew into a truly talented, experienced team. Divinity OS1-2 were their own little darlings and masterpieces. But BG3 just took it to a whole new level.

I... don't really see much point in going into depth with this review - the game already has 750k+ of overwhelmingly positive reviews. There's not much I can add here. The story is largely great, the characters are cool, memorable, and voice acting+motion capture is phenomenal. Graphics are great, soundtrack is epic, gameplay is DnD 5e, but much better suited for the nuances of a videogame, and much better balance. The amount of content and options for replayability is absurdly big. Easily a 9/10, and a well deserved GOTY.

The only peeves that I had with this game:
[list]
[*] You start as level 1, yet you're the "chosen ones" right off the bat, and you don't really feel level 1 narratively; only statistically. There's no sense of standard DnD party of strangers gathering up, meeting in some metaphorical tavern, getting slowly dragged into the maelstrom of events. No - you are immediately the chosen ones, everyone is super important, unique and powerful, with a backstory that fits a level 7-10 character AT LEAST.
[*] Most of your companions have a stupid thing in common - some super dark secret that they're uncomfortable sharing, but expect you to just be chill with it and trust them without giving you a proper explanation for a while.
[*] The game is definitely meant for a single player experience. Playing in coop is... just ruining most of the story. Unless you are roleplaying with your friends, then playing as a bunch of custom characters is a poor decision - you're just going to miss out on a whole bunch of content that you'll witness with a party of your NPC companions.
[*] I'm not sure if it got fixed over the years, but Act 3 really felt poorly optimized and most bugged at release. Can't speak for it's current state
[*] A bit of a spoiler, but not crucial one: [spoiler]Consuming tadpoles to increase your illithid powers has... virtually zero consequences. No effect on the ending, no actual effect on your relationship with your comrades (even if they verbally disapprove) [/spoiler], So refusing to use those powers does not reward you in any way, you just handicap yourself.
[/list]

comment:
With any other FromSoftware game I wouldn't have even cared to leave a review. insanely hard fights just for the purpose of being hard and making the player suffer, impossible to comprehend lore, and toxic wannabe philosopher fan bases; but the titular game, ELDEN RING, is really quite different, and quite good.

Though the formatting of incredibly punishing combat has remained the same, the formula of which it is presented is wildly fun and unique compared to other games by the same dev team. Stuck on a boss? You have a massive and deep world to explore and level up in to strengthen yourself before returning. Like character customization? ELDEN RING has one of the best character creators I've ever had the pleasure of playing with possibly hundreds of builds to play around with in the Lands Between.

Graphically the game is beautiful as well, even if turned to potato settings.

Where this game still fails a bit: In terms of actual roleplay there isn't much, most dialogues consist of you just pressing "Accept" or "Decline" with often times the Decline option lacking consequences; There are a few endings to play towards, but a good number of them are extremely similar.
Then onto lore; from what I know the lore and background lore of the game is it written with a lot of passion, with even a helping hand from Game of Thrones writer George R.R. Martin being lent. However like most FromSoftware games, it feels very much as if it doesn't actually want you to learn it. The general information about the world and its characters is all extreme conjecture and bias, which can be good for a complex world; but having no (at least to my knowledge) concrete way to learn the definitive lore is a bit wacky to me.


All in All; a very good game, and for hardcore fans of the medieval video game genre, it is a must buy.

comment:
🟩 Cyberpunk 2077 & Phantom Liberty – Ultimate Edition  
Now Featuring: "Wait, people said this game was broken?" Edition

>Spent years hearing about the legendary 2020 launch disaster.
>Finally pick up the game post-Update 2.0 alongside Phantom Liberty.
>Brace myself for T-posing NPCs, launching cars, and flatlining save files.
>Instead, get hit with one of the most immersive, visually mind-melting RPGs ever made.
>Keanu Reeves is living rent-free in my head insulting my life choices.
>Idris Elba pulls me into a high-stakes Cold War espionage thriller in Dogtown.
>Look up from my screen: 120 hours have vanished, my V is an untouchable Sandevistan cyber-god dashing through bullets with a katana, and I'm crying over fictional mercenaries at 3 AM.
>Where were the bugs? Did I accidentally buy the right timeline?

10/10 neon depression, 0/10 launch trauma experienced.
CD Projekt Red cooked the greatest redemption arc in modern gaming, and skipping the rough patch was the best decision I ever made.

✅ Night City and Dogtown boast unmatched atmosphere, detail, and verticality
✅ Phantom Liberty’s story and espionage vibe rival the best expansions ever made (Blood and Wine tier)
✅ Update 2.0 combat overhaul turns cyberware builds into pure, addictive power trips
✅ Incredible voice performances from Keanu Reeves and Idris Elba

❌ Existential dread and emotional devastation hitting you in virtually every single ending
❌ Having literally zero relatable "launch day horror stories" to bond over on Reddit
❌ Ruining standard open-world city design for any other game you play afterward

🏙️ Would I recommend the game? 100%. Night City is an absolute masterpiece now.
🦾 Is Phantom Liberty worth getting with it? Non-negotiable. Skipping Dogtown is a straight-up cybercrime.

comment:
J’ai vraiment bien aimé Cyberpunk 2077. Au début, j’étais pas forcément à fond dans le jeu, mais plus j’avançais, plus j’ai accroché à l’histoire et aux personnages.

Le truc que j’ai le plus aimé, c’est clairement Night City. La ville est énorme et il y a toujours quelque chose à faire. Même quand on ne fait pas l’histoire principale, on peut faire des quêtes secondaires, des contrats, se balader ou juste découvrir la ville. Je trouve que l’ambiance est vraiment réussie, surtout la nuit avec tous les néons et les bâtiments.

L’histoire principale est aussi un gros point fort. J’ai bien aimé suivre V et surtout la relation avec Johnny Silverhand. Il y a pas mal de moments qui restent en tête et certaines missions sont vraiment excellentes. Les personnages secondaires sont aussi assez intéressants et certaines quêtes sont presque aussi bien que les missions principales.

Au niveau du gameplay, j’ai bien aimé avoir plusieurs façons de jouer. On peut utiliser des armes, des armes de corps à corps, le piratage ou jouer plus discrètement. Le système de cyberware permet aussi de rendre son personnage beaucoup plus puissant au fur et à mesure.

Graphiquement, je trouve le jeu encore très beau. Night City est vraiment impressionnante et certains endroits sont magnifiques. Avec de bons réglages graphiques, le jeu peut vraiment être incroyable.

J’ai aussi beaucoup aimé les quêtes secondaires parce qu’elles ne servent pas juste à gagner de l’argent ou de l’expérience. Certaines racontent vraiment des histoires intéressantes et permettent de mieux connaître les personnages.

Pour la durée de vie, je trouve qu’il y a largement de quoi faire. J’ai passé pas mal de temps dessus et je n’ai même pas terminé tout le contenu. Le jeu peut facilement occuper pendant plusieurs dizaines d’heures si on fait aussi les quêtes secondaires.

Pour Phantom Liberty, je ne peux pas encore donner mon avis complet parce que je ne l’ai pas terminé. Pour l’instant, j’aime beaucoup l’ambiance et les nouvelles missions, mais je préfère attendre d’avoir fini le DLC avant de donner une vraie note définitive.

Au final, je donnerais environ **10/10 à Cyberpunk 2077**. C’est un jeu que j’ai vraiment apprécié et dans lequel j’ai passé beaucoup de temps. Il n’est pas parfait, mais son histoire, son univers, ses personnages et tout ce qu’il y a à faire font que j’ai vraiment aimé l’expérience.

Pour Phantom Liberty, pour l’instant je partirais sur **9/10**, mais cette note pourra changer quand je l’aurai terminé.
